title: Meet the Raspberry Pi
headings: What you need to get started
What exactly is a Raspberry Pi?
What can you actually do with one?
How is it different from your everyday computer?
Why the Pi 5 is a big leap — and what more RAM unlocks
A quick visual tour of the ports and connectors
You almost certainly cannot break it
text: Welcome to your Raspberry Pi 5 — a complete, fully functional computer that fits in the palm of your hand. In this opening chapter you will find out what this little board actually is, why millions of people around the world use one, and which accessories you need to get started — whether you bought a starter kit or are gathering the pieces yourself. By the end, you will understand what you have in your hands and feel genuinely ready to start exploring. What you need to get started Before anything else, let's make sure you know what each item is and what it does. Many people start with a Raspberry Pi 5 "starter kit" that bundles most of these together; others buy the board and add accessories one by one. Either way works. Gather (or check off) each of the following: Item What it is Why it matters Raspberry Pi 5 board The main computer — a green or red circuit board roughly the size of a bank card. It comes in 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, and 16 GB RAM versions. This is the heart of everything. All other items plug into or around it. Any RAM version works for everything in this book. Active Cooler A small aluminium heatsink with a tiny fan that clips on top of the main chip. Keeps the processor cool during demanding tasks so it never has to slow itself down. Many starter kits include one already fitted; if yours didn't, the official Active Cooler is an inexpensive add-on that clips straight on. Case A protective enclosure — often a smart aluminium box or a plastic shell. Protects the board from bumps and dust. Most kits include one (sometimes with the Pi already installed inside). A case is optional but recommended. Power supply A mains plug with a USB-C cable. The official 27 W supply is rated 5.1 V / 5 A. Powers the Pi. The Pi 5 needs more power than older models, so use the official 27 W USB-C power supply (or any good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD supply). Do not substitute a typical phone charger. microSD card (and a card reader) A tiny memory card (commonly 32 GB or larger), plus a way to read it on your main computer — many cards come with a small USB adapter, or your computer may have a built-in SD slot. The microSD card is the Pi's main storage — it holds the operating system and all your files. Many kits include one, sometimes with Raspberry Pi OS already installed. Micro-HDMI to HDMI cable A video cable with a small connector at one end (for the Pi) and a full-size connector at the other (for your TV or monitor). Many kits include one; otherwise it is a cheap, widely available cable. Sends the picture and sound from the Pi to your screen. Note the Pi end is micro -HDMI — this connector is smaller than the standard HDMI you find on TVs. You cannot use a standard HDMI cable directly; you need a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable or adapter. Note: You will need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, and monitor (or TV with an HDMI input). Chapter 2 covers exactly which types work and how to connect everything up. Tip: Check whether your microSD card already has Raspberry Pi OS installed. Look at the card label, or look for a sticker on the packaging saying "pre-loaded" or "pre-flashed". If it is pre-loaded, Chapter 2 will walk you straight to first boot. If it is blank — or you don't have a card yet — Chapter 3 covers installing the operating system yourself — it takes about ten minutes. What exactly is a Raspberry Pi? A Raspberry Pi is a single-board computer — every component that makes up a full computer (the processor, memory, graphics, USB ports, Wi-Fi, and more) is soldered directly onto one small circuit board roughly the size of a bank card. There is no separate tower, no desktop box, no jumble of internal cables. It is just one neat, tidy board. In plain words: A "single-board computer" (often shortened to SBC) simply means that everything a computer needs — its brain, memory, and connections to the outside world — all live on a single flat piece of circuit board, rather than being spread across separate components inside a big box. When you power it on, it boots an operating system, shows a desktop on your screen, connects to the internet, plays videos, browses the web, runs programs, and does essentially everything a normal laptop or desktop computer can do — just in a much smaller, more energy-efficient, and far cheaper package. Raspberry Pi 5 board — labelled diagram A labelled diagram of the Raspberry Pi 5 board identifying: BCM2712 processor, RAM, four USB ports, Gigabit Ethernet, two micro-HDMI ports, microSD slot, USB-C power, 40-pin GPIO header, PCIe connector, and Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chip. BCM2712 Processor + VideoCore VII RAM LPDDR4X 2× USB 3.0 2× USB 2.0 Gigabit Ethernet 2× micro-HDMI microSD USB-C Power Power button 40-pin GPIO header Wi-Fi 5 Bluetooth 5.0 PCIe connector approx. 85 mm wide — about the size of a bank card The Raspberry Pi 5 board — every component of a full computer on a single piece of circuitry. If your board is enclosed in a case, this is what is inside. Note: The Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone socket. If you want to hear audio, connect your screen or TV via the micro-HDMI cable (most modern monitors and all TVs carry sound over HDMI) or plug in USB speakers or a USB audio adapter. Bluetooth headphones and speakers also work perfectly. A brief, friendly history The Raspberry Pi was created by the Raspberry Pi Foundation , a British educational charity. Back in 2011, a group of academics and engineers in Cambridge, England, noticed a worrying trend: fewer and fewer school-leavers were arriving at university with any real experience of programming or electronics. Kids in the 1980s had grown up with BBC Micros and Commodore 64s — machines you had to program, because there was little else to do with them. By 2010, most children only knew how to use apps on someone else's device. Their solution was radical in its simplicity: build an affordable, programmable computer — one cheap enough that a school or a child could actually buy one, tough enough to survive a backpack, and open enough that curious people could take it apart and put it back together in software without worrying about breaking anything expensive. The first Raspberry Pi (the Model B) launched in February 2012 and sold 100,000 units in the first day . It cost $35. People queued online for hours to order one. The Foundation expected to sell a few thousand to enthusiastic teachers; they ended up starting a global movement. Since then, the Foundation has sold well over 60 million boards across six main generations. Every penny of profit goes back into the charity's educational mission: funding projects, writing free learning materials, and training teachers worldwide. When you buy a Raspberry Pi, you are supporting that mission. The Raspberry Pi 5 , released in October 2023, is the most powerful yet. It is two to three times faster than the Pi 4 thanks to a brand-new processor, adds a proper PCIe connector for fast storage, and finally has a real power button. It comes in 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, and 16 GB versions; even the smaller ones are far more capable than many budget laptops, and the 16 GB model is the top-of-the-range configuration. What can you actually do with one? This is where things get exciting. Because the Pi runs a full Linux operating system and has physical pins you can connect to real-world electronics, the range of things people make with it is genuinely astonishing. Here is just a small taste: Media centre: Connect it to your TV and run Kodi or Jellyfin to stream your film and music collection — or watch YouTube and browse catch-up TV. It replaces a £100+ streaming box. Retro gaming console: Install RetroPie or Batocera, plug in a USB gamepad, and play thousands of classic arcade, NES, SNES, Mega Drive, and PlayStation 1 games using your own ROM files. Ad-blocker for your whole house: Run Pi-hole, a piece of software that intercepts advertising requests across your entire home network — every device benefits, including phones and smart TVs. Home server / NAS: Attach a USB hard drive and run Nextcloud to create your own private "cloud" — photos, documents, and videos accessible from anywhere, with no monthly subscription. Weather station: Connect temperature, humidity, pressure, and air-quality sensors to the GPIO pins and log real readings from your garden, displayed on a web page you build yourself. Robot: Wire up motors, sensors, and a camera to build a moving robot you control from your phone or program to navigate on its own. Smart-home hub: Run Home Assistant to control smart plugs, lights, heating, and security cameras — without sending any data to a third-party cloud. AI assistant: Run a local large-language model (a "chatbot" that runs entirely on your own hardware, offline, with no API costs) using software such as Ollama. Smaller models run on a 4 GB or 8 GB Pi, while an 8 GB or 16 GB Pi 5 can run surprisingly capable AI models. Web server: Host a real website — a personal blog, a family photo gallery, or a small business site — directly from your Pi, visible on the public internet. Learn-to-code machine: The Pi ships with Python, Scratch, and dozens of other tools pre-installed. It is arguably the best beginner coding platform ever made, because you can connect your code to real physical things. Security camera system: Mount a Pi Camera, run MotionEyeOS or Frigate, and record motion-triggered footage to a drive — a complete home security setup for the cost of the hardware. Print server: Plug in an old USB printer that no longer has up-to-date drivers for modern computers, and the Pi will make it work wirelessly for every device in your house using CUPS. VPN server: Run WireGuard so that your phone and laptop connect securely to your home network when you are abroad, as if you were sitting at home. Tip: You do not need to know how to do any of these things yet. This book will walk you through many of them step by step. The point right now is simply to appreciate that the small board in front of you is capable of an extraordinary range of tasks. How is it different from your everyday computer? You probably use a laptop or desktop every day — most likely running Windows, macOS, or Linux — so it is worth understanding clearly how the Raspberry Pi is different, and why those differences actually matter. Feature A typical laptop / desktop Raspberry Pi 5 Operating system Windows or macOS (or a desktop Linux) Raspberry Pi OS (based on Linux, free and open-source) Processor type x86-64 (Intel or AMD); Apple Silicon Macs use ARM ARM (Arm Cortex-A76, by Broadcom) Power consumption Typically 45 W – 300 W Typically 5 W – 12 W under load Physical size Full tower, small form-factor box, or laptop 85 mm × 56 mm — bank-card sized Headphone jack Usually built in None — audio goes via HDMI, USB, or Bluetooth GPIO pins None 40-pin header for connecting to real electronics (3.3 V logic) Moving parts Usually a cooling fan; possibly a hard disk Active Cooler fan only; solid-state storage Typical cost £300 – £2,000+ £70 – £90 for the board alone Software installation Download installers (.exe on Windows, .dmg on macOS) or use an app store Usually one apt install command in the terminal Recovery if things go wrong Can require a reinstall disc, hours of work Re-flash the microSD card in under 10 minutes The operating system: Linux, not Windows The biggest practical difference for you as a newcomer is the operating system. Most everyday computers run Windows (made by Microsoft) or macOS (made by Apple). The Raspberry Pi runs Linux — a separate family of operating systems that is free, open-source, and used everywhere from web servers to Android phones to supercomputers. In plain words: "Open-source" means the underlying code that makes the operating system work is publicly available for anyone to read, modify, and share. Nobody owns Linux in the way Microsoft owns Windows. It is maintained by a worldwide community of volunteers and companies working together. The specific flavour of Linux on your Pi is called Raspberry Pi OS , currently nicknamed "Bookworm" . Linux versions are traditionally given friendly codenames, and Bookworm is based on a widely-used Linux distribution called Debian 12. It looks and feels like a proper desktop: there is a taskbar, a desktop, a file manager, a web browser, and menus. If you have ever used a computer, you will recognise most of it within a few minutes. In plain words: "Bookworm" is just a nickname — it doesn't mean anything technical. Linux and Debian releases are traditionally named after characters from Toy Story. "Bookworm" is Debian version 12, released in 2023. The version after it (Debian 13, called "Trixie") is being developed, but Bookworm is what ships with the Pi 5 and what all instructions in this book are written for. The main difference you will notice is that many tasks that required clicking through installer windows on Windows or macOS are done with a single short command typed into the terminal — a text window where you give the computer instructions in plain text. This sounds intimidating, but it is actually faster and more powerful once you get used to it. Every terminal command in this book is explained line by line, so you will always know exactly what you are typing before you press Enter. The processor: ARM, not x86 Most Windows PCs use an Intel or AMD processor that belongs to a family called x86-64. The Raspberry Pi 5 uses a completely different family called ARM (specifically, four Arm Cortex-A76 cores running at 2.4 GHz). ARM chips are designed to be very efficient — they do a lot of computing work per watt of electricity — which is why they are in every smartphone in the world, and now in Apple's Mac computers too. For you as a user, this mostly does not matter. Software for Raspberry Pi OS is already compiled (prepared) for ARM, so you just install it normally. The practical upside is that your Pi sips electricity: running 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, it costs roughly £5–£10 in electricity — whereas a typical desktop PC left running constantly would cost £100 or more. GPIO pins: connecting to the real world Along the top edge of your Pi 5 is a row of 40 small metal pins — the GPIO header . GPIO stands for General-Purpose Input/Output. These pins let you connect your Pi directly to the physical world: sensors that detect temperature or light, motors that spin wheels, LEDs that flash, buttons you press, and much more. In plain words: GPIO (General-Purpose Input/Output) pins are tiny metal contacts on the Pi that you can connect wires to. You can tell each pin to either send an electrical signal (to switch something on) or read an incoming signal (to detect whether something is happening). They operate at 3.3 volts — gentle enough to be safe for the electronics, but powerful enough to control a huge range of devices. Careful: The GPIO pins on the Pi 5 operate at 3.3 volts . Connecting a signal that is higher than 3.3 V (for example, a 5 V signal from some Arduino components) can permanently damage the board. Always check the voltage of any component before wiring it to the GPIO header. The chapters on GPIO go slowly and carefully through this. A normal laptop or desktop has no equivalent of this. It is one of the features that makes the Raspberry Pi special: your programs can reach out and touch the physical world, not just live inside a screen. Why the Pi 5 is a big leap — and what more RAM unlocks Every new generation of Raspberry Pi has brought meaningful improvements, but the jump from Pi 4 to Pi 5 is particularly significant. What is new in the Pi 5 New processor: The BCM2712 chip uses four Arm Cortex-A76 cores running at 2.4 GHz. This is approximately 2–3× faster than the Pi 4's cores in real-world tasks. VideoCore VII GPU: The graphics processor supports hardware video decoding up to 4K at 60 frames per second, making it a genuinely capable media machine. Dual 4K displays: Two micro -HDMI ports mean you can plug in two monitors and run a proper multi-screen workspace. Note that both ports use the smaller micro-HDMI connector, so you need a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable or adapter (often included in starter kits). PCIe 2.0 connector: A dedicated expansion slot lets you connect a fast NVMe SSD (solid-state storage drive) using an optional add-on board, making the Pi 5 dramatically faster than relying on a microSD card alone. Real-time clock: A battery connector on the board lets it keep the correct time even when switched off — the Pi 4 forgot the time every time it lost power. Physical power button: A dedicated button on the board lets you safely turn the Pi on and off. Holding it for two seconds triggers a clean shutdown; a brief press wakes it from sleep. This replaces the old approach of just pulling the power cable — which could corrupt your microSD card. Improved USB and networking: USB 3.0 ports are now on a dedicated controller, meaning plugging in a USB hard drive no longer slows down the network — a known limitation of the Pi 4. Active Cooler support: The Pi 5 has dedicated mounting points and a connector for the official Active Cooler (included with many starter kits, and an inexpensive add-on otherwise), which keeps performance high during intensive tasks without slowing down the chip. Why the amount of RAM matters In plain words: RAM (Random-Access Memory) is your computer's short-term working space. Think of it as a desk: the bigger the desk, the more papers (tasks and data) you can have open at once without having to put things away and fetch them back. More RAM means more things running simultaneously without the system slowing down. The Raspberry Pi 5 is available with 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, or 16 GB of RAM. Everything in this book works on any of them; the more RAM your board has, the more ambitious you can be. Here is what extra RAM unlocks: Heavy multitasking: With 8 GB or more you can have a web browser with many tabs open, a document editor, a music player, and a running server — all at the same time — without the system slowing to a crawl. Desktop use as a daily driver: With 8 GB or 16 GB, the Pi 5 is comfortable running the same kinds of tasks you do on a budget laptop. Many people use it as their main computer. Running local AI models: Software like Ollama can load AI language models entirely into RAM and run them offline. With 2 GB or 4 GB you are limited to very small models; with 8 GB or 16 GB you can run genuinely useful models that can answer questions, summarise text, write code, and more — all on your own hardware, privately. Running several services simultaneously: If you want your Pi to be a media server and an ad-blocker and a home automation hub all at once, more RAM gives each service plenty of breathing room. Compiling and building software: Tasks like building programs from source code require holding a lot of data in RAM at once. More RAM makes this comfortable rather than agonisingly slow. Note: In everyday use — browsing the web, writing documents, watching videos — you will not see a dramatic difference between, say, 4 GB and 8 GB. The larger models shine when you start stacking up ambitious projects, running multiple services, or experimenting with AI. If you are choosing a board, more RAM is good future-proofing — but whatever version you have, the projects in this book are written to work on it. A quick visual tour of the ports and connectors Before you start connecting things, it helps to know where each port is and what goes into it. The diagram below shows the board from above; the list underneath it explains each port in plain English. Raspberry Pi 5 — port positions around the edges Diagram showing the four edges of the Pi 5 board and which connectors are on each side. GPIO (40 pins) USB ports (2× USB 3.0 top 2× USB 2.0 below) Gigabit Ethernet 2× micro-HDMI microSD USB-C Power Power button PCIe slot The four edges of the Raspberry Pi 5 board and where each connector lives. If your board is inside a case, the case cutouts align with these positions. Connector Location on board What you plug in USB-C (power) Bottom edge, left of centre The official 27 W USB-C power supply (or any good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD supply). Nothing else — a typical phone charger will not supply enough power. 2× micro-HDMI Right edge, lower section Your monitor or TV, using a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable. The port closest to the USB-C connector is HDMI 0 (use this one first). 2× USB 3.0 Left edge, upper two ports (blue tab inside) Fast USB devices: external hard drives, USB 3.0 flash drives, fast card readers. 2× USB 2.0 Left edge, lower two ports (black tab inside) Keyboard, mouse, USB hub, or any standard USB device. Everything works here — USB 3 is just faster. Gigabit Ethernet Right edge, upper section An RJ45 network cable for a wired internet connection. Optional if you use Wi-Fi. microSD slot Bottom edge, far left The microSD card containing your operating system. Push until it clicks in; push again to release. 40-pin GPIO header Top edge Electronics projects — sensors, LEDs, motors, displays. Leave this alone for now. Power button Bottom edge, near centre Press briefly to power on; hold 2 seconds to shut down cleanly. Accessible through a small hole in most cases. PCIe 2.0 x1 Near the bottom-left of the board An optional NVMe SSD add-on board for much faster storage. Not required to get started. You almost certainly cannot break it If you are nervous about experimenting, here is the single most reassuring thing we can tell you: In software, almost everything is reversible. If you install something and it goes wrong, you can uninstall it. If you accidentally change a setting that breaks something, you can change it back — or look up how to fix it, and this book will help. If things get truly confused and you cannot work out what happened, you can wipe the microSD card and re-install the operating system in about ten minutes, starting with a completely fresh system as if the Pi just came out of the box. You cannot physically damage the processor or memory by running the wrong command. The only hardware risks to be aware of are: Connecting the wrong voltage to GPIO pins could damage the board — but we will always tell you clearly what voltages to use, and the chapters on GPIO go slowly and carefully. Pulling the power cable out while the Pi is writing to the microSD card can sometimes corrupt the card — but this is rare, and again, a re-flash fixes it. Always use the power button or the proper shut-down option from the menu to switch off safely. Tip: Experimenting is not just allowed — it is the whole point. The Raspberry Pi was created precisely so that people would poke around, try things, break things, and learn from fixing them. Every professional developer and engineer in the world learned by making mistakes. Make them freely. How to use this book This book is designed to be read chapter by chapter, in order, at least the first time through. Each chapter builds gently on what came before. Later, once you are comfortable, you can jump directly to whichever topic interests you — each chapter is also written to stand on its own as a reference. Here are a few suggestions for getting the most from it: Have your Pi in front of you. The best learning happens when you follow each step in real time on your own machine. Do not just read — type the commands, press the buttons, and see what happens. Read the "explain" boxes under every code block. Immediately after every block of terminal commands or program code, there is a plain-English explanation of what each line does. Never type a command you do not understand — read the explanation first. Do not skip the callout boxes. The coloured boxes marked Note, Tip, Careful, and "In plain words" contain important safety information, helpful shortcuts, and definitions of technical terms. They are there for a reason. It is fine to go slowly. There is no test, no deadline, and no instructor watching the clock. If something is not clear, re-read it. If it still is not clear, try it on the Pi — practical experience often explains things better than words can. Use the Key terms section at the end of each chapter. If you forget what a word means, it is defined there. There is also a glossary at the back of the book covering the most common terms across all chapters. Note: Every command in this book has been written and tested for Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (64-bit) , which is the current version for the Pi 5 and the one most kits and downloads provide. If you are using a different version, some details may differ slightly. Ready? In the next chapter, you will connect your Pi to a screen, keyboard, and mouse for the first time, power it on, and complete the initial setup. Let us go. Key terms Single-board computer (SBC) — A complete computer built onto a single flat circuit board, with no separate components. Raspberry Pi Foundation — The British educational charity that designs and sells Raspberry Pi computers, using profits to fund computing education worldwide. ARM — A family of processor designs used in smartphones, tablets, and the Raspberry Pi; known for being very power-efficient. x86-64 — The processor family used in most Windows PCs and laptops, made by Intel or AMD. Linux — A free, open-source operating system used on the Raspberry Pi, web servers, Android phones, and supercomputers. Raspberry Pi OS — The official Linux-based operating system for Raspberry Pi, currently codenamed "Bookworm" (based on Debian 12). Bookworm — The codename for Debian 12, the Linux version that Raspberry Pi OS is currently based on. All instructions in this book apply to Bookworm. GPIO (General-Purpose Input/Output) — The 40-pin connector on the Pi that lets you connect it to sensors, LEDs, motors, and other electronics. Operates at 3.3 V. RAM (Random-Access Memory) — The short-term working memory of a computer; more RAM means more tasks can run simultaneously without slowdown. PCIe — A high-speed expansion connector on the Pi 5 that allows you to attach a fast NVMe SSD storage drive via an add-on board. microSD card — A tiny removable memory card, about the size of a fingernail, used as the main storage for the Raspberry Pi's operating system and files. micro-HDMI — A smaller version of the HDMI video connector, used on the Raspberry Pi 5. You need a micro-HDMI to HDMI cable or adapter to connect to a standard monitor or TV. Terminal — A text-based window where you type commands directly to the operating system; faster and more powerful than menus for many tasks. Open-source — Software whose underlying code is publicly available for anyone to read, modify, and redistribute freely. NVMe SSD — A type of very fast solid-state storage drive that can be connected to the Pi 5 via its PCIe slot using a suitable add-on board. Active Cooler — The official Raspberry Pi heatsink-and-fan combination that clips onto the Pi 5 chip to keep it cool under load. Included with many starter kits, and an inexpensive add-on otherwise. Chapter summary To get started you need a Raspberry Pi 5 board, a power supply (the official 27 W USB-C supply or an equivalent 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one), a microSD card, a way to read that card on your main computer, and a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable; a case and an Active Cooler are recommended. Many starter kits bundle these together, sometimes pre-assembled. A Raspberry Pi is a complete, credit-card-sized single-board computer — every part of a full computer on one small board. It was created by a British educational charity to make computing accessible and affordable for everyone, and every sale funds that mission. People use Raspberry Pis for an enormous range of projects: media centres, robots, home servers, ad-blockers, weather stations, security cameras, AI assistants, and much more. The Pi runs Linux (Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm), not Windows or macOS; it uses an ARM processor rather than Intel/AMD; and it has 40 GPIO pins (at 3.3 V) for connecting to real-world electronics — three things a typical laptop or desktop lacks entirely. The Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone jack — audio travels via HDMI, USB, or Bluetooth. The Raspberry Pi 5 is 2–3× faster than its predecessor, supports dual 4K displays (via two micro-HDMI ports), has a PCIe slot for fast SSD storage, and includes a physical power button for safe shutdown. The Pi 5 comes in 2/4/8/16 GB RAM versions; all of them run everything in this book, and the more RAM you have, the more comfortably it handles heavy multitasking, local AI models, and everyday desktop use. Almost nothing you do in software can permanently damage the Pi — if something goes wrong, a fresh re-install of the OS takes about ten minutes. Follow each chapter in order the first time, always read the explanations beneath code blocks, and above all: experiment freely.

title: Your Kit, Unboxed
headings: A Guided Tour of the Raspberry Pi 5 Board
A Quick-Reference Table: Ports and What to Plug In
The microSD Card: Inserting and Removing
Connecting Everything for the First Time
What You Will See When the Pi Starts
How to Turn the Pi Off Properly
text: A Raspberry Pi 5, the right power supply, a microSD card, and a cable to a screen are all you need to build a fully working desktop computer. In this chapter we take a slow, careful look at every single part: what it is, what it does, and exactly how to connect it all together for the very first time. If you bought a starter kit, much of this may already be assembled for you; if you are putting the pieces together yourself, this chapter shows you exactly how. A Guided Tour of the Raspberry Pi 5 Board Before you plug anything in, take the Pi out of its case if you can and lay it flat so you can see the top of the board. (Do not worry if it is already sealed inside a case — we will describe every connector so you know where to find it through the case openings.) The board is a small green rectangle roughly the size of a credit card. Everything on it — the processor, the memory, the connectors — is mounted directly on that green card. In plain words: A board (or PCB — printed circuit board) is the flat green card that holds all the electronic components. Think of it as the "motherboard" of a tiny computer. The Brain and the Memory: SoC and RAM The largest component on the top of the board is a shiny silver square topped with a metal lid. This is the SoC (System on a Chip). In the Pi 5 it is the Broadcom BCM2712, and it contains the entire processor — four Arm Cortex-A76 cores running at 2.4 GHz — plus the graphics chip (VideoCore VII), and all the internal wiring that ties everything together. Think of it as the brain of the computer. In plain words: A SoC (System on a Chip) packs everything a computer needs to think and draw pictures into a single chip. The metal lid on top helps spread heat away from it. Stacked on top of the SoC, or placed right next to it, is a smaller chip: the RAM . The Pi 5 comes with 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, or 16 GB of LPDDR4X RAM, depending on which version you have. RAM is the computer's short-term memory — it holds whatever the computer is doing right now. More RAM means you can have more browser tabs, more programs, or bigger files open at the same time without the computer slowing down. Even the smallest version is plenty for anything a beginner will do; if you have one of the larger ones, you simply have more headroom for ambitious projects later. In plain words: RAM (Random Access Memory) is like a very fast notepad the computer writes its current work on. When you turn the power off, everything on that notepad is erased — that is why you save files to a storage card or drive. Labelled Diagram of the Pi 5 Board 40-pin GPIO BCM2712 SoC + RAM LPDDR4X USB-C mHDMI 0 mHDMI 1 USB 3.0 ① USB 3.0 ② USB 2.0 ① USB 2.0 ② ETH GbE 1 Gbps μSD slot CAM/CSI DISP/DSI PCIe / FPC FAN RTC BATT PWR Active Cooler sits here 40-pin GPIO Digital I/O pins Gigabit Ethernet Wired network USB 3.0 ×2 (blue) Fast drives, hubs USB 2.0 ×2 (black) Keyboard, mouse micro-HDMI 0 Primary monitor micro-HDMI 1 Second monitor USB-C Power 27 W supply only microSD slot OS storage card PCIe / FPC NVMe SSD (HAT) CAM / CSI Pi Camera ribbon DISP / DSI Pi touchscreen Power button Start / shutdown Fan connector Top-down view of the Raspberry Pi 5 board with every connector labelled. The dashed purple border shows where the Active Cooler sits on top of the SoC. The Ports Along the Edges — One by One Working around the board edge by edge, here is what every socket and connector does. Right Edge: USB Ports There are four USB sockets in a stacked pair of pairs. The two nearest the top of the board are blue on the inside — these are USB 3.0 ports. The two below them are black on the inside — these are USB 2.0 ports. In plain words: USB (Universal Serial Bus) is the standard plug used by keyboards, mice, memory sticks, and hundreds of other devices. The number (2.0 or 3.0) tells you the maximum speed. USB 3.0 is about ten times faster than USB 2.0 for transferring data. For a keyboard or mouse, the speed does not matter — either colour port works equally well. Use the blue USB 3.0 ports for things where speed matters: a USB memory stick you want to copy files to and from quickly, an external hard drive, or a USB hub (a device that turns one USB port into several). Use either port for your keyboard and mouse — it makes no difference. Tip: If you plug a USB 3.0 device into a USB 2.0 (black) port by accident, it will still work — just at the slower 2.0 speed. The blue ports are simply the better choice for fast devices. Right Edge: Gigabit Ethernet Above the USB ports, at the very top-right corner, is a slightly wider socket with a small plastic tab. This is the Ethernet port (also called the RJ-45 socket). It accepts a standard network cable and gives you a wired internet connection running at up to 1 Gigabit per second — far faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi for most home setups. In plain words: Ethernet is the wired way of connecting a computer to a router. The cable looks like a very wide phone plug. Gigabit means the port can transfer up to 1,000 megabits of data every second. When you plug in a network cable, a small amber light on the socket flashes to show data is moving, and a green light shows the connection is live. Bottom Edge: micro-HDMI Ports (×2) Along the bottom short edge of the board there are two small sockets that look like a shrunken version of the HDMI port on your television. These are the micro-HDMI ports , numbered 0 (closer to the centre of the board) and 1 (closer to the USB-C socket). They carry both picture and sound to a monitor or television. In plain words: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) is the standard that sends video and audio down a single cable to a screen. Micro-HDMI is simply a smaller version of that same plug, used because the Pi board is too small for a full-size one. The Pi 5 can drive two monitors simultaneously , each at up to 4K resolution at 60 frames per second — an impressive feat for such a small board. For a single monitor, always use port 0. Careful: Micro-HDMI and mini-HDMI look similar but are NOT the same size. You need a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable or adapter matched to the Pi 5 (many starter kits include one). Do not try to force a mini-HDMI or full-size HDMI plug into this socket — you could damage the port. Note: The Raspberry Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone jack . Audio comes out through the HDMI cable to your monitor or TV speakers. If you need a headphone socket, you can add one via a small USB audio adapter (widely available for a few pounds or euros). Bluetooth headphones or speakers also work well — see Chapter 4 for Bluetooth setup. Bottom Edge: USB-C Power Input At the far right of the bottom edge is a USB-C socket . This is the power input only — it is where you plug in the power supply. Unlike the USB-C port on a laptop, this socket on the Pi 5 does not transfer data; it only receives power. Note: The Pi 5 needs a proper USB-C Power Delivery supply that can provide at least 5 V at 5 A (= 25 W). A typical phone charger will not supply enough current and the Pi will show a low-voltage warning — a yellow lightning bolt icon — in the top-right corner of the screen. Use the official 27 W USB-C power supply (or any good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD supply). Left Edge (Underneath): microSD Card Slot On the underside of the board, at the left edge, is a thin spring-loaded slot. This is the microSD card slot . The microSD card is the Pi's "hard drive" — it holds the operating system, all your files, and any programs you install. Unlike a laptop's internal drive, you can pop the card out, copy it to your main computer for a backup, or swap it for a different card with a different operating system. In plain words: A microSD card is a tiny storage chip, about the size of a fingernail, most commonly used in cameras and phones. In the Pi it acts as the computer's main storage disk. Top Edge: The 40-Pin GPIO Header Running along the full width of the top edge of the board is a double row of small metal pins. This is the 40-pin GPIO header . GPIO stands for General-Purpose Input/Output. These pins let you connect the Pi to physical electronics: LEDs, buttons, sensors, motors, and much more. The Pi 5's GPIO pins operate at 3.3 V — important to know if you ever connect external components, since applying a 5 V signal to these pins can permanently damage the board. In plain words: GPIO pins are like tiny programmable switches. Some can output a small electrical signal to light an LED; others can read whether a button is pressed. They are the gateway to physical computing and electronics projects. For this beginner guide we will leave the GPIO header alone for now — it is covered in detail in Chapter 10. Top Edge: Fan Connector Near the GPIO header, there is a tiny 4-pin socket. This is the fan connector (sometimes labelled J14 on the board). The Active Cooler's small fan plugs in here so the Pi can control the fan speed automatically — running it faster when the processor is hot and quieter when it is idle. Top Edge: RTC Battery Connector A small 2-pin socket near the centre-top is the RTC battery connector . RTC stands for Real-Time Clock. A tiny coin battery (not included in most kits) can be connected here so the Pi remembers the correct date and time even when it is unplugged. Without a battery, the Pi simply fetches the time from the internet when it connects. This is perfectly fine for most uses. In plain words: An RTC (Real-Time Clock) is a tiny circuit that keeps ticking like a wristwatch even with the main power off — but only if a backup battery is attached. Without one, the Pi asks the internet "What time is it?" every time it starts. Top Edge: Power Button The Pi 5 has a small tactile button near the corner of the board, labelled "PWR_BTN". This is a genuine improvement over earlier Raspberry Pi models, which had no power button at all. It works as follows: Press once when the Pi is off — starts the Pi (same as plugging in the power). Short press while the Pi is running — sends a polite "please shut down" signal to the operating system. The Pi will save everything and power off cleanly within a few seconds. This is the recommended way to turn the Pi off. Press and hold for about 5 seconds — forces an immediate power cut (emergency only; equivalent to yanking the plug). Use this only if the Pi has frozen completely and will not respond. Careful: Never simply pull out the power cable while the Pi is running. Because the operating system is writing to the microSD card almost continuously, cutting the power mid-write can corrupt the card and make the Pi unbootable. Always shut down properly first. CSI and DSI Connectors (Camera and Display Ribbons) On the left side of the board, between the GPIO header and the PCIe connector, are two flat ribbon-cable sockets. These are: CSI (Camera Serial Interface) — for attaching an official Raspberry Pi Camera Module using a flexible ribbon cable. DSI (Display Serial Interface) — for attaching the official Raspberry Pi Touchscreen Display. Both connectors have a small locking clip that you push down to lock a ribbon cable in place, or lift to release it. For initial setup you will not need either of these — they are for future projects. PCIe / FPC Connector Between the CSI/DSI connectors and the GPIO area, a long thin socket runs parallel to the top edge. This is the PCIe 2.0 x1 / FPC connector . With an optional add-on board called an M.2 HAT, you can attach a fast NVMe solid-state drive (SSD) here, giving the Pi storage that is many times faster than even the best microSD card. This is an advanced upgrade — your kit uses the microSD card, which works perfectly well to start with. In plain words: PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) is a fast data lane originally designed for desktop PC graphics cards. In the Pi 5, a single lane is exposed on a flat ribbon connector so you can add a speedy SSD. NVMe is the type of very fast solid-state storage that uses this lane. Your Accessories — Every Part Explained Now let's look at the individual accessories you use with the Pi and understand why each one matters. Whether they came in a starter kit or you bought them separately, these are the parts you will be handling. The Power Supply The recommended supply looks like a phone charger but is significantly more capable. The official Raspberry Pi 5 supply outputs 5.1 V at up to 5 A, giving 27 W of power. The Pi 5 can draw more power than earlier Pi models — especially if you have multiple USB devices attached — so a proper supply is essential. Why does the exact supply matter? A cheap phone charger typically provides 5 V at 1 or 2 A (5–10 W). When the Pi 5 draws more current than the charger can supply, the voltage drops below 5 V and the Pi displays a yellow lightning bolt in the top-right corner of the screen. In this low-voltage state the processor throttles itself to use less power — meaning the Pi runs noticeably slower. Use the official 27 W USB-C power supply, or any good 5 V / 5 A USB-C Power Delivery supply. Careful: Make sure the plug on your supply matches the sockets in your country. If you travel with the Pi, take the correct plug adapter — never force a foreign plug into a socket. The Active Cooler If your Pi has an Active Cooler fitted, you will see (or feel through the case) a small heatsink with a tiny fan on top sitting on the SoC. This is the Active Cooler . It does two jobs at once: the metal heatsink draws heat away from the chip by conduction, and the fan blows that heat away into the surrounding air. In plain words: A heatsink is a piece of metal (usually aluminium) with fins or ridges that absorbs heat from a chip and spreads it over a large surface area so air can carry it away. An active cooler adds a fan to speed that process up. Why does the Pi 5 need active cooling? The Arm Cortex-A76 processor in the Pi 5 is considerably more powerful than its predecessors. Under a heavy load — compiling software, running a 4K video, or playing a 3D game — it generates enough heat to throttle itself if left uncooled. The Active Cooler keeps the chip well below its 85 °C thermal limit even under sustained full load, so your Pi always runs at full speed. A heatsink alone (passive cooling) is insufficient for a Pi 5 under heavy use; the fan makes the difference. Note: Many starter kits ship with the Active Cooler already clipped on and the fan cable plugged into the board's fan connector. If yours is already fitted, you do not need to do anything — just appreciate that it is there keeping your Pi healthy. If it isn't, the official Active Cooler is an inexpensive add-on that clips straight on and plugs into the fan connector; for any demanding use it is well worth fitting. The Case A case (most kits include one) is typically made from aluminium or plastic. It serves three purposes: physical protection, additional passive heat dissipation (a metal case helps conduct heat away from the board), and a tidy appearance. A good case has cutouts for every port so all your cables can reach the board without opening it. A case is optional — the Pi works fine without one — but it is recommended to protect the board. On most cases the microSD card slot is accessible through an opening on the side — you do not need to open the case to swap cards. The microSD Card and a Card Reader You will need a microSD card (commonly 32 GB or larger; many kits include one), which may already have Raspberry Pi OS installed on it. To write or back up the card you also need a way to read it on your main computer: many cards come with a small USB card reader, or your computer may have a built-in SD slot. Either lets you write a fresh OS image, make a backup, or recover a broken system — useful no matter whether your main computer runs Windows, macOS, or Linux. Tip: Keep a card reader handy even if your card already has the OS on it. It is your rescue tool if anything goes wrong with the software later. The Micro-HDMI to HDMI Cable This cable has a small micro-HDMI connector at one end (the Pi end) and a full-size HDMI connector at the other end (the monitor or TV end). It carries both video and audio. A suitable cable supports HDMI 2.0, which is enough for 4K resolution at 60 frames per second. Many kits include one; otherwise it is a cheap, widely available cable or adapter. Note: Most modern monitors and televisions have at least one full-size HDMI input. If your monitor only has DisplayPort or VGA inputs, you will need a separate active HDMI-to-DisplayPort or HDMI-to-VGA adapter (not included). Check your monitor's inputs before your first setup session. A Quick-Reference Table: Ports and What to Plug In Port / Connector Location on board What you plug in Notes USB 3.0 × 2 (blue) Right edge, upper pair USB memory sticks, external drives, USB hubs Up to 5 Gbps; also works for keyboard/mouse USB 2.0 × 2 (black) Right edge, lower pair Keyboard, mouse, any USB device Up to 480 Mbps; fine for input devices Gigabit Ethernet Right edge, top RJ-45 network cable to router Up to 1 Gbps; more reliable than Wi-Fi micro-HDMI 0 Bottom edge, inner Primary monitor or TV (via a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable) Up to 4K @ 60 fps; use this one first micro-HDMI 1 Bottom edge, outer Second monitor (optional) Up to 4K @ 60 fps; for dual-display setups USB-C (power only) Bottom edge, far right Official 27 W USB-C supply (or a 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one) Data is NOT supported on this port microSD slot Underside, left edge microSD card (your OS and storage) Push to insert; push to eject (spring-loaded) 40-pin GPIO Top edge Electronics projects (LEDs, sensors, etc.) 3.3 V logic only; leave alone until Chapter 10 PCIe / FPC Left area, horizontal M.2 NVMe SSD (via M.2 HAT add-on board) Advanced upgrade; not needed for beginners CSI (camera) Left side, ribbon slot Raspberry Pi Camera Module ribbon cable For future camera projects DSI (display) Left side, ribbon slot Official Pi Touchscreen ribbon cable For future touchscreen projects Fan connector (J14) Near top edge Active Cooler fan cable (already connected) Pi controls fan speed automatically RTC battery Near top edge Small lithium coin battery (optional) Keeps time when unplugged; not in kit Power button (PWR_BTN) Top edge, corner Press to start; short-press to shut down Hold 5 s for emergency power cut only Audio output None (no headphone jack) Via HDMI cable or USB audio adapter Bluetooth audio also supported Recognising a Correct Assembly If your kit arrived pre-assembled — or once you have put the pieces together yourself — confirm it is correct before powering on for the first time. Here is what a good assembly looks like: The Active Cooler sits flat and firm on the SoC. If you can see the board, the cooler should not wobble or feel loose. The fan cable should be plugged into the small 4-pin socket on the board. The board sits snugly inside the case, with all the USB, Ethernet, HDMI, and power sockets lined up with the cutouts in the case. Nothing should be forced or misaligned. The microSD card is inserted in the slot. From the underside of the board (or through the left-side opening in the case), you should see the edge of the card sitting flush — it should not be sticking out at an angle. No loose screws, spare parts, or leftover components remain in the box. (It is normal if there are spare rubber feet or a thin instruction leaflet.) Note: Some kits include a spare set of thermal pads or a small tube of thermal paste. If your kit arrived with these separate items and the Active Cooler is already installed, the extras are simply spares — you do not need to do anything with them. The microSD Card: Inserting and Removing The microSD card slot is spring-loaded: push the card in until you feel a click, then release — the card locks in place. To remove it, push gently again until you feel a second click, then let go — the spring will pop the card out far enough to grip it with your fingers. Careful: Never remove the microSD card while the Pi is powered on and running. Doing so is like ripping a hard drive out of a running PC — it will almost certainly corrupt the card and you will have to reinstall the operating system. Always shut down the Pi fully before removing the card. If your card arrived already inserted with Raspberry Pi OS pre-installed, leave it in place for now. Chapter 3 covers what to do if you ever need to re-write the card from scratch. Connecting Everything for the First Time Order matters when connecting a Raspberry Pi for the first time. Follow the steps below in sequence — and always connect power last . Tip: Before you start, clear a flat, stable desk surface and have all your cables and peripherals to hand: monitor, keyboard, mouse, and your network cable (if using wired internet). Monitor Keyboard Mouse Router (optional) 27 W Power Supply Raspberry Pi 5 micro-HDMI cable USB USB Ethernet USB-C — LAST 1 2 3 4 6 ⑤ Check SD card Connection order for first setup. Connect devices 1–5 first, then plug in power (6) last. Dashed lines = plug in order shown; solid orange line = power, connected last. Connect the monitor. Plug the micro-HDMI end of your micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable into micro-HDMI port 0 on the Pi (the one nearer the centre of the board). Plug the full-size HDMI end into your monitor or TV. Switch the monitor on and set it to the correct HDMI input (usually labelled HDMI 1, HDMI 2, etc. — check your monitor's manual if unsure). Connect a keyboard. Plug a USB keyboard into any of the four USB ports on the right edge of the Pi. For a beginner first-boot it does not matter which USB port — any of the four will work. Connect a mouse. Plug a USB mouse into another USB port. If you have a wireless keyboard/mouse combo with a single USB dongle, plug the dongle in now. Connect to the network (optional but recommended). If your router is nearby, plug a standard Ethernet cable from the router into the Pi's Ethernet port (top-right of the board). Wired internet is faster and more reliable for the initial setup and system update. You can set up Wi-Fi from within the operating system later if you prefer. Check the microSD card is inserted. Confirm the card is seated in the slot — it should be flush and locked in place. If your kit came pre-installed, this is already done. Connect the power supply — last. Plug the USB-C end of the power supply (the official 27 W supply, or a 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one) into the USB-C power socket on the Pi's bottom edge, then plug the other end into a wall socket and switch the socket on. The Pi will start immediately. You will see a green LED on the board begin to flash, and within a few seconds the Raspberry Pi boot screen will appear on your monitor. Careful: Always connect peripheral devices (monitor, keyboard, mouse) BEFORE applying power. Plugging a monitor in after the Pi has booted can sometimes mean the display output is not detected correctly, and you may see a blank screen. Note: The Pi 5 also has built-in dual-band Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) and Bluetooth 5.0 — no antenna or extra hardware needed. However, for the smoothest first-boot experience, a wired Ethernet connection is recommended. Wi-Fi setup is covered in Chapter 4. What You Will See When the Pi Starts After applying power you should see the following sequence on your monitor, which takes roughly 20–30 seconds on first boot: A rainbow square flashes briefly in the corner — this is the Pi's bootloader testing the display connection. It disappears almost immediately. A Raspberry Pi logo appears on a dark background, with four smaller Pi logos in a row — one for each processor core starting up. A stream of white text scrolls past — this is the Linux kernel loading. Do not worry about reading it; it disappears quickly. The Raspberry Pi OS desktop appears, typically with a Setup Wizard asking you to choose language, keyboard layout, username, password, and Wi-Fi network. Chapter 3 walks you through this wizard step by step. Tip: If the screen stays blank after 30 seconds, check that the monitor is switched on and set to the correct HDMI input, and that the micro-HDMI cable is securely plugged into port 0 (the inner socket) on the Pi's bottom edge. How to Turn the Pi Off Properly When you are ready to stop for the day, do not pull the power cable out. Instead, use one of these two methods: From the desktop: Click the Raspberry Pi menu (the raspberry icon, top-left of the screen) → choose Logout or Shutdown → click Shutdown . The Pi will close all programs, save everything, and power off. The green LED will stop flashing when it is safe to unplug. With the power button: Give the power button a single short press. The Pi will do the same clean shutdown as above. Wait for the green LED to go dark before removing power. If the desktop has become unresponsive and you cannot click the menu, you can type a shutdown command into a terminal window (covered in Chapter 5). Open a terminal and type the following, then press Enter: sudo shutdown -h now This command tells the Pi to power off immediately. Here is what each word means: sudo — "superuser do": runs the next command with full administrator privileges. The Pi may ask for your password the first time you use sudo in a session. shutdown — the built-in Linux program that safely powers off or reboots the computer, making sure all files are saved first. -h — short for "halt": tells shutdown to fully power off the machine rather than just restarting it. now — do it immediately, with no countdown or delay. Note: An equally correct modern alternative is sudo systemctl poweroff , which does exactly the same thing. Both commands work on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. The shutdown -h now form is slightly more traditional and is used here because it is easy to remember. Tip: You can also restart (reboot) the Pi from the same desktop menu. A restart is useful after installing new software or changing system settings — it is faster than a full shutdown and power-on cycle. Key terms SoC (System on a Chip) — a single chip containing the processor, graphics unit, and all internal connections; the "brain" of the Pi. RAM (Random Access Memory) — fast, temporary memory that holds whatever the computer is currently doing; cleared when power is removed. microSD card — a fingernail-sized storage card that acts as the Pi's hard drive, holding the operating system and all files. USB 3.0 / USB 2.0 — two versions of the universal plug standard; 3.0 (blue) is about ten times faster than 2.0 (black) for data transfer. Ethernet — a wired network connection using an RJ-45 cable; faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi. micro-HDMI — a smaller version of the standard HDMI video and audio connector, used on the Pi 5 to save space on the board. GPIO (General-Purpose Input/Output) — 40 programmable pins that let the Pi communicate with external electronics; operates at 3.3 V only. Active Cooler — a heatsink combined with a fan that keeps the Pi's processor at a safe temperature so it never slows down due to overheating. Heatsink — a piece of metal that absorbs and spreads heat away from a chip so that air can carry the heat away. PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) — a high-speed data connection; the Pi 5 exposes one lane for attaching a fast NVMe SSD via an add-on board. NVMe — a type of very fast solid-state storage that connects via the PCIe lane on the Pi 5. CSI / DSI — flat ribbon-cable connectors for attaching an official Pi Camera (CSI) or official Pi Touchscreen (DSI). RTC (Real-Time Clock) — a circuit that keeps track of the date and time; needs a backup battery to remember the time when the Pi is unplugged. USB-C (power) — the socket on the Pi 5 that accepts the 27 W power supply; it carries power only, not data. sudo — a Linux command prefix meaning "run as administrator"; required for tasks that affect the whole system. Thermal throttling — when a processor deliberately slows itself down to avoid overheating; prevented by the Active Cooler. Chapter summary The Raspberry Pi 5 packs a powerful quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 processor, VideoCore VII graphics, and up to 16 GB of RAM (2/4/8/16 GB versions) onto a credit-card-sized board. The board has two fast blue USB 3.0 ports, two standard black USB 2.0 ports, a Gigabit Ethernet socket, two micro-HDMI video outputs, a USB-C power input, a microSD storage slot, and a 40-pin GPIO header for electronics projects. Additional connectors include CSI (camera ribbon), DSI (display ribbon), PCIe/FPC (for a fast NVMe SSD), a fan socket, an RTC battery socket, and a physical power button. The Pi 5 has no 3.5 mm headphone jack; audio is delivered through the HDMI cable, a USB audio adapter, or Bluetooth. A proper power supply is essential — the official 27 W USB-C supply (or a good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one); a weaker charger will cause the Pi to display a yellow lightning bolt warning and slow itself down. The Active Cooler (heatsink and fan) keeps the Pi 5 running at full speed under heavy loads; it is included with many kits already fitted, and an inexpensive clip-on add-on otherwise. Always connect the monitor, keyboard, and mouse first, and plug in the power supply last. Never pull the power cable out while the Pi is running — always shut down using the desktop menu, the power button, or the sudo shutdown -h now command, and wait for the green LED to go dark. The microSD card is the Pi's main storage; never remove it while the Pi is switched on.

title: The Absolute Basics
headings: RAM Versus Storage — A Crucial Distinction
Two Ways to Talk to the Computer
What Is ARM? And Why Does It Occasionally Matter?
Open Source and "Free" Software — What These Actually Mean
Putting It All Together — A Layers Picture
text: Before you press a single button, it helps to understand what is actually happening inside the little computer sitting on your desk. This chapter builds up a mental picture — using everyday analogies — of the key ideas you will meet again and again: operating systems, RAM, storage, booting, Linux, the terminal, files, users, and a few other concepts that sound technical but are really quite simple once you see them clearly. What Is an Operating System? Imagine a large restaurant kitchen. Ingredients sit in the fridge and cupboards. The hobs, ovens, and knives are the tools. But without a head chef who decides which ingredients to fetch, which chef cooks which dish, and how the orders from the dining room are handled, the kitchen would be chaos. The operating system is that head chef — it is the software that manages every piece of your computer's hardware and makes sure all the programs you run get what they need, without treading on each other's toes. In plain words: An operating system (OS) is the master program that runs invisibly in the background whenever the computer is on. It handles the screen, the keyboard, the memory, the storage, and every other program you open. Without it, the hardware is just expensive metal. Your everyday laptop or desktop runs an operating system such as Windows or macOS. Your Raspberry Pi 5 runs Raspberry Pi OS — a version of Linux specially designed for the Pi. It handles everything the same way those systems do, but it looks different and behaves slightly differently in places. Note: Raspberry Pi OS is free to download and free to use — forever. You do not need a licence key or a subscription. Hardware Versus Software These two words are used constantly, so it is worth being crystal clear about them before going any further. In plain words: Hardware is anything you can physically touch — the circuit board, the RAM chips, the microSD card, the case, the cables. Software is the set of instructions stored on the hardware that tells it what to do — the operating system, apps, games, and any programs you write yourself. A useful analogy: hardware is the DVD player; software is the film on the disc. The player cannot do anything interesting without a disc, and a disc without a player is just a shiny circle. They need each other. RAM Versus Storage — A Crucial Distinction People sometimes confuse RAM and storage because both are measured in gigabytes and both sound like "memory". They serve completely different purposes. RAM — Your Desk In plain words: RAM (Random Access Memory) is your computer's working space — like the surface of a desk. When you open a program, the computer loads it from storage onto the desk so it can work with it quickly. The bigger the desk, the more things you can have open at once without things slowing down. Your Raspberry Pi 5 has 2, 4, 8, or 16 GB of RAM, depending on which version you have. Even the smaller amounts comfortably run a web browser, a code editor, and a music player together; with 8 GB or 16 GB you can keep many more programs open at the same time without the computer struggling. Here is the critical thing about RAM: it is wiped clean every time you turn the power off . Whatever was on the desk gets swept onto the floor the moment the lights go out. That is why you must save your work to a file before switching off. Storage — Your Filing Cabinet In plain words: Storage is where files live permanently — like a filing cabinet. Unlike RAM, storage keeps its contents when the power is off. On a typical laptop, the filing cabinet is an internal hard drive or SSD. On your Raspberry Pi 5, the filing cabinet is the microSD card . Your Pi's microSD card (commonly 32 GB or larger) plays the role that a hard drive plays in a laptop. Raspberry Pi OS itself is installed on it, and every file you create, every program you install, and every setting you change is stored there. Careful: MicroSD cards are tougher than they look, but they can still be damaged by being pulled out while the Pi is running. Always shut down properly before removing the card. You will learn how to shut down safely in Chapter 4. RAM (Your Desk) Web Browser Code Editor Music Player Other Program Fast. Wiped when power off. 2–16 GB on your Pi 5 loads saves Storage (Filing Cabinet) Raspberry Pi OS Your Files & Documents Installed Programs Permanent. Survives power off. microSD card — your Pi's hard drive Working space — temporary Long-term storage — permanent RAM is the desk where the computer does its work; the microSD card is the filing cabinet where everything is stored permanently. Programs are loaded from the filing cabinet onto the desk to run, then saved back when you are done. What Does "64-bit" Mean? You will notice that Raspberry Pi OS is described as a 64-bit operating system. This comes up often enough that it is worth a brief explanation. In plain words: Bits are the smallest unit of information a computer works with — think of them as on/off switches. A 64-bit processor can handle 64 switches at a time; an older 32-bit processor handled only 32 at a time. More bits at once means the processor can address far more memory, work with bigger numbers in one step, and generally run modern software more efficiently. Your Pi 5 has a 64-bit ARM processor, and the version of Raspberry Pi OS on your card is the 64-bit edition. This is the recommended version for all Pi 5 boards. In practice, you will rarely need to think about this — just know that if a website ever offers you a choice between a 32-bit and 64-bit download for Linux, always pick 64-bit for your Pi 5. What Does "Booting" Mean? In plain words: Booting (or "starting up") is the process the computer goes through from the moment you switch it on until it is ready for you to use. The word comes from the old phrase "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps" — the computer is loading the instructions it needs to load more instructions, step by step, until the full operating system is running. Here is what happens when you plug in your Raspberry Pi 5: Power flows to the board. A tiny built-in chip (the bootloader) wakes up. The bootloader looks at the microSD card and finds Raspberry Pi OS. It loads the OS into RAM and hands over control. Raspberry Pi OS starts all its background services (Wi-Fi, screen, keyboard, and so on). The desktop appears and you can start working. On the Pi 5, this process takes roughly 20–30 seconds from power-on to a usable desktop. You will see a rainbow square briefly, then a bouncing Raspberry Pi logo, and then the desktop. Tip: The rainbow square is completely normal — it just means the GPU (graphics chip) has started. It disappears after a second or two. Two Ways to Talk to the Computer There are two fundamentally different ways of giving your Raspberry Pi instructions, and you will use both of them throughout this book. The Graphical Way (Desktop) This is the one that looks like the desktop on Windows or a Mac. You see a wallpaper, icons, a taskbar, windows that open and close. You use a mouse to click on things. Everything you want to do has a visual representation — a picture of a file, a button to press, a menu to open. Raspberry Pi OS's graphical desktop is called PIXEL (which stands for "Pi Improved Xwindows Environment, Lightweight" — but you will never need to remember that). It looks clean and simple, with the Raspberry Pi logo in the top-left corner as the main menu button. Note: If you have used Windows or a Mac before, the desktop will feel familiar within a few minutes. The icons and menus work in the same way, even if they are in slightly different places. The Terminal Way (Typing Commands) In plain words: The terminal (also called the command line , command prompt , or shell ) is a text window where you type instructions and the computer types back its response. There are no icons or buttons — just text. It looks old-fashioned, but it is extraordinarily powerful and is the method that most Pi projects and guides (including much of this book) rely on. You open the terminal on Raspberry Pi OS by clicking the black rectangle icon on the taskbar, or by going to the Raspberry Pi menu → Accessories → Terminal. When the terminal opens, you will see something like this: pi@raspberrypi:~ $ This line is called the prompt — the terminal's way of saying "I am ready, what would you like me to do?" It tells you four things at a glance: pi is your username (the name of the account you are logged in as); raspberrypi is the computer's name (its "hostname" on the network); ~ means you are currently in your home folder (the tilde character is a shortcut for your personal folder); and $ is the signal that you can now type a command. If your username is something other than pi — which is possible if the card was set up with a different name — you will see that name instead. You type a command and press Enter . The computer carries it out and shows the result. For example: date The command date asks the computer to display the current date and time. After pressing Enter, the terminal will print something like Fri 19 Jun 2026 10:30:05 BST and then show the prompt again, ready for the next command. This is harmless — a good first command to try the moment your terminal is open. Neither the graphical way nor the terminal way is "better" — they are two tools for two slightly different jobs. The desktop is convenient for browsing, opening documents, and adjusting settings. The terminal is faster and more precise for installing software, configuring the Pi, and running projects. This book teaches you both, so you will always choose the right tool for the task. What Is Linux? In plain words: Linux is a family of operating systems. Just as there are many brands of car (all with four wheels, a steering wheel, and an engine), there are many versions of Linux — they share the same core but look and behave a little differently. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, and Raspberry Pi OS are all members of the Linux family. Linux was created in 1991 by a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds. He made the source code — the recipe for how it works — publicly available so that anyone could read it, improve it, and share their improvements. Decades later, this collaborative effort has produced one of the most reliable, secure, and widely used operating systems in the world. Linux runs most of the world's web servers, every Android phone, and almost every supercomputer. In plain words: Open source means the recipe (source code) is published for anyone to read, use, modify, and share. Free software in the Linux world usually means free as in freedom — you have the right to study and change it — as well as free as in no cost . Raspberry Pi OS is both. Raspberry Pi OS is built on top of Debian , one of the oldest and most stable Linux distributions. The version currently installed on your Pi is called Bookworm (Debian 12, released 2023). Debian names its releases after characters from the film Toy Story . Tip: Because Linux is open source, there is a huge community of people who have solved the same problems you will encounter. Searching "Raspberry Pi [your question] Bookworm" on the web almost always finds a working answer. What Is ARM? And Why Does It Occasionally Matter? Most Windows laptops and desktops use a processor made by Intel or AMD (Apple's recent Macs are an exception — they already use ARM). Your Raspberry Pi 5 uses a processor designed around something called the ARM architecture . In plain words: A processor's architecture is the language it speaks internally — the set of instructions it understands. Just as a French speaker and a Japanese speaker cannot understand each other without a translator, a program built for Intel/AMD will not run directly on an ARM chip. The program must be compiled (built) specifically for the architecture it will run on. ARM stands for "Advanced RISC Machine" — but you never need to remember that. What matters is that ARM chips are designed to be extremely energy-efficient, which is why they are used in phones, tablets, and single-board computers like the Pi. The Pi 5's processor (Broadcom BCM2712, with four Arm Cortex-A76 cores running at 2.4 GHz) is powerful enough to run a full desktop operating system while drawing very little power. Feature Intel / AMD (typical Windows PC) ARM (Raspberry Pi 5, also Apple Silicon Macs) Architecture x86-64 AArch64 (64-bit ARM) Power use 65–125 W (desktop) / 15–45 W (laptop) 5–15 W (typical Pi 5 use) Typical use Desktop PCs, laptops Phones, tablets, embedded projects, Pi Software Windows .exe files (built for x86-64) ARM binaries (built for AArch64) In practice, for everyday tasks on the Pi — browsing the web, writing documents, running Python programs — you will never notice the difference. Raspberry Pi OS and its software repository already contain ARM-compiled versions of everything you are likely to need. The only time it matters is if you try to download a program built for another system — a Windows .exe file, a macOS app, or a Linux program compiled only for Intel — in which case it simply will not run. The solution is always to install software through Raspberry Pi OS's built-in package manager (covered in Chapter 6), which automatically gives you the right version for your chip. Files, Folders, and Paths You are probably familiar with files and folders from Windows or macOS. The concept is identical on Linux, but there are a few important differences in how they are organised and written about. Files and Folders A file is a named collection of data stored on the microSD card — a document, a photo, a program, a piece of music. A folder (also called a directory on Linux) is a container that holds files and other folders, letting you organise things into a hierarchy, just like real folders in a real filing cabinet. The Root and Your Home Folder On Windows, each storage drive gets a letter: C:\ , D:\ , and so on. Linux works differently. There is one single tree starting from a folder called the root , written simply as / . Everything — all your files, all installed programs, all the operating system itself — hangs off this single root. In plain words: On Linux, / (a single forward slash) is the very top of the file system — the trunk of a tree from which all other folders branch. It is called the root directory . Inside the root, there are several important folders. The one you will use most is your home folder : /home/pi (or /home/yourname if you chose a different username during setup). This is your personal space — much like the Documents or home folder on Windows or macOS. When you open the terminal, you start here automatically. The tilde symbol ~ is a shortcut that always means your home folder, so ~/Documents is the same as /home/pi/Documents . Note: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, if the microSD card was pre-installed for you (as some kits provide), your username and home folder may already be set to pi . If you set up the card yourself using Raspberry Pi Imager, you chose your own username. Either way, ~ always points to the right place, whatever your username is. Paths In plain words: A path is the full address of a file or folder — the set of directions that tells the computer exactly where to find something, starting from the root and working down through the folder tree. Paths on Linux use forward slashes / , unlike Windows, which uses backslashes \ . (macOS, like Linux, already uses forward slashes.) For example: /home/pi/Documents/hello.txt — a file called hello.txt inside the Documents folder inside your home folder. /usr/bin/python3 — the Python 3 program, stored in the system's program folder. ~/Pictures/holiday.jpg — a photo in your Pictures folder (using the ~ shortcut). Note: Linux file names are case-sensitive . A file named Hello.txt and a file named hello.txt are treated as two different files. Windows ignores case; Linux does not. This trips up many beginners — if a command complains it cannot find a file, check the capitalisation first. A Quick Look at the Folder Tree Here are the folders you are most likely to encounter. You do not need to memorise them all — just keep this table as a reference. Folder What it contains / The root — the very top of the file system /home/pi Your personal files (documents, pictures, projects). Replace pi with your own username if different. /home/pi/Desktop Files and shortcuts that appear on the desktop /etc Configuration files for the whole system /usr/bin Programs installed for all users /tmp Temporary files — wiped on every reboot /boot/firmware Files the Pi needs to start up (on Bookworm the boot files live in this subfolder — not in /boot directly) /media/pi Where USB drives and other external storage appear when you plug them in /var/log System log files — useful when something goes wrong Tip: You can explore these folders visually using the file manager on the desktop (the folder icon on the taskbar), just as you would with File Explorer on Windows or Finder on macOS. There is no need to use the terminal to browse files unless you prefer to. The Linux File System Tree / (root) /home /etc /usr /boot /media /home/pi Desktop Documents Pictures /usr/bin programs /boot/firmware Pi boot files /media/pi USB drives Key: ~ (tilde) = your home folder = /home/pi So ~/Documents is exactly the same as /home/pi/Documents All paths start from / and use forward slashes — not backslashes like Windows The Linux file system is a single tree rooted at / . Your personal space lives inside /home/pi . On Bookworm, the boot files are in /boot/firmware , not /boot directly. Users, the Administrator, and sudo Linux was designed from the very beginning to be used by many people at once (on a shared computer or server). Even though you are the only person using your Pi, Linux still thinks in terms of users . Your User Account When Raspberry Pi OS first starts on a pre-installed card, it either sets up a default account named pi , or — if you used Raspberry Pi Imager to prepare the card yourself — the username you chose during setup. You are logged in as that account whenever you are using the desktop or the terminal. Your user account can do almost everything you need day-to-day: create files, browse the web, run programs, write code. But certain things — installing software system-wide, changing core settings, or modifying files outside your home folder — require special permission. The Administrator (Root) In plain words: On Linux, the all-powerful administrator account is called root . Root can do literally anything to the system — delete every file, break the operating system, install anything. Because of this power, you almost never log in directly as root. Instead, you use a command called sudo to temporarily borrow root's powers for a single command. In plain words: sudo stands for "superuser do". You put it in front of a command to run that one command with administrator privileges. Think of it as showing your ID at a secure door — you do not move into the secure area permanently, you just get access for that one moment. You will see sudo constantly in Pi guides. Here is an example — updating the list of available software: sudo apt update Line by line: sudo — run the following command with administrator (root) powers; apt — this is the package manager , the built-in program that installs and updates software on Raspberry Pi OS; update — tells apt to download the latest list of available software packages from the internet, so your Pi knows what is available and what version is current. Without sudo , this command would be refused because only an administrator can modify system-wide software lists. You will run this command frequently throughout the book. Careful: Because sudo gives you full administrator power, a typo in a sudo command can cause real damage. Always double-check a command before pressing Enter when sudo is involved. Never copy a sudo command from an unknown website without understanding what it does. When you first use sudo in a terminal session, Raspberry Pi OS will ask for your password. Type it and press Enter. (The characters will not appear on screen as you type — this is intentional and is a security feature, not a bug.) Note: Your everyday account (for example, pi ) is a member of a group called sudo , which is what grants it permission to use the sudo command at all. You are already in this group on any standard Raspberry Pi OS setup — you do not need to do anything to enable it. Users and Groups — A Brief Mention Linux also organises users into groups . Groups are used to grant shared permissions — for example, the gpio group grants access to the Pi's physical pins, and the audio group grants access to audio devices. Your account is already added to all the groups it needs by default, so this is mostly invisible to you.
