You may occasionally encounter it in more advanced projects, and at that point the project's instructions will tell you exactly what to do. Open Source and "Free" Software — What These Actually Mean You will see the words "free" and "open source" everywhere in the Raspberry Pi community. They are worth understanding properly because they affect how you can use, share, and build on the software. Free as in Freedom In the computing world, "free software" does not just mean zero cost (though it usually is zero cost). It means you have four essential freedoms: Freedom to use the software for any purpose. Freedom to study how it works (by reading the source code). Freedom to share copies with others. Freedom to improve it and share your improvements. Raspberry Pi OS, Linux, Python, the LibreOffice suite, the Firefox web browser, and thousands of other programs you will use on the Pi are all free in this sense. Nobody can take them away from you, charge you a subscription, or prevent you from looking under the bonnet. Open Source In plain words: Source code is the human-readable set of instructions that a programmer writes. Open source means that source code is published publicly, so anyone can read, learn from, verify, and improve it. The opposite is proprietary or closed-source software, where the recipe is a trade secret (like Windows or macOS). Open source matters for practical reasons beyond philosophy. Because thousands of developers worldwide can inspect the code, bugs and security vulnerabilities are spotted and fixed faster. No single company can abandon the project and leave you stranded. And the huge library of open-source software available for Linux means there is almost always a free, capable alternative to any commercial program you might need. Tip: The Raspberry Pi Foundation itself publishes most of its tools as open source. If you ever become curious about how something works under the hood, the code is there for you to read. Putting It All Together — A Layers Picture How Your Raspberry Pi 5 Is Organised — The Layers YOU — clicking, typing, creating Applications — browser, editor, Python, games… Raspberry Pi OS (Linux) — the operating system Firmware / Bootloader — starts up the Pi Hardware — processor, RAM, microSD, GPIO pins… Every computer works in layers. The hardware at the bottom does the actual work; the firmware wakes it up; the operating system (Raspberry Pi OS / Linux) manages everything; applications sit on top; and you interact with the applications. Each layer only needs to talk to the one directly below it. Keep this picture in mind as you work through the rest of this book. When something goes wrong, you can often work out which layer the problem is in — is the hardware not responding? Is the OS confused? Is the app misbehaving? — and that points you towards the right solution. Key terms Operating system (OS) — the master program that manages all of a computer's hardware and software. Raspberry Pi OS — the official Linux-based operating system for the Raspberry Pi, based on Debian Bookworm. Hardware — the physical components of a computer (circuit board, chips, cables, case). Software — programs and data; the instructions that hardware follows. RAM — fast, temporary working memory; wiped when power is off. Storage — permanent memory (the microSD card on the Pi) that survives power-off. 64-bit — a processor (and OS) that handles 64 data switches at once; gives access to more memory and runs modern software more efficiently than older 32-bit systems. The Pi 5 and Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm are both 64-bit. Booting — the start-up process from power-on to a ready desktop. Terminal / command line — a text window where you type commands instead of clicking. Prompt — the text the terminal shows (e.g. pi@raspberrypi:~ $ ) to indicate it is ready for a command. PIXEL — the name of the graphical desktop environment used by Raspberry Pi OS. Linux — a family of open-source operating systems; Raspberry Pi OS is a member. Debian Bookworm — the specific version of Linux that Raspberry Pi OS is based on (version 12, released 2023). ARM — the processor architecture used by the Raspberry Pi 5; different from the x86-64 architecture in most Windows PCs. Architecture — the internal instruction language of a processor; software must be built for the right architecture to run. Root directory (/) — the very top of the Linux file system, from which all folders branch. Home folder (~) — your personal folder on Linux, typically /home/pi (or /home/yourname if you chose a different username). Path — the full address of a file or folder (e.g. /home/pi/Documents/hello.txt ). Case-sensitive — Linux treats Hello.txt and hello.txt as different files; capitalisation matters. root (user) — the all-powerful administrator account on Linux. sudo — a command prefix that runs a single command with administrator (root) privileges. apt — the package manager on Raspberry Pi OS; the built-in tool for installing and updating software. Open source — software whose source code is published for anyone to read, use, and improve. Source code — the human-readable instructions a programmer writes to create a program. Chapter summary The operating system is the head chef of the computer — it manages all hardware and software; your Pi runs Raspberry Pi OS , a friendly Linux based on Debian Bookworm. RAM is fast, temporary working space (like a desk); the microSD card is permanent storage (like a filing cabinet) and acts as the Pi's hard drive. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm is 64-bit , matching the Pi 5's 64-bit ARM processor — always choose 64-bit software downloads for your Pi. Booting is the automatic start-up sequence from power-on to ready desktop, taking about 20–30 seconds on the Pi 5. You can control the Pi two ways: the graphical desktop (the PIXEL environment — click with the mouse) or the terminal (type commands); both are valid and useful. Linux is an open-source OS family; Raspberry Pi OS is built on Debian Bookworm and is free to use, study, and share. The Pi 5 uses an ARM processor (AArch64), which is different from the Intel/AMD chips in most Windows PCs; software must be built for the right architecture to run. Linux organises files in a single tree starting from / (root); your personal folder is /home/pi (written as ~ ); paths use forward slashes and are case-sensitive . On Bookworm, boot files live in /boot/firmware . Your everyday user account (e.g. pi ) is in the sudo group; for administrator tasks you prefix commands with sudo to temporarily borrow root's powers for that one command. Open source means the recipe (source code) is public — anyone can read, improve, and share it; most Pi software is both open source and free of charge.

title: First Boot: Installing the Operating System
headings: Before You Begin: Two Paths to Your First Boot
Path A — Your Card Is Already Loaded
Path B — Flashing Your Own Card with Raspberry Pi Imager
Connecting Everything Up for the First Time
What You See on the Desktop
Running the First Update from the Terminal
Headless Setup: Running the Pi Without a Monitor
text: Switching on your Raspberry Pi for the first time is one of those genuinely exciting moments — within a few minutes you will see a full desktop appear on your screen, ready to explore. This chapter walks you through every step of that journey, whether your microSD card already has the software loaded or you prefer to put a fresh, clean copy on it yourself. Before You Begin: Two Paths to Your First Boot Your microSD card may have come with Raspberry Pi OS already installed on it. If that is the case, you can jump straight to Path A below. If the card is blank, or if you would simply prefer to start from a known-clean installation (always a good idea), follow Path B first to copy the operating system onto the card yourself. In plain words: A microSD card is the tiny memory chip — about the size of a fingernail — that acts as the Raspberry Pi's hard drive. The operating system (OS) is the core software that makes the computer work; on your Pi it is called Raspberry Pi OS . Flashing means copying that operating system onto the card so the Pi can start up from it. Path A — Your Card Is Already Loaded If your card arrived with Raspberry Pi OS pre-installed, the only thing you need to do before powering on is insert the card into the Pi. Hold the microSD card so the gold contacts (the shiny metal strips) face down and the printed label faces up. Slide the card into the microSD slot on the underside of the Raspberry Pi board (the slot is on the edge opposite the USB ports). Push it in gently until you feel a soft click. It should sit flush — it is not designed to stick out. Skip ahead to the section "Connecting Everything Up for the First Time" later in this chapter. Tip: If the card does not slide in smoothly, try turning it around — it only fits one way. Never force it. Path B — Flashing Your Own Card with Raspberry Pi Imager Even if your card came pre-loaded, following Path B is a great habit: it gives you a clean, up-to-date installation and lets you set up your password and Wi-Fi details before the Pi ever boots. You will use a free program called Raspberry Pi Imager on your main computer to do this. Raspberry Pi Imager runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, so whatever you use, the steps below are the same. In plain words: Raspberry Pi Imager is a simple free program that downloads Raspberry Pi OS and copies it onto your microSD card in one step. Think of it like burning a DVD, except onto a tiny memory card instead. Step 1 — Download and Install Raspberry Pi Imager On your main computer, open a web browser and go to: https://www.raspberrypi.com/software/ Click the download button for your system — "Download for Windows" , "Download for macOS" , or the Linux option. The page detects your computer and highlights the right one. The version number may be higher than any shown here — that is fine, always get the latest. Once downloaded, open the file from your Downloads folder and follow the installer: on Windows, double-click the .exe and approve the "allow this app to make changes" prompt; on macOS, open the .dmg and drag Raspberry Pi Imager into your Applications folder; on Linux, install the downloaded package (or use sudo apt install rpi-imager ). Raspberry Pi Imager is now installed on your computer. Step 2 — Insert the microSD Card into Your Computer Put the microSD card into a card reader — either a USB card reader plugged into a USB port, or your computer's built-in SD slot if it has one. Insert the card with the gold contacts facing down and the label up. Your computer may pop up a window offering to open or format the card (an "AutoPlay" prompt on Windows, or a Finder window on macOS) — simply close it. Do not let it format the card. Careful: Make sure you are using the microSD card you intend for the Pi and not a USB stick or another drive that contains files you need. Flashing permanently erases everything on the card. Step 3 — Open Raspberry Pi Imager and Choose Your Settings Open Raspberry Pi Imager — from the Start menu on Windows (search for "Raspberry Pi Imager"), from the Applications folder or Launchpad on macOS, or from your applications menu on Linux. You will see three big buttons: Raspberry Pi Device , Operating System , and Storage . Work through them left to right. Click "Choose Device" and select Raspberry Pi 5 from the list. Click "Choose OS" . The top option will be Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) — this is the correct one for your Pi 5. Select it. Click "Choose Storage" . Your microSD card will appear (it may show by its size, e.g. "64 GB", or by a drive letter like D: on Windows or a disk name on macOS/Linux). Select it. Note: Always choose the 64-bit version of Raspberry Pi OS when you see the option. Your Pi 5 has a 64-bit processor, and the 64-bit OS uses its full capability — it runs faster and more efficiently than the 32-bit version. Step 4 — Pre-configure Your Settings (the Edit Settings Button) This is the most important step that many guides skip. After you have made all three selections above and clicked Next , Imager will ask "Would you like to apply OS customisation settings?" — click "Edit Settings" . This opens a panel where you can set your username, password, and Wi-Fi details before the card is written. It saves significant time during first boot, and it is the only easy opportunity to enable remote access without a monitor. A settings panel opens. Fill in the following fields on the General tab: Hostname: a short name for your Pi on your home network, for example raspberrypi . You can leave the default if you like. Username: choose a username for your account, for example pi or your own first name (all lowercase, no spaces). Password: choose a strong password — at least 12 characters, mixing letters, numbers, and symbols. Write it down somewhere safe. (See the section "Choosing a Strong Password" near the end of this chapter.) Configure wireless LAN: tick this box, then type your home Wi-Fi network name ( SSID ) and password exactly as they appear. Set Wireless LAN country to your country (e.g. GB for the UK, FR for France, DE for Germany, CH for Switzerland, and so on). Set locale settings: choose your time zone (e.g. Europe/London , Europe/Paris , Europe/Zurich ) and keyboard layout (e.g. gb for a UK keyboard, fr for French). Switch to the Services tab. Tick "Enable SSH" and select "Use password authentication" . SSH lets you control the Pi from another computer over your home network — you do not need to use it straight away, but enabling it here is much easier than turning it on later. Click Save to close the settings panel, then click Yes to apply the settings. Careful: Your Wi-Fi password is sensitive. Make sure no one is looking over your shoulder when you type it into Imager, and close the program when you are done. In plain words: SSH (Secure Shell) is a way to type commands into your Pi from another computer across your home network — even without a monitor attached to the Pi. Think of it as a text-based remote control. Chapter 9 covers it in full detail. In plain words: Hostname is simply the name your Pi announces itself by on your home network — the same way your phone might appear as "Florian's iPhone" in your router's list of connected devices. In plain words: SSID is the technical term for a Wi-Fi network name — the name you see when you look for Wi-Fi on your phone or laptop. In plain words: Locale refers to your region settings — primarily the time zone and keyboard layout, so that the Pi knows where in the world it is and which keyboard symbols go with which keys. Step 5 — Write the Card Click Yes when Imager asks if you are sure you want to erase the card. Imager will now download the latest version of Raspberry Pi OS from the internet and write it to the card. This typically takes 5 to 15 minutes depending on your internet speed and card speed. A progress bar shows how far along it is. After writing, Imager automatically verifies the card — it reads it back to check for errors. Do not remove the card during this step. When you see the message "Write Successful" , click Continue . Tip: If the write fails with an error, try a different USB port, or re-insert the card reader and try again. Occasionally Imager may need to format the card first — it will usually offer to do this automatically. Step 6 — Eject the Card Safely Tell your computer to eject the card before you pull it out: Windows: click the Safely Remove Hardware icon in the taskbar (bottom right — a USB plug with a small tick or arrow), then click "Eject" next to your card reader and wait for the "Safe to Remove Hardware" message. macOS: drag the card's icon to the Trash (which becomes an Eject icon), or click the eject arrow next to it in a Finder window's sidebar. Linux: click the eject symbol next to the card in your file manager, or right-click it and choose "Eject" / "Safely Remove". Once your computer says it is safe, gently pull the card reader out of the USB port (or remove the card from the built-in slot). Remove the microSD card from the card reader. Careful: Always eject the card properly before removing it. Pulling it out without ejecting can corrupt the data you just wrote and you would have to start over. Raspberry Pi Imager — Step by Step 1. Download Raspberry Pi Imager from raspberrypi.com 2. Choose Device Select Raspberry Pi 5 3. Choose OS Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) 4. Choose Storage Your microSD card 5. Edit Settings Hostname · User · Password Wi-Fi · Locale · SSH 6. Write & Verify Wait for "Write Successful" Do not remove card 7. Eject safely Use "Safely Remove Hardware" then insert card into Pi What to fill in during Edit Settings (Step 5) General tab: • Hostname: e.g. raspberrypi • Username: e.g. pi (lowercase, no spaces) • Password: strong — min. 12 characters • Wi-Fi SSID: your home network name • Wi-Fi Password: exactly as on your router • Wi-Fi Country: GB / FR / DE / CH / etc. • Time zone: e.g. Europe/London • Keyboard layout: e.g. gb Services tab: • Enable SSH — tick it, use password authentication Figure 4.1 — The seven steps of using Raspberry Pi Imager (the same on Windows, macOS and Linux). Steps 1–4 run left to right across the top; steps 5–7 flow downward on the right. The white panel shows exactly what to fill in during step 5. Connecting Everything Up for the First Time With the microSD card ready and inserted into the Pi, it is time to connect your cables. The order matters — always connect power last . The diagram below shows where each port is on the Pi 5. In plain words: micro-HDMI is a smaller version of the HDMI connector you probably know from TVs and monitors. The Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI sockets along one edge; you connect a screen with a cable (or adapter) that has a small micro-HDMI plug on one end (for the Pi) and a standard full-size HDMI plug on the other (for your TV or monitor). Many starter kits include this cable. Raspberry Pi 5 — Port Layout (top view) Raspberry Pi 5 2–16 GB RAM USB-C Power HDMI0 (primary) HDMI1 (second) USB 3.0 USB 3.0 USB 2.0 USB 2.0 Ethernet (Gigabit) 40-pin GPIO microSD slot (underside) PWR button LEDs Connect your screen to HDMI0 (closest to the USB-C power port) for first boot. Figure 4.2 — Simplified top-view port layout of the Raspberry Pi 5. For first boot, plug your screen into HDMI0 (the socket closest to the USB-C power port). The microSD slot is on the underside (bottom edge). Insert the microSD card (gold contacts down) into the slot on the underside of the Pi if you have not already done so. Push until it clicks. Connect the micro-HDMI cable to your TV or monitor first (the standard HDMI end goes into the screen), then plug the small micro-HDMI end into the Pi. Use the port labelled HDMI0 — this is the socket closest to the USB-C power port. It is the primary display output and the one the Pi uses by default on first boot. Switch your TV or monitor on and select the correct HDMI input (often labelled HDMI 1 or HDMI 2 on your screen's remote — whichever socket you plugged the cable into). Plug in a USB keyboard into one of the larger USB ports (any of the four USB ports on the right side of the Pi will work). Plug in a USB mouse into another USB port. Optionally plug in an Ethernet cable from your home router into the Pi's Ethernet port (the socket that looks like a wide telephone jack, on the right edge). This gives you a wired internet connection — faster and more reliable than Wi-Fi, especially during the first big software update. Connect the USB-C power supply last. Plug the USB-C end into the power socket on the Pi, then plug the other end into the mains wall socket and switch the socket on. Careful: Always connect power last . Plugging in the power before connecting the display cable can cause the Pi to start up without detecting the screen, which may mean you see nothing on your TV or monitor. Note: Your Pi 5 does not have a 3.5 mm headphone jack. Sound comes out through the HDMI cable to your TV or monitor's built-in speakers, or through a USB audio adapter. If you need audio from a device without HDMI audio, a small USB audio adapter costs just a few pounds or euros and plugs into any USB port. Tip: Your Raspberry Pi 5 has a small physical power button on the board itself (next to the LED lights). Once the Pi is running, a brief press of this button will perform a clean, safe shutdown — much better than simply pulling the power cable. Understanding the LED Lights On the corner of the Raspberry Pi 5 board you will see two small indicator lights. They tell you at a glance what the Pi is doing. LED colour / state What it means Solid red Power is on and the voltage is good. This should stay on the whole time the Pi is running. Red light off No power reaching the board, or the power supply is not providing enough voltage. Check your cable and power adapter are fully connected. Green flashing The Pi is reading from or writing to the microSD card. This is completely normal during boot and whenever the system is busy. Green solid (not flashing) The Pi is running and currently idle — the microSD card is not being accessed at this moment. Green off entirely No SD card detected, or the card cannot be read. Check the card is fully inserted and the right way around. Careful: Never pull the power cable out while the green LED is flashing. The Pi is writing to the card at that moment, and cutting the power mid-write can corrupt the microSD card — meaning you would have to re-flash it from scratch. The First-Run Wizard The first time Raspberry Pi OS boots, it runs a short setup wizard called the Welcome to Raspberry Pi screen. This wizard walks you through a handful of important settings. Follow the steps on screen — here is what to expect at each stage. Note: The first boot takes longer than usual — typically 60 to 90 seconds. The screen may go dark briefly, the Pi may reboot itself once, and you may see lines of scrolling text. This is completely normal. Be patient and do not unplug anything. Country, language, and time zone: Select your country from the drop-down list. The language and time zone will fill in automatically. If you set the locale in Imager (Path B), these may already be correct — just confirm and click Next. Create user / set password: If you set a username and password in Imager, this step may be skipped or pre-filled. If not, enter a username and a strong password now. Write it down. You will need this password to install software, make system changes, and log in remotely. Set up screen: The wizard may ask whether there is a black border around your desktop. If you see a black frame around the edges of the picture, tick the box — this turns off "overscan" so the image fills your screen properly. Connect to Wi-Fi: A list of nearby Wi-Fi networks appears. Click your network name, type your Wi-Fi password, and click Next. If you entered Wi-Fi details in Imager, the Pi may already be connected — you will see a tick next to your network name. Choose browser: The wizard may ask which browser you want to use. Chromium (the default) is a good choice — it is fast and behaves very much like Google Chrome. Update software: The wizard will offer to check for and install updates. Click Next to allow this. It downloads the latest security patches and bug fixes. This step can take 10 to 15 minutes on a typical home broadband connection. Let it finish completely — do not touch anything. When updates are complete, click Restart . The Pi reboots and lands on the desktop — your Raspberry Pi is now fully set up. Careful: Do not unplug the power during the software update step. If the power is cut while the Pi is installing updates, it can leave the system in a broken, unbootable state. Wait until the Pi restarts on its own. Tip: If the first-run wizard does not appear and you see the desktop straight away, that is fine — it simply means the pre-installed image was already fully configured. You can still run updates manually (covered later in this chapter and in Chapter 5) and change any settings you like from the System Settings menu. What You See on the Desktop After the wizard completes and the Pi restarts, you will see the Raspberry Pi OS desktop . At the top is a panel (similar to the Windows taskbar) with a small raspberry logo on the left — this is the application menu, like the Start menu on Windows. To the right you will find icons for a file manager, a web browser, and a terminal window, followed by a Wi-Fi indicator, a Bluetooth icon, a speaker volume control, and a clock. The desktop itself shows a plain wallpaper by default. In Chapter 5 you will start exploring everything that is installed and how to make the desktop feel like home. For now, simply enjoy having a fully working computer in front of you. Running the First Update from the Terminal If the wizard's update step was skipped, or you simply want to make absolutely sure everything is fully up to date, you can run a manual update. You will use the Terminal — a text-based window where you type commands directly. In plain words: The Terminal (also called the command line or shell ) is a window where you type short text instructions to the computer. It can look old-fashioned at first, but it is the fastest and most reliable way to manage a Linux system. You do not need to memorise commands — just type them exactly as shown here. Open the Terminal by clicking the black rectangle icon in the taskbar near the top of the screen (it shows a small >_ symbol inside it), or by pressing Ctrl + Alt + T on your keyboard. When the Terminal opens, you will see a line of text ending with a $ symbol. This is the prompt — it means the Pi is ready for a command. Type the following line exactly, then press Enter: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y What each part of this command does: sudo — stands for "superuser do". It temporarily grants administrator permission for this one command. The first time you use sudo in a session, the Pi asks for your password. Type it and press Enter. You will not see the characters appear as you type — that is intentional security behaviour, not a fault. apt — the package manager: the Pi's built-in tool for finding, downloading, and installing software. update — tells apt to download the latest list of available software. This does not install anything yet; it just refreshes the catalogue so the next step knows what versions are available. && — means "and then, but only if the previous command succeeded". If the update check fails (for example, because there is no internet connection), the second part will not run, which prevents errors. sudo apt full-upgrade -y — actually downloads and installs all the waiting updates. full-upgrade is slightly smarter than plain upgrade : it can also replace older packages when needed, making it the safer choice. The -y flag automatically answers "yes" to any confirmation prompts so you do not have to babysit it. Once you press Enter and the command finishes (the $ prompt reappears), your Pi is fully up to date. Note: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (the version your Pi runs), the system Python is described as externally managed . This means you should not type pip install directly to add Python packages — it will refuse with an error message. Instead, install Python packages using sudo apt install python3-packagename , use the pre-installed Thonny editor's built-in package manager, or create a virtual environment. Chapter 8 explains all of this step by step. Shutting Down Safely Never simply pull the power cable out to turn off the Pi. Doing so while the operating system is running can corrupt the microSD card, potentially destroying your files and your installation. Always shut down properly. There are three easy ways to shut the Pi down: From the desktop menu: Click the raspberry logo in the top-left corner, then choose Shutdown from the menu, then Shutdown again in the confirmation box. The Pi will power off within a few seconds. From the Terminal: Type sudo shutdown now and press Enter. The Pi will shut down immediately. Using the power button: The Pi 5 has a small physical power button on the board. A brief single press will initiate a clean, safe shutdown — the same as using the menu. After the green LED goes off and stays off, it is safe to unplug the power cable. Careful: A long press (holding the power button for several seconds) forces an immediate hard shutdown — the equivalent of pulling the power cable. Only do this if the Pi has completely locked up and will not respond to any normal commands. Use the short press for everyday shutdowns. Headless Setup: Running the Pi Without a Monitor Sometimes you may want to use the Pi without a screen, keyboard, or mouse at all — perhaps tucking it away behind a TV or in a cupboard. This is called running the Pi headless . In plain words: Headless simply means the computer runs without a display attached — like a server tucked in a cupboard. You control it entirely from another computer using SSH (the remote connection we enabled in Imager). If you followed Path B and enabled SSH in Raspberry Pi Imager, and you entered your Wi-Fi details too, your Pi is already prepared for headless use. After it boots (which you can confirm after about 60 seconds by checking your router's connected-devices list for the Pi's hostname), you can connect to it from your main computer using the ssh command. Open a terminal — Terminal on macOS or Linux, or Windows Terminal / PowerShell on Windows (both come built into Windows) — and the ssh command works identically on all three. Full step-by-step instructions for SSH and headless access are in Chapter 9 . The key points to remember now are: SSH must be enabled in Imager before you write the card — or turned on later from the Pi's Preferences menu when you do have a screen attached. The Pi and your main computer must be on the same Wi-Fi or wired network. You connect using your Pi's hostname (for example raspberrypi.local ) or its IP address, which you can find in your router's device list. Tip: If you are not sure whether to go headless or use a monitor, start with a monitor for your very first boot. It is much easier to spot and fix problems when you can see what the Pi is doing. Once everything is working well, you can tuck the Pi away and switch to headless use any time. Troubleshooting Common First-Boot Problems Most first boots go smoothly, but here are the most common problems and how to solve them. Symptom Most likely cause What to try Screen stays black Wrong HDMI port, or TV on wrong input Make sure the cable is in HDMI0 (closest to the USB-C power port). Select the correct HDMI input on your TV using its remote. Check the cable is fully pushed in at both ends. Red LED on but no green LED — no boot microSD card not detected, missing, or incorrectly flashed Remove the card, check it is the right way around (gold contacts down), re-insert until it clicks. If still no green light, re-flash the card with Raspberry Pi Imager. Red LED off entirely Power supply not providing enough power, or loose connection Check both ends of the USB-C power cable are fully plugged in. Make sure you are using the official 27 W USB-C supply (or a good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one), not a typical phone charger. Try a different mains socket. Coloured square / rainbow square in top-right corner Under-voltage warning — the power supply is not giving enough current Use the official 27 W USB-C supply (or a good 5 V / 5 A USB-C PD one). Avoid long or thin USB-C cables. Do not plug too many power-hungry USB devices in at once. Pi boots but can't connect to Wi-Fi Wrong SSID or password entered in Imager, or wrong Wi-Fi country code Check your Wi-Fi name (SSID) and password are exactly correct (case-sensitive). Make sure the country code matches your country. Try connecting via the Wi-Fi icon in the desktop taskbar instead. First-run wizard does not appear Pre-installed image was already configured, or image is not from Imager This is normal — just proceed to the desktop. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y in the Terminal to get updates. Keyboard or mouse not responding USB device not recognised, or plugged into a non-working port Unplug and re-plug into a different USB port. Prefer the blue USB 3.0 ports. If using a wireless USB dongle, try plugging the dongle directly rather than through a hub. Choosing a Strong Password Your Pi will be connected to the internet, which means a weak password is a genuine security risk. Here is what "strong" actually means in practice: At least 12 characters long — the longer, the better. A mix of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols — for example: Sunny7!Harbour&Blue . Not a real word, name, or date — avoid raspberry , your name, or your birthday. Not re-used from another account — if this password is ever stolen, you do not want it to also unlock your email or bank. Written down somewhere safe — a physical notebook kept at home is perfectly fine. If you forget it, you will have to re-flash the card and start over. Careful: The old default Raspberry Pi password ( raspberry ) is publicly known and widely used by automated hacking tools that scan the internet. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm no longer allows a default password — you must create your own. Make it genuinely strong. Key terms microSD card — a tiny removable memory chip that acts as the Pi's hard drive, holding the operating system and all your files. Raspberry Pi OS — the official Linux-based operating system designed for Raspberry Pi computers, based on Debian 12 (codename Bookworm). Flashing — the process of copying an operating system image onto a microSD card, overwriting everything that was there before. Raspberry Pi Imager — the official free Windows/Mac/Linux tool used to write Raspberry Pi OS (or other operating systems) to a microSD card. Hostname — the name your Pi announces on your local network, used to find it without knowing its exact IP address (for example raspberrypi.local ). SSID — Service Set Identifier; the technical term for a Wi-Fi network's name (the name you see when searching for Wi-Fi on a phone or laptop). SSH (Secure Shell) — an encrypted method of remotely controlling your Pi from another computer using a text-based terminal, without needing a monitor connected to the Pi. Headless — running the Pi with no monitor, keyboard, or mouse connected; controlled entirely over the network from another computer. sudo — a command prefix that grants temporary administrator ("superuser") permission for a single terminal command. apt — the package manager for Raspberry Pi OS; the built-in tool used to install, update, and remove software packages. Locale — the region settings that tell the operating system your time zone and keyboard layout. micro-HDMI — the smaller HDMI connector format used on the Raspberry Pi 5; you use a micro-HDMI-to-HDMI cable or adapter (often included in starter kits) to connect it to a standard HDMI screen. HDMI0 — the primary display output socket on the Pi 5; it is the micro-HDMI port closest to the USB-C power socket, and the one to use for your first boot. Terminal — the text-based window on Raspberry Pi OS where you type commands directly; also called the command line or shell. Bookworm — the codename for Debian 12, which is the Linux foundation that the current version of Raspberry Pi OS is built on. Under-voltage — a warning state where the Pi is not receiving enough electrical power; shown by a rainbow-coloured square in the top-right corner of the screen. Chapter summary Your Pi can be started from a pre-loaded microSD card (Path A) or from a card you flash yourself using Raspberry Pi Imager on your main computer — Windows, macOS, or Linux (Path B) — both result in the same working system. Raspberry Pi Imager's Edit Settings panel lets you pre-configure hostname, username, password, Wi-Fi, locale, and SSH before writing the card — saving significant setup time and enabling headless use from day one. Always choose the 64-bit version of Raspberry Pi OS for the Raspberry Pi 5. Connect cables in order: display first, then keyboard and mouse, then network, and power last ; plug your screen into HDMI0 (the socket closest to the USB-C power port). The red LED confirms power is good; a flashing green LED means the microSD card is being accessed — never cut power while the green light is flashing. The first-run wizard sets your country, password, and Wi-Fi, then downloads updates — this is normal, can take 10–15 minutes, and must not be interrupted. Running sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y in the Terminal keeps your Pi fully up to date with the latest security fixes. Always shut down properly — via the menu, the Terminal ( sudo shutdown now ), or a brief press of the physical power button — never by pulling the power cable. Enabling SSH in Imager before writing prepares your Pi for headless (no-monitor) use; full details are in Chapter 9. Choose a strong, unique password of at least 12 characters — the old default raspberry password is publicly known and must never be used.

title: A Tour of the Desktop
headings: What You See When You First Log In
The System Tray: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Volume and More
Changing the Appearance and Desktop Background
Add / Remove Software: The Graphical App Store
Keeping Your Software Up to Date
How to Shut Down and Reboot — and Why It Matters
Exploring Safely: Good Habits from Day One
text: The moment you boot your Raspberry Pi 5 for the first time, you are greeted by a clean, friendly desktop that works much like Windows — but with its own personality and a few surprises. This chapter is your guided tour: we will walk every corner of the screen, open every important application, and leave you confident enough to explore on your own. What You See When You First Log In After the Raspberry Pi finishes starting up, you land on the Raspberry Pi OS desktop . At first glance it looks like any other computer — there is a background image, some icons, and a bar along the top. That bar is called the taskbar (sometimes called the "panel"), and it is the control centre for everything. In plain words: A desktop is just the main screen you see after your computer starts — the equivalent of a physical desk where you lay out your work. The taskbar is the strip of buttons and icons that gives you quick access to apps, settings, and the clock. Note: When you first boot a fresh Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm image, a setup wizard called the Welcome to Raspberry Pi assistant may appear. It will walk you through choosing your country, language, time zone, and a username and password. Complete this wizard before continuing — it sets up the most important personal settings in one go. If you skipped it or it did not appear, do not worry: we will cover all those settings manually in this chapter. A Map of the Desktop The diagram below labels every part of the default Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm desktop so you can follow along as we explore each section. 🍓 📁 🌐 ■ 📶 🔊 📱 14:32 Fri 19 Jun Raspberry Menu Quick-launch icons System tray (applets) Clock & calendar Window list — open windows appear here Open windows list D E S K T O P 🗑 Wastebasket Wastebasket Right-click the desktop for: • Desktop Preferences • Open Terminal Here • Open File Manager Here Desktop area The default Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm desktop. The taskbar runs across the top; the system tray and clock sit in the top-right corner. Right-clicking anywhere on the empty desktop reveals shortcut options. The Taskbar in Detail The taskbar runs across the very top of the screen. From left to right, you will find: The Raspberry Menu button — the small raspberry icon at the far left. Click it to open the main application menu. Quick-launch icons — small icons for the File Manager, Chromium browser, and Terminal sit right next to the menu button. One click and they open immediately. The window list area — the wide empty middle section. When you open an app, a button for it appears here so you can switch between open windows. Click a button to bring that window to the front; click it again to minimise it. The system tray — a cluster of small icons in the top-right corner for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, volume, and more. We will look at these shortly. The clock — at the very right, showing the time and date. Click it to see a small calendar. Tip: If you right-click any empty space on the taskbar, you get options to add or remove panels and applets, so you can customise what lives there over time. Managing Windows: Minimise, Maximise, Close Every open application window has three buttons in its top-right corner, just like on Windows: – (minus / dash) — minimises the window (hides it; it stays as a button in the window list area of the taskbar). □ (square) — maximises the window so it fills the whole screen. Click it again to restore it to its previous size. ✕ (cross) — closes the window. If you have unsaved work, the app will ask you to save first. You can also double-click the title bar of any window to maximise or restore it, and drag the title bar to move the window around the screen. The Raspberry Menu Click the raspberry icon (top-left) to open the main menu. This is your gateway to every installed application, organised into tidy categories. Menu Categories Explained Category What You Find There Examples Programming Tools for writing code Thonny (Python IDE), Scratch 3, Geany Internet Web and communication apps Chromium browser, Claws Mail Sound & Video Media players and audio tools VLC Media Player, Audacity (if installed) Graphics Image viewers and editors Image Viewer, LibreOffice Draw (if installed) Accessories Everyday utilities Text Editor, Calculator, Archive Manager Office Document, spreadsheet and presentation apps LibreOffice Writer, Calc, Impress (if installed) Preferences All system settings Raspberry Pi Configuration, Appearance, Screen Configuration Help Built-in documentation Raspberry Pi Help Note: The exact list of apps depends on which version of the Raspberry Pi OS image was pre-loaded on your microSD card. Some kits come with a "full" image that includes LibreOffice and extra tools; others use a lighter "desktop" image. If an app is missing, the section on Add/Remove Software later in this chapter shows you how to install it for free. At the bottom of the menu you will also see Shutdown — we will cover how to use that safely at the end of this chapter. The Bundled Applications Worth Knowing Let us take a closer look at the most useful programs that come pre-installed. Chromium Web Browser Chromium is the open-source version of Google Chrome. It looks and behaves almost identically — if you have used Chrome on Windows, you will feel right at home. You can sign in with your Google account to sync bookmarks, use extensions from the Chrome Web Store, and watch videos on YouTube. Find it in Internet → Chromium Web Browser , or click its icon on the taskbar. Tip: Chromium runs well on the Pi 5. The more RAM your Pi 5 has (it ships in 2, 4, 8, or 16 GB versions), the more browser tabs you can keep open at once without slowdown — something earlier Pis with less memory struggled with. Even on a smaller model, everyday browsing is comfortable. File Manager The File Manager (also called PCManFM) works like Windows Explorer. You can browse folders, copy and paste files, rename things, create new folders, and plug in a USB drive to see its contents. Find it in the taskbar quick-launch area or under Accessories → File Manager . Key points about the file system on your Pi: Your personal files live in your home folder . If your username is pi this is /home/pi ; if you chose a different name during setup (e.g. alice ), it is /home/alice . This is equivalent to C:\Users\YourName on Windows. The File Manager opens your home folder by default. The folder called / (just a forward slash, called "root") is the very top of the file system, like C:\ on Windows. USB drives and the microSD card appear automatically on the left side of the File Manager when you plug them in. Right-clicking a file or folder in the File Manager gives you options to copy, cut, paste, rename, delete, or check its properties — just like right-clicking in Windows Explorer. In plain words: On Linux (which Raspberry Pi OS is built on), file paths use forward slashes ( / ) instead of backslashes ( \ ) like on Windows. So a folder called "Documents" inside your home folder is written as /home/pi/Documents (or /home/alice/Documents if your username is alice). Tip: In the File Manager, press Ctrl+H to show hidden files and folders — those whose names start with a dot (such as .config ). These are system files and settings that are normally tucked out of sight to keep things tidy. Press Ctrl+H again to hide them. Text Editor Under Accessories → Text Editor you will find a simple editor similar to Notepad on Windows — perfect for jotting notes, editing configuration files, or looking at plain text. It does syntax highlighting (colour-coding) for many programming languages, which is handy when you start exploring code. Thonny Python IDE Thonny is found in Programming → Thonny . It is a beginner-friendly environment for writing Python programs. Chapter 10 covers Thonny in detail, but for now just know it is there and ready to use — no installation needed. In plain words: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is a program that helps you write, run, and fix code all in one place. Think of it as a very smart text editor that understands programming languages. Scratch 3 Found in Programming → Scratch 3 , Scratch is a visual programming environment where you build programs by snapping colourful blocks together — no typing required. It is wonderfully beginner-friendly and a great way to understand how programming logic works before moving to text-based languages like Python. It is used in schools worldwide and is just as fun for adults learning to code. LibreOffice (if present) If your image includes LibreOffice, you will find it under the Office menu. It contains: LibreOffice Writer — a full word processor, very similar to Microsoft Word. It can open and save .docx files. LibreOffice Calc — a spreadsheet program like Microsoft Excel. It can open and save .xlsx files. LibreOffice Impress — a presentation maker like Microsoft PowerPoint. It can open and save .pptx files. If LibreOffice is not installed, you can add it from Add/Remove Software (covered later in this chapter). Raspberry Pi Imager If you ever need to write a new operating system to a microSD card, Raspberry Pi Imager makes it easy. It may already be installed under Accessories → Imager . You choose an OS image from a built-in menu, select your card, and click Write — the tool does the rest. Chapter 3 covers this in full detail; it is mentioned here so you know where to find it. Terminal The Terminal is a text-only window where you type commands directly at the computer. It looks intimidating but is incredibly powerful once you are comfortable with it. On Bookworm it is called LXTerminal and lives in Accessories → Terminal , or you can click the black rectangle icon on the taskbar. You can also right-click anywhere on the empty desktop and choose Open Terminal Here to open a Terminal directly in the folder you were looking at. Chapter 7 is entirely dedicated to using the Terminal, so do not worry about it for now — just know where to find it. The System Tray: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Volume and More The cluster of small icons in the top-right corner of the taskbar is called the system tray . Each icon is called an applet — a tiny mini-program that controls one aspect of your system. In plain words: An applet is just a very small program that lives in the taskbar and lets you control one specific thing — like the volume or the Wi-Fi connection — with a single click. Wi-Fi Applet Click the network icon (it looks like signal-strength bars or a pair of computers) to see available Wi-Fi networks. Click your network name, type the password when prompted, and you are connected. Once connected, the icon shows your signal strength. If you are using a wired Ethernet cable instead of Wi-Fi, this applet shows two small rectangles (representing network plugs). Tip: The Pi 5 supports both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi. If your router offers both, pick the 5 GHz network for faster speeds — it will usually have "5G" or "5GHz" somewhere in its name. Bluetooth Applet Click the Bluetooth icon (a stylised "B" shape) to open the Bluetooth manager. From here you can pair a wireless keyboard, mouse, or headphones. Click Add Device , put your device into pairing mode (check its manual), and the Pi will find it automatically. Note: Remember that the Pi 5 has no headphone jack . If you want audio through speakers or headphones, you need either HDMI audio (your TV or monitor's built-in speakers), a USB audio adapter, or a Bluetooth speaker or headphones paired through this applet. Volume Applet Click the speaker icon to see a volume slider. Drag it left to go quieter, right to go louder. Right-click the same icon to choose which audio output device to use — for example, switching between HDMI audio and a USB speaker. Eject / Removable Media When you plug in a USB drive, an eject icon appears in the system tray. Always click this icon and choose "Eject" before unplugging a USB drive. This tells the Pi to finish writing any data before the drive is removed, preventing file corruption. Careful: Pulling out a USB drive without ejecting it first can corrupt the files on that drive — just like on Windows. Always eject first, then unplug. Software Update Notifications A small shield or update icon sometimes appears in the system tray to let you know that software updates are available. Click it to open a graphical update manager that lists what will be updated and lets you apply the changes with one click. Keeping your software up to date is important for security and stability, so do not dismiss these notifications — install the updates when you have a few spare minutes. Clock and Calendar Click the clock in the top-right corner to pop up a small calendar. You can scroll through months. The time is set automatically if you are connected to the internet (the Pi uses a service called NTP — Network Time Protocol — to sync with internet time servers). In plain words: NTP (Network Time Protocol) is an invisible background service that checks the correct time over the internet and keeps your computer's clock accurate. You never need to touch it. Preferences: Raspberry Pi Configuration Go to Raspberry Menu → Preferences → Raspberry Pi Configuration . This is the most important settings window on your Pi — a one-stop shop for tuning how the system works. It has five tabs. Let us go through each one. Note: Some changes in this window require a reboot to take effect. The Pi will tell you when that is necessary. System Tab This tab controls fundamental behaviour: Password — change the password for your user account. Do this early if you have not already. The default password on older images is well known and is a security risk on any network. Hostname — the name your Pi announces on the local network. Change it from the default raspberrypi to something personal like florians-pi (use only letters, numbers, and hyphens — no spaces). Boot — choose whether the Pi boots straight to the desktop (recommended for beginners) or to a command-line screen. Auto login — when enabled, the Pi skips the login screen and goes straight to the desktop. Convenient at home; turn it off if others can access the machine. Network at Boot — if ticked, the Pi waits for a network connection before finishing start-up. Useful if you have services that need the internet immediately. Splash screen — the decorative image shown during boot. You can turn it off to see the technical boot messages instead (useful when diagnosing problems). Tip: Changing your password is the single most important security step for a Pi on any network. Go to the System tab now and set a strong password you will remember. Display Tab Controls what appears on your screen: Headless Resolution — if you ever run the Pi without a monitor attached (called "headless"), this sets the virtual screen size used for remote desktop access. Underscan — on some older TVs, the edges of the screen are cut off or have a black border. Toggle this to fix it. Pixel Doubling — makes everything appear twice as large. Useful on very high-resolution monitors where text is tiny. Screen Blanking — if enabled, the screen turns off after a period of inactivity to save power. Disable it if you find your screen going black annoyingly. In plain words: Headless means running the Pi without a keyboard, mouse, or monitor connected directly — you control it entirely from another computer over the network. It is a common setup once you are more comfortable with the Pi. Interfaces Tab This tab switches on or off various technical connections. By default most are off to keep the system secure: Interface What It Does When to Enable SSH Lets you control the Pi remotely from another computer using a text terminal When you want to log in from your main computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux) without a keyboard on the Pi VNC Lets you see and control the Pi's full desktop from another computer When you want to use the Pi remotely with a graphical screen SPI A communication bus for certain electronics add-ons When connecting specific sensors or displays to the GPIO pins I2C Another communication bus for electronics add-ons When connecting I2C-compatible sensors (temperature, pressure, etc.) Serial Port Enables the hardware serial connection on GPIO pins When connecting GPS modules, Arduino boards, or similar devices 1-Wire A simple bus used mainly for temperature sensors When using a DS18B20 temperature sensor Remote GPIO Allows another computer to control the Pi's GPIO pins over the network Advanced use only Careful: Only enable SSH and VNC if you need them. Leaving unnecessary interfaces enabled widens the attack surface of your Pi, especially on a shared or public network. Enable them only after you have set a strong password. Performance Tab This tab lets you adjust how hard your Pi works: GPU Memory — how much RAM (in megabytes) is reserved for the graphics chip. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, graphics memory is largely managed automatically using a modern system called CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocation), so the default value of 128 MB works well for everyday use. You generally do not need to change this unless a specific application asks you to. Overlay File System — an advanced option that makes the microSD card read-only to protect it from corruption. Leave it off unless you have a specific reason. Fan — the Pi 5 has a connector for the Active Cooler's fan. This panel lets you choose between always-on, temperature-controlled (recommended), or off. Temperature-controlled is the default: the fan spins up when the chip gets warm and quietens down when it cools. In plain words: GPU stands for Graphics Processing Unit — the part of the chip that draws images on your screen. CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocation) is a behind-the-scenes technique that lets the system share RAM between the main processor and the graphics chip intelligently, rather than permanently reserving a fixed chunk for graphics. Localisation Tab This tab makes your Pi feel at home in your country: Locale — sets the language, number format, and date format. For the UK choose en_GB.UTF-8 ; for France choose fr_FR.UTF-8 ; for Germany de_DE.UTF-8 ; for Switzerland you can choose any of the four national languages. Timezone — sets the region and city for your local time. Pick the nearest city in your timezone (e.g. Europe/London , Europe/Paris , Europe/Zurich ). Keyboard — sets the keyboard layout. If your keyboard has different symbols than what appears on screen, this is what to change (e.g. gb for a UK keyboard, fr for a French AZERTY keyboard, de for a German QWERTZ keyboard). Wi-Fi Country — sets the radio regulations for Wi-Fi. Always set this to your country — using Wi-Fi channels not permitted locally is illegal in most jurisdictions. Tip: If you find that pressing Shift+2 gives you " instead of @ , or the @ and " keys are swapped, the keyboard layout is set wrong. Go to the Localisation tab and correct it immediately — it affects everything you type. Screen Configuration Tool Go to Raspberry Menu → Preferences → Screen Configuration . This tool opens a graphical editor that shows your physical monitors as rectangles. The Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI ports, so it can drive two separate monitors at once. With Screen Configuration you can: Drag the monitor rectangles to set which screen is "left" and which is "right" — matching your physical desk layout. Set the resolution and refresh rate for each screen. The Pi 5 supports up to 4K (3840 × 2160) at 60 frames per second on each port. Mirror or extend — "mirror" shows the same picture on both screens; "extend" gives you one large continuous desktop spread across both. Rotate a screen — useful if you mount a monitor in portrait orientation. After making changes, click Apply in the top-left corner of the Screen Configuration tool, then confirm the change within a few seconds (the tool reverts automatically if you do not confirm, so you cannot lock yourself into a broken display). Note: If you use only one monitor, plug the HDMI cable into the micro-HDMI port labelled HDMI0 — it is the one closest to the USB-C power socket. The Pi 5 defaults to HDMI0 as the primary display. Changing the Appearance and Desktop Background Go to Raspberry Menu → Preferences → Appearance Settings . This window has several tabs: Desktop — change the background image or colour. You can pick from the built-in images, or click the folder icon to choose any image file from your home folder. You can also set different backgrounds on each monitor if you have two screens. Menu Bar — change the colour and size of the taskbar, and the size of the icons in it. System — choose a theme (controls the colour of window borders, buttons, and menus). The built-in choices include light and dark variants. Defaults — a set of preset combinations of wallpaper, theme, and icon style. A quick way to give your desktop a completely different look. You can also right-click anywhere on the empty desktop and choose Desktop Preferences to jump straight to the background settings. Tip: You can use any JPEG or PNG image as your wallpaper. Download a photo you love in Chromium, save it to your Pictures folder (in your home folder), and set it as your wallpaper here. Add / Remove Software: The Graphical App Store Go to Raspberry Menu → Preferences → Add / Remove Software . This opens a window that works much like an app store — you can search for free software, tick what you want, and click OK to install it automatically. Behind the scenes it is using Debian's software archive, which contains tens of thousands of free and open-source programs. Everything is free of charge and safe to install from this source. Installing an App (Step by Step) Open Raspberry Menu → Preferences → Add / Remove Software . Type what you are looking for in the search box at the top (for example, type vlc to find the VLC media player). A list of matching programs appears. Read the short description next to each result to make sure you have the right one. Tick the checkbox next to the program you want. Click OK . You will be asked for your password. The Pi downloads and installs the software. This may take a minute or two, depending on the size of the program and your internet speed. Once done, the program appears in the appropriate menu category. It is ready to use immediately — no restart required. Note: To remove an app you no longer want, open Add / Remove Software, search for it, un-tick its checkbox, and click OK. This frees up space on your microSD card. Installing Software from the Terminal Power users often install software faster by typing a single command in the Terminal. The command tool that manages software on Raspberry Pi OS is called apt . Here is how to install VLC as an example: sudo apt update sudo apt update — Downloads the latest list of available software from Debian's servers on the internet. Think of it as refreshing the app store catalogue so the system knows about the newest versions. sudo means "run this as administrator" (short for "superuser do") — some commands need elevated permission to make system-level changes. You will be asked for your password. sudo apt install vlc sudo apt install vlc — Tells the package manager to download and install the program called vlc . The Pi will ask you to confirm by pressing Y then Enter. Replace vlc with the name of any program you want to install — for example, sudo apt install libreoffice to install the full LibreOffice suite. In plain words: sudo is like clicking "Run as Administrator" on Windows — it temporarily grants you the highest level of permission to make system-level changes. You will be asked for your password the first time you use it in a Terminal session. On subsequent commands in the same session it remembers for a few minutes. Careful: Only run sudo commands from a trustworthy source — the official Raspberry Pi documentation, this book, or a well-known tutorial site. A malicious sudo command has the power to make serious, hard-to-reverse changes to your system. Note: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, if you try to install a Python package by typing pip install something without any extra steps, you will see an error saying the environment is "externally managed". This is a protection to prevent accidentally breaking the system. For Python packages, use Thonny's built-in package manager, install them with sudo apt install python3-packagename , or use a virtual environment (Chapter 10 explains all of these). Keeping Your Software Up to Date Software updates bring security fixes, bug corrections, and new features. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, updates arrive in two ways: Graphically — a shield icon appears in the system tray when updates are ready. Click it and follow the prompts to apply them. From the Terminal — run the two commands below. Many guides combine them onto one line, but here they are shown separately so you can see exactly what each one does. sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade Line 1 — sudo apt update : Contacts the Debian software servers and downloads an up-to-date list of all available packages and their latest version numbers. This does not install anything yet — it just refreshes the catalogue. Line 2 — sudo apt upgrade : Compares your currently installed software against the catalogue just downloaded, then downloads and installs any newer versions it finds. You will be shown a list of what will be upgraded and asked to confirm with Y then Enter. Tip: Run these two commands every week or two. It is one of the best habits you can build. If the system suggests a reboot afterwards, do so to make sure all updates are fully active. How to Shut Down and Reboot — and Why It Matters This is one of the most important habits to build. Never just unplug the power cable to turn off the Pi. Raspberry Pi OS, like all Linux systems, constantly writes data to the microSD card in the background. If you cut the power mid-write, you can corrupt the file system — sometimes badly enough that the card will not boot. Careful: Unplugging the Pi while it is running is the most common cause of microSD card corruption for new users. Always shut down properly through the menu or with the power button first, then wait for the activity light to go out before unplugging. Shutting Down from the Menu Click the Raspberry Menu (top-left raspberry icon). Click Shutdown at the bottom of the menu. A small window appears with three buttons: Shutdown , Reboot , and Logout . Click Shutdown to turn the Pi off completely, or Reboot to restart it. Wait until the screen goes dark and the green activity light on the Pi stops flashing. Then — and only then — you can safely unplug the power. Shutting Down from the Terminal If you are already working in a Terminal window, you can shut down or reboot with a command. Run one or the other — not both at the same time: sudo shutdown now sudo shutdown now — Immediately begins a safe shutdown. The Pi saves everything, stops all running programs cleanly, and powers itself off. Wait for the green activity LED to go dark before removing power. sudo reboot sudo reboot — Cleanly restarts the Pi, as if you chose Reboot from the Raspberry Menu. Use this after installing updates or making configuration changes that require a restart. Using the Physical Power Button The Raspberry Pi 5 has a small physical button on the board (usually accessible through a small hole in the lid of your case). A single short press initiates a safe, clean shutdown — exactly the same as choosing Shutdown from the menu. This is the quickest and safest way to power off if your keyboard or mouse is not responding. Note: Holding the power button down for several seconds forces an immediate power cut without saving — only do this as a last resort if the Pi is completely frozen and will not respond to anything. Exploring Safely: Good Habits from Day One The desktop is yours to explore, and you really cannot break anything simply by opening apps and clicking menus. Here are a few habits that will keep your Pi healthy: Always shut down properly — never unplug the power mid-session. Keep software updated — security fixes and improvements arrive regularly. Run sudo apt update followed by sudo apt upgrade in the Terminal every week or two, or click the shield icon in the system tray when it appears. Set a strong password — do this in Raspberry Pi Configuration → System as soon as possible if you have not already. Eject USB drives before unplugging — use the system tray eject icon. Read error messages — the Pi usually tells you in plain language when something goes wrong. Do not just click OK without reading. Back up your microSD card — Chapter 13 covers this. A microSD card can wear out or get corrupted; a backup means you can be back up and running in minutes. Tip: If you accidentally delete something from the File Manager, open the Wastebasket — right-click the bin icon on the desktop and choose Open, or look for it in the File Manager's left-hand panel. Files deleted from the File Manager go there first, just like the Recycle Bin on Windows. Files deleted from the Terminal, however, are gone immediately — the Terminal has no wastebasket. Key terms Taskbar — the strip along the top of the screen containing the menu, quick-launch icons, window list, system tray applets, and clock. Applet — a tiny program embedded in the taskbar that controls one aspect of your system (Wi-Fi, volume, etc.). System tray — the cluster of small applet icons in the top-right corner of the taskbar. Raspberry Menu — the main application launcher, opened by clicking the raspberry icon at the top-left of the taskbar. Chromium — the open-source web browser included with Raspberry Pi OS, almost identical to Google Chrome. Thonny — a beginner-friendly Python programming environment pre-installed on the Pi. Scratch 3 — a visual, block-based programming environment great for learning coding concepts without typing code. LibreOffice — a free, open-source office suite compatible with Microsoft Office file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx). Terminal — a text-based window where you type commands directly at the system; covered in depth in Chapter 7. SSH — Secure Shell; a way to control the Pi remotely from another computer's terminal over a network. VNC — Virtual Network Computing; lets you see and control the full Pi desktop from another computer over a network. GPU — Graphics Processing Unit; the part of the chip that handles drawing images and video on your screen. CMA — Contiguous Memory Allocation; a modern technique used on Bookworm to share RAM flexibly between the processor and graphics chip. Locale — a setting that tells the system which language, number format, and date format to use. Headless — running the Pi without a directly connected keyboard, mouse, or monitor; controlled remotely over the network. apt — the command-line software manager for Debian/Raspberry Pi OS; used to install, update, and remove programs. sudo — a prefix for commands that need administrator-level permission; equivalent to "Run as Administrator" on Windows. NTP — Network Time Protocol; a background service that keeps your Pi's clock accurate by syncing with internet time servers. Shutdown — the safe process of stopping all software and powering off the Pi without corrupting data. Chapter summary The taskbar runs across the top of the screen and holds the Raspberry Menu, quick-launch icons, a window list, the system tray applets, and the clock. The Raspberry Menu organises all installed apps into categories: Programming, Internet, Sound & Video, Graphics, Accessories, Office, Preferences, and Help. Key bundled apps include Chromium (web browser), File Manager, Text Editor, Thonny (Python IDE), Scratch 3 (visual coding), and optionally LibreOffice. Right-clicking anywhere on the empty desktop reveals shortcuts to Desktop Preferences, Open Terminal Here, and Open File Manager Here. The system tray applets control Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, volume, removable media, and software update notifications — always eject USB drives before unplugging them. Raspberry Pi Configuration (Preferences menu) is a five-tab settings window covering System, Display, Interfaces, Performance, and Localisation — set your password and localisation settings there first. The Screen Configuration tool lets you arrange, resize, and configure up to two monitors connected to the Pi 5's dual micro-HDMI ports. Appearance Settings let you change the desktop background, taskbar colour, and window theme. Add / Remove Software is a graphical app store with tens of thousands of free programs; you can also install software with sudo apt install <name> in the Terminal. Keep software up to date by running sudo apt update then sudo apt upgrade every week or two, or by clicking the shield update icon in the system tray. Always shut down the Pi using the Raspberry Menu, the sudo shutdown now command, or the physical power button — never unplug the power cable during use, as this can corrupt the microSD card. Good habits — proper shutdown, regular updates, a strong password, and USB ejection — protect your Pi from the most common everyday problems.

title: The Terminal, Demystified
headings: What is the Terminal, and Why Should You Care?
Reading the Prompt — Every Part Explained
The Filesystem: a Single Tree Starting at /
Editing Files in the Terminal with nano
Pipes and grep — Connecting Commands Together
Working Smarter: Shortcuts That Save Typing
Putting it All Together: A Practice Session
Quick Reference: Commands at a Glance
text: The terminal is probably the most misunderstood tool on any computer — it looks like something from a 1970s science-fiction film, but once you spend ten minutes with it you will wonder how you ever managed without it. This chapter strips away the mystery, teaches you how to read every part of the screen, walks you through the commands you will use every single day, and shows you how to edit files and run commands with administrator privileges — everything you need to feel genuinely at home in the Linux command line. What is the Terminal, and Why Should You Care? When you use a normal desktop application, you point at things and click. Behind the scenes, the computer is still receiving text commands — the graphical interface just hides them from you. The terminal (sometimes called the command line or console ) lets you type those commands directly. There is no middleman. In plain words: A terminal is a window that accepts typed commands and shows their output as text. A shell is the program running inside that window — it reads what you type, runs it, and prints the result. Raspberry Pi OS uses a shell called Bash (Bourne Again SHell). Think of the terminal as the telephone handset, and Bash as the person answering at the other end. Why bother with it when there is already a desktop? Speed. A three-word command can do in one second what would take ten mouse-clicks. Power. Many tools — especially for programming, electronics, and servers — are only available from the command line. Precision. Commands do exactly what you say, every time, with no guessing. Automation. You can save a list of commands in a file and run them all at once. Remote control. You can control your Pi over the network without ever plugging in a keyboard or screen, using only text. Note: Nothing you type in the terminal can hurt your Pi's hardware. The worst that can happen with the commands in this chapter is deleting a file you did not mean to delete — which we will flag clearly and show you how to avoid. Opening the Terminal There are three easy ways to open a terminal window on Raspberry Pi OS: Look at the taskbar (the bar at the top of the screen). You will see a small black rectangle icon that looks like a screen — click it. A terminal window opens instantly. Click the Raspberry Pi menu (top-left corner, the raspberry icon) → Accessories → Terminal . Press the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + Alt + T — if nothing happens, use method 1 instead. A dark window appears with some text and a blinking cursor. Do not worry about what it says yet — we will read it carefully in the next section. Reading the Prompt — Every Part Explained Before you can type anything, the shell prints a prompt : a short line of text that tells you who you are, which machine you are on, and where you are in the file system. It looks something like this: pi@raspberrypi:~$ This is your prompt. It is made of four pieces joined together: pi — your username (the account you are logged in as). The default user on Raspberry Pi OS is pi , though you may have chosen a different name when you first set up the Pi. @ — just the "at" symbol, meaning "logged in at". raspberrypi — the hostname of the machine (its name on the network). You can change this in Settings. : — a colon separating the machine name from the current folder. ~ — a tilde symbol, which is a shortcut meaning "your home folder" (more on this in a moment). $ — the dollar sign signals "I am ready; type your command here." If you ever see a # instead, it means you are running as the all-powerful root administrator — proceed carefully. So the full prompt pi@raspberrypi:~$ means: "You are the user called pi, on the machine called raspberrypi, currently sitting in your home folder, and I am waiting for your command." pi @ raspberrypi : ~ $ █ username machine name current folder ready for input cursor Anatomy of the Bash prompt. Each coloured segment tells you something different about your current session. The Filesystem: a Single Tree Starting at / On Windows your files live on drives such as C:\ and D:\ . Linux (and therefore Raspberry Pi OS) works differently: there is exactly one big tree, and everything hangs off a single root. In plain words: The filesystem is the way your operating system organises files into folders. On Linux the entire structure is one big upside-down tree. The very top of that tree is called root and is written as a single forward slash: / . Every folder and every file on the system lives somewhere below that slash. The key folders you will encounter are: Folder path What lives there / The very top of the tree — "root". Every path starts here. /home Personal folders for all user accounts on the machine. /home/pi (or your username) Your personal home folder. This is where your documents, downloads, and projects live. Also written as ~ . /etc System-wide configuration files — Wi-Fi settings, user lists, service settings. /var "Variable" data: log files, print queues, emails — things that change while the system runs. /usr Installed programs and their shared files live here (think of it as the equivalent of C:\Program Files ). /tmp Temporary files. The system wipes this on every reboot — never save anything important here. /boot/firmware Files the Pi reads when it first powers on, including the kernel and configuration. Leave this alone unless a guide specifically tells you to edit something here. /dev Device files — the terminal, USB drives, the GPIO pins, etc. Everything on Linux is treated as a file, including hardware. /proc A virtual folder showing live information about running processes and hardware. Not real files — they are generated on the fly by the kernel. Here is a simplified picture of the tree: / /home /etc /usr /var /tmp /boot /home/pi (your files, ≈ ~) Documents Downloads /var/log (system logs) /boot/firmware (boot config) System folder Your home folder Sub-folder The Linux filesystem tree. Everything starts at / . Your personal files live under /home/pi , which is also written as ~ . The Anatomy of a Command Every command you type follows the same pattern: command -options argument(s) command — the name of the program you want to run (e.g. ls , cp , mkdir ). -options (also called flags ) — extra instructions that modify how the command behaves. They usually start with a hyphen and a single letter ( -l ) or two hyphens and a word ( --help ). They are optional. argument(s) — the thing(s) the command should act on: a filename, a folder path, some text. Also optional depending on the command. For example: ls -l /home/pi — the command is ls (list files), the option is -l (long format), and the argument is /home/pi (the folder to list). ls -l /home/pi command option / flag argument "list /home/pi in long format" Every Linux command follows the same three-part pattern: the command name, optional flags, and the thing to act on. Tip: Linux is case-sensitive . ls and LS are two different things. File names work the same way: Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files. Always type commands in lower case unless told otherwise. Your First Commands pwd — Where Am I? pwd stands for Print Working Directory . It answers the question "which folder am I currently in?" pwd pwd — prints the full path of the folder you are currently in. When you first open the terminal this will be your home folder, so the output will be something like /home/pi . ls — List What is in a Folder ls stands for list . It shows you the contents of a folder, just like opening a folder in the file manager but in text form. ls ls -l ls -a ls -lah ls — lists all visible files and folders in your current folder. Folders are usually shown in a different colour (blue by default). ls -l — long format. Shows one item per line with extra detail: permissions, owner, file size, and the date it was last changed. ls -a — shows all files, including hidden ones. Hidden files have names that start with a dot (e.g. .bashrc ). They are hidden by default to keep the home folder tidy. ls -lah — combines three flags at once: long format ( -l ), all files ( -a ), and human-readable file sizes ( -h , so you see "4.0K" instead of "4096"). You can combine most single-letter flags like this. In plain words: Permissions are rules that control who is allowed to read, change, or run a file. You will see a string like -rwxr-xr-x at the start of each line in ls -l output. For now, just know they exist — Chapter 8 covers them fully. cd — Change Directory (Move Between Folders) cd is how you "walk" through the filesystem tree. Think of it as double-clicking a folder, but in text form. cd Documents cd /home/pi/Downloads cd ~ cd .. cd - cd Documents — move into the Documents folder that is inside your current folder.
