Use sudo raspi-config to enable hardware interfaces (camera, SSH, SPI, I2C) that some software requires before it will work.

title: Getting Connected: Network & Remote Control
headings: Step Zero: Change Your Password First
How Your Home Network Fits Together
Remote Access Option A: SSH — Command Line
Remote Access Option B: Full Remote Desktop with VNC
Remote Access Option C: Raspberry Pi Connect — Access from Anywhere
Copying Files Between Your Computer and the Pi
Setting Up SSH Key Authentication (Optional, but Recommended)
Keeping Your Pi Secure on the Network
Changing or Checking Your Pi's Hostname
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 becomes far more powerful the moment it can talk to the rest of your home network — and even more so when you can control it from your main computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux) without ever touching a keyboard or mouse connected to the Pi. This chapter walks you through networking basics in plain words, shows you how to find your Pi on your home network, and then takes you step by step through four ways to reach your Pi remotely: a command-line connection, a full remote desktop, a cloud-based browser link, and file copying. The good news: the core tools ( ssh , scp , ping ) are built into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux and behave identically, so the steps work whatever computer you start from. Careful: Before you enable any form of remote access, change the default password on your Raspberry Pi. Anyone on your home network — or, with some tools, anyone on the internet — could log in using the factory default. We cover this right at the start. Step Zero: Change Your Password First If you set up your Pi using the Raspberry Pi Imager (covered in Chapter 3), you will have created a username and password during that process. If you did not, or if you are not sure, do the following before anything else in this chapter. Open a Terminal on your Pi (the black screen icon on the taskbar, or go to Applications > Accessories > Terminal ). Type the command below and press Enter : passwd This runs the passwd command, which lets you change the password for the account you are currently logged in to. It will ask for your current password first, then your new password twice. Nothing appears on screen as you type — that is completely normal. Choose a password that is at least 12 characters long and that you will remember. A short phrase with a number works well — for example BlueSky!Clouds7 . Tip: Write the new password down and keep it somewhere safe. If you forget it and cannot log in, recovering access is possible but inconvenient (it requires booting from the microSD card on another computer to reset it). Networking for Total Beginners Before we connect anything, let us understand what is actually happening when two devices talk to each other. What a home network is In plain words: A network is simply a group of devices that can send information to each other. Your home network is the collection of phones, laptops, smart TVs, and other gadgets all connected through your internet router. At the centre of your home network sits a router — the box your internet provider gave you, or one you bought yourself. The router acts like a post office: every device on your network has its own address, and the router makes sure messages get to the right place. In plain words: An IP address is the unique number that identifies a device on a network — just like a street address identifies a house. A typical home IP address looks like 192.168.1.42 . The numbers before the last dot ( 192.168.1 ) identify your local network; the last number ( 42 ) identifies the specific device. In plain words: A hostname is a human-friendly name for a device, so you do not have to remember its number. Your Raspberry Pi's default hostname is raspberrypi . You can change it in settings. How the Pi gets its address automatically (DHCP) In plain words: DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It sounds complicated, but it just means "the router automatically hands out IP addresses to every device that connects." You do not need to do anything — when your Pi connects to your network, the router gives it a free address automatically, usually within a few seconds. The downside of DHCP is that the router might give your Pi a different number the next time it restarts. This matters for remote access because you need to know the address to connect. We will look at how to deal with this later in this chapter. Wired Ethernet vs Wi-Fi Your Pi 5 has two ways to join your home network: Method Speed Reliability Setup needed Best for Wired Ethernet Up to 1,000 Mbps (Gigabit) Excellent — no interference Plug in a cable. Done. Desks near a router; servers; anything that needs a stable connection Wi-Fi Up to ~300–600 Mbps (dual-band 2.4 / 5 GHz) Good, but walls and distance reduce it Choose your network and enter the password Anywhere without a cable run; casual use Tip: If you are going to use your Pi as a server or for regular remote access, a wired Ethernet cable is strongly recommended. It is faster, does not drop out, and does not need you to enter a Wi-Fi password again if you move the Pi. Connecting via Ethernet Plug one end of a standard network cable (also called an RJ45 or Ethernet cable — any cheap one from a shop or online works) into the Ethernet port on the Pi 5, and the other end into any spare port on your router or a network switch. That is all. You should see a small green or amber LED on the Pi's Ethernet port light up within a few seconds, and the network icon in the Pi's taskbar will change to show a wired connection. In plain words: An Ethernet cable is the flat, rectangular-plugged cable you may have seen connecting computers to routers. The Pi 5's Ethernet socket gives you a full Gigabit connection — fast enough to stream video, copy large files, or run a home server with ease. Connecting via Wi-Fi Look at the top-right corner of the Pi desktop. Click the network icon (it looks like two small arrows or a fan shape). A list of available Wi-Fi networks appears. Click on your home network's name. A small box asks for the Pre Shared Key — this is your Wi-Fi password. Type it in and click OK . After a few seconds the icon changes to show signal bars, and the Pi is connected. Note: The Pi 5 supports both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi bands. If your router shows two network names (for example MyHome and MyHome_5G ), the 5 GHz one is faster but has a shorter range. Either will work fine for remote access. Connecting to Wi-Fi without a screen (headless) If your Pi has no monitor attached, you can still set up Wi-Fi by adding a configuration file to the microSD card before first boot. However, the easier method is to use Raspberry Pi Imager to pre-configure the Wi-Fi credentials when you write the OS to the card — this is covered in Chapter 3. If you already have the Pi running and just want to join a different network without a screen, use the command below in an SSH session (covered later in this chapter): sudo nmtui sudo — runs the command with administrator privileges. nmtui — opens NetworkManager's Text User Interface, a simple menu-driven tool for managing network connections. Use the arrow keys to navigate, select "Activate a connection", choose your Wi-Fi network, enter the password, and confirm. No mouse needed. How Your Home Network Fits Together The Internet Home Router e.g. 192.168.1.1 Ethernet Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi 5 hostname: raspberrypi IP: 192.168.1.42 raspberrypi.local Your computer Windows / macOS / Linux IP: 192.168.1.10 SSH / VNC / SFTP Figure 9-1: A typical home network. The router connects the Pi (via Ethernet cable) and your main computer (via Wi-Fi) and provides access to the internet. SSH, VNC, and file-copy tools let your computer talk directly to the Pi across this same local network — and they work the same whether that computer runs Windows, macOS, or Linux. Finding Your Pi's IP Address You need to know your Pi's IP address (or its hostname) before you can connect to it remotely. Here are three ways to find it, from easiest to most involved. Method 1: Ask the Pi directly (quickest) If you have a keyboard and screen connected to your Pi, open a Terminal and type: hostname -I This prints the IP address (or addresses) currently assigned to your Pi. The first number is almost always the one you want — it will look something like 192.168.1.42 . The capital letter -I is a flag meaning "show all IP addresses this machine has right now." You can also find what hostname the Pi is announcing on the network: hostname This prints the short hostname — by default raspberrypi . On a local network you can usually reach the Pi by typing raspberrypi.local instead of its number, thanks to a technology called mDNS (explained below). Method 2: The desktop network applet On the Pi desktop, hover your mouse over the network icon in the top-right corner of the taskbar and leave it there for a second. A small tooltip appears showing the current IP address. Alternatively, right-click the network icon and choose Connection Information to see full details including the IP address, network speed, and MAC address. Method 3: Check your router's device list Every router has an admin page you can open in any browser. The address is usually printed on a sticker on the bottom of your router — common ones are 192.168.1.1 , 192.168.0.1 , or 10.0.0.1 . Open that address in a browser on your main computer, log in (credentials are also on the sticker), and look for a section called "Connected Devices", "DHCP Clients", or "LAN Clients". Your Pi should appear there with its current address. Tip: Once you find your Pi in the router's device list, many routers let you reserve that IP address so the Pi always gets the same number. Look for a button labelled "Reserve", "Static DHCP", "DHCP Reservation", or "Lease Binding" next to your Pi's entry. Once reserved, the Pi will have the same address every time it restarts — so you never need to look it up again. The Magic of raspberrypi.local In plain words: mDNS (multicast DNS) is a trick that lets devices on a local network find each other by name — without needing a central server. On Raspberry Pi OS it is provided by a service called Avahi . It works out of the box on every modern computer: Windows 10 and 11 include built-in mDNS support, macOS has had it for years (Apple calls it Bonjour), and most Linux distributions ship Avahi too. What this means in practice: instead of typing ssh yourname@192.168.1.42 , you can type ssh yourname@raspberrypi.local and it just works — as long as both devices are on the same home network. The .local suffix tells your computer to look for the device by name on the local network rather than searching the internet. Note: If you renamed your Pi's hostname to, say, mypi , you would use mypi.local . To change the hostname, open Raspberry Pi Configuration (from the Applications menu > Preferences), go to the System tab, and edit the hostname field. Restart the Pi for the change to take effect. Note: On rare occasions, .local addresses do not work — for example, on some business or school networks. If you type raspberrypi.local and get an error saying "could not resolve host", simply use the Pi's numeric IP address instead (for example 192.168.1.42 ). Remote Access Option A: SSH — Command Line In plain words: SSH stands for Secure Shell. It is a way to open a text-based window on your Pi from another computer, so you can type commands as if you were sitting right in front of it. Everything is encrypted, so nobody can eavesdrop on what you type — even on a shared network. SSH is powerful because it is lightweight (works even on a slow connection), is built directly into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux with no extra software to install, and gives you full control over your Pi. Enabling SSH on the Pi If you set up your Pi with Raspberry Pi Imager and ticked "Enable SSH" in the advanced settings, SSH is already on and you can skip to the next section. If you are not sure, you can enable it in one of two ways. Using the graphical configuration tool (easiest): Click the raspberry icon (top left) to open the Applications menu. Go to Preferences > Raspberry Pi Configuration . Click the Interfaces tab. Next to SSH , click Enable . Click OK . SSH is now active and will start automatically on every boot. Using the terminal (also works if you are already connected via SSH): sudo systemctl enable --now ssh sudo — runs the command with administrator ("superuser") privileges, which is required for changing system services. systemctl enable — tells the system to start the SSH service automatically every time the Pi boots up. --now — also starts it immediately right now, without needing a reboot. ssh — the name of the SSH service on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm (provided by the openssh-server package, which is pre-installed). Using raspi-config (useful if you have no display — for example, connecting to a brand-new Pi via serial cable): sudo raspi-config nonint do_ssh 0 sudo raspi-config — runs the Raspberry Pi configuration tool with administrator rights. nonint — tells raspi-config to run without an interactive menu (just carry out the instruction and exit). do_ssh 0 — enables SSH. (The 0 means "on"; 1 would mean "off".) Tip: You can also enable SSH permanently before first boot by placing a file called ssh (no extension, empty) in the bootfs partition of the microSD card when it is inserted into your main computer. The Raspberry Pi Imager does this automatically when you tick "Enable SSH" — so for most people, this is already done. Connecting from your computer Every modern computer already includes a built-in SSH client — you do not need to install anything extra. The command itself is identical everywhere; only how you open a terminal differs: Windows 10/11: press Windows key + X and click Windows Terminal — or search for "Terminal" or "PowerShell" in the Start menu and open it. macOS: open Terminal from Applications > Utilities (or search for it with Cmd + Space ). Linux: open your distribution's Terminal application (often Ctrl + Alt + T ). Open a terminal on your main computer using the method above for your operating system. Type the following, replacing yourusername with the username you set up on the Pi: ssh yourusername@raspberrypi.local ssh — the command that starts a Secure Shell connection. yourusername — the account name on the Pi you want to log in to. This is the username you created in Raspberry Pi Imager (commonly something like pi or your own first name). @raspberrypi.local — the address of your Pi on the local network. Replace raspberrypi with your Pi's hostname if you changed it. If the .local address does not work, use the Pi's numeric IP address instead (for example ssh yourusername@192.168.1.42 ). The first time you connect, you will see a message like this: The authenticity of host 'raspberrypi.local (192.168.1.42)' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:AbCdEfGhIjKlMnOpQrStUvWxYz1234567890abcdef. Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? This is a one-time security check. Your computer is saying: "I have never talked to this device before. Here is its unique identity fingerprint. Do you trust it?" On your home network where you know the Pi is yours, it is safe to type yes and press Enter. Your computer saves this fingerprint and will not ask again next time. Type yes and press Enter . You will be asked for your Pi's password. Type it (nothing appears on screen as you type — that is normal) and press Enter . You are now logged in to your Pi remotely. The prompt changes to show the Pi's hostname — for example yourusername@raspberrypi:~ $ . Any command you type now runs on the Pi, not on your own computer. Careful: If you ever see the "authenticity" fingerprint warning on a connection you have made before (and you have not replaced or re-flashed the Pi), stop. This could indicate that something unexpected is happening on your network. Type no and investigate before proceeding. Useful things to try once connected via SSH ls pwd df -h sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y exit ls — lists the files and folders in the current directory on the Pi (short for "list"). pwd — shows the full path of the folder you are currently in. The letters stand for "Print Working Directory". After logging in you are normally in /home/yourusername . df -h — shows how much storage space is used and free on your Pi's microSD card. The -h flag makes the numbers human-readable (showing GB instead of raw bytes). sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y — fetches the latest list of available software updates ( update ), then installs all available updates without asking you to confirm each one ( upgrade -y ). The && means "only run the second command if the first one succeeded." exit — closes the SSH session and returns you to your computer's own terminal. SSH connection diagram Your computer Windows / macOS / Linux ssh user@raspberrypi.local encrypted SSH tunnel Router local network Raspberry Pi 5 SSH server (port 22) runs your commands All traffic is encrypted end-to-end on port 22 Figure 9-2: How SSH works. Your computer sends an encrypted connection request through the router to the Pi. The Pi's SSH server listens on port 22 and responds. Every command you type and every result you receive travels inside this encrypted tunnel. Remote Access Option B: Full Remote Desktop with VNC In plain words: VNC (Virtual Network Computing) lets you see and control the Pi's full graphical desktop from your main computer — icons, windows, menus and all. Instead of just a text prompt, you get the complete visual experience, as if you had a second screen and mouse plugged directly into the Pi. How VNC changed in Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm There is something important to know about VNC on Bookworm: the older version of Raspberry Pi OS came with RealVNC's server pre-installed. Bookworm moved to a newer display system called Wayland , and with it a new VNC server called wayvnc . This is what you get when you enable VNC through the graphical configuration tool. In plain words: Wayland is the modern system that draws the desktop (windows, icons, menus) on screen. It replaces the older "X11" system. You do not need to understand it deeply — just know that Bookworm uses Wayland by default, and the VNC server that goes with it is called wayvnc . Enabling VNC on the Pi Using the graphical configuration tool (recommended): Open Preferences > Raspberry Pi Configuration from the Applications menu. Click the Interfaces tab. Next to VNC , click Enable . Click OK . The wayvnc service starts automatically and will do so on every boot. Or from the terminal: sudo systemctl enable --now wayvnc sudo systemctl enable — configures the wayvnc service to start automatically at login. --now — also starts it immediately without requiring a restart. wayvnc — the name of the VNC server for Wayland, which is the display system used by Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. Note: wayvnc only runs while someone is logged in to the Pi's desktop session. This is fine for most home uses. If you need VNC access on a Pi that is not logged in (a so-called "headless" server), Raspberry Pi Connect (Option C below) is a better choice. Connecting with RealVNC Viewer You need a VNC viewer on your main computer. The official free option — RealVNC Viewer — is compatible with wayvnc , is simple to use, and is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux: On your main computer, open a browser and go to realvnc.com/en/connect/download/viewer/ . Download the free VNC Viewer for your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux) and install it. Open VNC Viewer. In the address bar at the top, type raspberrypi.local (or the Pi's numeric IP address if .local does not work) and press Enter . You will be asked for a username and password — use the same credentials you use to log in to the Pi desktop. The Pi's full desktop appears in a window on your computer. You can use it just as if you were sitting in front of it — click, type, open applications, everything. Tip: In VNC Viewer you can press F8 to open a menu with options to send special key combinations (like Ctrl+Alt+Del) to the Pi, change the screen quality, or go full screen so the Pi desktop fills your entire display. Note: VNC works best on your local home network. If you want to access your Pi from outside your home (from work or a coffee shop, for example), using Raspberry Pi Connect (Option C below) is much easier and more secure than trying to configure VNC over the internet. Remote Access Option C: Raspberry Pi Connect — Access from Anywhere Raspberry Pi Connect is an official service from the Raspberry Pi Foundation. It lets you see and control your Pi's desktop — or open a terminal window — from any web browser, anywhere in the world, without any complicated network setup or router changes. It works through a secure relay server, so you do not need to know your home router's address or configure anything. Note: Raspberry Pi Connect requires a free account at connect.raspberrypi.com and an internet connection on both the Pi and the device you are controlling from. It is free for personal use. Setting up Raspberry Pi Connect On your Pi, open a Terminal and install Raspberry Pi Connect: sudo apt update sudo apt install -y rpi-connect sudo apt update — refreshes the Pi's list of available software packages from the internet. sudo apt install -y rpi-connect — downloads and installs the Raspberry Pi Connect software. The -y flag means "yes to all questions", so the installation runs without stopping to ask you to confirm. Start the Connect service so it runs automatically when you log in: systemctl --user enable --now rpi-connect systemctl --user — manages services that belong to your user account (not system-wide services). enable — tells the system to start this service automatically every time you log in to the Pi. --now — also starts it immediately right now, without needing to log out and back in. Link your Pi to your Raspberry Pi account: rpi-connect signin This command prints a short URL in the terminal. Open that URL in any web browser — either on the Pi itself or on your main computer. Log in to your Raspberry Pi account (or create a free one if you do not have one yet). Once you do, your Pi will be securely linked to your account. On your main computer (or any device with a browser), go to connect.raspberrypi.com , sign in, and you will see your Pi listed. Click Connect , then choose: Screen sharing — to see and control the full Pi desktop in your browser. Remote shell — to open a terminal window in your browser (like SSH but without any software to install). Tip: Raspberry Pi Connect is the easiest remote-access option for most beginners. It does not require any router changes, works even on restrictive hotel or school networks, and only takes a few minutes to set up. If you only need a terminal (not the full desktop), the "Remote shell" option is especially lightweight. Checking whether rpi-connect is running rpi-connect status This shows whether Raspberry Pi Connect is running and whether your Pi is signed in and visible at connect.raspberrypi.com . If it shows "not signed in", run rpi-connect signin again and follow the URL it gives you. Copying Files Between Your Computer and the Pi Once you can connect remotely, you will often want to move files between your main computer and the Pi — perhaps to copy a photo from the Pi, or to send a script you wrote on your computer across to run on the Pi. Here are two practical ways to do this: a command-line tool that works the same on every operating system, and a graphical drag-and-drop option (with a recommended app for whichever OS you use). Method 1: scp — Secure Copy (command line) In plain words: scp is like copying a file on your computer, but over an SSH connection to another machine. It uses the same security as SSH, and it is already built into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux — no extra software needed. Open a terminal on your main computer (Windows Terminal or PowerShell on Windows; Terminal on macOS or Linux). The scp command is the same everywhere — only the way you write the local file path differs (Windows uses paths like C:\Users\YourName\Pictures , while macOS and Linux use paths like /Users/yourname/Pictures or /home/yourname/Pictures ). To copy a file FROM your Pi TO your computer (Windows path shown; on macOS/Linux use a path like ~/Pictures/photo.jpg ): scp yourusername@raspberrypi.local:/home/yourusername/photo.jpg C:\Users\YourName\Pictures\photo.jpg scp — the secure copy command. yourusername@raspberrypi.local: — connect to the Pi as this user. The colon at the very end separates the machine address from the file path on the Pi. /home/yourusername/photo.jpg — the full path to the file on the Pi you want to copy. Replace yourusername with your actual username on the Pi. C:\Users\YourName\Pictures\photo.jpg — where to save the file on your computer. On Windows, replace YourName with your Windows username; on macOS or Linux, use a path such as ~/Pictures/photo.jpg instead. To copy a file FROM your computer TO the Pi: scp C:\Users\YourName\Documents\script.py yourusername@raspberrypi.local:/home/yourusername/ The source and destination are simply swapped compared to the previous example. Here the file script.py on your computer is copied to the home folder on the Pi. On macOS or Linux, the source would be a path like ~/Documents/script.py . The trailing / after the remote path means "put it inside this folder, keeping the same filename." To copy an entire folder and everything inside it: scp -r yourusername@raspberrypi.local:/home/yourusername/myproject C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\ -r — the "recursive" flag, which tells scp to copy a folder and everything inside it (all files and sub-folders). Without this flag, scp cannot copy folders — only individual files. myproject — the name of the folder on the Pi to copy. C:\Users\YourName\Desktop\ — the destination on your computer; on Windows the folder will appear on your Desktop. On macOS or Linux, use a path such as ~/Desktop/ instead. Method 2: A graphical drag-and-drop file browser (SFTP) If you prefer to drag and drop files rather than type commands, a graphical SFTP program gives you a two-panel file browser — your computer on one side, your Pi on the other — so you can drag files between them just like in your normal file manager. There is a free option for every operating system: Windows: WinSCP (from winscp.net ) — a classic two-panel transfer tool. macOS: Cyberduck (from cyberduck.io ), or connect directly in Finder via Go > Connect to Server . Linux: your file manager (Files/Nautilus, Dolphin, and others) can usually open an SFTP location directly — look for "Connect to Server" or type sftp://raspberrypi.local in the address bar. FileZilla is a cross-platform alternative that also runs on Windows and macOS. In plain words: SFTP stands for SSH File Transfer Protocol. It is a secure way to browse and copy files over an SSH connection — and it works on every operating system. All the tools above use SFTP under the hood. Note: SFTP is completely different from the old "FTP" protocol — it is encrypted and safe. The steps are the same idea in any of these tools. Using WinSCP on Windows as the example: On your computer, download and install your chosen tool (WinSCP from winscp.net , Cyberduck from cyberduck.io , or FileZilla from filezilla-project.org ). Open it and start a new connection. Fill in: File protocol: SFTP Host name: raspberrypi.local (or the Pi's IP address) User name: your Pi username Password: your Pi password Click Login (or Connect). If you see a fingerprint prompt (similar to SSH), accept it — it is safe on your home network. Two panels appear side by side. Navigate to any folder on either side and drag files across to copy them. You can also right-click to rename, delete, or create new folders. Tip: These tools can save your login details so you do not have to type them each time. Look for a "Save" or bookmark option in the connection window. You can also choose to remember the password if you are the only person who uses your computer. Setting Up SSH Key Authentication (Optional, but Recommended) Every time you connect via SSH or SFTP, you currently have to type your password. SSH keys are a more convenient and more secure alternative: your computer holds a secret "key" file, and the Pi holds the matching "lock". When you connect, the two match automatically and you are let in — no password typing needed. The ssh-keygen tool used here is built into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux alike. Note: This section is optional. If you find typing the password tedious, or if you want to be able to automate tasks between your computer and your Pi, follow these steps. If you are happy typing the password, skip to the next section. Step 1: Generate an SSH key pair on your computer Open a terminal on your main computer (Windows Terminal or PowerShell on Windows; Terminal on macOS or Linux) and type: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "pi-access" ssh-keygen — the tool that creates an SSH key pair (a private key that stays on your computer, and a public key that goes to the Pi). -t ed25519 — specifies the type of key to create. ed25519 is a modern, compact, and very secure type. It is strongly preferred over the older rsa type. -C "pi-access" — a comment that labels this key. You can put anything here — it is just for your own reference, like a name tag on the key. When asked where to save the key, press Enter to accept the default location (on Windows that is C:\Users\YourName\.ssh\id_ed25519 ; on macOS or Linux it is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ). When asked for a passphrase, you can press Enter twice to leave it empty (for convenience) or set a passphrase for extra security. Step 2: Copy the public key to your Pi On Windows , still in Windows Terminal (PowerShell), run: type $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub | ssh yourusername@raspberrypi.local "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys" type $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub — reads your public key file from your Windows PC. | ssh yourusername@raspberrypi.local "..." — sends (pipes) that content over SSH to the Pi, where the quoted commands run on the Pi. mkdir -p ~/.ssh — creates the .ssh folder in your Pi home directory if it does not already exist. The -p flag means "no error if it already exists". cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — appends the public key to the Pi's list of trusted keys ( authorized_keys ). The >> means "add to the end" rather than overwriting anything already there. chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — sets the permissions on that file so only your user account can read it. SSH refuses to use the file if the permissions are too open. On macOS or Linux , there is an even simpler built-in helper. In your Terminal, run: ssh-copy-id yourusername@raspberrypi.local ssh-copy-id — a small tool included on macOS and Linux that automatically copies your public key into the Pi's authorized_keys file and sets the correct permissions for you — doing in one step what the longer Windows command above does manually. You will be asked for your Pi password this one last time. After this, SSH will use your key instead. Step 3: Test it ssh yourusername@raspberrypi.local Run the usual SSH command. If everything worked, you will be logged in immediately without being asked for a password. If you set a passphrase on your key in Step 1, you will be asked for that passphrase instead — which is shorter and faster than the Pi password and never travels over the network. Careful: Keep your private key file ( id_ed25519 , without the .pub ) safe. Anyone who has that file can log in to your Pi without a password. Do not email it or put it in a shared folder. Keeping Your Pi Secure on the Network Enabling remote access is powerful but does carry some responsibility. Here is a short checklist of good habits: Use a strong, unique password. Not the default. Not your birthday. A phrase or a random string of at least 12 characters. Keep software updated. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y regularly (or set a monthly reminder) to get security fixes. Only enable what you need. If you are not using VNC, leave it off. Fewer open services mean fewer potential entry points. Prefer Raspberry Pi Connect over opening ports. If you want to reach your Pi from outside your home, Raspberry Pi Connect is much safer than configuring your router to forward ports to the internet. Port-forwarded SSH and VNC are regularly scanned and attacked by automated bots. Raspberry Pi Connect avoids this entirely. Consider SSH key authentication. Setting up SSH keys (explained above) means no password is sent over the network at all. This is the gold standard for SSH security. There is no firewall to configure. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm does not include a firewall turned on by default, and on a home network behind your router's NAT (which blocks unsolicited incoming connections from the internet), this is fine for most users. Your router is your first line of defence. Note: On your home network, behind your router, your Pi is not directly reachable from the internet unless you deliberately configure your router to allow it. SSH and VNC connections on your local network are private to your home. Changing or Checking Your Pi's Hostname If you have more than one Raspberry Pi on the same network, they cannot both be called raspberrypi — the .local addresses would clash. Here is how to give each Pi a unique name. sudo hostnamectl set-hostname mypi5 sudo hostnamectl — the tool for reading and changing the system's hostname, run with administrator rights. set-hostname mypi5 — sets the hostname to mypi5 . Replace mypi5 with any name you like — use only letters, numbers, and hyphens; no spaces or special characters. After a reboot your Pi will be reachable at mypi5.local . Note: You can also change the hostname graphically via Preferences > Raspberry Pi Configuration > System > Hostname . Either method requires a restart for the change to take full effect. Quick-Reference: All Connection Methods Method What you get Works from outside home? Extra software on PC? Difficulty SSH (built-in) Text command line Only with port forwarding (not recommended) None — built into Windows 10/11, macOS, Linux Easy VNC (wayvnc + RealVNC Viewer) Full graphical desktop Only with port forwarding (not recommended) Free RealVNC Viewer (Windows/macOS/Linux) Easy Raspberry Pi Connect Desktop or terminal, in any browser Yes — works anywhere in the world None — just a web browser Very easy scp (file copy) Copy individual files or folders Only with port forwarding (not recommended) None — built into Windows 10/11, macOS, Linux Moderate SFTP (graphical file transfer) Graphical two-panel file browser Only with port forwarding (not recommended) Free app: WinSCP (Windows), Cyberduck (macOS), FileZilla (any OS) Easy SSH keys (optional) Password-free SSH login Only with port forwarding (not recommended) None — built into Windows 10/11, macOS, Linux Moderate one-time setup Tip: For most beginners, the recommended combination is: Raspberry Pi Connect for remote desktop access (especially from outside your home), and a graphical SFTP app for moving files (WinSCP on Windows, Cyberduck on macOS, or FileZilla on any OS). All are free, graphical, and require no ongoing command-line knowledge after the initial setup. Use SSH when you need to run quick commands or update the system. Key terms Network — a group of devices connected so they can share information. Router — the box that connects your home devices to each other and to the internet; acts like a post office, directing traffic to the right address. IP address — a unique number that identifies a device on a network, like a street address (e.g. 192.168.1.42 ). Hostname — a human-readable name for a device (e.g. raspberrypi ). DHCP — the system by which a router automatically hands out IP addresses to devices when they connect. DHCP reservation — a router setting that ensures a specific device always receives the same IP address. mDNS — a technology that lets devices on a local network find each other by name, enabling convenient .local addresses like raspberrypi.local . SSH (Secure Shell) — a secure, encrypted way to run command-line instructions on a remote computer over a network. SSH key pair — a matched pair of files (a private key and a public key) that allow password-free SSH login; the private key stays on your computer, the public key goes to the Pi. Wayland — the modern system that draws the graphical desktop on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, replacing the older X11 system. VNC (Virtual Network Computing) — a system for viewing and controlling another computer's full graphical desktop remotely. wayvnc — the VNC server built for Wayland, used by Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm when you enable VNC. Raspberry Pi Connect — an official, free service from the Raspberry Pi Foundation that lets you access your Pi's desktop or a terminal from any web browser, anywhere in the world. scp — Secure Copy; a command-line tool for copying files securely over an SSH connection. SFTP — SSH File Transfer Protocol; a secure way to browse and transfer files, used by graphical tools like WinSCP (Windows), Cyberduck (macOS), and FileZilla (any OS). Fingerprint (SSH) — a unique code that identifies a device; checked the first time you connect via SSH to confirm you are talking to the right machine. Port forwarding — a router setting that lets external internet traffic reach a specific device inside your home network. Useful but carries security risks if not set up carefully. NAT — Network Address Translation; the mechanism your router uses to share a single internet address among all your home devices. It also acts as an automatic barrier against most unsolicited connections from the internet. Chapter summary Always change your Pi's password before enabling any remote access — the default is not safe. Your Pi joins your home network automatically via Ethernet (plug in a cable) or Wi-Fi (choose a network and enter the password); the router assigns an IP address automatically through DHCP. Find your Pi's current IP address with hostname -I on the Pi, by hovering over the desktop network icon, or by checking the router's admin page. You can usually reach your Pi by the convenient name raspberrypi.local instead of memorising its number, thanks to mDNS — this works on Windows 10/11, macOS (Bonjour), and Linux with no extra software. Use DHCP reservation in your router's settings to give your Pi a permanent, fixed address so it never changes. SSH (built into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux) gives you a secure encrypted command-line connection to your Pi from a terminal — type ssh username@raspberrypi.local . VNC (using wayvnc on Bookworm, plus the free RealVNC Viewer for Windows, macOS, or Linux) lets you see and control the full Pi desktop remotely over your home network. Raspberry Pi Connect is the easiest remote-access option — it works from any web browser, anywhere in the world, without changing router settings, and only needs a free Raspberry Pi account. Copy individual files with the command-line scp tool (already built into Windows 10/11, macOS, and Linux), or use a free graphical SFTP app (WinSCP on Windows, Cyberduck on macOS, FileZilla on any OS) for drag-and-drop file transfers. SSH key authentication lets you log in to the Pi without typing a password every time — more convenient and more secure than passwords. For accessing your Pi from outside your home without complexity or security risk, Raspberry Pi Connect is the recommended choice for beginners.

title: Storage, Backups & Booting from an SSD
headings: Understanding How the Pi Stores Its Data
Checking How Much Space You Have
Using USB Drives and External Hard Drives
Backing Up Your Pi — Why It Matters
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 keeps everything it knows — the operating system, your files, your programs — on a small microSD card that slips into a slot on the underside of the board. In this chapter you will learn how to look after that card, make regular backups so you never lose your work, connect extra drives, and eventually upgrade to a much faster solid-state drive so your Pi feels like a completely different machine. Understanding How the Pi Stores Its Data Every computer needs somewhere to keep its files permanently — even when the power is off. On a laptop that is usually a built-in hard drive or SSD. On a Raspberry Pi 5, the default storage is a microSD card : the same type of tiny card you might use in a camera or smartphone. In plain words: "Storage" means the place your computer writes files to keep them safe long-term — just like a filing cabinet. "Memory" (RAM) is different: it is the scratchpad the computer uses while it is working, and it empties itself the moment you switch off. Your microSD card is storage; the RAM inside your Pi 5 (the Pi 5 comes in 2, 4, 8, or 16 GB versions) is memory. The microSD card works perfectly well for everyday use, but it has two important weaknesses you should know about from the start: Wear. Every time data is written to a microSD card, a tiny part of it wears out. Most cards are rated for a limited number of write cycles. A Pi that is running a busy project — writing logs, updating files, running a web server — can wear out a cheap card faster than you might expect. Corruption on sudden power loss. If the Pi is writing a file at the exact moment the power is cut, that file (and sometimes nearby parts of the filesystem) can become scrambled and unreadable. This is called filesystem corruption . In plain words: The "filesystem" is the system of rules and structures that keeps your files organised on a storage device — like the tabs and dividers inside a filing cabinet. When corruption strikes, it is as if someone spilt water on the cabinet and the labels dissolved. Careful: Never pull the power lead out of your Pi without shutting it down first. Always use the shutdown option from the desktop menu or the command line. This is the single most important habit to protect your data. Always Shut Down Properly To shut down from the desktop, click the Raspberry Pi menu (top-left), then choose Logout → Shutdown . Wait until the screen goes dark and the green activity light on the board stops blinking before you unplug anything. To shut down from the terminal (the black command-line window), type: sudo shutdown now sudo — short for "superuser do". It runs the command with administrator privileges, which is required for system-level actions like shutting down. shutdown now — tells the Pi to shut itself down immediately, saving all open files first. The word now means do it straight away, with no delay. You will see a few lines of text scroll past, and then the Pi will halt safely. The green activity light will stop blinking. Only then should you disconnect power. Tip: Your Pi 5 has a small physical power button on the corner of the board. A quick single press triggers a clean shutdown — just like choosing Shutdown from the menu. This is very handy if the button is accessible through your case. Checking How Much Space You Have Before you start downloading things or installing programs, it is good practice to check how much free space remains on your card. The command for this is df , which stands for disk free . df -h df — the disk-free command; it shows how much space each storage device is using and how much is left. -h — stands for "human-readable". Without this flag the numbers are shown in raw blocks of bytes, which is hard to read. With -h you see figures in megabytes (MB) and gigabytes (GB) instead. The output will look something like this (your exact numbers will differ): Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/mmcblk0p2 119G 12G 102G 11% / /dev/mmcblk0p1 512M 64M 448M 13% /boot/firmware tmpfs 7.7G 0 7.7G 0% /dev/shm Filesystem — the internal name the Pi uses for each storage area. /dev/mmcblk0p2 — your main microSD card partition: the big one holding the operating system and all your files. mmc stands for MultiMediaCard — the standard that microSD uses. p2 means partition 2. Size — the total capacity of that partition (119 GB in this example, from a 128 GB card — some space is always used up by the card's own bookkeeping). Used — how much space is currently occupied (12 GB here). Avail — how much is still free (102 GB). Use% — the percentage used (11%). A good rule of thumb: keep this below 80%. Mounted on / — the forward-slash / is called the root of the filesystem. Everything on the Pi hangs off this one point. Think of it like the C:\ drive on Windows, but with a forward slash instead. /dev/mmcblk0p1 — the smaller boot partition, which holds the files the Pi reads when it first starts up. /boot/firmware — the mount point (location in the filesystem) for the boot partition on Bookworm. This is where bootloader configuration files live. tmpfs — a temporary area held in RAM, not on the card. Files here vanish when you reboot — it is not real storage. Tip: If your Use% is climbing above 80%, it is time to delete unwanted files, move things to an external drive, or upgrade to a bigger card or SSD. Listing All Connected Drives To see a cleaner picture of every storage device the Pi can see — including USB drives and SSDs — use lsblk : lsblk lsblk — stands for "list block devices". A "block device" is the technical name for any storage drive. This command prints a tree showing every drive and its partitions, their sizes, and where they are mounted. Your microSD card will appear as mmcblk0 , a USB drive as sda , and an NVMe SSD as nvme0n1 . The Filesystem Is Already Expanded for You When Raspberry Pi OS is first installed on a card, it normally occupies only a small portion of the card's capacity. On first boot, the system automatically expands the filesystem to fill the entire card — so all the space on your 64, 128, or 256 GB card becomes usable. You do not need to do anything; it happens in the background. If you ever re-flash the card, you can trigger this manually via Raspberry Pi Configuration → Performance → Expand Filesystem , or by running sudo raspi-config and choosing Advanced Options → Expand Filesystem . Using USB Drives and External Hard Drives Plugging in a USB memory stick, an external hard drive, or an external SSD is one of the easiest ways to add more storage or to move files between your Pi and your main computer. Where USB Drives Appear When you plug a USB drive into one of the Pi's USB ports, Raspberry Pi OS automatically mounts it — meaning it makes the drive accessible and gives it a location in the filesystem. In plain words: "Mounting" a drive means connecting it to the filesystem tree so you can reach its files. Think of it like plugging a new drawer into the filing cabinet. "Unmounting" (or ejecting) does the reverse — it safely disconnects the drive so you can remove it without risking data loss. The drive will appear in the file manager (the folder icon in the taskbar) on the left panel. On the command line, its files will be at a path such as: /media/your-username/MY-USB-DRIVE Replace your-username with the username you chose during setup (the default is pi ). The MY-USB-DRIVE part is whatever name (label) was given to the drive when it was formatted. Note: The Pi 5 has two USB 3.0 ports (the ones with blue plastic inside) and two USB 2.0 ports (black plastic). For the fastest transfers with a USB 3.0 drive, plug it into one of the blue ports. Copying Files to and from a USB Drive You can drag and drop files in the file manager exactly as you would on Windows. Or, from the terminal, use the cp (copy) command: cp ~/Documents/my-report.txt /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE/ cp — the copy command. ~/Documents/my-report.txt — the file to copy. The tilde ~ is a shortcut for your home folder (e.g. /home/pi ). /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE/ — the destination: the root folder of the USB drive. Replace pi with your username and MY-USB-DRIVE with the actual label of your drive. The trailing slash / tells cp you are copying into a folder, not renaming the file. To copy a whole folder and everything inside it, add -r (for "recursive"): cp -r ~/Projects /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE/ -r — tells cp to copy recursively, meaning it copies the folder itself and every file and sub-folder inside it. Without -r , cp will refuse to copy a folder. Keeping a Folder in Sync with rsync The cp command always copies everything from scratch. If you run it a second time, it copies all files again even if most have not changed. The rsync command is smarter: it only copies files that are new or have changed since the last time. This makes it much faster for large folders and ideal for regular backups. rsync -av ~/Documents/ /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE/Documents-backup/ rsync — "remote sync", a tool for efficiently copying and synchronising files. It compares source and destination and only transfers what has changed. -a — "archive mode". This one flag does a lot of useful things at once: it copies folders recursively, preserves file permissions, timestamps, and symbolic links. Think of it as "copy everything faithfully". -v — "verbose". Prints the name of each file as it is copied, so you can see what is happening. ~/Documents/ — the source folder. The trailing slash / here is important: it means "copy the contents of Documents, not the Documents folder itself". /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE/Documents-backup/ — the destination folder on your USB drive. Replace the drive name with yours. Tip: Run the same rsync command again the next day — it will only copy files that have changed since yesterday, making it very quick. This is an easy habit that keeps a current copy of your work on a separate drive. Safely Ejecting a USB Drive Before you pull out a USB drive, you must tell the Pi to finish writing and disconnect it cleanly. In the file manager, right-click the drive in the left panel and choose Eject . Or from the terminal: sudo umount /media/pi/MY-USB-DRIVE sudo — administrator privileges are needed for hardware operations. umount — the unmount command. Note the spelling: it is umount , not unmount — a long-standing quirk of Linux. This safely disconnects the drive from the filesystem. Once the command completes with no error message, it is safe to physically unplug the drive. Careful: Pulling out a USB drive without ejecting it first can corrupt the files on the drive, just as with the microSD card. Always eject first — it only takes a second. Formatting a New Drive (If Needed) If you buy a brand-new USB drive or a new SSD enclosure, it may arrive already formatted and ready to use, or it may need formatting first. The easiest way to format a drive on the Pi is through the Disks graphical tool (also called GParted in some versions). Open the application menu → Accessories → Disks (if Disks is not listed, open a terminal and run sudo apt install gnome-disk-utility to install it). Select the drive you want to format from the list on the left. Be very careful to pick the correct drive — formatting erases all data permanently. Click the menu button (three horizontal lines, top-right) and choose Format Disk . For the partition type, choose GPT . Click Format. Once the disk is blank, click the + button to create a new partition. Choose the full size, and select Ext4 as the filesystem type for a Linux drive, or FAT32 / exFAT if you also want to read it on Windows or macOS. Give it a label (a name) and click Create. Note: Ext4 is the standard Linux filesystem — fast and reliable on the Pi, but Windows and macOS cannot read it without extra software. exFAT works on Windows, macOS, and the Pi without any extra tools, making it ideal for drives you share between your Pi and your main computer. Backing Up Your Pi — Why It Matters A microSD card can fail without any warning. It can be corrupted by a power cut. It can be lost or broken. If that happens and you have no backup, everything — your files, your settings, your programs — is gone. Backups are not optional; they are essential. There are two main approaches to backing up a Raspberry Pi: Image the whole card to your main computer — making a perfect copy of the entire card as a single file. Clone the card to another card or USB drive directly from the Pi, using the built-in SD Card Copier tool. What Is a Disk Image? In plain words: A "disk image" (often a .img file) is a single file that contains a perfect, byte-for-byte copy of an entire storage device. It is like a photograph of the entire card — every file, every setting, the operating system itself. If your card dies, you can write the image back to a new card and your Pi will be exactly as it was. Method 1 — Making an Image on Your Main Computer This method uses your main computer and requires you to remove the microSD card from the Pi (shut down first!), insert it into a USB card reader (many Pi kits include one; otherwise any inexpensive microSD-to-USB reader works), and plug that into your computer. Two free tools can do this. Raspberry Pi Imager runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, so it is the option to use whatever computer you own. Win32DiskImager is a popular Windows-only alternative; on macOS the equivalent graphical tool is Raspberry Pi Imager or balenaEtcher , and on Linux you can use Raspberry Pi Imager or the dd command (see "The dd Command" below). Tool Best for Where to get it Raspberry Pi Imager (Windows / macOS / Linux) Writing a fresh OS image AND backing up (it can read a card to a .img.gz file) raspberrypi.com/software — free download Win32DiskImager (Windows only) Simple, dedicated tool for reading and writing raw disk images ( .img ) sourceforge.net/projects/win32diskimager — free download The example below uses Win32DiskImager on Windows to back up your card (if you are on macOS or Linux, use Raspberry Pi Imager's "read" feature instead, which follows the same idea of choosing the card and saving it to an image file): Shut down your Pi properly and remove the microSD card once the board has fully powered off and the green light has stopped blinking. Insert the card into the USB card reader and plug the reader into your computer. Open Win32DiskImager. You may need to run it as Administrator (right-click → Run as administrator). In the Image File field, click the folder icon and choose where to save the backup file. Give it a clear name, such as pi-backup-2026-06-19.img , and click Save. In the Device dropdown, select the drive letter that corresponds to your microSD card. Check Windows Explorer (File Explorer) to confirm which letter your card reader has been assigned — it is usually something like E: or F:. Be very careful: choosing the wrong drive letter could overwrite data on your PC. Click Read . Win32DiskImager will copy the entire card into the image file. This may take 10–30 minutes depending on the card size and your PC's speed. When it says "Read Successful", click OK. Your backup is complete. Remove the card reader and put the microSD card back into the Pi. Note: A raw backup image will be roughly the same size as your card's capacity (e.g. a 128 GB card produces a ~128 GB image file), even if the card is mostly empty. This is because a raw image copies every sector of the card, used or not. Make sure you have enough free space on your computer before starting. To save space, you can compress the finished .img file with a free archiver — 7-Zip (7-zip.org) on Windows, or the built-in compression / a tool like Keka on macOS, or gzip on Linux — and a mostly-empty 128 GB image can often compress to 5–15 GB. To restore the backup to a new card, simply use Win32DiskImager again, but click Write instead of Read, choosing the .img file as the source and the new card as the destination. Careful: When clicking Write in Win32DiskImager, double-check the device letter one more time before clicking. Writing an OS image to the wrong drive will erase everything on it with no undo. Method 2 — SD Card Copier (Clone Card-to-Card on the Pi) Raspberry Pi OS includes a built-in tool called SD Card Copier that lets you clone your current microSD card to a second card (or a USB drive) while the Pi is still running. This is the simplest backup method because you do not need to shut down or use another computer at all. Insert a second microSD card (via the USB card reader) or a USB drive into one of the Pi's USB ports. It must be at least as large as your current card. Open Applications menu → Accessories → SD Card Copier . In the Copy From Device dropdown, select your internal card (listed as something like /dev/mmcblk0 ). In the Copy To Device dropdown, select the destination card or drive. Make sure New Partition UUIDs is ticked. This gives the cloned card its own unique identity so the Pi does not get confused if both cards are ever plugged in at the same time. Click Start . Progress is shown on screen. It may take 15–45 minutes depending on the card size. When complete, you will see a success message. The cloned card is now a perfect working copy of your Pi's card — you could boot from it immediately if needed. Tip: Store your backup image or cloned card somewhere safe — a labelled envelope in a drawer, or uploaded to cloud storage (if you compress it first). Make a fresh backup whenever you have finished a big project or installed a lot of new programs. Once a month is a reasonable habit for general use. The dd Command — For the Curious You may come across references to a Linux command called dd for making disk images directly in the terminal. It is a powerful low-level tool that can copy an entire drive to a file. However, it has no safety prompts — a single typo can silently wipe the wrong drive — so it is not recommended for beginners. The tools above (SD Card Copier and Win32DiskImager) do the same job more safely and with a visual progress indicator. If you are curious, dd stands for "data duplicator", and it is worth exploring once you are comfortable with the terminal. Upgrading to a Solid-State Drive (SSD) Once you have been using your Pi for a while, you may notice that some tasks — opening programs, loading large files, running a busy web server — feel a little sluggish. The microSD card is often the bottleneck. The solution is to add or switch to a solid-state drive (SSD) . In plain words: A "solid-state drive" (SSD) is a type of storage that is much faster than a microSD card and far more durable for heavy, continuous use. Unlike an old-style hard drive, it has no moving parts — it stores data on chips. An "NVMe SSD" is a particular type of very fast SSD that uses a connector standard called M.2 and a communication protocol called NVMe, designed to take full advantage of the Pi 5's high-speed PCIe connection. The Pi 5 gives you two practical ways to add an SSD: PCIe NVMe SSD via a HAT — the fastest option, using the Pi's built-in PCIe slot. USB SSD — a simpler option using any of the Pi's USB 3.0 ports, no extra board needed. Three storage options compared microSD Card Speed: 20–80 MB/s read Write: 10–30 MB/s Durability: moderate Extra hardware: none Cost: already included Good for: getting started USB 3.0 SSD Speed: 200–450 MB/s read Write: 150–400 MB/s Durability: excellent Extra hardware: USB enclosure Cost: £20–40 Good for: easy upgrade NVMe via HAT Speed: 400–900 MB/s read Write: 300–700 MB/s Durability: excellent Extra hardware: HAT + SSD Cost: £30–70 Good for: maximum speed Storage options at a glance. The NVMe route is the fastest but costs a little more and requires an extra board. The USB SSD is a great middle ground that needs no extra board at all. Option A — PCIe NVMe SSD (the Fast Way) The Pi 5 has a PCIe 2.0 x1 connector — a small slot on the edge of the board that enables very fast data transfer, the same technology used in full-size desktop computers for high-speed storage. On its own, this connector cannot directly accept a standard M.2 NVMe SSD; you need an additional accessory board called a HAT that bridges the two. In plain words: "PCIe" (PCI Express) is a high-speed data pathway between the processor and a storage device. "NVMe" (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is the protocol that tells data how to travel along that pathway very quickly. "M.2" is the physical shape and connector of the SSD itself — a small rectangular stick about the size of a stick of chewing gum. A "HAT" (Hardware Attached on Top) is a small add-on board that clips or connects to the Pi to give it new capabilities — here, an M.2 socket connected to the PCIe slot via a short ribbon cable. Popular HAT options include: HAT Notes Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+ (official) The official board from the Raspberry Pi Foundation. Supports 2230 and 2242 M.2 NVMe SSDs. Connects via the PCIe ribbon cable and the 40-pin GPIO header for power. Recommended for beginners — it is well documented and fully supported. Pimoroni NVMe Base A popular third-party option that mounts under the Pi for a compact build. Supports the longer 2280 drives (the most widely available and cheapest size). Various third-party HATs Many manufacturers make PCIe-to-M.2 HATs. Ensure yours explicitly says "Raspberry Pi 5 compatible" and supports "PCIe Gen 2 x1" — otherwise it may not work at all. Note: The HAT and the M.2 NVMe SSD are usually sold separately — most starter kits do not include them, so check what came in your kit before buying. When buying an SSD, look for an M.2 NVMe drive in a size your HAT supports (2230, 2242, or 2280 — these numbers describe the length in millimetres). A 256 GB or 512 GB drive is plenty for most Pi projects and very affordable. Raspberry Pi 5 40-pin GPIO header (power) PCIe connector ribbon cable M.2 HAT+ M.2 socket NVMe SSD (M.2 "stick") How the NVMe SSD connects to the Pi 5 The M.2 HAT+ connects to the Pi 5 via a short PCIe ribbon cable (teal). The NVMe SSD plugs into the M.2 socket on the HAT. Power for the HAT comes from the 40-pin GPIO header. Step 1 — Update the Bootloader First Before fitting the HAT, it is important to ensure your Pi's bootloader (the tiny program that runs before the operating system) is up to date. Older bootloader versions may not support NVMe boot at all. Do this while still booted from your microSD card: sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade -y sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a sudo reboot sudo apt update — refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet so the next commands know about the latest versions. sudo apt full-upgrade -y — installs all available updates, including any updated bootloader package. The -y automatically answers "yes" to any prompts. sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a — checks for a newer version of the Pi's EEPROM (the chip that holds the bootloader) and schedules the update to be applied on next boot. -a means "apply any available update". The update itself is applied during the reboot. sudo reboot — restarts the Pi so the bootloader update is written into the EEPROM chip. After this reboot your bootloader is current and NVMe boot will be fully supported. Tip: Even if you are not planning to add an SSD, keeping your bootloader updated is good practice. It brings bug fixes and performance improvements. Step 2 — Physically Install the HAT and SSD Follow the instructions included with your HAT carefully. In general: Power off the Pi completely and disconnect the power lead. Locate the PCIe FPC connector (a small black latch near the edge of the board) and lift the latch gently, then insert the ribbon cable included with the HAT, gold contacts facing down. Press the latch closed. Connect the other end of the ribbon cable to the HAT in the same way. If your HAT mounts on top of the Pi, align it with the 40-pin GPIO header and press it gently down until the pins are fully seated. Slide the M.2 NVMe SSD into the socket at a slight angle (about 30°), then press it flat and secure it with the small retaining screw. Reconnect power. The Pi should boot from the microSD card as normal, and the new SSD should now be visible to the system. Step 3 — Verify the SSD Is Detected lsblk lsblk — lists all block (storage) devices. You should now see both your microSD card ( mmcblk0 ) and the NVMe SSD, which will appear as nvme0n1 . If nvme0n1 is not listed, check that the ribbon cable is seated properly at both ends and the SSD is fully pushed into the socket. Step 4 — Clone the MicroSD Card to the SSD Use SD Card Copier to clone your entire system to the new SSD: Open Applications → Accessories → SD Card Copier . Set Copy From Device to your microSD card ( /dev/mmcblk0 ). Set Copy To Device to the NVMe SSD ( /dev/nvme0n1 ). Tick New Partition UUIDs and click Start . Wait for it to finish — this can take 10–30 minutes. Step 5 — Set the Boot Order Tell the Pi to try the NVMe SSD before the microSD card when it starts up: sudo raspi-config raspi-config — the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool. It opens a menu-driven interface for changing system settings without editing configuration files by hand. Use the arrow keys to navigate and Enter to select. In the menu, navigate to Advanced Options → Boot Order → NVMe/USB Boot and press Enter to select it. Then arrow down to Finish and press Enter. When asked if you want to reboot, choose Yes . Note: Choosing "NVMe/USB Boot" does not mean the Pi ignores the microSD card forever. It means: "try NVMe or USB drive first; if neither is found, fall back to the microSD card." This is a safe setting — if anything goes wrong with the SSD, you can still put the microSD card back in and the Pi will boot from it. Step 6 — Test the SSD Boot After the Pi reboots, open a terminal and run lsblk to confirm the system is running from nvme0n1 — you should see it listed as mounted at / . If everything looks correct, power off the Pi, remove the microSD card, and power back on. If the Pi boots successfully to your desktop, the SSD is working as the sole boot drive. Store the microSD card somewhere safe as an emergency fallback — you can always boot from it if the SSD ever has a problem. Tip: Once you are running from an NVMe SSD, the difference is immediately noticeable. The Pi boots in 5–10 seconds rather than 20–30, programs open almost instantly, and file-heavy tasks like compiling code or processing large images are dramatically faster. Option B — USB SSD Boot (The Simpler Way) If you do not want to buy a HAT, you can boot from an external SSD connected via USB — specifically into one of the blue USB 3.0 ports . You need an SSD in a USB 3.0 enclosure (readily available online for £10–20). No HAT required. The process is almost identical to the NVMe method: Connect the USB SSD to one of the blue USB 3.0 ports on the Pi (while still booted from the microSD card). Use SD Card Copier to clone the microSD card to the USB SSD, just as described above. Run sudo raspi-config → Advanced Options → Boot Order → NVMe/USB Boot to set the boot priority. Reboot. Remove the microSD card if desired. The Pi should now boot from the USB SSD. A USB SSD is not quite as fast as a PCIe NVMe drive (USB 3.0 is capped at roughly 450 MB/s in ideal conditions), but it is still many times faster than a microSD card and far more reliable for heavy continuous use. It is an excellent middle-ground upgrade that costs very little and requires no hardware modifications to the Pi. A Note on Power for Bus-Powered Drives Careful: Some larger external drives (particularly 2.5-inch mechanical spinning hard drives) draw more power than the Pi's USB ports can safely provide. This can cause the drive to disconnect randomly or the Pi to reboot unexpectedly. If you use an external drive, prefer one that is labelled "SSD" (solid-state, low power draw) or one that has its own separate power supply. Compact 2.5-inch SSDs in a USB enclosure typically draw well under 1 W and work fine. If you see a lightning-bolt icon in the top-right corner of the screen, the Pi is warning you that it is under-powered — switch to a powered USB hub or a drive with its own power brick. Note: The Pi 5 with the official 27 W USB-C power supply is more capable than earlier Pi models, but the total power budget across all USB ports is still limited. Bear this in mind if you have several USB devices connected at once. Quick Reference: Storage Commands Task Command What it does Check free space df -h Shows used and free space on all drives in MB/GB List all drives lsblk Shows every storage device and partition tree Shut down safely sudo shutdown now Powers off the Pi cleanly, saving all files first Safely eject a USB drive sudo umount /media/pi/DRIVE-NAME Disconnects the drive so it is safe to unplug Open Pi configuration sudo raspi-config Menu for changing system settings including boot order Copy a file to USB drive cp ~/file.txt /media/pi/DRIVE-NAME/ Copies a single file to the drive Copy a whole folder to USB drive cp -r ~/MyFolder /media/pi/DRIVE-NAME/ Copies a folder and all its contents Sync a folder (smart backup) rsync -av ~/Documents/ /media/pi/DRIVE-NAME/backup/ Copies only new or changed files — much faster on repeat runs Update bootloader sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a Schedules a bootloader update to apply on next reboot Key terms MicroSD card — the small removable card that holds the Pi's operating system and files by default; convenient but vulnerable to wear and corruption from sudden power loss. Filesystem — the rules and structures that organise files on a storage device, like the dividers and labels inside a filing cabinet. Filesystem corruption — damage to stored data caused by a sudden loss of power during a write operation. df -h — a terminal command that displays disk usage in human-readable units (MB/GB). lsblk — a terminal command that lists all storage (block) devices connected to the Pi and their partitions. Mount / unmount — connecting (mounting) or safely disconnecting (unmounting) a drive so the operating system can access it or release it cleanly. Disk image (.img) — a single file containing a perfect byte-for-byte copy of an entire storage device; can be written back to a new card to restore the Pi exactly. SD Card Copier — a built-in Raspberry Pi OS graphical tool for cloning the current card to another card or drive. rsync — a command-line tool that copies only new or changed files between two locations, making repeat backups fast and efficient. SSD (Solid-State Drive) — a fast, durable storage device with no moving parts; much faster and more reliable than a microSD card for continuous use. NVMe — a communication protocol for SSDs that uses PCIe lanes; delivers the highest storage speeds on the Pi 5. M.2 — the physical form factor used by NVMe SSDs — a small rectangular stick. Sizes like 2230, 2242, and 2280 describe length in millimetres. HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) — an add-on board that connects to the Pi to add capabilities, such as an M.2 socket for an NVMe SSD. PCIe (PCI Express) — a high-speed data bus built into the Pi 5 that enables very fast communication with an NVMe SSD via a HAT. EEPROM / bootloader — a small chip and program on the Pi board that runs before the operating system starts; it decides which drive to boot from. Keeping it updated ensures NVMe boot works correctly. rpi-eeprom-update — the command to check for and apply bootloader (EEPROM) updates on a Raspberry Pi. raspi-config — a menu-driven terminal tool for configuring Pi system settings, including boot order. Boot order — the sequence of storage devices the Pi tries when starting up; can be set to prefer NVMe or USB over the microSD card. Bus-powered — a drive that draws its power from the USB port rather than its own power supply; small SSDs work fine this way, but large spinning hard drives often need external power. exFAT — a filesystem format readable by Windows, macOS, and Raspberry Pi OS without extra software; ideal for drives shared between your Pi and your main computer. Ext4 — the standard Linux filesystem used by Raspberry Pi OS; fast and reliable on the Pi, but not readable by Windows without third-party software. Chapter summary Always shut down the Pi properly before cutting power — the physical power button, the desktop menu, or sudo shutdown now all do this safely — to protect the microSD card from corruption. Use df -h to check free space and lsblk to see all connected drives; keep disk usage below 80%. Raspberry Pi OS automatically expands the filesystem to fill your entire card on first boot — no action needed. USB drives appear in the file manager automatically; always eject them via right-click or sudo umount before unplugging. rsync -av is smarter than cp for regular backups — it only copies files that have changed, making repeat runs fast. Back up your Pi regularly by imaging the card to your main computer with Raspberry Pi Imager (Windows/macOS/Linux) or Win32DiskImager (Windows), or by cloning it with the built-in SD Card Copier; store the backup somewhere safe. Before adding an NVMe SSD, update the Pi's bootloader with sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a and reboot to ensure NVMe boot is fully supported. The Pi 5's PCIe slot supports a very fast NVMe SSD via an M.2 HAT+, delivering speeds 10–30 times greater than a microSD card. A USB SSD connected to a blue USB 3.0 port is a simpler, slightly slower upgrade that needs no extra HAT — set the boot order via raspi-config and you are done. Small SSDs draw very little power and work safely from the Pi's USB ports; large mechanical hard drives may draw too much and need their own power supply.

title: Your First Code with Python
headings: Two ways to run Python code
Putting it all together — a number-guessing game
Errors are normal — do not panic
Adding extra Python libraries — the Bookworm-correct way
text: Python is the perfect first programming language — it reads almost like plain English, runs instantly, and comes pre-installed on every Raspberry Pi. In this chapter you will write your very first lines of code, understand what they do, build up to a complete mini-game, and learn how to add extra Python tools the safe, Bookworm-correct way. What is programming? A computer does exactly what you tell it — nothing more, nothing less. A program is simply a list of very precise instructions written in a language the computer can follow. Every instruction is carried out in order, from top to bottom, unless you deliberately tell the computer to jump around. Imagine a recipe for making toast: Put bread in toaster. Press the lever down. Wait until the bread pops up. Spread butter on the toast. Serve. A Python program works exactly like that recipe. Each line is one instruction. The computer reads line 1, carries it out, then reads line 2, carries it out, and so on. If you leave out a step, or write one in the wrong order, you get the wrong result — just like forgetting to put bread in the toaster first. In plain words: Programming means writing a list of instructions in a special language that a computer can understand and carry out automatically. Why Python? There are dozens of programming languages. Python is chosen as the default on the Raspberry Pi for good reasons: Its instructions look like short English sentences, so beginners can guess what code means even before they have learned it properly. You can test a single line of code immediately without building an entire project. There is an enormous library of ready-made tools for everything from controlling GPIO pins to analysing spreadsheets. It is one of the most-used languages in science, education, automation, and professional software development worldwide. The Raspberry Pi Foundation has built a beginner-friendly editor called Thonny that makes writing and running Python programs as easy as using a word processor. Two ways to run Python code On your Pi you have two main routes to writing and running Python. Both are useful and you will use both regularly. Method 1 — Thonny (the easy visual editor) Thonny is a purpose-built Python editor designed for people who have never programmed before. It has a big text area where you type your code, a green Run button you click, and a panel at the bottom (called the Shell ) that shows you what happens when the program runs. You can also type single lines directly into the Shell to test them instantly. To open Thonny, click the raspberry icon in the top-left corner of the desktop, go to Programming , and click Thonny . You can also type thonny in a terminal and press Enter. Thonny — Python IDE ▶ Run ■ Stop Code editor (type your program here) print("Hello, world!") name = input("What is your name? ") print("Nice to meet you,", name) Shell (output and interactive commands appear here) Hello, world! What is your name? _ The Thonny editor. Type code in the top panel, click Run, and see the output in the Shell panel below. You can also type single commands directly into the Shell. Method 2 — the terminal (python3 myfile.py) Once you have saved a Python file you can also run it from the terminal without opening Thonny at all. This is quicker when you already know the code is ready. Open a terminal window (the black icon on the taskbar, or from the menu under Accessories → Terminal ). If your file is called hello.py and you saved it in your home folder, type: python3 hello.py python3 — launches the Python 3 interpreter (the program that reads and runs Python code). On Raspberry Pi OS always write python3 , not just python , to make sure you get the modern version. hello.py — the name of the file to run. Python files always end in .py . Tip: Use Thonny while you are learning — it highlights errors, shows line numbers, and lets you run code one step at a time. Switch to the terminal later when you are comfortable. Method 3 — the interactive Python shell (REPL) There is a third option that is perfect for quick experiments: the Python REPL (Read-Evaluate-Print Loop). You launch it by typing python3 in a terminal and pressing Enter, with no filename. You then type one line of Python at a time and see the result instantly. In plain words: REPL stands for Read-Evaluate-Print Loop. Python reads your line, evaluates it (runs it), prints the result, and then waits for the next line. It is like a calculator that understands Python. python3 python3 (with no filename after it) — starts the interactive Python shell. Your prompt changes to >>> , which means Python is waiting for your input. Once you see the >>> prompt, try these: >>> 2 + 2 4 >>> print("Hello from the REPL!") Hello from the REPL! >>> name = "Raspberry Pi" >>> name 'Raspberry Pi' >>> exit() >>> 2 + 2 — you type the expression after the >>> prompt; Python immediately prints the answer 4 on the next line. print("Hello from the REPL!") — works exactly as in a script. name = "Raspberry Pi" — creates a variable. Variables created in the REPL persist for the whole session. name — typing a variable name on its own (without print ) shows its value. This only works in the REPL, not in a saved script. exit() — closes the Python shell and returns you to the normal terminal prompt. Tip: You can also use the REPL from inside Thonny — it is the Shell panel at the bottom. Click in it and type away. Your first Python building blocks The rest of this chapter introduces the core ideas of Python one at a time. Each section has a short runnable example. Open Thonny, type each example in the editor panel, and press the green Run button to see what happens. Do not just read — actually type the code. Your fingers will remember it. print() — showing things on screen print() is the simplest instruction in Python. It tells the computer to display whatever is inside the brackets on screen. print("Hello, world!") print("I am learning Python.") print(42) print(3.14) print("Hello, world!") — displays the words Hello, world! followed by a new line.
