This chapter shows you two practical paths: the quick-and-simple way with a built-in Python trick, and the modern, tidy way using Docker containers. What Is a Web Server, Really? When you type a web address into your browser, your browser sends a request over the network asking "Please send me that page." A web server is simply a program sitting on another computer, waiting for those requests and then sending back the web page (an HTML file) in reply. The word "server" just means "something that serves requests" — it has nothing to do with the size or power of the computer. Your Pi 5 is perfectly capable of being a web server for every device on your home Wi-Fi. In plain words: A web server is a program that listens for browsers asking for pages and hands them back, the same way a library assistant hands you a book when you ask for one. Every device on your home network has a local address called an IP address — a set of four numbers like 192.168.1.42 . Once your Pi is running a web server, any other device on the same Wi-Fi can open a browser and visit http://192.168.1.42 to see whatever page the Pi is serving. (Finding your Pi's IP address was covered in Chapter 5; the quick reminder is to open a Terminal on the Pi and type hostname -I .) Note: Everything in this chapter works on your home network only, until you deliberately open it to the outside world. That is the safe default — we discuss the outside internet at the end of the chapter. Part A — Serve a Simple Web Page There are two easy approaches. The first uses a tool that is already installed; the second installs the professional-grade web server software called Nginx . Both end with you viewing a page from another device. Method 1: The One-Command Python Server Python 3 is already installed on Raspberry Pi OS and includes a tiny built-in web server. It takes one command and serves every file in a folder. This is great for a quick demo or sharing files on your home network — but it is not meant to run permanently or to handle heavy traffic. Open a Terminal on your Pi. Create a test folder and move into it: mkdir ~/my-website cd ~/my-website mkdir ~/my-website — creates a new folder called my-website inside your home directory. The ~ is a shortcut that always means "my home folder" (usually /home/pi ). cd ~/my-website — changes your current location to that new folder so the next commands work there. Create a simple web page: nano index.html nano index.html — opens the Nano text editor to create a new file called index.html . A file named index.html is the conventional "home page" that web servers look for first when a visitor arrives at the address without asking for a specific file. Type (or paste) this into Nano: My Pi Website

Hello from my Raspberry Pi 5!

This page is being served by my Pi.

This is a minimal HTML web page. The declaration tells the browser this is a modern HTML5 document.

creates a large heading;

creates a paragraph. The browser will display both. You can write anything you like here — it is your page. Press Ctrl + O then Enter to save, then Ctrl + X to exit Nano. Start the web server: python3 -m http.server 8080 python3 -m http.server 8080 — tells Python 3 to run its built-in web server module ( http.server ) and listen on port 8080 . A port is like a numbered door on your Pi — different services listen on different door numbers. The standard web port is 80, but we use 8080 here to avoid needing extra administrator permissions. You will see a message like Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 8080 . The Terminal is now busy running the server — leave it open. On any device on your home network (phone, laptop, another computer), open a web browser and go to: http://:8080 Replace with the actual IP address shown by hostname -I on the Pi (for example http://192.168.1.42:8080 ). The :8080 tells the browser which port to knock on. You should see your "Hello from my Raspberry Pi 5!" page. When you are done, go back to the Terminal and press Ctrl + C to stop the server. Tip: While the server is running, look back at the Terminal — it prints a line every time a device visits the page, showing the visitor's IP address, the time, and what file was requested. This is exactly what a real web server access log looks like. Method 2: Nginx — The Proper Web Server Nginx (pronounced "engine-ecks") is a fast, professional web server used by millions of websites worldwide. Unlike the Python one-liner, it runs as a background service that starts automatically when your Pi boots. This is the right choice if you want a page that is always available. In plain words: A service (also called a daemon ) is a program that runs quietly in the background all the time, without needing a Terminal window open. Your Pi starts its services automatically when it boots up, so you never have to remember to start them. Open a Terminal and install Nginx: sudo apt update sudo apt install nginx -y sudo apt update — refreshes the list of available software packages from the internet. Always do this before installing something new to make sure you get the latest version. sudo apt install nginx -y — downloads and installs Nginx. The -y answers "yes" automatically to the "do you want to continue?" question, so you do not have to type it yourself. When the installation finishes, Nginx starts automatically and is immediately listening for web traffic. Check that it is running: sudo systemctl status nginx sudo systemctl status nginx — asks the system service manager ( systemctl ) to report the current status of the Nginx service. You should see the word active (running) highlighted in green. Press Q to exit the status view. On your Pi itself, open the Chromium web browser and go to http://localhost . The word localhost always means "this computer itself". You should see the Nginx welcome page — this confirms it is working. Now replace the default page with your own. The web files Nginx serves live in /var/www/html/ . Edit the default page: sudo nano /var/www/html/index.html sudo nano /var/www/html/index.html — opens the existing index file in the Nano editor. sudo is needed because the folder is owned by the system, not your user account, and without it Nano would not be able to save your changes. Select all the existing text (hold Ctrl + K repeatedly to delete line by line) and replace it with your own HTML — you can use the same simple page from Method 1, or write something new. Save with Ctrl + O , Enter , then Ctrl + X . From any device on your home network, open a browser and visit: http:// No port number is needed — Nginx listens on the standard web port 80, which browsers use automatically when you just type an http:// address without a colon and number. Your page appears! And it will still be there the next time you visit, even after you restart the Pi. Tip: You can drop any number of HTML files, images, or CSS files into /var/www/html/ and Nginx will serve them all. Create sub-folders for different pages and link between them with normal HTML links — you are building a real website. How a home network web server works Diagram showing a browser on a laptop sending an HTTP request to the Raspberry Pi, which has Nginx running and returns a web page. Both are connected through a home Wi-Fi router. Raspberry Pi 5 Nginx (web server) 192.168.1.42 : 80 /var/www/html/ GET http://192.168.1.42/ Here is index.html → Your Laptop / Phone Web browser Displays the page Home Wi-Fi Router (same network) A browser on any device on your home network asks the Pi's Nginx web server for a page. Nginx reads the HTML file from disk and sends it back. The whole conversation stays inside your home network, through the router. Part B — The Modern Way: Docker and Containers Serving a static HTML page is satisfying, but the real fun begins when you run complete self-hosted applications on your Pi — things like a home dashboard, a private notes app, an uptime monitor, or a media server. The cleanest way to do this in 2025 is with Docker . What Is Docker? In plain words: A container is like a pre-packed lunchbox for a program. It contains the program itself plus every library, tool, and configuration file it needs to run — all bundled together. You can drop the lunchbox onto any compatible computer and it just works, without touching or interfering with anything else on the machine. Docker is the most popular tool for creating and running these containers. Before Docker, installing a server application on Linux could mean following a long list of steps, installing dozens of extra packages, editing configuration files, and hoping nothing clashed with other software already on the machine. With Docker: You pull a ready-made container image from the internet (think of an image as the sealed lunchbox before you open it). Docker runs it in an isolated environment — it cannot accidentally break other things on your Pi. Removing an app is as simple as deleting its container and image — no leftover files scattered everywhere. The same container works the same way every time, on every machine that runs Docker. Docker containers on a Raspberry Pi Diagram showing Raspberry Pi OS at the base, Docker Engine on top of it, and three separate containers sitting side by side inside Docker, each with their own libraries and a port number. Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm) — the base system Docker Engine Container A Uptime Kuma Port 3001 (its own libraries) Container B Memos (Notes) Port 5230 (its own libraries) Container C Any other app Port 9000 (its own libraries) Three containers run side by side on the same Pi, each isolated with its own set of files and libraries. They share the underlying hardware through Docker but cannot interfere with each other or with the main Raspberry Pi OS. Installing Docker The official and recommended way to install Docker on Raspberry Pi OS is to use a script provided by Docker themselves. Here is how. Careful: The installation command below downloads a script from the internet and runs it with administrator rights on your Pi. This is only safe because it comes directly from Docker's own website, which is a trusted source. As a rule, never paste commands that run downloaded scripts unless you trust where they come from. In this case, Docker's official documentation recommends exactly this method for Linux systems. Open a Terminal and download the installer script: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh curl — a command-line tool for downloading files from the internet. -fsSL — a combination of flags: -f makes curl fail quietly on server errors, -s hides the download progress bar, -S still shows error messages even in silent mode, and -L follows any redirects automatically. https://get.docker.com — the official Docker installation script URL. -o get-docker.sh — saves the downloaded content to a file called get-docker.sh on your Pi rather than running it immediately, so you can inspect it first if you wish. Run the installer: sudo sh get-docker.sh sudo sh get-docker.sh — runs the downloaded script with administrator privileges ( sudo ). This installs the Docker Engine and all its dependencies. You will see a lot of text scrolling past — that is normal. It will take a few minutes. Add your user account to the docker group. By default, only administrators can run Docker commands. Adding yourself to the docker group means you can run them without typing sudo every time: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER sudo usermod — modifies a user account. -aG docker — appends ( -a ) the user to the group ( -G ) called docker . Using -a is critical: without it, the command would replace all your existing groups instead of adding to them, which could lock you out of things. $USER — the shell automatically replaces this with your own username (for example pi ). Careful: Being in the docker group is effectively the same as having administrator access, because Docker can manipulate system files. Only add trusted users to this group on your Pi. This group change does not take effect in your current Terminal session. You must log out and log back in, or simply reboot: sudo reboot sudo reboot — restarts the Pi. After it comes back on (give it about 30 seconds), open a Terminal and your user account will have Docker permissions. After rebooting, open a Terminal and verify Docker is working: docker --version docker run hello-world docker --version — prints the installed Docker version number. A successful output confirms Docker is installed correctly. docker run hello-world — downloads a tiny test container image called hello-world from the internet and runs it. The container prints a friendly success message and then exits on its own. This confirms Docker can pull images from the internet and run containers on your Pi's ARM64 processor. You should see a message that includes "Hello from Docker!" — Docker is ready. Essential Docker Commands Before running a real app, here are the key commands you will use day-to-day. These are worth bookmarking — you will reach for them often. Command What it does docker ps Lists all running containers — their names, what image they are based on, and which ports they are listening on. docker ps -a Lists all containers, including stopped ones. docker stop Gracefully stops a running container. Replace with the container's name. docker start Starts a container that has been stopped. docker restart Stops then immediately starts a container — useful after changing settings. docker logs Prints the recent output (messages and errors) from a container — the first place to look when something is not working. docker logs -f Follows the logs in real time as they are written. Press Ctrl + C to stop watching. docker rm Deletes a stopped container. Your data in volumes is kept safe — only the container itself is removed. docker images Lists all downloaded images (the "sealed lunchboxes") on your Pi, with their sizes. docker rmi Deletes a downloaded image from disk to free up storage space. docker pull Downloads an image from Docker Hub without running it yet. docker system prune Cleans up all stopped containers, unused images, and unused networks in one go — useful for reclaiming disk space. It asks for confirmation before deleting anything. In plain words: A Docker image is the recipe — a sealed, downloadable package. A Docker container is what you get when you actually run that recipe — a live, running instance of the app. You can run the same image multiple times to get multiple separate containers, just as you can bake the same recipe multiple times to get multiple cakes. Running Your First Real App: Uptime Kuma Uptime Kuma is a beautiful, free self-hosted monitoring dashboard. You give it a list of websites or services to watch, and it checks them regularly and shows you whether they are up or down — with a clean visual interface and optional alerts. It is a perfect first Docker app because it installs in one command and needs nothing else. Run Uptime Kuma: docker run -d \ --name uptime-kuma \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3001:3001 \ -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data \ louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker run — the command to create and start a new container. -d — runs the container detached , meaning it runs in the background. You get your Terminal prompt back immediately. --name uptime-kuma — gives this container a human-readable name so you can use it in other commands (like docker stop uptime-kuma ) instead of a random ID. --restart unless-stopped — tells Docker to automatically restart this container if the Pi reboots or if the container crashes, unless you manually stop it with docker stop . This is what makes it feel like a real always-on service. -p 3001:3001 — maps port 3001 on your Pi to port 3001 inside the container . The format is always Pi-port:container-port . This is what lets your browser reach the app from outside the container. -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data — creates a named storage area managed by Docker called uptime-kuma-data and links it to the folder inside the container where Uptime Kuma stores its data. Without this, all your settings and monitoring history would be lost every time the container is restarted. louislam/uptime-kuma:1 — the image to use. Docker downloads it automatically from Docker Hub (the main public library of images) if it is not already on your Pi. louislam is the developer's account, uptime-kuma is the image name, and :1 is the version tag — the latest version in the 1.x series, which supports ARM64 (your Pi's processor type). The backslash \ at the end of each line simply means "this command continues on the next line" — it is there for readability. You could write the whole thing on one line if you preferred. Docker will download the image (this may take a minute or two the first time, depending on your internet speed) and then start the container. You will see a long container ID printed — that means it is running. Check that it is running: docker ps docker ps — shows all currently running containers. You should see uptime-kuma in the list with a status of Up and the port 0.0.0.0:3001->3001/tcp shown, which means port 3001 on your Pi is connected to port 3001 inside the container. On your Pi's browser, or on any device on your home network, open a browser and go to: http://:3001 Replace with your Pi's actual local IP address — for example http://192.168.1.42:3001 . The :3001 is the port number you mapped in the -p flag. The Uptime Kuma setup page appears. Create an admin account and start adding websites or services to monitor. Tip: The --restart unless-stopped flag means Uptime Kuma will automatically start again every time you reboot your Pi. You never need to remember to start it manually. To stop it permanently, run docker stop uptime-kuma . Docker Compose — Managing Multi-Part Apps Some apps are made of several containers working together — for example, a web application plus a separate database container. Typing a long docker run command for each one is tedious and error-prone. Docker Compose solves this with a single text file that describes all the containers, and one command to start them all. In plain words: A docker-compose.yml file is a recipe card that lists all the containers an app needs, their settings, and how they connect to each other. Running docker compose up reads the card and starts everything in one go. Note: Modern Docker (version 20 and later, which is what you just installed) includes Compose built-in. The command is docker compose (two words, no hyphen). If you see older tutorials using docker-compose (with a hyphen), that is an older separate tool — the built-in version works the same way. Here is an example using Memos , a lightweight private notes app. You type notes into a clean interface and they are stored entirely on your Pi — no third-party server involved. Create a folder for this app and move into it: mkdir ~/memos && cd ~/memos mkdir ~/memos — creates a folder called memos in your home directory. && — runs the second command only if the first one succeeded (a safety check). cd ~/memos — moves into that new folder so the next commands work there. Create the Compose file: nano docker-compose.yml Opens Nano to create a new file called docker-compose.yml . The name and the .yml extension are important — Docker Compose looks for exactly this filename in the current folder. Paste in this content exactly. Indentation matters in YAML files — use spaces, not tabs, and keep the spacing exactly as shown: services: memos: image: neosmemo/memos:stable container_name: memos restart: unless-stopped ports: - "5230:5230" volumes: - ./data:/var/opt/memos services: — the top-level section that lists all the containers this Compose file manages. memos: — the name we give to this service within Compose. It can be anything you like. image: neosmemo/memos:stable — the Docker image to use, pulled automatically from Docker Hub. The :stable tag means the latest stable release. container_name: memos — the name Docker will give the running container, so you can use commands like docker logs memos . restart: unless-stopped — auto-restart on reboot, same as before. ports: - "5230:5230" — maps port 5230 on the Pi to port 5230 inside the container. volumes: - ./data:/var/opt/memos — maps a folder called data in the current directory ( ./data ) to the data folder inside the container. Docker will create the data sub-folder for you automatically the first time. This is where your notes are permanently stored — they survive container restarts and updates. Save and exit Nano: Ctrl + O , Enter , Ctrl + X . Start the app: docker compose up -d docker compose up — reads the docker-compose.yml file in the current folder and creates and starts all the services listed in it. Docker downloads the image if it is not already on your Pi. -d — runs everything in the background (detached), so your Terminal is free again. Visit it on your network by opening a browser on any device and going to: http://:5230 The Memos sign-up page appears. Create an account and start writing private notes — they are stored on your Pi, not on anyone else's server. To stop everything in the Compose file (run this from inside the ~/memos folder): docker compose down docker compose down — stops and removes all the containers defined in the Compose file. Your notes and data stored in the ./data folder are not deleted — they stay safely on your Pi's storage. Run docker compose up -d again at any time to start the app back up. Tip: There is a huge community of self-hosted apps with ready-made Docker Compose files. Good places to discover them are Awesome-Selfhosted (a curated list at github.com/awesome-selfhosted/awesome-selfhosted ) and the r/selfhosted community on Reddit. Home media servers, password managers, recipe organisers, photo libraries, and hundreds more can be running on your Pi in minutes. Updating a Docker Container Docker images are periodically updated by their authors to add features or fix security issues. Updating a container is a three-step process: pull the new image, stop and remove the old container, then run a new container from the updated image. For Compose apps it is even simpler. For a single container (like Uptime Kuma): docker pull louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker stop uptime-kuma docker rm uptime-kuma docker run -d \ --name uptime-kuma \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3001:3001 \ -v uptime-kuma-data:/app/data \ louislam/uptime-kuma:1 docker pull louislam/uptime-kuma:1 — downloads the latest version of the image. Even if the :1 tag has not changed, this fetches any updates published under that tag. docker stop uptime-kuma — gracefully stops the running container. docker rm uptime-kuma — removes the old container. Your data is safe because it lives in the named volume uptime-kuma-data , not inside the container itself. The final docker run block — creates and starts a fresh container from the newly downloaded image, with all the same settings as before. Your data in the volume is automatically reconnected. For a Compose app (like Memos) — from inside the app's folder: cd ~/memos docker compose pull docker compose up -d cd ~/memos — moves into the Memos folder so Docker Compose can find the docker-compose.yml file. docker compose pull — downloads the latest version of every image listed in the Compose file. docker compose up -d — restarts all services using the newly pulled images. Any container whose image has changed is automatically recreated. Your data in the ./data folder is untouched. Tip — Portainer, a graphical Docker dashboard: If you prefer clicking over typing commands, Portainer is a free, self-hosted web interface for managing all your Docker containers, images, and volumes through a browser. You can install it with a single docker run command (search for "Portainer CE install" on their official site at portainer.io ). It makes updating, starting, and stopping containers as easy as clicking a button, and it is a great way to see everything Docker is doing on your Pi at a glance. Reaching Your Pi from Outside Your Home Network Everything so far works only on your home network — devices in your house can reach the Pi, but not anyone on the wider internet. You may wonder: how do I access my Pi when I am away from home, or share something with a friend? Careful — read this before opening your router to the internet. The most obvious method — opening a port on your home router (called "port forwarding") — directly exposes your Pi and everything running on it to the entire internet. Automated bots constantly scan the internet for open ports and attempt to break in. If your Pi is exposed without proper security measures (HTTPS encryption, strong authentication, firewall rules, and regular updates), it is likely to be compromised within hours or days. Do not attempt port forwarding without significant technical knowledge and careful preparation. The good news is that there are modern, safer alternatives that do not require opening any router ports at all. These tools create an encrypted tunnel between your Pi and their servers, so you can reach your Pi securely from anywhere without ever exposing a raw port to the internet. Safer Alternatives to Port Forwarding Tool What it does Free tier? Best for Tailscale Creates a private, encrypted virtual network (a VPN) between your devices. Your Pi gets a stable private IP address accessible from your phone or laptop anywhere in the world, as if they were all on the same home network. No open router ports needed. Yes — free for up to 3 users / 100 devices Personal access to your own Pi from anywhere Cloudflare Tunnel The Pi makes an outgoing connection to Cloudflare's network. Cloudflare gives you a public URL (optionally your own domain name) and routes traffic to your Pi with HTTPS automatically. No open router ports. Yes — free for personal use Sharing a web app publicly with a proper https:// web address Raspberry Pi Connect The Raspberry Pi Foundation's official remote access tool. Lets you reach the Pi desktop or a Terminal through a plain web browser, using your Raspberry Pi account. Very beginner-friendly to set up. Yes — free Remote desktop and Terminal access to the Pi itself Setting Up Tailscale (Recommended for Beginners) Tailscale is the easiest option for personal use — install it on your Pi and on your phone or laptop, sign in with a free account, and your devices can reach each other from anywhere securely, with no technical configuration of your router required. On your Pi, install Tailscale: curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sudo sh curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh — downloads the Tailscale installation script from their official servers. The flags mean the same as before: fail on error, silent, show errors, follow redirects. | sudo sh — the | (called a "pipe") sends the downloaded script directly into sudo sh to run it as administrator. This is the method Tailscale's own documentation recommends for Linux. Connect the Pi to your Tailscale account: sudo tailscale up sudo tailscale up — starts the Tailscale connection and authentication process. It will print a URL in the Terminal. Open that URL on any device — your phone, laptop, or the Pi's own browser — to log in with your Tailscale account (or create a free one). Once you log in, the Pi joins your private Tailscale network immediately. Install Tailscale on your phone or laptop too. Free apps are available for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. Visit tailscale.com/download and sign in with the same account you used in the previous step. Find your Pi's Tailscale IP address: tailscale ip -4 tailscale ip -4 — prints your Pi's private Tailscale IP address. It will look something like 100.x.x.x . This address only works when you are connected to Tailscale on both the Pi and the device you are browsing from, but it works from anywhere in the world — your home, a cafe, or another country — through an encrypted connection, with no router ports open. For example, if your Tailscale IP is 100.64.10.5 , you could reach Uptime Kuma from anywhere by visiting http://100.64.10.5:3001 . Note: Tailscale's free tier supports up to 3 users and 100 devices — more than enough for personal and family use. If you ever want to share an app publicly with a real https:// web address that anyone can visit without installing Tailscale, look at Cloudflare Tunnel — but that is a more advanced step beyond this chapter. Quick Reference: Ports Used in This Chapter Service Default port Access URL on your home network Python http.server (temporary) 8080 http://:8080 Nginx (permanent web server) 80 http:// (no port needed) Uptime Kuma (monitoring) 3001 http://:3001 Memos (private notes) 5230 http://:5230 Tip — find your Pi's IP address quickly: Open a Terminal on the Pi and type hostname -I . The first number shown (e.g. 192.168.1.42 ) is your Pi's local IP address. Use that number everywhere you see in this chapter. Key terms Web server — a program that listens for browser requests and sends back web pages in reply. Nginx — a popular, fast, professional web server that runs as a permanent background service on your Pi. IP address — a unique number (like 192.168.1.42 ) that identifies a device on a network. Port — a numbered "door" on a networked device; different services listen on different port numbers so many services can run on the same machine simultaneously. localhost — a special name that always means "this computer itself"; typing http://localhost in a browser on the Pi reaches the Pi's own web server. Docker — software for running applications inside isolated containers on your Pi. Container — a self-contained, isolated running instance of an application, bundled with everything it needs, that cannot interfere with the rest of the system. Image — the sealed, downloadable package from which a container is created; the recipe that Docker runs to produce a container. Docker Hub — the main public online library where Docker images are stored and downloaded from. Volume — a Docker-managed storage area that keeps your data (settings, databases, files) safe even when a container is stopped, updated, or replaced. Docker Compose — a tool that reads a YAML file describing one or more containers and starts them all with a single command. Port forwarding — a router setting that sends incoming internet traffic to a specific device on your home network; risky without expert-level security measures. Tailscale — a free VPN tool that creates a private, encrypted connection between your devices so you can reach your Pi from anywhere without opening any router ports. Cloudflare Tunnel — a free service that gives a Pi-hosted app a public HTTPS web address without opening any router ports. Service / daemon — a program that runs quietly in the background, starting automatically each time the Pi boots, with no Terminal window required. ARM64 — the processor architecture used by the Raspberry Pi 5. When choosing Docker images, look for ones that support linux/arm64 or arm64/v8 — most popular images do. Chapter summary A web server is simply a program that responds to browser requests with web pages — your Pi 5 can be one right now with no special hardware. python3 -m http.server 8080 instantly serves any folder as a temporary website — useful for quick tests but stops when you close the Terminal. Nginx is a proper, always-on web server installed with sudo apt install nginx ; drop HTML files into /var/www/html/ and they are immediately available on your network, even after a reboot. Docker lets you run self-hosted applications as isolated containers — one command installs a complete app without touching anything else on the Pi. Key Docker habits: always use --restart unless-stopped so apps survive reboots; always use a volume ( -v ) so your data is preserved; check docker logs first when something goes wrong. Docker Compose describes multi-container apps in a single docker-compose.yml file and starts everything with docker compose up -d ; updates are as simple as docker compose pull followed by docker compose up -d . Access your apps on the home network at http://: ; use Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Raspberry Pi Connect for safe remote access from outside your home — never open raw router ports without expert security knowledge.

title: Run AI on Your Pi
headings: What is an AI language model, in plain English?
How models are measured — and what fits on a Pi
Setting honest expectations before you start
Chatting with a model in the terminal
Controlling the model from a Python script
Using the official Ollama Python library (optional)
Other on-device AI: speech-to-text with Whisper
Simple image recognition with TensorFlow Lite
The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ — optional hardware for serious speed
Privacy: why running AI locally matters
text: This chapter tackles one of the most exciting things you can do with your Raspberry Pi 5: run a genuine artificial-intelligence language model entirely on your own device, with no internet connection required, no cloud subscription, and nothing leaving your home. It is genuinely remarkable — and with honest expectations about speed, completely achievable. The Pi 5 comes in several memory sizes (2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, and 16 GB), and the amount of RAM your model can use is the main thing that decides how large a model you can run — so this chapter works for any Pi 5, with the right model chosen to match its memory. What is an AI language model, in plain English? You have probably heard of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, or similar tools that you type questions to and receive surprisingly thoughtful answers. Behind the scenes, each of those services runs a large language model — a piece of software that has been trained to understand and generate human language. In plain words: A "large language model" (LLM) is a program that has read an enormous amount of text — books, websites, articles — and learned the patterns of how words and ideas connect. When you ask it a question, it predicts, word by word, what a useful and sensible answer looks like. It does not truly "think" or "know" things the way a person does, but the results can be remarkably helpful for writing, answering questions, summarising text, and generating code. The difference between what you see on the internet and what you can run on your Pi comes down to model size . The biggest commercial models (the ones powering ChatGPT and Gemini) have hundreds of billions of parameters and require vast data centres filled with specialised hardware. The ones you can run at home are much smaller — but still impressively capable. In plain words: "Parameters" are the millions or billions of internal numbers that a language model learned during training. Think of them like the settings on a very complicated machine. More parameters generally means a smarter model — but also one that needs more memory and runs more slowly. A model with 3 billion parameters is a small, efficient machine; a model with 70 billion parameters is a much larger one that needs far more RAM. How models are measured — and what fits on a Pi Model sizes are described in billions of parameters, written as "B". Common sizes you will encounter include 1B, 3B, 7B, 8B, and 13B. As a rough guide, the bigger the number, the smarter the answers — but also the more RAM needed and the slower it runs. There is a clever technique called quantisation that makes models much more practical for home hardware. In plain words: "Quantisation" is a form of compression applied to an AI model. The original model stores each parameter as a precise 32-bit or 16-bit number. Quantisation rounds those numbers down to 4 bits or 8 bits each — losing a tiny amount of accuracy but shrinking the model to roughly one quarter or one eighth of its original size. A 7B model that would normally need about 14 GB of RAM can, after 4-bit quantisation, fit in around 4–5 GB. The quality difference is usually small enough that you will not notice it for everyday tasks. The amount of RAM your Pi 5 has is the main limit on the size of model you can run — quite simply, the more RAM your Pi 5 has, the larger the model you can run. The Pi 5 is sold in 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, and 16 GB versions. A 2 GB or 4 GB Pi handles the small, fast 1B–3B models comfortably, while leaving enough memory for the operating system to keep running smoothly alongside them. An 8 GB Pi opens the door to 7B models, and a 16 GB Pi can run 7B–8B models with room to spare and even squeeze in a 13B model. Whatever size your Pi 5 is, there is a capable model that will fit — you simply match the model to the memory you have. Model size Approx. RAM needed (4-bit quantised) Which Pi 5 can run it? Speed (tokens/second, approx.) 1B parameters ~1 GB Any Pi 5 (2 GB and up), easily 15–30 tokens/sec (fast) 3B parameters ~2–3 GB 4 GB and up, easily 8–15 tokens/sec (comfortable) 7B–8B parameters ~5–6 GB 8 GB and up, with room to spare 3–7 tokens/sec (readable) 13B parameters ~9–10 GB 16 GB only, just fits 1–3 tokens/sec (slow but usable) 70B parameters ~45+ GB No Pi 5 — not enough RAM N/A Note: "Tokens per second" is how AI speed is measured. A token is roughly three quarters of a word on average — so 5 tokens per second is about 4 words per second. That is slower than a fast typist but perfectly readable as the text appears on screen, one word at a time. Setting honest expectations before you start Before installing anything, please read this section — it will save you frustration. Speed: Your Pi 5 runs AI on its main processor (CPU), not on a specialised AI chip. Expect text to appear at a readable pace — roughly like watching someone type — not instantly. A 7B model generating a paragraph may take 15–30 seconds. Smaller models are noticeably faster. No image generation: Generating photorealistic images (like Stable Diffusion does) requires a powerful graphics card. The Pi 5 cannot do this at any practical speed. What we cover here is text — asking questions and getting answers. Context length: Small models have a limited "memory" within a conversation. If you have a very long chat, the model may forget what was said at the beginning. Accuracy: Small local models can make mistakes or "hallucinate" (confidently state something false). Always verify important facts from other sources. Privacy: This is the genuine superpower. Everything stays on your device. No company sees your prompts, no data is sent anywhere, and it works with no internet connection at all. For sensitive documents, personal questions, or offline environments, this is a real advantage. Cloud AI (ChatGPT etc.) Your device (prompt typed here) Internet Data Centre Answer returned Your prompts travel over the internet and are processed on remote servers. Requires internet. Data leaves device. Local AI (your Pi 5) Raspberry Pi 5 Prompt ► Ollama ► Model All processing stays here Answer ◄◄◄◄◄◄◄◄ Everything happens inside your Pi. Works offline. Nothing sent anywhere. Private. No subscription needed. Cloud AI sends your prompts across the internet to remote servers. Local AI on your Pi processes everything on your own device — privately, offline, and free. Installing Ollama Ollama is a free, open-source tool that makes running AI models on your own computer as simple as typing one command. It handles downloading models, setting them up, and providing a straightforward way to chat with them. It also runs a small local web server in the background so that programs (like Python scripts) can send it questions and receive answers automatically. Open a Terminal window (click the black screen icon in the taskbar, or go to the Applications menu and look under Accessories). Then type the following command exactly and press Enter: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh This is a single command split into two parts connected by a pipe ( | ): curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh — curl is a program that fetches content from the internet. The flags -fsSL tell it to fail silently if something goes wrong ( -f ), suppress the progress bar ( -s ), still show errors if they occur ( -S ), and follow any web redirects ( -L ). The result is the Ollama installation script, downloaded directly into memory. | sh — the pipe sends that downloaded script straight to sh (the shell, your command interpreter), which runs it immediately. This is a common one-line installation pattern in Linux. In plain English: download the official Ollama installer and run it. The script detects that you are on a Raspberry Pi (Linux, 64-bit ARM) and installs the correct version automatically. You will see progress messages scrolling past. When you see your terminal prompt ( pi@raspberrypi:~ $ ) again, installation is complete. Careful: Running a script piped directly from the internet grants it full control over your system. Only do this for trusted, well-known projects. Ollama is a reputable open-source project at ollama.com — but as a general rule, always check the URL carefully before running such a command. Confirm the installation was successful by asking Ollama for its version number: ollama --version ollama --version — runs the ollama program with the --version flag, which asks it to print which version is installed. If you see something like ollama version 0.9.x , everything worked. If you see "command not found", close the terminal window, open a fresh one, and try again — a new terminal session picks up the newly installed program. Note: Ollama also installs itself as a background service that starts automatically every time your Pi boots. This means the AI server will always be ready when you want to use it, without any extra steps. Pulling your first model Ollama uses the word "pull" to mean "download a model from the internet and store it on your Pi". You only need to do this once per model — afterwards it lives on your microSD card and works completely offline. In plain words: "Pulling" a model is similar to downloading an app. Once downloaded, you run it locally — no internet needed to use it, only to download it the first time. Start with a small, fast model to make sure everything works. Gemma 3 1B is Google's efficient 1-billion-parameter model, quantised to fit in about 800 MB. It downloads quickly and is a good first test: ollama pull gemma3:1b ollama pull gemma3:1b — tells Ollama to download the Gemma 3 model at the "1b" (1 billion parameter) size. The part after the colon ( :1b ) is the tag , which selects which size or variant you want. Ollama will display a download progress bar. The file is about 815 MB, so on typical home broadband this takes one to three minutes. Once that has downloaded, try a more capable model. Llama 3.2 3B is Meta's 3-billion-parameter model — noticeably smarter than Gemma 1B but still quick on your Pi: ollama pull llama3.2:3b ollama pull llama3.2:3b — downloads Meta's Llama 3.2 model at the 3-billion-parameter size. This is around 2 GB and takes a few minutes. It gives clearly better answers than the 1B model for most everyday tasks, while still running at a comfortable speed. If your Pi 5 has 8 GB or 16 GB of RAM, you can pull an 8-billion-parameter model for the best quality. This takes longer to download (around 5 GB) and generates text more slowly, but produces impressively thorough answers. (On a 2 GB or 4 GB Pi, skip this one and stick with the 1B and 3B models above — there is not enough memory for an 8B model to run well.) The recommended 8B model is Llama 3.1 8B (note: Meta's Llama 3.2 series only goes up to 3B; the 8B model belongs to the Llama 3.1 series): ollama pull llama3.1:8b ollama pull llama3.1:8b — downloads the 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model. At approximately 4.7 GB download size, it uses around 5–6 GB of RAM while running — comfortable on an 8 GB or 16 GB Pi 5. Many users find this the best balance of quality and speed for a home device. Expect the download to take 15–30 minutes on typical home broadband. Note: Model names and available tags change over time as new models are released. To see the full catalogue, visit ollama.com/library in your web browser. Popular choices for beginners include gemma3 , llama3.2 , llama3.1 , phi4 (Microsoft — very strong for its size), and mistral (excellent for summarisation). Each model has different strengths; feel free to experiment. To see all the models you have downloaded so far: ollama list ollama list — displays a table of every AI model currently stored on your Pi, including its name, tag, file size, and when it was last used. Use this to keep track of what you have downloaded and how much space each model takes. Chatting with a model in the terminal Now comes the rewarding part. To start a conversation with a model, use ollama run followed by the model name: ollama run llama3.2:3b ollama run llama3.2:3b — loads the Llama 3.2 3B model into your Pi's RAM and starts an interactive chat session right in the terminal. The first time you run a model after a reboot, there may be a short pause of a few seconds while it is loaded into memory. Once you see the >>> prompt appear, the model is ready and waiting for your message. After a brief loading pause, you will see a prompt like this: >>> Send a message (/? for help) The >>> is Ollama's interactive chat prompt. Type your question or message and press Enter. The model will begin generating a response, word by word. When it finishes, the >>> prompt returns and you can ask another question. The model remembers everything said earlier in the session, so you can have a natural back-and-forth conversation. Try typing something like this at the prompt: >>> Explain what a Raspberry Pi is, in two sentences, for someone who has never heard of one. Type this (or any question you like) after the >>> prompt and press Enter. Words will appear one by one at a comfortable reading pace. On a 3B model, a two-sentence answer typically takes about 5–10 seconds. On the 8B model, expect 15–25 seconds for the same question. When you want to end the conversation and return to the normal terminal, type: /bye /bye — a special Ollama command (note the slash at the start, which distinguishes it from a question you would type to the model) that ends the chat session, unloads the model from memory, and returns you to the normal terminal prompt. You can also press Ctrl + D to exit. Tip: Inside an Ollama chat session, type /? and press Enter to see all available slash commands. Useful ones include /clear (start a fresh conversation, making the model forget everything said so far), /show info (display technical details about the currently loaded model), and /set system "..." (give the model a persona or background instructions, for example /set system "You are a friendly French tutor" ). How an Ollama chat session works You type a question Ollama receives prompt AI Model generates reply answer returned, word by word Answer appears Everything stays on your Pi. No internet required. The model remembers your whole conversation until you type /bye. How Ollama processes a chat: your question goes to the local model, which generates a reply word by word — all within your Pi. Controlling the model from a Python script Chatting in the terminal is enjoyable, but the real power comes from writing Python programs that can talk to the AI model automatically. Ollama runs a small web server in the background at all times while it is installed — your programs can send it questions and receive answers using simple web requests. In plain words: A "web server" is a program that listens for requests and sends back responses — just like a website, but running locally on your own Pi. Ollama's built-in server listens at the address http://localhost:11434 . "Localhost" means "this very machine" — the request never leaves your Pi. Your Python script sends a prompt to that address, and Ollama sends back the AI's answer. Open Thonny (the Python editor — find it in the Programming section of the Applications menu). Create a new file, paste in the script below, and save it as ai_chat.py in your home folder. This script uses only Python's built-in libraries, so no extra installation is needed. import urllib.request import json MODEL = "llama3.2:3b" def ask(prompt): url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" data = { "model": MODEL, "prompt": prompt, "stream": False } body = json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8") req = urllib.request.Request( url, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST" ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: result = json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8")) return result["response"] question = "What are three good reasons to learn Python programming?" print("Asking the AI:", question) print() answer = ask(question) print("AI says:") print(answer) Here is what each part of this script does: import urllib.request — loads Python's built-in tool for making web requests. We use this to talk to Ollama's local server. Using the built-in library means no extra packages need to be installed. import json — loads Python's built-in JSON tool. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a simple text format used to package data — it looks like {"key": "value"} . Ollama communicates using JSON. MODEL = "llama3.2:3b" — stores the model name in a variable so it is easy to change in one place. To use a different model, just update this line. def ask(prompt): — defines a reusable function called ask . You give it a question (the prompt ) and it returns the AI's answer. Everything indented below this line is part of the function. url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" — this is Ollama's local web address for text generation. localhost means "this Pi", 11434 is the port Ollama listens on (a port is like a numbered door on a server), and /api/generate is the specific endpoint that accepts prompts. data = {...} — creates a Python dictionary (a collection of labelled values) containing the request. model tells Ollama which model to use, prompt is the question, and "stream": False tells Ollama to wait until the full answer is ready before sending it back all at once (rather than word by word). body = json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8") — converts the Python dictionary into a JSON-formatted text string, then encodes it into bytes (the raw binary format needed for sending over a network). req = urllib.request.Request(...) — builds a web request object specifying the URL, the data to send, a header telling Ollama the data is in JSON format, and POST as the HTTP method (meaning "send data to this address and expect a response"). with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as response: — sends the request to Ollama and opens the response. The with keyword ensures the network connection is cleanly closed when we are done reading. result = json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8")) — reads the raw bytes of the response, decodes them into a text string, and parses the JSON into a Python dictionary we can work with. return result["response"] — extracts just the AI's text answer from the dictionary and returns it. Ollama's reply contains several fields; the actual generated text is under the key "response" . question = "What are three good reasons..." — stores the question we want to ask. Change this to anything you like. print("Asking the AI:", question) — prints the question to the screen so you can see what was sent. answer = ask(question) — calls our ask function, sending the question to Ollama and waiting for the answer. This may take 10–30 seconds depending on the model and question length. print("AI says:") / print(answer) — prints the AI's response to the output panel at the bottom of Thonny. Note: Before running this script, make sure Ollama is running in the background. Because Ollama installs as a system service, it starts automatically when your Pi boots. You can verify it is running by opening a terminal and typing ollama list — if it shows your models without an error, the server is ready. To run the script in Thonny, click the green Run button (the triangle) in the toolbar, or press F5 . After a wait of 10–30 seconds, you should see the AI's answer printed in the panel at the bottom of Thonny. Tip: Change the question variable to anything you like — ask it to summarise a paragraph of text you paste in, suggest a recipe, explain a concept, or help you draft an email. To use a smaller, faster model, change MODEL to "gemma3:1b" . For more thoughtful answers at the cost of extra waiting time, change it to "llama3.1:8b" . Using the official Ollama Python library (optional) The script above uses only Python's built-in libraries, which is great for learning. However, if you want a cleaner way to work with Ollama in Python, there is an official ollama library that simplifies the code considerably. Because Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm manages system Python packages carefully, the safest way to install it is inside a virtual environment . In plain words: A "virtual environment" is a self-contained folder that holds a private copy of Python and any extra libraries you install into it. It keeps your project's packages separate from the rest of the system, avoiding conflicts. Think of it as a clean, isolated workbench just for one project. Open a terminal and create a folder for your AI project, then create a virtual environment inside it: mkdir ~/ai-project cd ~/ai-project python3 -m venv venv mkdir ~/ai-project — creates a new folder called ai-project in your home directory ( ~ is a shortcut for your home folder). cd ~/ai-project — moves into that new folder. python3 -m venv venv — creates a virtual environment in a subfolder called venv . The -m venv part tells Python to run its built-in virtual environment tool. Activate the virtual environment and install the Ollama library: source venv/bin/activate pip install ollama source venv/bin/activate — activates the virtual environment. Your terminal prompt will change to show (venv) at the start, confirming it is active. While active, any pip install commands install packages only inside this private environment, not system-wide. pip install ollama — downloads and installs the official Ollama Python library from the Python Package Index (PyPI). This is safe inside a virtual environment. Create a new Python file called ai_simple.py in the same folder with the following content: import ollama response = ollama.generate( model="llama3.2:3b", prompt="Explain in two sentences what the Raspberry Pi 5 is good for." ) print(response["response"]) import ollama — loads the Ollama library you just installed. response = ollama.generate(...) — sends a prompt to your locally running Ollama server and waits for the full answer. The model and prompt arguments work just like in the manual version earlier. print(response["response"]) — prints the AI's text answer to the screen. Run the script from the terminal (make sure the virtual environment is still active): python3 ai_simple.py python3 ai_simple.py — runs your Python script. After 10–30 seconds, the AI's answer will be printed in the terminal. When you have finished working in the virtual environment, type deactivate and press Enter to return to the normal terminal. Note: When you return to this project in the future, you will need to activate the virtual environment again before running your scripts: navigate to the folder ( cd ~/ai-project ) and then run source venv/bin/activate . Your prompt will show (venv) to confirm it is active. Managing your models — saving space Each AI model takes up significant space on your microSD card — anywhere from 800 MB to 5 GB or more. To see how much space is currently used, run: ollama list ollama list — shows all downloaded models with their sizes. Use this to decide which models to keep and which to remove. If you want to remove a model you no longer use, simply run: ollama rm llama3.1:8b ollama rm llama3.1:8b — deletes the specified model from your Pi, freeing up the disk space it was using. Replace llama3.1:8b with whichever model name you want to remove. You can always re-download it later with ollama pull . Tip: If your microSD card is getting full, start by removing larger models you do not use regularly. The 8B model takes nearly 5 GB, while the 1B model is under 1 GB. Keep whichever model you use most, and re-download others as needed. Other on-device AI: speech-to-text with Whisper Language models are not the only AI you can run locally. Whisper , made by OpenAI and released as open-source software, is a speech-to-text system — it listens to an audio recording and converts it to written text. A fast compiled version called whisper.cpp runs well on the Pi 5 CPU without needing any cloud service. In plain words: "Speech-to-text" means automatically turning spoken words into written ones — like live captions or a dictation tool. "Compiling from source code" means downloading the program as raw instructions and building it into a runnable application on your own computer. It takes a few minutes but is a one-time step. Installing whisper.cpp requires building it from source code. Here are the full steps: Install the build tools needed to compile the program: sudo apt install -y build-essential git sudo apt install -y build-essential git — installs two packages. build-essential provides the compiler (the tool that turns source code into a runnable program), and git is a tool for downloading source code from the internet. The -y flag automatically confirms all prompts. Download the whisper.cpp source code to your Pi: git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp — copies (clones) the entire whisper.cpp project from GitHub onto your Pi into a new folder called whisper.cpp . This is the source code you will compile in the next step. Enter the folder and compile the program: cd whisper.cpp make -j4 cd whisper.cpp — moves into the newly downloaded folder. make -j4 — compiles the source code into a runnable program. The -j4 flag tells make to use all four CPU cores of your Pi 5 simultaneously, which speeds up the build significantly. This step typically takes 2–5 minutes. You will see many lines of output scrolling past — this is normal. Download a small English speech model: bash ./models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en bash ./models/download-ggml-model.sh base.en — runs the download script included with whisper.cpp to fetch the "base" English model. base.en is a fast, reasonably accurate model optimised for English speech. It is about 140 MB. Larger models ( small.en , medium.en ) are more accurate but slower. Transcribe an audio file (it must be in WAV format): ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-base.en.bin -f your_recording.wav ./build/bin/whisper-cli — runs the whisper.cpp transcription program that was built in step 3. The ./ prefix means "in the current folder". -m models/ggml-base.en.bin — tells whisper.cpp which model file to use (the one downloaded in step 4). -f your_recording.wav — specifies the audio file to transcribe. Replace your_recording.wav with the actual filename of your audio file. The file must be in WAV format (you can convert MP3 or other formats using the ffmpeg tool: sudo apt install -y ffmpeg , then ffmpeg -i input.mp3 output.wav ). Note: Whisper can also transcribe other languages and even detect the language automatically, using larger multilingual models (remove the .en from the model name, e.g. base instead of base.en ). It is useful for transcribing voice memos, meeting recordings, or interview audio — entirely on your own device, with no data sent anywhere. Simple image recognition with TensorFlow Lite For basic image recognition (identifying everyday objects in photographs), the Pi 5's VideoCore VII graphics processor can accelerate lightweight models using TensorFlow Lite , which is available directly through the apt package manager. In plain words: "Image recognition" means teaching a computer to identify what is in a photograph — a cat, a car, a banana. TensorFlow Lite is a lightweight version of Google's machine-learning framework, designed specifically for small devices like the Raspberry Pi. It uses pre-trained models, meaning the AI has already been taught to recognise thousands of objects; you just need to give it a photo. sudo apt install -y python3-tflite-runtime sudo apt install -y python3-tflite-runtime — installs TensorFlow Lite for Python 3 directly from the official Raspberry Pi OS software repository. This is the recommended method on Bookworm because it uses the system package manager rather than pip, avoiding any conflicts with the system Python. The -y flag automatically confirms the installation. With TensorFlow Lite installed, you can run pre-trained image classification models to identify everyday objects in photos taken with a Raspberry Pi Camera or loaded from files. The Raspberry Pi Foundation's official documentation at raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/camera_software.html contains complete step-by-step examples with sample code. Tip: A good beginner project combining TensorFlow Lite and the Pi Camera is a "bird feeder identifier" — a Pi with a camera pointed at a bird feeder that automatically logs which species visit, entirely without a cloud service. The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ — optional hardware for serious speed If you find that the Pi 5's CPU speed is too slow for your AI ambitions, there is an optional add-on board made by the Raspberry Pi Foundation called the AI HAT+ . It contains a Hailo-8L neural network accelerator chip that connects to the Pi's PCIe slot. In plain words: A "neural network accelerator" is a chip specially designed to perform the mathematical operations that AI models need, far faster than a general-purpose CPU can. Think of it as adding a dedicated AI co-processor to your Pi. The PCIe slot (a small connector on the underside of the Pi 5 board) is a high-speed data connection; the AI HAT+ uses it to communicate at maximum speed. The AI HAT+ provides up to 13 TOPS (Tera Operations Per Second) of AI processing power, which is roughly 10–20 times faster than the Pi 5 CPU alone for vision tasks. It is designed particularly for real-time video analysis — detecting people, vehicles, faces, or objects in a live camera stream at full frame rates. Task type Best approach on Pi 5 Why Chat / text generation (LLMs) Ollama on CPU LLMs run on CPU RAM; AI HAT+ does not accelerate them significantly Real-time object detection in video AI HAT+ (optional) HAT+ is 10–20× faster for vision models; CPU is too slow for real-time video Speech-to-text (Whisper) CPU (whisper.cpp) Works well on Pi 5 CPU; HAT+ does not help here Image classification (TensorFlow Lite) CPU or AI HAT+ CPU fine for single images; HAT+ needed for live video classification Note: The AI HAT+ is available from official Raspberry Pi retailers for approximately £50–70 (around €55–80 in mainland Europe). Installation involves fitting it onto the 40-pin GPIO header and connecting a short ribbon cable to the PCIe slot — straightforward but it adds significant height, so check your case has room (an open-top or tall case works best). Privacy: why running AI locally matters Cloud AI services — ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and others — are powerful, but every question you type is sent to servers owned by a company, stored, potentially used to improve future models, and subject to that company's privacy policy, data protection laws, and any future policy changes. When you run AI on your Pi: Your prompts never leave your home network. Your questions are not stored or logged by any company. It works with no internet connection at all — useful on a train, in a remote location, or anywhere connectivity is limited or expensive. There is no subscription fee. Once downloaded, the model is yours to use indefinitely. You are in complete control of what model is running and how it behaves. This makes local AI genuinely useful for tasks involving personal information — summarising private documents, asking questions about medical or financial topics you would rather keep private, or working with confidential text. Tip: If you would like a proper graphical chat interface (similar to the ChatGPT website, but talking to your local models), search for Open WebUI — a free, open-source web application that connects to Ollama and runs on your Pi. You access it by opening a browser on your Pi and going to http://localhost:3000 after installation. Full instructions are at openwebui.com . Troubleshooting common problems Ollama says "command not found" after installation Close your terminal window and open a fresh one. The installation adds Ollama to your PATH (the list of locations the terminal searches for commands), and a new terminal session picks up the change automatically. If the problem persists, type the following and try again: source ~/.bashrc ollama --version source ~/.bashrc — reloads your shell configuration file without closing and reopening the terminal. This picks up any changes made to your PATH during installation. ollama --version — checks whether Ollama is now found and prints its version number. If this still fails, try restarting your Pi ( sudo reboot ) and trying again. The model download is very slow AI models are large files — 1–5 GB is normal. On a typical home broadband connection this takes anywhere from 5 minutes to half an hour. Connect your Pi via an Ethernet cable rather than Wi-Fi for a faster and more reliable download. Downloads can be resumed — if a download is interrupted, just run the same ollama pull command again and it will continue from where it left off. Running a model makes the Pi very sluggish While a large model is generating text, it uses most of the Pi's CPU. This is normal and expected — wait for the response to finish and the Pi will return to its normal responsiveness. If things are uncomfortably slow, switch to a smaller model (for example, gemma3:1b instead of llama3.1:8b ). You can also close other applications while the model is generating. The Python script says "Connection refused" Ollama's background server may not be running. Check its status with: sudo systemctl status ollama sudo systemctl status ollama — checks whether the Ollama background service is currently running. You will see either Active: active (running) highlighted in green, meaning all is well, or a stopped or failed status. If it is not running, start it with the next command. If it is stopped, start it manually: sudo systemctl start ollama sudo systemctl start ollama — starts the Ollama service immediately. To make it start automatically every time the Pi boots (which is the default after installation), run sudo systemctl enable ollama . The model gives wrong or strange answers This is a known limitation of all current language models, especially smaller ones. It is called hallucination — the model confidently produces text that sounds plausible but is factually incorrect. Always verify important information from a reliable source. Smaller models hallucinate more often than larger ones. Providing more context in your prompt often helps: instead of "What is the boiling point of water?", try "You are a physics teacher. Please explain the boiling point of water at sea level." Whisper.cpp build fails with an error Make sure build-essential and git are installed (run sudo apt install -y build-essential git again). Also ensure you have enough free disk space — the build process temporarily needs several hundred megabytes. Run df -h ~ to check how much free space you have on your microSD card. df -h ~ df -h ~ — shows the disk usage of the filesystem where your home folder lives. The -h flag makes the sizes human-readable (showing GB or MB rather than raw bytes). The "Available" column tells you how much free space remains. You need at least 1 GB free for the build, plus space for model files. Key terms Large Language Model (LLM) — a type of AI program trained on vast amounts of text, capable of understanding and generating human language. Parameters — the numerical values learned during AI training; measured in billions (e.g. 7B = 7 billion). More parameters generally means a more capable but larger, slower model. Quantisation — a compression technique that reduces a model's file size and RAM usage by storing its numbers at lower precision, with only a small loss of quality. Ollama — a free, open-source tool for downloading and running AI language models locally on your own device. Tag — the part after the colon in an Ollama model name (e.g. :3b , :8b ) that specifies which size or variant of a model to download. Token — roughly three quarters of a word; the unit AI models use internally. "Tokens per second" measures how fast a model generates text. Localhost — a special network address meaning "this computer itself". Ollama's local server is accessed at http://localhost:11434 , which never leaves your Pi. Port — a numbered "door" on a server that allows different services to listen on the same machine. Ollama uses port 11434. API — Application Programming Interface; a defined way for programs to talk to each other. Ollama provides an API so Python scripts can send prompts and receive answers automatically. Virtual environment — a self-contained folder holding a private copy of Python and its installed packages, keeping a project's dependencies separate from the rest of the system. Hallucination — when an AI model confidently generates text that is factually incorrect. A known limitation of all current language models, more common in smaller models. Whisper / whisper.cpp — an open-source speech-to-text AI made by OpenAI; whisper.cpp is a fast compiled version that runs efficiently on the Pi 5 CPU. TensorFlow Lite — a lightweight machine-learning framework for small devices, used for image classification and other AI tasks on the Pi without a cloud service. AI HAT+ — an optional Raspberry Pi add-on board containing a Hailo neural network accelerator chip, dramatically speeding up real-time vision AI tasks. PCIe — a high-speed hardware connection on the Pi 5 used by add-on boards like the AI HAT+ to communicate at fast data rates. TOPS — Tera Operations Per Second; a measure of AI chip performance. The AI HAT+'s Hailo chip delivers up to 13 TOPS. Chapter summary A large language model (LLM) is an AI program trained on text; it generates answers word by word based on patterns it learned during training. Model size is measured in billions of parameters (1B, 3B, 7B, 8B…); larger models give better answers but need more RAM and run more slowly. Quantisation compresses models to roughly a quarter of their original size with minimal quality loss, making 7B–8B models practical on home hardware. RAM is the main limit on model size: a 2–4 GB Pi 5 runs 1B–3B models, an 8 GB Pi runs 7B models, and a 16 GB Pi runs 7B–8B (even 13B) models — match the model to the memory your Pi 5 has. Ollama installs with a single terminal command and handles downloading, storing, and running models automatically; it also starts as a background service on every boot. Use ollama pull <name> to download a model, ollama run <name> to chat interactively, and ollama list to see what is stored. Note that Llama 3.2 only comes in 1B and 3B sizes; the recommended 8B model is llama3.1:8b . A Python script using only built-in libraries can send prompts to Ollama's local API and display the AI's answers; the optional ollama Python library simplifies this further when used inside a virtual environment. Whisper.cpp provides offline speech-to-text; TensorFlow Lite enables image recognition — both run on the Pi CPU without any cloud service. The optional Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ (Hailo accelerator) dramatically speeds up vision tasks like real-time object detection; it does not significantly help text generation. Running AI locally means complete privacy — your prompts never leave your device, no subscription is needed, and it works with no internet connection. Expect text to appear at a readable but modest pace; small models can hallucinate (state incorrect facts confidently), so always verify important information elsewhere.

title: Security & Good Habits
headings: Step One: Change the Default Password
Step Two: Keep the System Updated
Step Three: SSH Keys — Log In Without a Password
Step Four: A Simple Firewall with ufw
Step Five: Do Not Expose the Pi Directly to the Internet
Step Six: fail2ban — Blocking Repeated Bad Login Attempts
Step Seven: Disable Unused Interfaces with raspi-config
Step Eight: Backups as a Security Measure
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is a capable little computer — and like any computer connected to a network, it deserves a few sensible precautions. This chapter walks you through the most important habits: locking down access, keeping software fresh, adding a firewall, and protecting the hardware itself. None of it requires a security background — just a few minutes of your time and a willingness to follow the steps. Why Bother with Security? A Raspberry Pi running on your home network is unlikely to be attacked within minutes of being switched on. But over time, a few real risks build up: Anyone on your Wi-Fi — a guest, a compromised smart TV, or a neighbour who knows your password — could log in to the Pi if it still uses the default password. If you ever open the Pi to the internet, even for a few minutes, automated scanners called "bots" will find it and try common passwords within hours. An out-of-date system may have known security holes that are trivially exploited. The good news is that a handful of straightforward steps make the Pi extremely resistant to the vast majority of threats, without turning your life into a cybersecurity course. Step One: Change the Default Password When you first set up Raspberry Pi OS, the installer asked you to create a username and password. If you skipped that step or used something obvious like raspberry , now is the time to fix it. Careful: The old default username was pi and the old default password was raspberry . Many automated attack scripts try this combination first. If your Pi still uses them, change both immediately. What makes a strong password? A strong password is long, random, and unique — used nowhere else. You do not need to memorise a string of symbols; a passphrase made of four or five random words is both memorable and very secure. For example: kettle-purple-moon-46-fence is far stronger than P@ssw0rd! . In plain words: A passphrase is a password made of several words strung together. Length beats complexity — a 30-character passphrase of common words is harder to crack than an 8-character mix of symbols. To change your password, open a Terminal on the Pi (or connect via SSH) and run: passwd This command opens the "change password" tool for your own user account. It will ask you to type your current password, then ask you to type the new password twice to confirm it. The characters you type will not appear on screen — this is normal and deliberate. Tip: Use a password manager (such as Bitwarden, which is free) to generate and store a strong, unique password. You only need to remember one master password, and the manager handles everything else. Checking for other user accounts On a freshly set-up Pi 5 running Bookworm there should only be your own user account (plus the system root account that runs in the background). It is worth confirming no unexpected accounts exist: awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 && $1 != "nobody" { print $1 }' /etc/passwd This command reads the file /etc/passwd (which lists every user account on the system) and prints only the ones with a user ID of 1000 or above. Those are the "real" human user accounts. On a fresh Pi you should see just your own username. If you see names you do not recognise, investigate before continuing. Note: The root account is a special all-powerful administrator account built into Linux. On Raspberry Pi OS, the root account does not have a password set and cannot be logged into directly — you use sudo instead. Do not set a root password unless you have a specific reason to. Step Two: Keep the System Updated Software updates fix security vulnerabilities — holes that attackers could use to take control. Running apt regularly is one of the single most effective things you can do. In plain words: apt is the Raspberry Pi OS package manager — the tool that downloads and installs software and updates from the official Raspberry Pi and Debian servers. We covered this in detail in Chapter 6. As a recap, run these two commands: sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade -y Line 1 — sudo apt update : Downloads the latest list of available packages and versions from the internet. It does not change anything on your system yet — it only refreshes the catalogue. Line 2 — sudo apt full-upgrade -y : Installs every available update, including updates that require removing or replacing existing packages (which is what full-upgrade does that plain upgrade does not). The -y flag answers "yes" automatically to any confirmation prompts. Tip: Make this a habit — run it once a week, or at least once a month. It takes only a minute or two on a fast connection. Automatic security updates If you want the Pi to install security-related updates on its own in the background, you can install the unattended-upgrades package: sudo apt install unattended-upgrades -y sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades Line 1: Installs the unattended-upgrades tool, which can apply security updates automatically without you needing to run apt manually. Line 2: Opens a simple text-based configuration screen asking whether you want automatic updates enabled. Choose Yes . The tool will then download and apply official security patches in the background each day. Note: Unattended-upgrades only installs security updates automatically. Major version upgrades and new software still require your manual approval. Step Three: SSH Keys — Log In Without a Password In Chapter 11 you learned to connect to the Pi remotely using SSH (Secure Shell). By default, SSH asks for your password every time. There is a smarter, more secure method: SSH keys . Once set up, you never type a password to SSH in — and you can disable password login entirely, which blocks automated attackers completely. What is an SSH key pair? In plain words: An SSH key pair is a pair of matching digital files — a public key (like a padlock) and a private key (like the only key that opens that padlock). You put the public key (the padlock) on the Pi. You keep the private key (the opening key) on your main computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux). When you connect, your computer proves it holds the matching key — without ever sending the key itself over the network. No password is needed. The private key must stay on your main computer and never be shared. The public key can be placed on any number of servers — it is safe to share because it can only be used to verify the private key, never to impersonate it. Your computer Private Key (secret) Keep this file safe! proves match (no password) Raspberry Pi Public Key (padlock) ~/.ssh/authorized_keys You keep this Pi stores this How SSH key authentication works: your PC holds the private key; the Pi holds the matching public key. A connection is granted only when the two match — no password is transmitted. Generating a key pair on your computer Every modern desktop operating system ships with a built-in SSH client, so you do not need to install anything extra. The ssh-keygen command below is identical on all three — only the way you open a terminal differs: Windows: open a PowerShell (or Windows Terminal) window — press Win + X and choose "Terminal" or "PowerShell". macOS: open the Terminal app (in Applications → Utilities, or search for it with Spotlight). Linux: open your usual terminal application.
