In the terminal window, type the following and press Enter: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my-pi-key" ssh-keygen : The key-generation program built into Windows, macOS, and Linux alike. -t ed25519 : Tells it to use the Ed25519 algorithm — a modern, fast, secure algorithm that produces short keys. This is the recommended choice over the older RSA algorithm. -C "my-pi-key" : Adds a comment label to the key so you can identify it later (you can use any text you like here). The program asks: Enter file in which to save the key . Press Enter to accept the default location (on Windows that is C:\Users\YourName\.ssh\id_ed25519 ; on macOS and Linux it is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ). Two files will be created: id_ed25519 — your private key. Never share this file. id_ed25519.pub — your public key. This is the one you will copy to the Pi. The program then asks for a passphrase . This is an optional extra layer of protection: if someone steals the private key file, they still cannot use it without this passphrase. You can press Enter twice to skip it, but setting a passphrase is recommended — every operating system can remember it for you via a feature called the SSH Agent, so you only type it once per session. Note: If you already have a key pair from a previous project (you see a message like "already exists"), you can reuse it — just press n when asked to overwrite, and skip to the next section. Copying the public key to the Pi Now you need to place the public key into a special file on the Pi called ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . There are two ways to do this. In plain words: The tilde ( ~ ) is a shortcut that means "your home folder". So ~/.ssh/authorized_keys means the file named authorized_keys inside the hidden .ssh folder inside your home folder on the Pi. Method A — using ssh-copy-id (easiest, on macOS, Linux, or Git Bash) On macOS and Linux the ssh-copy-id helper is built in. On Windows, the built-in PowerShell does not include it, but if you have Git for Windows installed (which gives you Git Bash), you have it there. Wherever ssh-copy-id is available, run: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub yourname@raspberrypi.local ssh-copy-id : A helper tool that reads your public key and appends it to the authorized_keys file on the remote machine automatically. -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub : Tells it which public key file to use. yourname@raspberrypi.local : Replace yourname with the username you chose when you set up the Pi, and raspberrypi.local with the Pi's hostname or IP address. It will ask for your Pi's password one last time to authenticate and copy the key. Method B — paste it manually (works on any computer) On your computer, display the contents of your public key so you can copy it. On Windows (PowerShell), run: Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub" On macOS or Linux (Terminal), run instead: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub This reads and prints the contents of your public key file to the screen. The output is one long line starting with ssh-ed25519 . Select it all and copy it to your clipboard (Ctrl+C on Windows/Linux, Cmd+C on macOS). Now SSH into the Pi using your password as normal: ssh yourname@raspberrypi.local Opens an SSH session to the Pi, logging in with your password as before. Replace yourname and raspberrypi.local with your actual username and Pi address. On the Pi, create the .ssh directory if it does not already exist, and open the authorized_keys file: mkdir -p ~/.ssh chmod 700 ~/.ssh nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Line 1 — mkdir -p ~/.ssh : Creates the hidden .ssh folder in your home directory. The -p flag means "don't complain if it already exists". Line 2 — chmod 700 ~/.ssh : Sets the folder's permissions so that only your own user account can read or write it. SSH refuses to work if the folder permissions are too open. Line 3 — nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys : Opens the nano text editor to create (or edit) the authorized_keys file. In the nano editor, paste the public key you just copied (right-click in the terminal window to paste, or use Ctrl+Shift+V). It must be all on one single line. Press Ctrl + X , then Y , then Enter to save and exit. Set correct permissions on the file: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Sets the authorized_keys file to be readable and writable only by your own user. SSH will refuse to use the file if anyone else can read it — this permission setting satisfies that requirement. Testing the key login Without closing your current SSH session (keep it open as a safety net in case something goes wrong), open a new terminal window (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS or Linux) and try connecting: ssh yourname@raspberrypi.local If the key is set up correctly, the Pi will log you in without asking for a password — it silently verified your private key against the stored public key. If it still asks for a password, re-check that you pasted the key correctly on a single line with no extra spaces, and that the file permissions on the Pi are exactly 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . Optionally disabling password login (advanced — read carefully first) Once key login is confirmed to be working, you can disable password authentication entirely. This means only computers that hold the correct private key can log in via SSH — brute-force password guessing becomes impossible. Careful: If you disable password login and then lose your private key (for example, your computer fails and you had no backup), you will be permanently locked out of SSH. Before doing this, either back up your key files to a USB drive or cloud storage, or make sure you have a keyboard and monitor you can plug into the Pi so you can still log in locally. Confirm key login works perfectly before taking this step. On the Pi, open the SSH server configuration file: sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config Opens the SSH server configuration file in the nano text editor with administrator ( sudo ) privileges. This file controls how the SSH server behaves. Find the line that says PasswordAuthentication . If it starts with a # , that means it is commented out (ignored). Remove the # and change the line to read exactly: PasswordAuthentication no This line tells the SSH server to refuse password-based login attempts. Only key-based authentication will be accepted. Make sure the line does not start with a # character — a # at the start means the setting is ignored. Save the file ( Ctrl + X , then Y , then Enter ), then restart the SSH service: sudo systemctl restart ssh Restarts the SSH server so it reads the new configuration. Your current SSH session stays open — the restart only affects new connections from this point onward. Test immediately by opening a fresh terminal window (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS or Linux) and connecting again. If it works, you are done. If it does not, your existing session is still open so you can undo the change — re-open the file and set PasswordAuthentication yes , then restart ssh again. Tip: You can also change the default SSH port from 22 to a high, non-standard port number (for example 2222 or 51234). This does not stop a determined attacker but does dramatically reduce the number of automated probing attempts that reach the Pi. To do this, add a line Port 2222 to /etc/ssh/sshd_config , then run sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp before restarting ssh . When connecting you would then use ssh -p 2222 yourname@raspberrypi.local . Step Four: A Simple Firewall with ufw In plain words: A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and which are blocked. ufw stands for "Uncomplicated Firewall" — it is a beginner-friendly tool built on top of Linux's powerful but complex built-in firewall system. For a home Pi, the default Raspberry Pi OS setup is fairly safe already, but adding ufw gives you explicit control and an extra layer of defence if you ever install a new service by accident. Install ufw: sudo apt install ufw -y Downloads and installs ufw from the official Raspberry Pi OS software repository. The -y flag confirms the installation automatically. Allow SSH connections — do this before enabling the firewall, otherwise you will lock yourself out of remote access: sudo ufw allow ssh Tells ufw to always permit incoming connections on the SSH port (port 22). Without this rule, enabling the firewall would immediately cut off your remote access. If you are running a web server on the Pi and want to allow normal web traffic, add these rules too — skip them if you have no web server: sudo ufw allow 80/tcp sudo ufw allow 443/tcp Line 1: Allows unencrypted web traffic (HTTP) on port 80. Line 2: Allows encrypted web traffic (HTTPS) on port 443. Enable the firewall: sudo ufw enable Turns on the firewall immediately and configures it to start automatically every time the Pi boots. It will warn you that existing SSH connections may be disrupted — type y to confirm. Because you added the SSH rule in step 2, SSH connections will continue to work fine. Check the current status and active rules: sudo ufw status verbose Prints a summary of whether ufw is active and lists all the rules currently in effect — which ports are allowed or blocked, and in which direction. You should see Status: active and a rule permitting SSH. Here is what a typical ufw status looks like for a Pi used for SSH access and a web server: To (port) Action From 22/tcp (SSH) ALLOW IN Anywhere 80/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 443/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere Everything else DENY IN Anywhere Note: ufw blocks incoming connections by default while allowing all outgoing connections. This means the Pi can freely browse the web, download updates, and contact external services — only unsolicited connections arriving from outside are filtered. Step Five: Do Not Expose the Pi Directly to the Internet This is one of the most important rules in this chapter. Never open ports on your home router to forward traffic directly to your Pi unless you are an experienced network administrator who understands the implications. Here is why: The moment a port is open to the internet, automated scanners will find it — usually within an hour. Even with a strong password and SSH keys, a misconfigured service or an unpatched vulnerability can be exploited. Home internet connections typically have a dynamic IP address that changes, making direct access unreliable anyway. Instead, use one of these safer approaches: Tool What it does Best for Tailscale Creates a private, encrypted virtual network between your devices. Only your approved devices can reach the Pi. SSH access from anywhere; connecting Pi to your laptop and phone securely. Raspberry Pi Connect Official Raspberry Pi remote desktop and shell service. Free, easy, no router configuration needed. Beginners who want to see the Pi's desktop from another computer. Cloudflare Tunnel Publishes a web service running on the Pi through Cloudflare's network, with HTTPS and DDoS protection built in. Sharing a website or web app running on the Pi with the public. Tip: Tailscale is free for personal use with up to 100 devices and is the simplest way to access your Pi securely from anywhere. Install it on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm using Tailscale's official installer script — do not use a plain apt install as the package is not in the default Raspberry Pi OS repository. Open a Terminal on the Pi and run: curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh This downloads and runs the official Tailscale installation script directly from tailscale.com. The script detects your operating system (Debian Bookworm on a Pi 5), adds the correct package repository, and installs Tailscale. After it completes, run sudo tailscale up and follow the link it shows to sign in and approve the Pi in your Tailscale account. Careful: Running a script piped directly from the internet (the curl … | sh pattern) is only safe when you trust the source completely. Only do this with well-known, reputable services such as Tailscale, and always verify you are typing the URL correctly. Step Six: fail2ban — Blocking Repeated Bad Login Attempts In plain words: fail2ban watches your system's log files for repeated failed login attempts and automatically blocks the IP address of whoever is trying. Think of it as a bouncer who notices someone trying the wrong door code five times in a row and then bars the door to them for an hour. Even if you have SSH keys enabled and password login disabled, fail2ban is good practice: it reduces log clutter and slows down any scanners that probe your Pi. Install fail2ban: sudo apt install fail2ban -y Downloads and installs fail2ban from the software repository. Once installed, it starts running automatically in the background and begins watching the SSH login logs immediately. Create a local configuration file so your settings survive future package updates: sudo cp /etc/fail2ban/jail.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.local Copies the default configuration file to a new file called jail.local . fail2ban always reads jail.local in preference to jail.conf , so any customisations you make here will not be overwritten when fail2ban is updated. Check that the SSH protection is active: sudo fail2ban-client status sshd Asks the fail2ban service to report the status of its SSH "jail". You should see that the jail is active and a count of currently banned IP addresses (probably zero on a freshly set-up Pi). If the command returns "sshd is not a valid jail", try sudo fail2ban-client status ssh instead. The default settings ban an IP address for 10 minutes after five failed login attempts within 10 minutes. You can adjust these values in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local if you wish, but the defaults are sensible for most home Pi setups. Step Seven: Disable Unused Interfaces with raspi-config The raspi-config tool lets you switch hardware interfaces (SSH, VNC, the camera connector, and so on) on or off. Disabling anything you are not using is good security practice — an interface that is switched off cannot be attacked. In plain words: An interface here means a communication channel — for example, the SSH network service, or the I2C bus used by electronic sensors. If you are not using it, turning it off removes a potential entry point. sudo raspi-config Opens the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool in the terminal. Use the arrow keys to navigate and Enter to select. Go to Interface Options to enable or disable SSH, VNC, the camera connector, I2C, SPI, and other interfaces. Select Finish when done; the Pi may ask you to reboot. A sensible starting point for a Pi used as a desktop or SSH server: Interface Recommended setting Why SSH Enabled Needed for remote terminal access. VNC Only if you use it Disable if you only use SSH; VNC opens another port. Camera Only if connected Disable if you have no camera module attached. I2C / SPI / Serial Only if wiring electronics Disable if you are not connecting GPIO components. 1-Wire Off by default — leave off Only needed for specific temperature sensors. Step Eight: Backups as a Security Measure Security is not only about keeping attackers out — it is also about recovering quickly if something goes wrong. A ransomware attack, a corrupted microSD card, or an accidental deletion can all destroy your work. Backups are your safety net. We covered backups in detail in Chapter 17. The most important points to remember from a security perspective are: Keep at least one backup off the Pi itself — on a USB drive, another computer, or cloud storage. A backup that lives only on the Pi is lost if the Pi is lost. Test your backups occasionally. A backup you have never restored from is a backup you cannot trust. Use the rpi-clone tool (Chapter 17) to clone the entire microSD card to a USB drive, so you can be up and running again in minutes if the card fails. Tip: The rclone tool (free, open-source) can automatically copy important files from the Pi to Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, or many other cloud services. Install it with: sudo apt install rclone -y Downloads and installs rclone from the Raspberry Pi OS repository. After installation, run rclone config in the terminal to follow an interactive setup wizard that connects rclone to your preferred cloud service. Once configured, you can back up a folder to the cloud with a single command. Step Nine: Physical Safety Software security is only half the picture. The physical setup of your Pi matters too. Use the correct power supply The Pi 5 requires a 27 W USB-C Power Delivery supply at 5.1 V / 5 A . If you bought a starter kit it most likely included one; otherwise the official Raspberry Pi 27 W USB-C power supply is the safest choice. Using a lower-rated charger (for example, a phone charger rated at 5 W or 18 W) can cause instability and data corruption. In plain words: The undervoltage warning is a lightning-bolt icon that appears in the top-right corner of the Pi's desktop when the power supply cannot keep up with demand. If you see it, stop what you are doing and switch to the correct supply — running under-voltage can corrupt the microSD card and make the Pi unusable. Careful: If you see a yellow lightning-bolt icon in the corner of the screen, or the message "Under-voltage detected!" in the terminal, your power supply is not delivering enough power. Switch to the official 27 W USB-C supply immediately. Continuing to run under-voltage risks file system corruption. Always shut down cleanly Never simply pull the power cable out of the Pi while it is running. The Pi writes data to the microSD card constantly; cutting power mid-write can corrupt the file system in a way that is difficult or impossible to repair. Always shut down using one of these methods: From the desktop: click the Raspberry Pi menu → Logout → Shutdown . From the terminal or SSH: sudo shutdown now Tells the operating system to close all programs safely, write any unsaved data to the card, and then cut power. The Pi 5 has a power button — after this command completes, the green activity light will go out, and pressing the power button will then remove the remaining standby power. Press the physical power button on the Pi 5 board once — this sends a clean shutdown signal (equivalent to the command above). Do not hold it down for more than a few seconds or it will force-cut power. Protect the GPIO pins In plain words: GPIO stands for General Purpose Input/Output — the 40 metal pins along the edge of the Pi board that let you connect physical components like LEDs, sensors, and buttons. We explore them in Chapter 18. Careful: The GPIO pins run on 3.3 V logic , not 5 V. Connecting a 5 V signal directly to a GPIO input pin can permanently destroy the Pi. Always check the voltage requirements of any component before wiring it up. Also never short (accidentally connect) the 5 V power pins to the ground pins or to each other — this can blow a fuse or damage the board. Always double-check your wiring before applying power when working with GPIO. Keep the Pi away from metal surfaces and loose components that could bridge the pins. Consider using a GPIO pin protector cap or keeping the board in a case (most starter kits include one, and inexpensive cases are widely available) when you are not doing electronics work. Security Checklist Use this checklist to confirm you have taken the most important steps. Work through it once now, and revisit it whenever you install a major new service on the Pi. Security Quick-Check Change default password — use a long passphrase Run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y monthly Install unattended-upgrades for automatic security patches Generate SSH key pair on your computer; copy public key to Pi Test key login, then optionally set PasswordAuthentication no Enable ufw — allow ssh first, then sudo ufw enable Never forward router ports — use Tailscale or Pi Connect instead Install fail2ban to auto-block repeated login failures Disable unused interfaces in raspi-config Make regular backups stored off the Pi — test one Use 27 W USB-C supply; always shut down cleanly; protect GPIO pins Print or bookmark this checklist. The first three items are the most important — tackle them before anything else. Change the default password. Run passwd and set a long, unique passphrase. Store it in a password manager. Update the system. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y and repeat monthly. Optionally install unattended-upgrades . Set up SSH keys. Generate a key pair on your computer, copy the public key to the Pi, test that key login works. Optionally disable SSH password login. Set PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config only after confirming key login works. Enable ufw. Run sudo ufw allow ssh then sudo ufw enable . Add only the ports you genuinely need. Never forward ports directly. Use Tailscale, Raspberry Pi Connect, or Cloudflare Tunnel for remote access instead. Install fail2ban. Run sudo apt install fail2ban -y and leave it running in the background. Disable unused interfaces. Run sudo raspi-config and switch off anything you are not using. Make regular backups. Keep at least one backup off the Pi. Test it. Use rpi-clone for a full card image. Use the correct power supply. 27 W USB-C PD only. If you see a lightning-bolt icon, investigate immediately. Always shut down cleanly. Use the menu, sudo shutdown now , or the power button — never yank the cable. Be GPIO-careful. Check voltages before wiring. Keep the Pi in its case when not working with electronics. Note: You do not need to do all of these on day one. The most important three are: change the password, keep the system updated, and use SSH keys. The rest can be added gradually as you become more comfortable. Key terms passwd — the Linux command that lets you change your user account's password. apt — the Raspberry Pi OS package manager, used to install, update, and remove software. SSH (Secure Shell) — an encrypted protocol for remotely controlling a computer via a terminal. SSH key pair — two mathematically linked files: a private key (kept on your PC) and a public key (placed on the Pi). Together they prove identity without transmitting a password. Ed25519 — a modern SSH key algorithm: fast, secure, and recommended over the older RSA algorithm. authorized_keys — a file on the Pi listing every public key permitted to log in via SSH. sshd_config — the SSH server configuration file, located at /etc/ssh/sshd_config . ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) — a beginner-friendly firewall tool for Linux that blocks unwanted incoming connections. fail2ban — a tool that automatically bans IP addresses that make too many failed login attempts. Tailscale — a free service that creates a private encrypted network between your devices, making remote access safe without opening router ports. raspi-config — the Raspberry Pi configuration tool used to enable or disable hardware interfaces and other system settings. Undervoltage warning — a lightning-bolt icon shown when the Pi is not receiving enough power; signals a risk of data corruption. GPIO — the 40-pin header on the Pi used to connect physical electronic components; runs on 3.3 V logic. unattended-upgrades — a package that automatically installs security updates in the background. passphrase — a password made of several words; longer than a typical password, easier to remember, and very hard for an attacker to guess. Interface (in raspi-config) — a hardware or network communication channel on the Pi, such as SSH, VNC, or I2C, that can be individually switched on or off. Chapter summary Change the default password immediately and use a long, unique passphrase stored in a password manager. Run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y monthly — or install unattended-upgrades for automatic security patches. SSH key pairs replace passwords with a public/private key system: generate a pair on your computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux) with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 , copy the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the Pi, and optionally disable password login in sshd_config . Install ufw with sudo apt install ufw -y , allow SSH before enabling, then run sudo ufw enable to block unexpected incoming connections. Never open router ports to expose the Pi directly to the internet — use Tailscale (installed via the official curl script), Raspberry Pi Connect, or Cloudflare Tunnel instead. Install fail2ban to automatically ban IP addresses that repeatedly fail to log in. Disable hardware interfaces you are not using via sudo raspi-config to reduce the attack surface. Backups are part of security: keep a copy off the Pi and test it occasionally. Use the correct 27 W USB-C power supply, always shut down cleanly, and treat the 3.3 V GPIO pins with care. The twelve-point security checklist in this chapter gives you a complete, actionable to-do list — the first three items are the most critical.

title: Maintenance & Troubleshooting
headings: Routine Care: Keeping Your Pi Healthy
Reading Logs: What Is the Pi Telling You?
When a Clean Re-Flash Is the Fastest Fix
text: Your Raspberry Pi 5 is a sturdy little machine, but like any computer it benefits from a small amount of regular care — and every computer occasionally misbehaves. This chapter gives you everything you need to keep your Pi running smoothly, understand what its warning lights mean, and solve the most common problems without needing to call anyone for help. Routine Care: Keeping Your Pi Healthy A well-maintained Raspberry Pi can run continuously for years. The three pillars of routine care are keeping the software up to date, watching the temperature, and making sure the storage card is treated gently. None of this takes more than a few minutes a week. Keeping Software Up to Date Raspberry Pi OS receives regular updates that fix security holes, squash bugs, and occasionally add new features. Applying them is a two-command process that you can run from the Terminal application any time. In plain words: A package is a bundle of software that your Pi can install, update, or remove. The package manager ( apt ) is the tool that fetches and installs those bundles automatically, handling all the complicated dependency juggling behind the scenes. sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade -y Line 1 — sudo apt update : Asks your Pi to download a fresh list of available packages from the internet. It does not install anything yet; it just refreshes the catalogue so the next command knows what is new. Line 2 — sudo apt full-upgrade -y : Downloads and installs every update that is now available. The full-upgrade variant (rather than the older upgrade ) is recommended for Raspberry Pi OS because it is allowed to remove or replace packages when needed to apply a complex update. The -y flag answers "yes" automatically to any confirmation prompts so you do not have to sit and watch. Tip: Run these two commands roughly once a week, or at least once a month. Good moments to remember: before starting a new project, or just after you turn the Pi on for the day. After a major upgrade you may see a message saying a reboot is needed. If so, type: sudo reboot Tells the Pi to restart cleanly. All running programs close gracefully, the system powers down, and then boots back up with the new software active. Tip: You can also check whether a reboot is pending by looking for the file /run/reboot-required . If that file exists after an upgrade, a reboot is needed. You can check with: test -f /run/reboot-required && echo "Reboot needed" || echo "No reboot needed" . Checking the Temperature The Pi 5's processor is powerful, and under heavy work it generates heat. If you have a cooler fitted — such as the official Active Cooler, the little heatsink-and-fan combination that clips to the board, or a fan built into your case — it handles this well, but it is good to know how to check the temperature yourself. (A cooler is strongly recommended on the Pi 5; if yours did not come with one, the official Active Cooler is inexpensive and easy to fit.) In plain words: Throttling means the processor deliberately slows itself down to avoid overheating. It is a safety mechanism, not a failure — but it does make your Pi feel sluggish, so you want to avoid it. vcgencmd measure_temp Reads the temperature sensor built into the Pi's processor chip and prints it to the screen. A typical result looks like temp=47.2'C . The vcgencmd command is a special Raspberry Pi utility for querying the hardware directly. Here is a quick guide to what the temperature readings mean: Temperature What it means Action needed Below 60 °C Cool and happy None — all is well 60–75 °C Warm under load Normal during intensive tasks; no action needed if it drops when idle 75–80 °C Getting hot Check airflow around the case; make sure the fan is spinning Above 80 °C Throttling will occur Improve cooling; see the Troubleshooting section below Tip: You can watch the temperature update in real time every two seconds by running: watch -n 2 vcgencmd measure_temp . Press Ctrl + C to stop. Checking for Throttling and Undervoltage The Pi reports throttling events in a special status register. You can read it with one command: vcgencmd get_throttled Reads a hidden status word from the Pi's hardware and prints a hexadecimal (base-16) number. The most reassuring result is throttled=0x0 , which means nothing bad has happened since the last reboot. The number returned is a bitmask — a code where each digit position carries a separate meaning. You do not need to memorise the arithmetic; just use this table: Result value What it means Likely cause 0x0 All clear — no throttling ever recorded Everything is fine Bit 0 set (e.g. 0x1 ) Undervoltage right now Power supply is too weak or cable is poor quality Bit 1 set (e.g. 0x2 ) Arm frequency capped right now Temperature or voltage is borderline Bit 2 set (e.g. 0x4 ) Currently throttled Too hot — check cooling Bit 16 set (e.g. 0x10000 ) Undervoltage occurred since last reboot Power dip happened at some point Bit 18 set (e.g. 0x40000 ) Throttling occurred since last reboot Temperature spike happened at some point Values can be combined — for example 0x50005 means undervoltage and throttling are happening right now and both have also occurred since last boot. The Lightning-Bolt Warning Icon On the Raspberry Pi OS desktop you may occasionally see a small yellow lightning-bolt icon appear in the top-right corner of the screen. This is the desktop's visual alert for undervoltage — the Pi is not receiving enough power. It is the graphical equivalent of the bits above. The good news: a proper 27 W USB-C power supply (5.1 V / 5 A) made for the Pi 5 — the official Raspberry Pi supply, or the equivalent one included with many starter kits — prevents virtually all undervoltage warnings when used correctly. If you do see the lightning bolt: Make sure you are using a proper 27 W USB-C supply made for the Pi 5, not a phone charger. Check that the USB-C cable is pushed firmly into both the Pi and the power supply. Avoid using a USB hub to power the Pi — it must be powered directly from its own supply. Careful: Persistent undervoltage can cause data corruption on your microSD card. If you see the lightning bolt regularly, fix the power supply before doing anything else. Checking Free Storage Space Your microSD card has a finite amount of space. If it fills up, programs start behaving strangely or refusing to run. df -h df stands for "disk free". The -h flag means "human-readable", so sizes are shown in megabytes (MB) and gigabytes (GB) rather than raw byte counts. The output shows every storage area ("filesystem") mounted on your Pi, how big it is, how much is used, and how much is free. The line you care about most is the one whose "Mounted on" column reads / — that is your main microSD card. A typical healthy result looks like this: Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/mmcblk0p2 58G 12G 43G 22% / This example shows a 64 GB card with 12 GB used and 43 GB free — plenty of headroom. If the "Use%" column climbs above 85–90%, it is time to tidy up. The device name /dev/mmcblk0p2 refers to the second partition on your microSD card — this is normal and expected. Tidying Up: Freeing Disk Space Over time, packages you install leave behind cached files and old versions. Two commands clean most of this up safely: sudo apt autoremove -y sudo apt clean Line 1 — sudo apt autoremove -y : Removes packages that were installed automatically as dependencies of something else but are no longer needed by anything. These orphaned packages are safe to delete. Line 2 — sudo apt clean : Deletes the downloaded package files that apt keeps in a cache folder after installation. The software itself is still installed; only the now-unnecessary installer files are removed. This can reclaim hundreds of megabytes. Tip: Combine all four maintenance commands into one tidy habit: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y && sudo apt autoremove -y && sudo apt clean . The && symbol means "run the next command only if the previous one succeeded". Checking CPU and Memory Usage If your Pi feels sluggish, it is useful to see what is using the processor and memory. The simplest way is the htop tool — a live, colourful dashboard of everything running on the Pi. htop Opens an interactive view showing all running processes, how much processor time each one is using (%), and how much memory each one is consuming. The bars at the top show overall CPU usage across all four processor cores and total memory use. Press Q to quit back to the terminal. If htop is not installed, run sudo apt install htop first. Tip: If you want a quick, non-interactive snapshot of the top resource users without opening a live view, type top -b -n 1 | head -20 . This prints a one-shot summary of the twenty busiest processes and exits immediately. Understanding Your Pi's Status LEDs The Raspberry Pi 5 has a red LED and a green LED on the board. Learning what they signal is often the fastest way to diagnose a problem. Raspberry Pi 5 PWR ACT Red LED (PWR) Solid ON = power is good (normal) OFF or flickering = power problem Check cable and power supply Green LED (ACT) Irregular flashing = reading/writing SD card Solid ON or no flash at all = boot problem Repeating blink pattern = boot error code The two status LEDs on the Raspberry Pi 5 board and what they tell you. LED colour Behaviour What it means Red (PWR) Solid on Power supply is good — normal Red (PWR) Off entirely No power reaching the board; check the cable and supply Red (PWR) Flickering Undervoltage — power supply is struggling Green (ACT) Irregular flashing Actively reading or writing to the microSD card — normal during boot and use Green (ACT) Steady on or off after initial flash Boot has stalled — corrupted card, wrong image, or card not seated properly Green (ACT) Specific blink patterns (e.g. 4 flashes, pause) A boot error code — count the flashes; see the Boot Error Codes table below Boot Error Codes (Green LED Blink Patterns) If the green LED flashes in a regular repeating pattern during boot rather than irregularly, count the flashes between the pauses. Each number points to a specific problem: Flash count What it means What to do 3 flashes start.elf not found or corrupted Re-flash the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager 4 flashes start.elf cannot be launched Re-flash the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager 7 flashes kernel.img not found Re-flash the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager 8 flashes SDRAM (memory) not recognised Try a different microSD card; if that fails, the board may need checking Note: All single-digit blink-code problems are almost always fixed by re-flashing the microSD card. The Pi 5's bootloader is very reliable; what fails is usually the card or the image written to it. Reading Logs: What Is the Pi Telling You? When something goes wrong, your Pi keeps a record of what happened in its system logs . You do not need to understand everything in them — just knowing how to glance at the end of the log is often enough to find a clear error message. In plain words: A log is like a diary that the operating system writes automatically. Every time a service starts, crashes, or encounters a problem, it writes a timestamped entry. Reading logs is the first step professionals take when diagnosing any Linux system. Viewing Recent Log Entries journalctl -xe journalctl is the command for reading the system journal (log). The -x flag adds helpful explanatory text around error entries. The -e flag jumps to the end of the log (the most recent entries) rather than starting from the beginning. Use the arrow keys to scroll up and down; press Q to quit. Viewing Boot Messages dmesg | tail -30 dmesg prints the kernel ring buffer — the messages the Linux kernel itself generated, especially during boot. The | symbol (called a "pipe") sends that output to the next command. tail -30 shows only the last 30 lines, which are usually the most relevant. Look for lines containing the words error , fail , or warning . Tip: If you see an unfamiliar error message, copy the exact text and search for it in a web browser. The Raspberry Pi forums at forums.raspberrypi.com and general Linux Q&A sites almost always have someone who has seen the same thing before. Viewing Logs for a Specific Service If a particular program (called a service when it runs in the background) is misbehaving, you can read just its log: journalctl -u ssh -n 50 Shows the last 50 log lines specifically for the ssh service (the remote-access tool). Replace ssh with the name of any other service — for example bluetooth or NetworkManager — to see its log instead. The -u flag means "unit" (the systemd name for a service) and -n 50 means "show the last 50 lines". The raspi-config Configuration Tool Raspberry Pi OS includes a dedicated configuration tool called raspi-config . It gives you a simple menu-driven interface for changing the most important system settings without needing to edit any configuration files by hand. In plain words: A configuration file is a plain text file that tells the operating system how to behave. Editing them directly requires care. raspi-config does the editing for you safely. sudo raspi-config Opens the Raspberry Pi Configuration menu in the terminal. Use the arrow keys to move up and down, Enter to select, and Tab or the left/right arrows to move between the menu buttons at the bottom (such as <Select> and <Finish>). Press Escape or choose <Finish> to exit. Changes often take effect after a reboot. The most useful things you can do in raspi-config : Menu section What it does System Options > Password Change your login password System Options > Hostname Give your Pi a memorable name on the network (e.g. mypi ) Interface Options > SSH Enable or disable remote terminal access Interface Options > VNC Enable graphical remote desktop access Localisation Options > Timezone Set the correct local time zone Localisation Options > WLAN Country Set the Wi-Fi country code (required for Wi-Fi to work) Advanced Options > Expand Filesystem Make the OS use all available space on the microSD card Note: Raspberry Pi Imager normally expands the filesystem automatically when it writes the card. However, if you ever re-flash manually and notice the available space seems smaller than expected, run sudo raspi-config and choose Advanced Options > Expand Filesystem. Troubleshooting: The Big Reference Table Below is a comprehensive table of the most common Raspberry Pi problems, their likely causes, and how to fix them. Work through the "Fix" steps in order — the simplest checks come first. Problem Likely cause(s) Fix Nothing on the screen — blank display Wrong micro-HDMI port used; monitor on wrong input; cable not fully inserted; Pi not booted yet See detailed steps below the table Pi will not boot (green LED solid or wrong blink pattern) Corrupted microSD card; card not seated properly; wrong OS image written to card See detailed steps below the table No Wi-Fi — cannot connect to any network Wi-Fi country not set; or trying to connect before country was configured in the imager See detailed steps below the table Cannot SSH — "connection refused" or "host not found" SSH not enabled; wrong hostname or IP address; not on the same network See detailed steps below the table Pi running hot or feeling slow Throttling due to heat or poor power; fan not spinning; case blocking airflow See detailed steps below the table microSD card corruption / Pi freezes randomly Sudden power loss; poor-quality power supply; card wear See detailed steps below the table "externally-managed-environment" error when using pip Bookworm protects the system Python from pip by default See detailed steps below the table App will not install / "package not found" Package list is stale; package name wrong; package not in default repositories Always run sudo apt update first, then retry the install command No sound from HDMI monitor Monitor speakers not selected as audio output; monitor has no speakers Right-click the speaker icon in the taskbar and select the HDMI audio device; or use USB speakers Pi loses the correct time after a power cut No RTC battery installed; NTP time sync not working Connect to the internet to sync time automatically; or fit a real-time clock battery to the RTC connector Nothing on the Screen / Blank Display This is the most common beginner shock. Work through these steps in order: Check which micro-HDMI port you are using. The Pi 5 has two micro-HDMI sockets side by side. The primary port is the one closest to the USB-C power socket (labelled HDMI 0 on the board). Plug your cable into that port first. If you are already in it, try the other one. Check your monitor's input source. Most monitors have multiple inputs (HDMI 1, HDMI 2, DisplayPort, etc.). Use your monitor's menu button or input-select button to switch to the HDMI input your cable is connected to. This is the single most common reason for a blank screen. Check the cable is seated firmly. The micro-HDMI connector is small — push it in until it clicks. Do the same at the monitor end. Wait for the Pi to finish booting. The first boot after a fresh installation can take 60–90 seconds before the desktop appears. Watch the green ACT LED: if it is flashing, the Pi is working. Be patient. Try a different HDMI cable or a different monitor. Cables do fail. If you have another monitor or TV in the house, try plugging in there. Look at the green LED. If it shows a repeating pattern of short flashes (for example, 4 flashes then a pause), count them — each pattern is a boot error code. See the Boot Error Codes table above. In most cases, re-flashing the card (see the section on re-flashing below) will fix it. Note: There is no 3.5 mm headphone socket on the Pi 5. Audio output is via HDMI or USB. If your monitor has no built-in speakers, you will need USB speakers or a USB audio adapter for sound. Pi Will Not Boot Reseat the microSD card. Power the Pi off by unplugging it. Remove the microSD card from its slot on the underside of the board, then push it back in firmly until you feel it click. Reconnect power. Check whether the card is recognised. During boot the green LED should flash irregularly. If it does not flash at all after 30 seconds, the Pi cannot read the card. Re-flash the microSD card. Connect the card (using a USB card reader, or your computer's built-in SD slot) to your main computer — Windows, macOS, or Linux. Use the Raspberry Pi Imager application (download free from raspberrypi.com/software , available for all three) to write a fresh copy of Raspberry Pi OS to the card. This takes about 5–10 minutes. Then reinsert the card in the Pi and try again. Re-flashing erases the card but is completely safe and free — it is the fastest fix for most boot problems. Careful: Re-flashing erases everything on the microSD card. If there are files on it you want to keep, copy them to your main computer first using a USB card reader or an SD slot. See the "Backing Up Your Files" section later in this chapter. No Wi-Fi The Pi 5 has built-in dual-band Wi-Fi, but it will refuse to connect if the country code has not been set. This is a legal requirement — Wi-Fi radios must operate within the power limits of the country they are in. Click the Raspberry Pi menu (top-left), go to Preferences > Raspberry Pi Configuration . Click the Localisation tab. Click Set WiFi Country and choose your country (United Kingdom, France, Germany, etc.). Click OK, then reboot when prompted. After rebooting, click the Wi-Fi icon in the top-right corner of the taskbar and select your network. You can also set the country from the Terminal: sudo raspi-config nonint do_wifi_country GB sudo reboot Line 1: Runs the Raspberry Pi configuration tool in non-interactive (command-line) mode and sets the Wi-Fi country to the United Kingdom ( GB ). Replace GB with your two-letter country code: FR for France, DE for Germany, CH for Switzerland, NL for the Netherlands, and so on. Line 2: Reboots the Pi so the new country setting takes effect. Wi-Fi will be available after the restart. Cannot SSH (Remote Access) In plain words: SSH (Secure Shell) lets you control your Pi's terminal from another computer over the network, without needing a monitor plugged into the Pi at all. Make sure SSH is enabled. On the Pi desktop, go to Preferences > Raspberry Pi Configuration > Interfaces and ensure SSH is set to Enabled . Alternatively, in the Terminal: sudo raspi-config nonint do_ssh 0 Enables SSH using raspi-config in non-interactive mode. The 0 means "enable" (and 1 would mean "disable"). After running this, SSH is active immediately — no reboot required. Check you are on the same network. Your Pi and the computer you are connecting from must be connected to the same router — either both on the same Wi-Fi, or the Pi on Ethernet into the same router. SSH will not work across different networks. Find the Pi's IP address. Run the following command on the Pi (when you have a monitor and keyboard connected), then use the printed address when connecting from your main computer. hostname -I Prints the Pi's current IP address (or addresses) on the network. The first number (e.g. 192.168.1.42 ) is the one to use when connecting from another computer. You can then connect from your main computer by opening a terminal (Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows; Terminal on macOS or Linux) and typing ssh yourusername@192.168.1.42 — the command is identical on all three. Use the right hostname. If you do not have a monitor available, try connecting using the Pi's hostname: ssh yourusername@raspberrypi.local . If you changed the hostname in raspi-config , use that name instead (e.g. ssh yourusername@mypi.local ). Check for a firewall. By default, Raspberry Pi OS does not run a firewall, so this is rarely the problem. But if you installed one, make sure port 22 is allowed. Tip: You can verify your internet connection from the Pi's terminal at any time with: ping -c 4 raspberrypi.com Sends four small test packets to the Raspberry Pi website and waits for replies. If you see responses with times in milliseconds, the internet connection is working. If you see "Network unreachable" or "Name or service not known", the Pi is not online — check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection first. Running Hot or Feeling Slow Check the temperature with vcgencmd measure_temp and the throttle status with vcgencmd get_throttled . A non-zero throttle value confirms the Pi has slowed down. Check the fan is spinning. The Active Cooler fan should spin when the Pi is warm. Listen for it, or look through any ventilation slots in the case. If the fan is silent when the Pi is hot, it may not be connected properly — the fan connector attaches to a small header on the Pi's board. Power the Pi off and reseat the connector. Check for airflow. Make sure the case's ventilation slots are not blocked by books, walls, or fabric. The Pi needs air to flow over it. Check the power supply. Throttling can be caused by undervoltage, not just heat. Confirm you are using the included 27 W supply (not a phone charger), and the cable is undamaged. Check what is using resources. Run htop to see which programs are consuming the most CPU or memory, and close what you do not need. You can also use the System Monitor application in the Raspberry Pi menu under Accessories. microSD Card Corruption The microSD card is the most fragile part of the Pi setup. Corruption — where files become garbled or unreadable — usually happens when the card loses power while it is in the middle of writing data. Symptoms include: the Pi freezes randomly, refuses to boot, shows a "kernel panic" message, or the file system appears read-only. How to prevent it: Always shut down properly using the desktop menu ( Raspberry Pi menu > Shutdown > Shutdown ) or the terminal command sudo shutdown -h now . Wait for the green LED to stop flashing before disconnecting power. Use the physical power button on the Pi 5 board: a single press triggers a clean shutdown. Use a good-quality power supply (a proper 27 W USB-C supply for the Pi 5 is correct). Cheap phone chargers that struggle to deliver enough power cause micro-dropouts that corrupt cards. Consider upgrading to an NVMe SSD on the PCIe connector for projects that involve heavy disk writing — SSDs are far more durable than microSD cards. How to fix it: If the card is already corrupted, the quickest fix is to re-flash it using Raspberry Pi Imager on your main computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux) as described in the section below. Before you do, if the Pi still boots at all, back up your files first. Tip: If the Pi boots but reports the filesystem is read-only, you may be able to check and repair it without re-flashing. Shut the Pi down cleanly, remove the microSD card, and insert it into your main computer. On Windows , run the disk error-checking tool (right-click the drive in File Explorer > Properties > Tools > Check). On macOS , use Disk Utility's First Aid. On Linux , run fsck on the card's partition from a terminal. This sometimes fixes minor corruption. The "externally-managed-environment" Error with pip On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, if you try to install a Python library directly with pip install something , you will see an error like: error: externally-managed-environment This is not a bug. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm deliberately blocks pip from installing packages into the system Python environment, to protect the operating system from accidentally broken libraries. This is the correct and intentional behaviour. You have three safe ways around this: Option 1 — Use apt (best for well-known libraries): sudo apt install python3-requests Many popular Python libraries are available as official Raspberry Pi OS packages with the prefix python3- . Replace requests with the name of the library you need (for example python3-numpy or python3-pillow ). This is the safest and most reliable method because the package has been tested to work with your exact version of Python. Option 2 — Use a virtual environment (best for projects): python3 -m venv myproject-env source myproject-env/bin/activate pip install requests Line 1: Creates a self-contained Python environment in a new folder called myproject-env . This environment is completely separate from the system Python, so nothing you install inside it can break the operating system. You only need to do this once per project. Line 2: "Activates" the environment — from this point on, python3 and pip refer to the versions inside this folder, not the system ones. You will see the environment name appear in brackets at the start of your prompt: (myproject-env) . You need to run this activation line each time you open a new terminal and want to work on this project. Line 3: Now that the virtual environment is active, pip install works normally and installs only into this safe, isolated folder. To deactivate the environment when you are done, simply type deactivate . Option 3 — Use Thonny (easiest for beginners): The pre-installed Thonny code editor manages its own Python environment separately from the system. Open Thonny, go to Tools > Manage packages , and search for the library you want. Thonny installs it into its own space without triggering the error. An App Will Not Install Always run sudo apt update first. If your package list is more than a few days old, apt may look for a package version that no longer exists and fail with a confusing error. Refresh the list first, then retry. Search for the correct package name. Package names are case-sensitive and sometimes use hyphens where you might expect underscores. Use the search command below to find matching packages. Check your internet connection. Run the ping command shown earlier in this chapter to confirm you are online. If there is no response, fix your network first. apt-cache search image viewer Searches the local package catalogue for any package whose name or description contains the words "image viewer". This is useful when you know what kind of software you want but are not sure of the exact package name. No internet connection is needed — it searches the already-downloaded list. Replace the search words with whatever you are looking for. Backing Up Your Files The simplest backup is to copy your important files to a USB drive or to your main computer. For whole-system backups — a complete snapshot of everything on the card — you have two practical options. Copying Files to a USB Drive First, plug a USB drive into any of the Pi's USB ports. It will appear in the file manager automatically. Then, to copy your documents folder to it from the terminal, use: cp -r /home/yourname/Documents /media/yourname/MYUSBDRIVE/ cp is the copy command. The -r flag means "recursive" — it copies a folder and everything inside it, including any sub-folders. Replace yourname with your actual username (the name you created when you set up the Pi). Replace MYUSBDRIVE with the actual name of your USB drive, which you can see in the file manager when you plug it in. The path /media/yourname/MYUSBDRIVE/ is where Raspberry Pi OS automatically makes USB drives accessible. Tip: To find out your exact username, type whoami in the terminal and press Enter. The Pi will print your username. Whole-Card Image Backup (from your main computer) The most thorough backup is a complete image of the entire microSD card, made from your main computer. This captures the operating system, all installed programs, and all your files — so you can restore everything exactly as it was if the card ever fails. The right tool depends on your computer's operating system, but the idea is the same on all three. Shut down the Pi cleanly ( Raspberry Pi menu > Shutdown ), wait for the green LED to stop flashing, then remove the microSD card. Insert the card into a USB card reader (or your computer's built-in SD slot) and plug it into your computer. Make the image with the tool for your operating system: Windows: download and install Win32 Disk Imager (free, from sourceforge.net/projects/win32diskimager ). Open it, choose an image file name and location to save to (e.g. pi-backup-2025-06.img on your desktop or an external drive), select the correct drive letter for your microSD card, then click Read . macOS: open Terminal , run diskutil list to identify the card's disk (e.g. /dev/disk4 ), then run sudo dd if=/dev/diskN of=~/pi-backup-2025-06.img bs=4m (replace diskN with the right number). Linux: open a terminal, run lsblk to identify the card (e.g. /dev/sdb ), then run sudo dd if=/dev/sdX of=~/pi-backup-2025-06.img bs=4M status=progress (replace sdX with the right letter). Wait for the read operation to complete. The result is a single .img file that is an exact copy of your card. Store this .img file somewhere safe — an external hard drive or cloud storage. If your Pi's card ever fails, you can write this image back to a new card to restore everything: with Win32 Disk Imager's Write button on Windows, the same dd command with if and of swapped on macOS or Linux, or Raspberry Pi Imager's "Use custom" option on any operating system. Careful: Whichever tool you use, make absolutely sure you select the correct microSD card. Choosing the wrong drive — the wrong drive letter in Win32 Disk Imager, or the wrong /dev/disk in a dd command — can overwrite or destroy data on a different disk. The dd command in particular is unforgiving, so double-check the device name before you press Enter. Note: The .img backup file will be the same size as your microSD card (e.g. 64 GB). Make sure the destination has enough free space. When a Clean Re-Flash Is the Fastest Fix Experienced Raspberry Pi users have learnt that re-flashing the card — wiping it and starting fresh — is often the fastest solution to a stubbornly misbehaving Pi. Do not be afraid of it. Here is why it is not as drastic as it sounds: It is free and takes about 10 minutes using Raspberry Pi Imager. Your personal files are easy to back up first — just copy the contents of /home/yourname/ to a USB drive or your main computer before you re-flash. A fresh system has no accumulated clutter, broken configurations, or partial updates — it is a clean slate. Raspberry Pi Imager lets you pre-configure your username, password, Wi-Fi credentials, and SSH settings before writing, so the re-flashed Pi comes up connected and ready to use. If you have spent more than an hour trying to fix a problem and are going in circles, take a step back, back up your files, and re-flash. You will almost certainly solve the problem in less time than you have already spent on it, and you will feel a satisfying sense of a fresh start. Note: Re-flashing is not a defeat. It is a professional technique. Even experienced Linux administrators re-image systems to fix stubborn problems. The difference between a beginner and an expert is often just knowing when to take this shortcut. A Maintenance Checklist Pin this list somewhere convenient as a quick reminder of good habits: How often Task Command or action Weekly (or before a new project) Update all software sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y Monthly Clean up old packages and cache sudo apt autoremove -y && sudo apt clean Monthly Check free disk space df -h Any time it feels slow Check temperature and throttling vcgencmd measure_temp and vcgencmd get_throttled Any time it feels slow Check CPU and memory usage htop Before any risky change Back up personal files Copy /home/yourname/ to USB drive or your main computer Occasionally Full card image backup Image the card from your computer (Win32 Disk Imager on Windows; dd on macOS/Linux) Every session Shut down cleanly Raspberry Pi menu > Shutdown, or sudo shutdown -h now Key terms apt — the package manager for Raspberry Pi OS; it installs, updates, and removes software. Throttling — the processor deliberately running slower than normal to avoid overheating or to cope with insufficient power. Undervoltage — when the Pi is not receiving enough electrical voltage, usually due to a weak power supply or poor-quality cable. vcgencmd — a Raspberry Pi-specific command-line tool for querying hardware status, including temperature and throttling. journalctl — the command for reading the system journal (log) on Raspberry Pi OS and other modern Linux systems. dmesg — displays messages from the Linux kernel, especially those generated during startup. SSH (Secure Shell) — a method of remotely controlling a computer's terminal over a network using an encrypted connection. Virtual environment (venv) — a self-contained Python installation that is separate from the system Python, making it safe to install any libraries without risk of breaking the OS. externally-managed-environment — the Bookworm-era protection that prevents pip from installing directly into the system Python; solved by using a venv, apt, or Thonny. ACT LED — the green activity LED on the Pi board; irregular flashing means the microSD card is being read or written. PWR LED — the red power LED on the Pi board; solid on means power is good; flickering or off means a power problem. Re-flashing — erasing a microSD card and writing a fresh operating system image to it; the fastest fix for many boot problems. df -h — a command that shows how much disk space is used and free on each storage device, in human-readable sizes. htop — an interactive terminal program that shows a live view of CPU and memory usage for every process running on the Pi. raspi-config — a menu-driven tool built into Raspberry Pi OS for changing system settings such as the hostname, Wi-Fi country, and enabled interfaces. Win32 Disk Imager — a free Windows program that can read an entire microSD card into a single backup image file, and write that image back to a card to restore it. On macOS and Linux the equivalent is the built-in dd command (or Raspberry Pi Imager's "Use custom" option, which works on any operating system). Boot error code — a repeating pattern of green LED flashes during startup that points to a specific hardware or software problem; almost always fixed by re-flashing the card. Chapter summary Run sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y weekly to keep your Pi secure and up to date. Use vcgencmd measure_temp to check temperature and vcgencmd get_throttled to check for throttling; a result of 0x0 means all is well. The yellow lightning-bolt icon on the desktop means undervoltage — always use the included 27 W power supply, not a phone charger. Check free disk space with df -h and clean up with sudo apt autoremove -y && sudo apt clean . Use htop to see which programs are consuming the most CPU or memory when the Pi feels slow. The red LED shows power status; the green LED shows microSD card activity — a frozen green LED or a regular blink pattern during boot points to a card problem. A blank screen is most often caused by the wrong micro-HDMI port, the wrong monitor input, or a loose cable — not a broken Pi. No Wi-Fi almost always means the Wi-Fi country has not been set; fix it in Raspberry Pi Configuration under Localisation, or with sudo raspi-config . The "externally-managed-environment" pip error is intentional; use apt install python3-packagename , a virtual environment, or Thonny instead. Always shut down cleanly to protect the microSD card from corruption; the physical power button on the Pi 5 triggers a safe shutdown. Make a complete image backup of your microSD card from your main computer — Win32 Disk Imager on Windows, the dd command on macOS or Linux — and store it somewhere safe. Re-flashing the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager is free, takes ten minutes, and fixes the vast majority of stubborn problems — back up your files first, then do not hesitate.

title: Where to Go Next
headings: How to Ask for Help Effectively
Keeping Your Pi Up to Date
A Few Principles for the Road Ahead
text: You have come a long way. You unboxed a tiny computer, set it up from scratch, learned the command line, wrote your first programs, wired up real electronics, and made things happen that would have seemed like magic a few weeks ago. This final chapter is your launchpad — a collection of inspiring project ideas, honest advice on which accessories are worth buying, a map of the best places to keep learning, and a few good habits to carry with you for the rest of your Raspberry Pi life. You Are Already a Maker Every expert you will ever meet online started exactly where you are now — staring at a tiny board and wondering what on earth to do with it. The Raspberry Pi community is one of the friendliest in technology, and there is no shortage of people willing to share knowledge, troubleshoot problems, and celebrate your first blinking LED. The only thing left to do is pick a project and start. The sections below are not a checklist. They are a menu. Read through them, let your imagination wander, and pay attention to the ideas that make you think "I would actually use that." Those are the ones worth building. A Gallery of Project Ideas These projects range from very beginner-friendly to happily challenging. All of them are well-documented online, and the Raspberry Pi community has built guides for every single one. Weather Station Connect a small sensor — the BME280 is a favourite, costing around £5 — to your GPIO pins and you can measure temperature, humidity, and air pressure in real time. Add a simple Python script and a web page, and you have your own personal weather station that you can read from any phone or computer in your house. More ambitious builders add a small outdoor housing, a solar panel for power, and send the readings to a cloud service to build up years of local weather data. Security Camera The official Raspberry Pi Camera Module (described in the accessories section below) clips directly onto the Pi's camera connector. A free piece of software called Motion , installed in a single terminal command, turns the Pi into a motion-detecting security camera that saves video clips when something moves in front of it. You can view the live feed in a web browser from anywhere in your house. Add a waterproof outdoor housing and you have a garden or doorbell camera for a fraction of the cost of a commercial one — with complete privacy because everything stays on your own hardware. Time-Lapse Photography Plug in the Camera Module, write a short Python script that takes a photo every few minutes, and you can capture a flower blooming, clouds rolling over a hillside, or a construction project across the street — compressed into a beautiful few-second video. The Pi can run this script automatically every time it boots, so you can leave it pointing at a window for weeks and collect thousands of frames without touching it. Retro Handheld Games Console A free operating system called RetroPie turns your Raspberry Pi into a machine that plays games from old consoles. You flash it onto a microSD card instead of Raspberry Pi OS — it is a completely separate system that you switch to just for gaming. Pair it with a small screen, a USB gamepad, and an optional 3D-printed case, and you have a pocket games console. It is one of the most popular Pi projects of all time, with hundreds of thousands of builds documented online. Note: Playing old games legally requires owning the original game cartridge and making your own backup copy. Downloading game files you do not own is against copyright law in most countries, including the UK and EU. Small Robot or Rover Robotics kits designed for the Raspberry Pi — such as the CamJam EduKit Robotics board or the Pimoroni Explorer HAT — let you drive small motors from your GPIO pins. You can build a wheeled rover that follows a line of black tape, avoids obstacles using an ultrasonic distance sensor, or is controlled remotely from a phone. This is one of the most satisfying projects because the Pi does something physical and visible in the real world. Home Dashboard / Magic Mirror A "Magic Mirror" is a touchscreen — or a monitor mounted behind a two-way mirror — that shows a personal dashboard: the time and date, today's weather, your calendar, the latest news headlines, and anything else you find useful. The open-source MagicMirror² software (free, runs on the Pi) has hundreds of community-made modules, from bus timetables to compliment generators. The result is something that genuinely looks futuristic in a hallway or kitchen. Print Server If you have an older USB printer that is not Wi-Fi capable, a Raspberry Pi running a free piece of software called CUPS (Common Unix Printing System) can share it wirelessly with every device in your home — Windows PCs, phones, tablets, and Macs alike. It is a two-hour weekend project that gives an old printer a second life. Music Streamer Software called Volumio or moOde turns your Pi into a dedicated hi-fi music player. Connect a USB DAC (a small device that converts digital audio to analogue sound), plug it into your stereo amplifier, and you have a high-quality network music player that can play music from local files on a hard drive, internet radio streams, and supported streaming services — all controlled from a phone. Audiophiles praise these builds for sounding better than many commercial streamers costing hundreds of pounds. In plain words: A DAC (Digital-to-Analogue Converter) is a small device, often about the size of a USB memory stick, that takes digital audio data from the Pi and turns it into an electrical signal your speakers or headphones can use. The Pi 5 has no headphone jack of its own, so a USB DAC is the standard way to get high-quality sound out. Network Ad Blocker A free tool called Pi-hole turns your Pi into a network-wide advertisement and tracker blocker. Every device on your home Wi-Fi — phones, laptops, smart TVs — automatically has adverts blocked at the network level, without installing anything on those devices. Pi-hole also gives you a beautiful dashboard showing how much of your internet traffic is advertising. A companion tool called Uptime Kuma can monitor your home network devices and send you alerts if something goes offline. Bird-Feeder Camera with AI This is one of the most delightful projects in the Pi community. Mount a Camera Module on a garden bird feeder, connect an AI model that can identify bird species from photos, and you have an automatic bird-watching log. The open-source BirdNET-Pi project uses sound analysis to identify birds by their calls. A camera-based version can snap a photo every time a bird lands, run it through a small AI model, and log the species, time, and date — building up a wildlife diary of your garden over months and years. This project brings together cameras, GPIO sensors, Python programming, and machine learning all at once. A taste of what you can build next Weather Station Security Camera Magic Mirror Network Ad Blocker Retro Gaming Robot Rover Time-lapse Camera Music Streamer Print Server Bird AI Camera Pi 5 powers all Every one of these projects runs on the Pi 5 you already own. Ten project directions, one tiny computer. All of these are achievable by a beginner with free online guides. Accessories Worth Buying (and Why) A basic setup is enough to do a great deal. But as you grow, certain accessories unlock entirely new capabilities. Here is an honest guide to what is worth spending money on — and what each thing does. In plain words: A HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) is an add-on circuit board that stacks neatly on top of your Raspberry Pi, connecting through all 40 GPIO pins at once. Think of it like a module you slot onto the Pi to give it a new superpower — more storage, artificial intelligence, an uninterruptible power supply, and so on. The GPIO header acts as the universal connector. M.2 NVMe SSD + the M.2 HAT+ The microSD card most people start with is convenient, but it is slower and less durable than a proper solid-state drive. An M.2 NVMe SSD is a small, flat storage chip — typically the size of a stick of chewing gum — that connects to the Pi 5 through its built-in PCIe connector via an official add-on board called the M.2 HAT+ . In plain words: PCIe (pronounced "PCI Express") is a high-speed data connection built into the Pi 5, designed originally for connecting graphics cards and fast storage inside desktop computers. The Pi 5 has one PCIe 2.0 lane — a single high-speed channel — which is what makes plugging in an M.2 HAT+ or AI HAT+ possible. Together the M.2 HAT+ and an NVMe SSD give you storage that is three to five times faster than a microSD card and far more reliable for daily use. If you plan to use your Pi as a proper desktop computer or a server that runs 24 hours a day, this upgrade is the single most impactful thing you can buy. Typical cost: £12–20 for the HAT+, plus £20–50 for a 250 GB to 500 GB NVMe SSD. Tip: The Pi 5 supports NVMe SSDs in the "M.2 2230" and "M.2 2242" form factors (these numbers refer to the physical size in millimetres). When you are shopping, make sure the SSD you buy is one of those sizes and uses the NVMe interface — not the older SATA interface, which the M.2 HAT+ does not support. The Camera Module 3 The Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 is the official camera for the Pi. It connects via a flat ribbon cable to the dedicated camera connector on the Pi 5 board (labelled CAM/DISP 0 or CAM/DISP 1 ). The Module 3 shoots up to 12 megapixel stills and 1080p video, has autofocus, and is fully supported by the Pi's built-in camera software with no driver installation needed. You can capture a photo from the terminal with a single command. It is the heart of the security camera, time-lapse, and bird-feeder AI projects described above. Typical cost: around £25. There is also a Camera Module 3 Wide with a wider-angle lens, and a Camera Module 3 NoIR with the infrared filter removed (for night-vision projects when paired with an infrared LED). Choose based on what you want to build. A GPIO / Electronics Starter Kit If the electronics chapters of this book sparked an interest in building circuits, a GPIO starter kit is a great next step. These kits — available from Pimoroni, The Pi Hut, CPC Farnell, and many other UK/EU electronics retailers for around £15–30 — typically include a breadboard, a selection of LEDs, resistors, buttons, sensors (temperature, distance, light), a buzzer, and jump wires. They give you the components to build dozens of small projects and experiment freely without worrying about running out of parts. Look for kits specifically labelled as compatible with the Raspberry Pi. A UPS HAT (Uninterruptible Power Supply) If you run your Pi as a server — storing files, hosting a website, running Pi-hole, or anything else that should stay on — a sudden power cut can corrupt your storage card or SSD. A UPS HAT is a small board that sits on top of your Pi and contains a battery. If the mains power fails, the battery takes over instantly and keeps the Pi running long enough to shut itself down cleanly. Brands like Waveshare and PiJuice make popular models, typically costing £20–40. For a Pi running 24/7, this is genuine peace of mind. The AI HAT+ The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ is an official add-on that adds a dedicated neural network processor to your Pi 5, giving it the ability to run AI models — particularly image recognition and object detection — many times faster than the Pi's main processor can manage on its own. It connects via the same PCIe connector as the M.2 HAT+. This is the accessory that powers the bird-feeder AI camera project at full speed, and it opens up a world of real-time computer vision projects: counting people in a room, identifying plants, detecting when a cat door is being used. Typical cost: around £50. If AI interests you, this is a genuinely exciting accessory. Note: The AI HAT+ and the M.2 HAT+ both use the Pi 5's single PCIe connector — you can only use one of them at a time unless you add a special PCIe expansion board. For most beginners, choose the one that fits your project best. Accessory What it does Best for Approx. cost (UK) M.2 HAT+ + NVMe SSD Fast, reliable internal storage Desktop use, servers, daily driver £30–70 Camera Module 3 12 MP autofocus camera Security cam, time-lapse, bird AI ~£25 GPIO starter kit LEDs, sensors, breadboard, wires Electronics experiments £15–30 UPS HAT Battery backup for clean shutdowns 24/7 servers, always-on projects £20–40 AI HAT+ Fast AI / neural network processor Real-time image recognition, AI projects ~£50 USB DAC Converts Pi audio to analogue for speakers Music streamer, hi-fi audio £10–40 Where to Keep Learning Books are a great starting point, but the Raspberry Pi world moves quickly and the community produces an astonishing amount of free, high-quality learning material. Here are the best places to go next. The Official Raspberry Pi Documentation The official documentation lives at www.raspberrypi.com/documentation . It is written by the people who built the hardware and software, kept continuously up to date, and covers everything from first boot to advanced hardware hacking. Whenever you buy a new accessory — a camera, a HAT, a sensor — the official docs should be your first stop. The "Getting Started" section in particular is excellent for reviewing the basics or looking up something you half-remember. The MagPi Magazine The MagPi is the official Raspberry Pi magazine, published monthly. Every issue contains step-by-step project guides, reviews of new accessories, coding tutorials, and interviews with builders around the world. Crucially, every past issue is available as a free PDF download from magpi.raspberrypi.com . The archive stretches back to 2012 and contains hundreds of projects. Search it when you have an idea — chances are someone has written a guide for something very similar. A sister publication, HackSpace Magazine , covers the broader making and electronics world. The Official Raspberry Pi Forums The forums at forums.raspberrypi.com have been running since the Pi was first released and contain millions of posts. Whatever problem you run into, somebody has almost certainly had the same one. Use the search box before posting — your question has probably been answered. The community is friendly, patient with beginners, and responsive. When you do post a question (more on how to do this well below), you will typically get a helpful reply within hours. Reddit: r/raspberry_pi The subreddit r/raspberry_pi (visit www.reddit.com/r/raspberry_pi ) is one of the largest Raspberry Pi communities online, with millions of members. People share finished projects with photos, ask for help, discuss new products, and post beginner questions all day long. The weekly "Help and Discussion" thread is a welcoming place for new questions. You will also find inspiration there daily — someone always seems to be building something brilliant. Project and Tutorial Sites Beyond the official resources, several websites specialise in Raspberry Pi project guides: projects.raspberrypi.org — The official project site, with guided, beginner-friendly tutorials organised by difficulty level. A great place to start when you want a structured project to follow. Instructables (instructables.com) — A huge library of user-submitted project guides covering everything from simple LED blinkers to full robots. Search "Raspberry Pi" and you will find thousands of results. Hackaday (hackaday.com) — A daily news site for makers and hackers. More advanced content, but a wonderful source of inspiration for where technology and creativity intersect. The Pi Hut blog (thepihut.com/blogs/raspberry-pi-tutorials) — The UK's leading Pi retailer also publishes free tutorials. Practical, clear, and specifically aimed at UK beginners. Adafruit Learning System (learn.adafruit.com) — Electronics retailer Adafruit publishes some of the best-written tutorials in the hobby electronics world, with excellent explanations of how things work, not just instructions to copy. Video Learning If you prefer learning by watching, YouTube has a huge library of Raspberry Pi content. The channels NetworkChuck , Jeff Geerling , ExplainingComputers , and The Raspberry Pi Guy all produce high-quality, beginner-accessible videos. Jeff Geerling in particular is well-known for deep, honest technical reviews of Pi hardware and accessories. For Python, the channel Corey Schafer produces some of the clearest Python tutorials available anywhere. Learning Python Further Python is the main programming language of the Raspberry Pi world. Here are the best ways to go deeper, all of them free or nearly free: Thonny's built-in help — Thonny, the editor already installed on your Pi, has a built-in "Assistant" that explains errors in plain English. Use it whenever Python gives you a confusing message. Python.org tutorials (docs.python.org/3/tutorial) — The official Python tutorial, clear and authoritative. Work through it chapter by chapter at your own pace.
