Automate the Boring Stuff with Python (automatetheboringstuff.com) — A free, practical book focused on real-world tasks: manipulating files, reading spreadsheets, sending emails. One of the most-recommended Python books for non-programmers. Tip: On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, the system Python is "externally managed" — this means if you try to install a Python library with pip install something , you will see a warning and it may refuse. The safe alternatives are: install via sudo apt install python3-something (for well-known libraries), or create a virtual environment first with python3 -m venv myenv && source myenv/bin/activate and then use pip inside it. Thonny handles this automatically. See Chapter 10 for a full explanation. How to Ask for Help Effectively At some point, you will get stuck. Something will not work, an error message will make no sense, or a project will simply refuse to behave. This is completely normal — even experienced engineers get stuck. The difference is that experienced engineers know how to ask for help in a way that gets them a useful answer quickly. When you post a question in a forum or subreddit, include all of the following: What you are trying to do. "I am trying to run a Python script that reads temperature from a BME280 sensor connected to the I²C pins." What you expected to happen. "I expected to see a temperature reading printed in the terminal." What actually happened. Copy and paste the exact error message, in full. Do not paraphrase it — the exact wording matters. Your hardware and software. For example: "Raspberry Pi 5 (state your RAM size), Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, 64-bit." Run the following two commands in your terminal and paste the output into your question: uname -a cat /etc/os-release uname -a — prints a single line describing your Linux kernel: the operating system name, the hostname of your Pi, the kernel version number, and whether it is a 64-bit system. This tells helpers exactly which version of the core software you are running. cat /etc/os-release — reads and prints a small text file that your operating system stores about itself. It shows the OS name ("Raspberry Pi OS"), the version ("12" for Bookworm), and the codename. This confirms to helpers that you are on Bookworm and not an older release. What you have already tried. This shows you have made an effort and prevents people from suggesting things you have already ruled out. Your code, if relevant. Paste it using the forum's code formatting (usually triple backticks on Reddit) so it is easy to read. A question that contains all of this information will get a fast, helpful response. A question that says "it doesn't work, help?" may get ignored or a frustrated reply asking for more details. Tip: Before posting anywhere, try putting the exact error message into a search engine surrounded by quotation marks. Nine times out of ten, someone else has had the same error and the first result will be a forum thread with the solution. Keeping Your Pi Up to Date Even after you have finished this book, one habit is worth keeping: run the system update command regularly — perhaps once a month. It downloads security patches, bug fixes, and improvements to all the software on your Pi. sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y sudo — runs the command as an administrator (the "superuser"). Installing and updating software requires administrator permission on Linux, just as it does on Windows. apt update — contacts the internet repositories (software libraries) and downloads an up-to-date list of which packages are available and what their latest versions are. This does not yet change anything on your Pi — it only refreshes the list. && — means "if the first command succeeded, then run the next one". If the update step fails (for example, because there is no internet connection), the upgrade step will not run. apt full-upgrade -y — downloads and installs all available updates based on the list just fetched. full-upgrade is preferred over plain upgrade on Raspberry Pi OS because it will also handle packages that need to be removed or replaced as part of the update — which is normal for kernel and firmware updates. The -y flag automatically answers "yes" to any confirmation prompts, so the command runs without interruption. Careful: On a Pi that is running as a server — Pi-hole, a print server, a music streamer — it is wise to check the forums or the project's own release notes before a major operating system upgrade, in case a new version has known compatibility issues with the software you are using. For most casual desktop use, keeping the system updated regularly is simply good practice. Note: You may occasionally see advice online to run sudo rpi-update . This command updates the Pi's firmware to a development (testing) version and is not recommended for everyday use — it can introduce instability. The apt full-upgrade command above keeps your firmware up to date through the stable, tested release channel, which is what you want. A Few Principles for the Road Ahead Experienced makers share a few habits that are worth knowing about now, before you form different ones: Back up before you build. Before you start a big project, take a backup image of your microSD card using the Raspberry Pi Imager software on your main computer (Windows, macOS, or Linux). If something goes wrong, you can restore it in minutes rather than starting from scratch. One change at a time. When something stops working, it is almost always because of the most recent change you made. If you change several things at once, finding the cause becomes much harder. Change one thing, test it, then move on. Read the error message. Error messages feel intimidating at first, but they almost always contain the answer. The last line is usually the most important. Copy it and search for it online. Document what you do. Keep a simple text file or notebook where you write down what you installed, why you wired things up a certain way, and any configuration changes you made. Future you — returning to a project after three months — will be very grateful. Use virtual environments for Python projects. When you install Python libraries for a project, do it inside a virtual environment so they do not conflict with each other or with the system. This keeps your Pi tidy and your projects self-contained. Thonny can manage this for you automatically. Share what you make. Post a photo in the subreddit. Write a short guide on a forum. The Pi community runs on generosity — the tutorials you read were written by people who had exactly the same experience as you, and chose to give something back. A Warm Closing Word When the Raspberry Pi Foundation launched the first Pi back in 2012, their hope was to put affordable, programmable computers into the hands of curious people — particularly young people — and see what would happen. What happened was rather extraordinary. Millions of people around the world discovered they could build things with technology, not just consume it. They built satellites and weather balloons and telescope mounts and schools and hospitals and their own radio stations. You are now part of that tradition. You have a powerful computer, a set of skills, and a community of millions of people who love the same thing you are just beginning to discover. The Raspberry Pi 5 on your desk is not the end of anything — it is the beginning of a very long and enjoyable journey. Whatever you build next, enjoy the process. The blinking LEDs, the cryptic error messages, the moments when something finally works after three attempts — all of it is the hobby. Keep tinkering. Key terms HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) - An add-on circuit board that stacks onto the Raspberry Pi's 40-pin GPIO header, giving the Pi new capabilities such as storage, AI processing, or battery backup. M.2 NVMe SSD - A small, fast, flat storage chip that connects via the Pi 5's PCIe connector (using the M.2 HAT+) and is significantly faster and more reliable than a microSD card. PCIe (PCI Express) - A high-speed data connection built into the Pi 5, used to connect the M.2 HAT+ (for NVMe storage) or the AI HAT+ (for AI processing). The Pi 5 has one PCIe 2.0 lane. Camera Module 3 - The official Raspberry Pi camera, connecting via a ribbon cable to the camera connector on the Pi board, with 12 MP resolution and autofocus. DAC (Digital-to-Analogue Converter) - A device, often USB, that converts the Pi's digital audio into an analogue signal suitable for speakers or headphones. Required on the Pi 5, which has no built-in headphone jack. UPS HAT - An Uninterruptible Power Supply board for the Pi; contains a battery so the Pi can shut down safely during a power cut rather than losing data. AI HAT+ - An official Raspberry Pi add-on that adds a dedicated AI processor for running neural networks much faster than the Pi's main CPU can manage. Pi-hole - Free, open-source software that turns a Raspberry Pi into a network-wide advertisement and tracker blocker. Motion - Free, open-source software that turns a Pi with a camera into a motion-detecting security camera. MagPi - The official monthly Raspberry Pi magazine; every issue is available as a free PDF download from magpi.raspberrypi.com. RetroPie - A free operating system (flashed separately onto a microSD card) that turns the Raspberry Pi into a retro gaming device by emulating old games consoles. CUPS (Common Unix Printing System) - Free software that turns a Pi into a wireless print server, sharing a USB printer with all devices on your network. Virtual environment - An isolated Python workspace on your Pi that keeps the libraries for one project separate from other projects and from the system Python. Created with python3 -m venv . apt full-upgrade - The recommended terminal command for updating all software on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, including the kernel and firmware, via the stable release channel. Chapter summary The Raspberry Pi community is large, friendly, and produces enormous amounts of free learning material — you are never alone in a project. Popular next projects include a weather station, security camera, retro games console, Pi-hole ad blocker, magic mirror dashboard, robot, and an AI bird-feeder camera. The most impactful upgrades are the M.2 HAT+ with an NVMe SSD (for speed and reliability) and the Camera Module 3 (for all camera-based projects). A HAT is an add-on board that stacks on the GPIO header to give the Pi new capabilities; the AI HAT+ and M.2 HAT+ share the Pi 5's single PCIe connector, so only one can be used at a time. The best free resources are the official Raspberry Pi documentation, the free MagPi magazine PDF archive, the official forums, and the r/raspberry_pi subreddit. Effective help requests include the exact error message, your hardware and OS version (from uname -a and cat /etc/os-release ), what you expected, what happened, and what you have already tried. Keep the habit of running sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y monthly to keep your system secure and up to date via the stable release channel; avoid sudo rpi-update for everyday use. On Bookworm, install Python libraries via apt or inside a virtual environment rather than with a bare pip install , which the system will refuse. Back up your SD card before major projects, change one thing at a time when troubleshooting, read error messages carefully, and document your work. The Pi 5 you already own is powerful enough for every project in this chapter — you have everything you need to keep building.

title: Welcome to the Maker Lab: Your Toolkit & Salvaging E-Waste
text: Welcome to the Maker Lab — the part of the course where you stop reading about electronics and start building real things you can hold, switch on, and show off. Over the next nine lessons you will build a traffic light, a reaction game, a singing sound machine, a glowing mood lamp, a parking sensor, a plant logger, a motion alarm, and finally a web dashboard you can open on your phone. Every build teaches a named Python idea and a named electronics idea, and a thread running through all of them is one of the most satisfying skills in the maker world: bringing dead electronics back to life by salvaging their parts. This first lesson is your kit-out and safety briefing — no complex wiring yet, just the toolkit, the languages on your Pi, and the rules that will keep you (and your Pi) safe. How the Maker Lab Works Every chapter in this Part is a complete, working project. You will not just copy code — each build introduces a fundamental and teaches it properly with a tiny example first, then puts it to work in the project. By the end you will have written real programs that: switch lights on and off in sequences (loops and lists); read buttons and time your reactions (conditionals, randomness, timing); play tunes through a salvaged speaker (dictionaries, tone generation); fade colours on a recycled-jar lamp (functions, PWM brightness); measure distance and log data to a file (classes, files, timestamps); detect motion and raise an alarm (event-driven callbacks); and serve all of it as a live web page from your Pi (a little HTML, CSS and JavaScript). In plain words: a fundamental is a core idea you will reuse forever. A for loop , a function , a resistor , LED polarity — learn each one once, properly, and it pays off in every project after. We will always name the fundamental out loud so you know exactly what you are learning. You do not need a fortune in parts. A modest beginner starter kit — a breadboard, a handful of jumper wires, some LEDs, resistors, a couple of buttons, and a cheap multimeter — covers most of the Part. The rest you can salvage from broken electronics destined for the bin , which is exactly what the recycling thread is about. By the end of this lesson you will know how to tell a treasure-filled gadget from a genuinely dangerous one. What You'll Learn This is a kit-and-safety lesson, so the fundamentals are foundations rather than a single build. Here is what you will walk away knowing: Area Fundamentals (named) Python recap variables , print() , f-strings , functions , import ; running code in Thonny and with python3 file.py ; the Bookworm PEP 668 rule for installing packages with pip A second language Bash scripting basics: the shebang #!/bin/bash , chmod +x , running ./script.sh ; which languages live on the Pi and when to use each Electronics toolkit the breadboard, jumper-wire types, resistors, LEDs, buttons, the multimeter; reading resistor colour bands ; LED polarity Testing parts using a multimeter for continuity , resistance (Ω) , the diode test , and DC volts to check salvaged components Recycling (core) what is safe to open and harvest vs what is dangerous — never open ; how to harvest a component and test it The Maker Toolkit Let us meet the tools and parts you will use again and again. None of them is expensive, and most come in a starter kit. The figure below labels the essentials. Your Maker Lab Toolkit Breadboard Jumper wires Resistors long + short − LED Push button 330Ω Multimeter red & black probes The core toolkit: a solderless breadboard, jumper wires, resistors, LEDs, push buttons, and a digital multimeter with its red and black probes. The breadboard In plain words: a breadboard is a plastic board full of holes with hidden metal strips inside. You push wires and component legs into the holes and the metal connects them — no soldering, no glue, and you can pull everything out and start again. It is the workbench for every build in this Part. Inside, the holes are connected in groups. The two long rails down each edge (marked + and − ) are the power rails — every hole along a rail is joined. In the central area, each short numbered half-row is joined across (e.g. holes 10a – 10e ), but a gap down the middle separates the left half from the right half. You will use this layout in every wiring project from the next chapter onward; for now, just know that pushing two legs into the same half-row connects them. Jumper wires Jumper wires are short flexible wires with rigid connectors on each end. They come in three flavours, named by what is on each end: Type Ends Typical use Male-to-male (M–M) a pin on both ends breadboard hole → breadboard hole Female-to-male (F–M) a socket on one end, a pin on the other Pi GPIO pin (needs the socket) → breadboard hole Female-to-female (F–F) a socket on both ends module header pin → Pi GPIO pin directly Tip: the Pi's GPIO header is a row of pins , so any wire going to the Pi needs a female (socket) end there. For connecting the Pi to a breadboard, female-to-male wires are what you want. A small bundle of each type will see you through the whole Part. Resistors, LEDs and buttons A resistor slows electricity down. Its job in nearly every project here is to protect an LED (and the GPIO pin) by limiting current. The standard beginner value is 330 Ω for an LED on a 3.3 V pin; you will also meet 1 kΩ as a base resistor for transistors later. In plain words: an LED (Light-Emitting Diode) is a tiny lamp that only lets current flow one way. It has a longer leg (the anode, +) and a shorter leg with a flat edge on the plastic rim (the cathode, −) . Current must enter the long leg and leave the short leg, or it will not light. A push button (a tactile switch) is just a momentary connection: press it and two sides join; release and they part. You will wire your first one in the reaction-timer game two chapters from now. Reading Resistor Colour Bands Resistors are tiny, so their value is printed as coloured bands rather than numbers. A standard 4-band resistor reads: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance . The first two bands are digits, the third tells you how many zeros (the multiplier), and the last (set slightly apart, usually gold) is the manufacturing tolerance. Colour Digit Multiplier Black 0 ×1 Brown 1 ×10 Red 2 ×100 Orange 3 ×1,000 Yellow 4 ×10,000 Green 5 ×100,000 Blue 6 ×1,000,000 Violet 7 — Grey 8 — White 9 — Gold — tolerance ±5% Let us read the two values you will use most. A 330 Ω resistor is orange–orange–brown–gold : orange (3), orange (3), brown (×10) → 33 × 10 = 330 Ω, ±5%. A 1 kΩ resistor is brown–black–red–gold : brown (1), black (0), red (×100) → 10 × 100 = 1,000 Ω = 1 kΩ, ±5%. Resistor-band reader 330 Ω Orange 3 Orange 3 Brown ×10 Gold ±5% = 330 Ω 3 3 × 10 1 kΩ Brown Black Red Gold = 1,000 Ω 1 0 × 100 Reading the two resistors you will use most. 330 Ω = orange–orange–brown–gold; 1 kΩ = brown–black–red–gold. The first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier, the gold band is ±5% tolerance. Tip: if the bands are ambiguous (some colours are hard to tell apart in poor light), do not guess — set your multimeter to the ohms (Ω) range and measure the resistor directly. We will do exactly that below. Reading the bag label from a starter kit is the fastest method of all. LED Polarity An LED is a one-way street. Get the direction right and it lights; get it backwards and it simply stays dark (no harm done — an LED will not be damaged by being put in the wrong way round at these low voltages). There are three ways to spot which leg is which: Leg length: the longer leg is the anode (+) ; the shorter leg is the cathode (−) . The flat edge: the plastic rim has a tiny flat on the cathode (−) side. Inside the dome: the larger metal piece (the anvil) inside the plastic is the cathode (−). Note: in every wiring project in this Part, current flows from a GPIO pin, through a 330 Ω resistor, into the LED's long leg (anode) , out of the short leg (cathode) , and back to GND. Memorise "long leg to the positive side" and you will rarely wire an LED backwards. Using a Multimeter A multimeter is the single most useful tool for testing parts — especially salvaged ones, where you cannot trust a label. It is a dial (or buttons) surrounded by settings, with a red probe and a black probe. Four settings cover almost everything you will do in this Part. Setting Symbol What it does Continuity sound-wave / 🔊 beeps if the two probes are joined by an unbroken wire — tests cables, switches, solder joints Resistance Ω (omega) measures resistance in ohms — reads a resistor's value, or checks a coil/speaker Diode test ▷∣ (arrow + bar) checks diodes and LEDs for direction; lights an LED dimly when probes are the right way round DC volts V… (V with straight lines) measures direct-current voltage — battery level, a sensor's output, the Pi's 3.3 V/5 V pins Continuity — is this wire alive? Set the dial to continuity (the speaker/sound-wave symbol). Touch the two probes together first — it should beep, confirming the meter works. Now touch one probe to each end of a wire or each side of a switch: a beep means an unbroken connection; silence means a break. This is how you test a salvaged USB cable, a jumper wire, or whether a button actually closes when pressed. Resistance — what value is this resistor? Set the dial to a resistance range above your expected value (e.g. the 2 kΩ range for a 330 Ω resistor). Touch one probe to each leg — resistors have no polarity, so direction does not matter. The display shows the value; a 330 Ω resistor will read somewhere around 314–347 Ω (within the ±5% tolerance). This is the foolproof way to confirm bands you cannot quite read. Diode test — which way round is this LED? Set the dial to the diode symbol (▷ with a bar). Touch the red probe to the LED's long leg (anode) and the black probe to the short leg (cathode) : the LED should glow faintly and the meter shows a forward voltage (roughly 1.5–3.5 V depending on colour). Swap the probes and it stays dark with no reading. This both proves the LED works and confirms its polarity — invaluable when a salvaged LED's legs have been trimmed to the same length. DC volts — how much is this supplying? Set the dial to DC volts (V with a solid and dashed line) on a range above what you expect (e.g. the 20 V range for a 9 V battery). Touch the red probe to the positive terminal and black to negative. A 1.5 V cell reading 0.9 V is nearly flat; a salvaged battery reading near 0 V is dead. You will also use this to confirm a Pi pin really is at 3.3 V before trusting it. Careful: only ever measure low-voltage DC (batteries, sensor outputs, the Pi's pins) with a hobby multimeter. Never put the probes into a mains socket or onto mains wiring — household mains is lethal and well beyond what beginner gear and beginner skills should touch. If a part is connected to mains, it is off-limits (see the recycling section). A Quick Python Refresher Python is the main language of this whole course, so let us make sure the foundations are solid before the builds begin. If you have done the earlier chapters this will be a recap; if you are jumping in here, it is everything you need to follow along. Two ways to run a program You will run Python in two ways throughout this Part: In Thonny — the friendly editor preinstalled on Raspberry Pi OS. Open it from the Raspberry Pi menu → Programming → Thonny, type your code in the top pane, and click the green Run button (▶) or press F5 . Output appears in the Shell at the bottom. Thonny is best while writing and debugging because you can run a line at a time and inspect variables. From the terminal with python3 file.py — this is how a "real" program is launched, and how your projects will eventually run on their own. Open a terminal, move to the folder holding your file, and run it. python3 hello.py python3 : the command that starts the Python 3 interpreter. On Raspberry Pi OS always use python3 (and pip3 ), never bare python , to be sure you are on Python 3. hello.py : the file to run. Python reads it top to bottom and executes each line. The file must be in your current folder, or you give its full path. Variables, print() and f-strings A variable is a named box that holds a value. print() displays things in the console. An f-string (a string prefixed with f ) lets you drop variables straight into text inside {curly braces} . name = "Maker" leds = 3 print("Hello, " + name) print(f"You have {leds} LEDs and {leds * 2} legs to wire.") Line 1 — name = "Maker" : creates a variable called name holding the text (a string ) "Maker". Line 2 — leds = 3 : creates a variable holding the whole number (an integer ) 3. Line 3 — print("Hello, " + name) : joins two strings with + and prints Hello, Maker . Line 4 — the f-string: the f before the quotes lets you insert variables and even do maths inside the braces. {leds} becomes 3 and {leds * 2} is calculated to 6 , printing You have 3 LEDs and 6 legs to wire. f-strings are the tidiest way to build messages, and you will use them constantly. Functions A function is a named, reusable block of code. You define it once with def and call it as often as you like. Functions can take inputs (called parameters ) and hand back a result with return . def greet(who): print(f"Welcome to the Maker Lab, {who}!") def add(a, b): return a + b greet("everyone") total = add(2, 3) print(total) Lines 1–2 — def greet(who): : defines a function named greet that takes one parameter, who . The indented line is its body; it runs only when the function is called. Lines 4–5 — def add(a, b): return a + b : defines add , which takes two parameters and return s their sum back to whoever called it. Line 7 — greet("everyone") : calls greet , passing "everyone" in as who ; it prints the welcome. Line 8 — total = add(2, 3) : calls add and stores the returned value (5) in total . Line 9 — print(total) : displays 5 . Wrapping repeated steps in functions keeps your project programs short and readable. import — borrowing other people's code The import keyword pulls in a module or library — a bundle of ready-written code — so you do not have to write everything yourself. You will start nearly every project with imports. import random from gpiozero import LED print(random.randint(1, 6)) led = LED(17) Line 1 — import random : brings in Python's built-in random module; you then use its tools with the random. prefix. Line 2 — from gpiozero import LED : imports just the LED object from the gpiozero library, so you can write LED(17) directly without a prefix. gpiozero is preinstalled on Bookworm and is the library you will use for every electronics build. Line 4 — random.randint(1, 6) : rolls a whole number from 1 to 6, like a die. Line 5 — led = LED(17) : creates an LED object on GPIO 17 — a taste of what is coming next chapter. Installing Packages: the Bookworm Rule (PEP 668) Most of the time you will import libraries that are already installed ( gpiozero , random , time ). Occasionally a project needs an extra one. On older systems you might have typed pip install something straight away — but on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm that is deliberately blocked. In plain words: PEP 668 is a Python rule that marks the system Python as "externally managed". It means: do not let pip scribble over the Python that the operating system itself depends on, because that can break your whole desktop. If you try a plain system-wide pip install on Bookworm, you will get an error: externally-managed-environment message — that is the rule protecting you, not a bug. There are two correct ways to install a package on Bookworm: Option 1 — use apt (simplest when a Pi package exists): sudo apt install python3-gpiozero sudo apt install python3-<name> : installs a Debian-packaged Python library system-wide, the operating-system-approved way. Many common libraries are available as python3-… packages (e.g. python3-gpiozero , python3-flask ). This sidesteps PEP 668 entirely because apt, not pip, manages it. Option 2 — make a virtual environment (a venv) and pip-install inside it: python3 -m venv myenv source myenv/bin/activate pip install some-library Line 1 — python3 -m venv myenv : creates a private, self-contained Python environment in a folder called myenv . Anything you install here is kept apart from the system Python, so it cannot break your desktop. Line 2 — source myenv/bin/activate : switches your terminal into that environment. Your prompt gains a (myenv) prefix to remind you. Now python and pip point inside the venv. Line 3 — pip install some-library : installs into the venv freely — no PEP 668 error, because you are no longer touching the system Python. Type deactivate to leave the venv later. Careful: you may see advice online to "just add --break-system-packages " to force a system-wide pip install. The flag's own name is the warning: it can break the tools your Pi relies on. Prefer apt or a venv. We will use a venv properly in the final capstone chapter when we install Flask. A First Taste of Bash Python is not the only language living on your Pi. The black terminal window you type commands into is itself running a language called Bash . Every ls , cd or sudo apt install you type is a Bash command — and you can save a list of those commands into a file to run them all at once. That file is a Bash script . In plain words: Bash is the language of the command line. A Bash script is a plain text file full of terminal commands that run top to bottom. It is perfect for gluing together jobs you would otherwise type by hand — backups, updates, launching your Python program at boot. Here is a tiny script. Open Thonny or any text editor, type this, and save it as hello.sh : #!/bin/bash echo "Hello from Bash!" echo "Today the Pi says:" date Line 1 — #!/bin/bash : the shebang . This special first line tells the system "run this file with the Bash program". Without it, the system would not know which language the file is written in. Line 2 — echo "Hello from Bash!" : echo is Bash's version of print() — it prints text to the terminal. Line 3 — another echo : prints a second line of text. Line 4 — date : runs the built-in date command, printing the current date and time. A Bash script is mostly just commands you could have typed yourself. Before you can run a script with ./ , you must mark the file as executable — give it permission to run as a program: chmod +x hello.sh ./hello.sh Line 1 — chmod +x hello.sh : chmod ("change mode") sets file permissions; +x adds the "executable" permission. You only need to do this once per script. Line 2 — ./hello.sh : runs the script. The ./ means "the file in this current folder" — without it, the shell would search the system folders for a command called hello.sh and not find your file. The shebang then makes Bash interpret it. Tip: a quick rule of thumb — reach for Bash when the job is mostly running other programs and shuffling files; reach for Python when the job involves real logic, maths, data, or talking to hardware. You will use both in this Part: Python for the projects, and the occasional Bash command to install or launch them. Which languages live on the Pi? Your Pi can run several programming languages out of the box. Here are the four you are most likely to meet, and when each shines: Language Best at Where you'll see it in this course Python readable, beginner-friendly logic; hardware control via gpiozero ; data, files, the web every project in this Part Bash running commands, automating the terminal, installing and launching things installs, scripts, running your programs C maximum speed and tiny memory; the language the Linux kernel and many Pi libraries are written in under the hood; not written directly here JavaScript making web pages interactive in the browser the capstone web dashboard (ch31) Note: you do not need to learn all four. Python carries the whole Part; Bash gives you a handful of handy commands; you will taste a little JavaScript right at the end to build a web dashboard; and C runs quietly beneath everything without you writing a line of it. The E-Waste Pile: Salvaging Safely Here is the maker's open secret: a huge amount of the gear you need is sitting in cupboards, charity-shop "spares or repair" bins, and recycling skips. A dead printer is a bag of motors and rods. An old mouse is a tidy micro-switch and an LED. A broken toy is a speaker and a gearbox. Learning to harvest and test these parts is good for your wallet and the planet — but it comes with one absolutely firm rule. Careful — read this before opening anything: the danger in old electronics is not the little 3.3 V and 5 V parts we play with. It is mains electricity and the large capacitors that store it. A capacitor can hold a lethal charge for a long time after the device is unplugged . Some devices must never be opened, full stop. The two-column figure below is your rule of thumb. Safe to harvest vs Dangerous — never open ✓ SAFE (low voltage) unplug first · battery-/USB-powered • Broken printers — stepper & DC motors, rods, gears, optical/limit switches • Mice & keyboards — micro-switches, LEDs, USB cable • Old toys — small motors, speakers, gears • Dead routers/modems — LEDs, buttons, connectors, heatsinks • TV remotes — IR LEDs, rubber buttons • Broken speakers/headphones — drivers, wire • Old USB cables — for 5 V power leads Always unplug & remove batteries first. ✗ DANGEROUS — NEVER OPEN mains voltage · stored lethal charge • CRT TVs & monitors — 20,000–30,000 V anode; the tube can implode • Microwave ovens — capacitor holds a lethal 4,000+ V even when unplugged • Mains PSUs & adapters — big filter caps store dangerous charge • Anything with large capacitors inside • Lithium-ion batteries — fire/explosion if punctured, crushed or shorted Recycle these whole, at a proper e-waste / WEEE collection point. Your salvage rule of thumb. The left column is low-voltage and safe to open once unplugged. The right column can hold a lethal charge — never open these; take them whole to an e-waste recycling point. Dangerous — never open these Careful — CRT TVs and monitors. The old, deep, glass-tubed sets. The picture tube runs at an anode voltage of 20,000–30,000 V , and internal capacitors can hold that charge for a long time after unplugging . The glass tube is also under vacuum and can implode into flying shards if cracked. Never open one. Recycle it whole. Careful — microwave ovens. A microwave's high-voltage capacitor can store a lethal 4,000 V or more even when the oven is unplugged . People have been killed by them. Always treat that capacitor as charged. Never open a microwave oven — recycle it whole. Careful — mains power supplies and adapters. Anything that plugs into the wall and converts mains down (PC power supplies, laptop bricks, plug-in chargers) contains large filter capacitors that store a dangerous charge on the mains side. Discard the whole adapter rather than opening it. The neat low-voltage USB cable hanging off a charger is fine to keep — just cut it free of the brick and never open the brick itself. Careful — lithium-ion batteries. The rechargeable cells in phones, laptops and power banks will catch fire or explode if punctured, crushed, bent or short-circuited . Never cut into one, never deform a swollen one, and never throw them in normal bin or fire. Take them to a battery recycling point. Note: the safe rule is simple — if it plugs into the mains wall socket, or has a big can-shaped capacitor, or a lithium battery, do not open it. Take it whole to a WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) recycling point. Everything we build in this Part runs from the Pi's gentle 3.3 V/5 V or small batteries — there is no reason to ever go near mains. Safe to harvest — the treasure list Now the fun part. These devices are low-voltage, battery- or USB-powered, and full of useful parts. Always unplug them and remove any batteries first , but once that is done they are safe to open and explore: Broken printers — a goldmine: stepper motors, DC motors, metal rods, gears, and optical/limit switches. Mice and keyboards — tactile micro-switches (great buttons), LEDs, and a USB cable. Old toys — small DC motors, speakers, gearboxes, and sometimes LEDs. Dead routers and modems — indicator LEDs, buttons, connectors, and small heatsinks. TV remotes — infrared (IR) LEDs and lovely rubber buttons. Broken speakers and headphones — speaker drivers and thin wire. Old USB cables — ready-made 5 V power leads. How to harvest a component and test it Most parts are either plugged in, screwed in, or soldered to a circuit board. Here is the routine: Make it safe. Unplug the device from any power and remove all batteries. Confirm there is no mains adapter still attached. Only safe-list devices, please. Open it up. Undo the screws (some hide under rubber feet or labels) and gently prise the case apart. Take a photo first so you remember how it goes together. Free the part. If it is held by a plug or screws, simply remove it. If it is soldered, you will need to desolder it: heat the joint with a soldering iron and lift the leg free, or use a solder sucker/braid to remove the molten solder. Work in a ventilated space and never touch the hot tip. Test it with your multimeter. Now prove the part actually works before you build with it: a salvaged LED → use the diode test ; red probe on the long leg should make it glow. a switch or button → use continuity ; it should beep only when pressed. a resistor → use the resistance (Ω) range to read its value. a speaker or motor coil → resistance should read a few ohms, not "open" (infinite) or "0" (a dead short). a salvaged cable → continuity end-to-end to find which wire is which and that none is broken. Label and store it. A little box of tested, labelled parts is worth more than a drawer of mystery junk. Careful: a soldering iron runs at around 350 °C — hot enough for a serious burn and to start a fire. Use a stand, keep it away from cables and skin, solder in a ventilated room, and let parts cool before handling. If you are under 16 or new to it, do desoldering with an adult nearby. Make It Your Own You have not wired anything yet, but you can already practise the skills that make every later build easier. Try these: Sort your kit. Open your starter kit and identify every part using this chapter: name each resistor by its colour bands, find the long leg on each LED, and test which jumper-wire types you have. Meter practice. Measure three resistors with the Ω range and check they match their bands. Diode-test an LED both ways round. Continuity-test a USB cable. Write and run a Bash script. Make a hello.sh that prints a greeting and the date, chmod +x it, and run it with ./hello.sh . Practise f-strings. Write a short Python program that stores your name and the number of parts in your kit, then prints a tidy summary line with an f-string. Start a salvage box. Find one safe-list dead gadget (an old mouse is perfect), open it, harvest the micro-switch and any LED, test them, and label them. You have just earned your first salvaged parts. What You've Learned This was your kit-out and safety briefing — the foundation for the whole Maker Lab. You now know: the toolkit : breadboard, the three jumper-wire types, resistors, LEDs, buttons, and a multimeter; how to read resistor colour bands (330 Ω = orange-orange-brown-gold; 1 kΩ = brown-black-red-gold) and how to spot LED polarity ; how to use a multimeter for continuity , resistance , the diode test and DC volts to test parts; a Python refresher — variables, print(), f-strings, functions, import , running code in Thonny and with python3 file.py , and the Bookworm PEP 668 rule (use apt or a venv, not a system-wide pip); a first taste of Bash — the shebang #!/bin/bash , chmod +x , running ./script.sh — and which languages live on the Pi; and the most important lesson of all: what is safe to salvage and what to never open . Next chapter the building begins in earnest: you will wire three LEDs and a breadboard into a working UK traffic-light controller, and learn lists and for loops along the way. Grab your kit — you have earned your Salvage Scout badge.

title: Traffic-Light Controller
headings: The Current Budget: Why Three LEDs Is Fine
text: A real set of traffic lights is just three lamps switched on and off in a fixed order — and that is exactly the kind of thing a Raspberry Pi is brilliant at. In this project you will wire up a red, an amber and a green LED, then teach your Pi to run a proper UK traffic-light sequence in an endless loop. Along the way you will learn four Python fundamentals you will use forever — lists , for loops , functions and time.sleep() for timing — and the electronics idea of driving several outputs at once while staying inside the Pi's current budget . What You'll Build & Learn By the end of this chapter you will have a working model traffic light that cycles forever, and then a smarter version that waits for a pedestrian to press a button before changing. More importantly, you will have met the building blocks that nearly every program is made from. The Python fundamentals Lists — a single name that holds several things in order, like [red, amber, green] . Instead of three separate variables, you keep your three LEDs together in one tidy container. The for loop — a way to repeat an action once for every item in a list, without copying and pasting the same line three times. Functions — named, reusable blocks of code (with parameters you can pass in) so you can write a step once and call it as often as you like. time.sleep() and sequencing — pausing the program for a set number of seconds so each light stays on long enough to see, in the right order. The electronics fundamentals Driving multiple outputs — controlling three LEDs from three separate GPIO pins at the same time. One resistor per LED — every LED gets its own 330 Ω current-limiting resistor; you never share one resistor between several LEDs. The current budget — each GPIO pin can safely supply only about 16 mA , and the whole header together should stay under roughly 50 mA . Three well-behaved LEDs fit comfortably; we will do the sums so you can see why. Note: This chapter assumes you have met the GPIO header, breadboards and the single-LED blink circuit from earlier in the course. If the words "GPIO 17 means physical pin 11" are new to you, it is worth a quick look back before continuing. Everything else we will build up gently from there. Parts List You can find every one of these in a basic Raspberry Pi starter kit, or salvage the LEDs and resistors from old electronics (see the "From the e-waste pile" box later). A Raspberry Pi 5, set up and running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. 3 × LEDs — ideally one red, one amber/yellow and one green, but any three colours work. 3 × 330 Ω resistors — colour bands orange-orange-brown-gold. One per LED, no exceptions. A half-size or mini breadboard. 4 × female-to-male jumper wires — three for the GPIO signals, one for the shared ground. (For the pedestrian variant only) 1 × push button and 1 more jumper wire. In plain words: a female-to-male jumper wire has a little socket on one end (the "female" end, which slides over a GPIO pin) and a stiff pin on the other (the "male" end, which pushes into a breadboard hole). The Current Budget: Why Three LEDs Is Fine Before we wire anything, let us understand the single most important safety idea in this chapter. The GPIO pins are wonderful, but they are delicate . They can only push a small amount of electrical current before they overheat and fail. In plain words: current is how much electricity flows per second, measured in milliamps (mA). Think of voltage as water pressure and current as the actual amount of water moving through the pipe. Too much current through a thin wire — or a GPIO pin — makes it overheat. Two limits matter on the Pi 5: Per pin: keep each GPIO pin under about 16 mA . Whole header: keep the total drawn from all the 3.3 V pins combined under about 50 mA . How much does one LED with a 330 Ω resistor actually draw? We can work it out with Ohm's Law ( current = voltage ÷ resistance ). A standard LED "uses up" about 2 V, leaving 3.3 − 2 = 1.3 V across the resistor. So: 1.3 V ÷ 330 Ω ≈ 0.0039 A ≈ 4 mA per LED Four milliamps is well under the 16 mA per-pin limit, so each pin is happy. Three LEDs together draw about 3 × 4 = 12 mA — comfortably under the 50 mA whole-header limit. This is exactly why we can light three LEDs straight from the Pi, and exactly why each LED still needs its own resistor: that resistor is what keeps the current down to those safe few milliamps. The GPIO current budget Per pin: 16 mA max ~4 mA used one LED + 330 Ω ≈ 4 mA Whole header: 50 mA max ~12 mA used (3 LEDs) plenty of headroom Ohm's Law check 3.3 V − 2 V (LED) = 1.3 V on resistor 1.3 V ÷ 330 Ω ≈ 4 mA per LED Each LED with its own 330 Ω resistor sips about 4 mA. Three of them stay far inside both the per-pin (16 mA) and whole-header (50 mA) limits. Careful: if you removed the resistors and connected the LEDs straight to 3.3 V, each would try to pull far more than 16 mA. The LED could burn out, and the GPIO pin behind it could be destroyed — permanently, with no fuse to save it. One 330 Ω resistor per LED, always. Never share a single resistor between two LEDs either: each LED needs its own, or they will rob current from one another and behave unpredictably. The Circuit: Common-Cathode Layout All three LEDs share one thing: the ground (GND) connection. The long leg (anode, +) of each LED connects through its own resistor to its own GPIO pin. The short leg (cathode, −) of every LED connects to a shared ground rail, which runs back to a single GND pin on the Pi. Because all the cathodes meet at a common point, this is called a common-cathode layout. In plain words: common-cathode just means "all the negative legs join together." It saves wires — you only need one ground wire back to the Pi instead of three. We will use these three GPIO pins (the BCM/GPIO numbers your code uses, with the physical header position in brackets): LED GPIO (BCM) Physical pin Red GPIO 25 Pin 22 Amber GPIO 8 Pin 24 Green GPIO 7 Pin 26 Careful: power off and unplug your Pi before doing any wiring. Shut down from the menu (Raspberry Pi menu > Shutdown), wait for the green activity light to go out, then pull the power lead. Remember the Pi 5 GPIO is 3.3 V logic only — never feed 5 V into a GPIO pin. Fit one 330 Ω resistor per LED, and double-check every wire before you plug the power back in. Wiring diagram Traffic-Light Wiring (3 LEDs, common cathode) GPIO Header Pin 22 (GPIO 25) Pin 24 (GPIO 8) Pin 26 (GPIO 7) Pin 20 (GND) − ground rail (all cathodes meet here) 330Ω R 330Ω A 330Ω G Current path: GPIO pin → resistor → LED anode → cathode → ground rail → GND Each LED has its own GPIO pin and its own 330 Ω resistor. All three short legs (cathodes) join the shared ground rail, which returns to a single GND pin — the common-cathode layout. Connection table From To Via GPIO 25 (pin 22) Red LED long leg (anode) 330 Ω resistor GPIO 8 (pin 24) Amber LED long leg (anode) 330 Ω resistor GPIO 7 (pin 26) Green LED long leg (anode) 330 Ω resistor Red LED short leg (cathode) Ground rail direct Amber LED short leg (cathode) Ground rail direct Green LED short leg (cathode) Ground rail direct Ground rail GND (pin 20) jumper wire Step-by-step wiring Power off. Shut the Pi down fully and unplug it before touching any wires. Place the three LEDs. Push each LED into the breadboard so its two legs land in different numbered rows. Keep the long legs (anodes) all on one side and the short legs (cathodes) all on the other side of the centre gap. Fit one resistor per LED. For each LED, push a 330 Ω resistor so one leg shares the row with that LED's long leg, and the other leg sits in a free row where a GPIO wire can reach it. Run the three GPIO wires. Connect GPIO 25 (pin 22) to the red LED's resistor, GPIO 8 (pin 24) to the amber resistor, and GPIO 7 (pin 26) to the green resistor. Build the ground rail. Connect all three LED short legs (cathodes) to the breadboard's blue − rail. Then run one jumper wire from the − rail back to a GND pin (pin 20) on the Pi. Check LED direction. Long leg toward the resistor/GPIO side; short leg toward ground. A backwards LED simply will not light — no harm done, just turn it around. Reconnect power only once every wire is checked, then boot to the desktop. Fundamental 1: Meet the List Before the full program, let us learn each fundamental on its own with a tiny example. Open Thonny and try these in the editor. A list is one name that holds several values in order, written inside square brackets and separated by commas. Here is a list of three LED objects: from gpiozero import LED red = LED(25) amber = LED(8) green = LED(7) lights = [red, amber, green] Lines 3–5 — red = LED(25) etc.: create three separate LED objects, one per GPIO pin. Each variable controls one physical LED. Line 7 — lights = [red, amber, green] : bundles all three into a single list called lights . The square brackets make it a list; the order is remembered, so lights[0] is the red one, lights[1] is amber, and lights[2] is green. (Lists count from zero — that catches everyone out at first.) In plain words: a list is like an egg box. The box has one name, but holds several eggs in numbered slots. You can reach into slot 0, slot 1, slot 2, and so on. Fundamental 2: The for Loop Now that the LEDs live in a list, a for loop lets us do the same thing to every one of them without repeating ourselves. Try this: from gpiozero import LED from time import sleep lights = [LED(25), LED(8), LED(7)] for light in lights: light.on() sleep(0.5) light.off() Line 4 — lights = [LED(25), LED(8), LED(7)] : creates the three LEDs straight inside the list — no need for separate variables if we do not want them. Line 6 — for light in lights: : this is the loop. It runs the indented block once for each item in lights . On the first pass, light means the red LED; on the second, amber; on the third, green. light is just a temporary name we chose for "the current item." Lines 7–9 — light.on() / sleep(0.5) / light.off() : switch the current LED on, wait half a second, then switch it off. Because the loop repeats, you see each LED flash in turn — a chase effect — from one short block of code. Tip: the indentation (the spaces at the start of lines 7–9) is what tells Python which lines belong inside the loop. Thonny adds it automatically when you end a line with a colon. Keep it consistent — four spaces is the Python convention. Fundamental 3: Functions with Parameters A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you like, just by calling its name. A function can take parameters — values you hand in each time — so the same function can do slightly different jobs. Here is a function that turns exactly one light on and the others off: from gpiozero import LED from time import sleep red = LED(25) amber = LED(8) green = LED(7) lights = [red, amber, green] def show(on_light, seconds): for light in lights: light.off() on_light.on() sleep(seconds) show(green, 3) show(amber, 1) show(red, 3) Line 9 — def show(on_light, seconds): : def starts a function definition. We name it show and give it two parameters : on_light (which LED to light) and seconds (how long to wait). These are placeholders filled in each time we call the function. Lines 10–11 — for light in lights: light.off() : a small for loop that switches all the LEDs off first, so we always start from a clean state. Line 12 — on_light.on() : switches on just the LED that was passed in. Line 13 — sleep(seconds) : pauses for the number of seconds passed in, holding that light on. Lines 15–17 — show(green, 3) etc.: call the function three times with different arguments. Green for 3 seconds, amber for 1, red for 3. Writing the logic once and calling it three times is the whole point of a function. In plain words: a function is a recipe with blanks to fill in. show is the recipe; on_light and seconds are the blanks (parameters); show(green, 3) fills them in (those are the arguments) and runs the recipe. The UK Traffic-Light Sequence UK traffic lights follow a very specific four-phase cycle. The one phase people forget is the red-and-amber together step, which warns drivers that green is coming so they can get ready to move. Phase Lights on Meaning 1 Red Stop 2 Red + Amber Stop, but get ready — green is next 3 Green Go (if the way is clear) 4 Amber Prepare to stop The UK four-phase cycle 1. Stop 2. Get ready 3. Go 4. Slow down → → → The UK sequence loops forever: Red → Red+Amber → Green → Amber → back to Red. The Red+Amber phase (2) is the one that does not exist in many other countries. The Full Program Now we put the fundamentals together. Open a new file in Thonny, type this in, and save it as traffic.py . from gpiozero import LED from time import sleep # One LED object per pin, kept together in a list red = LED(25) amber = LED(8) green = LED(7) all_lights = [red, amber, green] def all_off(): for light in all_lights: light.off() def phase(reds, ambers, greens, seconds): all_off() if reds: red.on() if ambers: amber.on() if greens: green.on() sleep(seconds) print("Traffic lights running. Press Stop to quit.") while True: phase(True, False, False, 4) # Red: stop phase(True, True, False, 1) # Red + Amber: get ready phase(False, False, True, 4) # Green: go phase(False, True, False, 1) # Amber: slow down Lines 1–2: import LED from gpiozero and sleep from the built-in time module so we can pause between phases. Lines 5–8: create the three LEDs and store them in the list all_lights — our list fundamental in action. Lines 10–12 — def all_off(): : a small function that loops over the list (a for loop ) and switches every LED off. Calling all_off() is now a one-word way to reset everything. Line 14 — def phase(reds, ambers, greens, seconds): : the heart of the program. Four parameters say which lights should be on (each is True or False ) and for how long. Line 15 — all_off() : start every phase from a clean, all-off state so old lights never linger. Lines 16–21 — the three if checks: switch on only the lights asked for. if reds: means "if reds is True, turn the red LED on." This lets the very same function produce all four phases, including Red+Amber together. Line 22 — sleep(seconds) : hold this phase for the requested time — sequencing with time.sleep() . Line 25 — while True: : repeat forever, so the lights cycle endlessly like the real thing. Lines 26–29 — four phase(...) calls: the UK sequence, in order, with the Red+Amber phase included. Because the timings are just arguments, you can tweak them without touching the function. Running it Save the file as traffic.py in your home folder (File > Save). Run it with the green ▶ button or F5. Watch the cycle: red, then red+amber together, then green, then amber, repeating. The console prints a start message. Stop with the red ◼ button when you have seen enough. All LEDs go off. The Elegant Version: TrafficLights The program above works perfectly and taught us lists, loops and functions. But gpiozero already knows about traffic lights! It has a ready-made object called TrafficLights that bundles a red, amber and green LED together for you. Here is the entire sequence again, far shorter: from gpiozero import TrafficLights from time import sleep lights = TrafficLights(red=25, amber=8, green=7) while True: lights.red.on() sleep(4) lights.amber.on() # red still on -> the Red+Amber phase sleep(1) lights.off() lights.green.on() sleep(4) lights.green.off() lights.amber.on() sleep(1) lights.amber.off() Line 1 — from gpiozero import TrafficLights : imports the ready-made traffic-light object. Line 4 — lights = TrafficLights(red=25, amber=8, green=7) : creates one object that owns all three LEDs. The red= , amber= , green= parts are keyword arguments — they make it crystal clear which pin is which colour. Wiring is unchanged: each LED still has its own 330 Ω resistor. Lines 7–8 — lights.red.on() then sleep(4) : you reach each colour through the object: lights.red , lights.amber , lights.green are ordinary LEDs you can turn on and off. Line 9 — lights.amber.on() : because red is still on, switching amber on as well gives the Red+Amber phase for free. Line 11 — lights.off() : a handy shortcut that switches all three off at once. Lines 12–17: green for 4 s, then amber alone for 1 s, before the loop returns to red. Tip: TrafficLights even has a built-in demo. Try lights.blink() to flash all three together, or explore the gpiozero documentation at gpiozero.readthedocs.io for more ready-made objects like LEDBoard , which groups any number of LEDs. Note: both versions drive the same wiring and obey the same current budget. The hand-written version teaches you the fundamentals; the TrafficLights version shows how a good library lets you say what you mean in fewer lines. Real programmers move between both styles all the time. The Pedestrian-Crossing Variant Real crossings change for people, not just on a timer. Let us add a push button: while no one presses it, the lights stay green for traffic; press it, and the lights run through amber to red so pedestrians can cross, then back to green. Wire a push button alongside the LEDs. With gpiozero's Button , the default wiring is one leg to a GPIO pin and the other leg to GND (gpiozero switches on an internal pull-up resistor, so a press reads as "pressed" without any extra parts). We will use GPIO 2 (physical pin 3) for the button. From To Via Button leg 1 GPIO 2 (pin 3) jumper wire Button leg 2 (opposite side) GND (pin 20 / ground rail) jumper wire Careful: power off again before adding the button. The button needs no resistor of its own, but the three LEDs still each need their 330 Ω resistor — nothing about the LED rules changes. from gpiozero import TrafficLights, Button from time import sleep lights = TrafficLights(red=25, amber=8, green=7) button = Button(2) # other leg to GND; internal pull-up by default def let_pedestrians_cross(): print("Button pressed - stopping traffic") lights.amber.on() sleep(1) lights.amber.off() lights.red.on() sleep(5) # walk time lights.red.off() lights.green.on() # traffic flows again # Start with green for the traffic lights.green.on() print("Lights green. Press the button to cross.") while True: button.wait_for_press() lights.green.off() let_pedestrians_cross() Line 1: import both TrafficLights and Button from gpiozero. Line 5 — button = Button(2) : the button on GPIO 2. By default pull_up=True , so wire the other leg to GND; pressing pulls the pin low and gpiozero reports it as pressed. Lines 7–15 — def let_pedestrians_cross(): : a function holding the whole "stop the traffic, let people walk, then resume" sequence: amber, red for a walk time, then back to green. Lines 18–19: before the loop, set green for traffic and print an instruction. Line 21 — while True: : loop forever, waiting for presses. Line 22 — button.wait_for_press() : pauses the program right here until the button is pressed. No busy-waiting, no wasted effort — the program simply sleeps until someone wants to cross. Lines 23–24: turn green off and call our crossing function. When it finishes, the loop returns to waiting for the next press. Note: we have used Button only lightly here. Buttons, debouncing and reaction-time games are the whole subject of the next chapter — so if the button misbehaves or seems to "press itself" twice, that is the bouncing problem you will learn to fix next. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause & fix One LED never lights It is probably in backwards. Long leg (anode) must face the resistor/GPIO side; short leg (cathode) faces ground. Pull it out and turn it round. No LEDs light at all Check the single ground wire from the − rail to the Pi's GND pin — if that is loose, none of the LEDs can complete their circuit. Wrong colour lights for a phase A GPIO wire is on the wrong resistor. Match GPIO 25→red, GPIO 8→amber, GPIO 7→green, and check your code uses the same numbers. LED is very dim or flickers A wire is barely making contact, or you used a much larger resistor than 330 Ω. Re-seat the wires; confirm orange-orange-brown-gold bands. No module named 'lgpio' Run sudo apt install python3-lgpio in a terminal, then restart Thonny. An LED stays dimly lit when it should be off Usually a stray wire bridging two rows on the breadboard. Trace each row and remove the accidental bridge. From the E-Waste Pile You do not need to buy LEDs and resistors — old electronics are full of them. Almost any dead gadget with indicator lights is a free supply. LEDs live in broken toys, old routers and modems (status lights), printer control panels, and cheap fairy lights. Desolder them gently with a soldering iron; the longer leg is still the anode. Resistors are scattered across almost every circuit board. Read the colour bands (orange-orange-brown-gold is your 330 Ω) or measure them with a multimeter on the Ω setting. Test before you trust: a multimeter in diode mode lights a good LED dimly when the red probe touches the anode; swap the probes if it stays dark. Careful: only ever harvest from low-voltage, unplugged equipment. Never open mains power supplies, microwave ovens, CRT televisions/monitors, or anything with large capacitors or lithium batteries — these can hold a dangerous or lethal charge even when unplugged. Stick to battery toys, USB gadgets and dead routers. Make It Your Own You have the fundamentals now — here are four ways to take the project further: Two-way junction. Add a second set of three LEDs for the cross-road and run the two sets in opposite phases (one red while the other is green). A list of two TrafficLights objects and a loop will keep it tidy. Adjustable timing. Move all the sleep durations into variables at the top ( go_time = 4 , warn_time = 1 ) so you can tune the whole cycle in one place. A green "walk" man. Add a fourth and fifth LED (red and green) for the pedestrian signal, and light the green walk LED while traffic is on red. Level crossing. Swap the sequence for two red LEDs that alternate (blinking left-right) like a railway level crossing — a great excuse to practise blink() and a list. Tip: every extension above still obeys the current budget. If you ever add many LEDs (say a whole row), add up the milliamps: stay under ~16 mA per pin and ~50 mA across the header, or switch to a driver chip designed to handle more. Key terms List — a single name holding several values in order, written in square brackets; items are numbered from 0. for loop — repeats a block of code once for each item in a list (or other sequence). Function — a named, reusable block of code, defined with def , that you run by calling its name. Parameter / argument — a parameter is a named "blank" in a function definition; an argument is the actual value you pass in when you call it. time.sleep() — pauses the program for a given number of seconds; the basis of timed sequencing. while True — a loop that repeats forever, used here to cycle the lights endlessly. Common cathode — a wiring layout where all the LED negative legs (cathodes) join a shared ground. Current budget — the safe limits on current: ~16 mA per GPIO pin and ~50 mA across the whole header. TrafficLights — a ready-made gpiozero object grouping a red, amber and green LED, created with TrafficLights(red=, amber=, green=) . LEDBoard — a gpiozero object that groups any number of LEDs so you can control them together. Chapter summary A list keeps related things (our three LEDs) together under one name, indexed from 0. A for loop runs the same code for every item in a list — perfect for switching all the LEDs off at once. Functions with parameters let you write a step once (like phase() ) and reuse it with different values. time.sleep() holds each phase long enough to see, giving you control over sequencing . The UK cycle is Red → Red+Amber → Green → Amber, including the easily forgotten Red+Amber "get ready" phase. Every LED needs its own 330 Ω resistor ; never share one or omit it. Respect the current budget : ~16 mA per pin, ~50 mA total; three resistor-limited LEDs draw only ~12 mA together. A common-cathode layout shares one ground wire for all three LEDs. gpiozero's TrafficLights(red=, amber=, green=) bundles the three LEDs into one elegant object that does the same job in fewer lines. Adding a Button (one leg to a GPIO pin, the other to GND) turns the project into a pedestrian crossing — a gentle taste of the next chapter. Always power off and unplug before wiring, and keep to 3.3 V on every GPIO pin.

title: Reaction-Timer Game
headings: How a Button Talks to the Pi
Fundamental 3: Timing with the time Module
text: How fast are your reflexes, really? In this project you will build a reaction-timer game: an LED lights up after a random, unpredictable delay, and you must slam a button as quickly as you can. The Pi measures your reaction time in milliseconds and keeps track of your best score across rounds. Building it teaches you a whole cluster of core Python ideas — variables , the random module, the time module, conditionals , while loops and f-strings — plus the electronics of reading a button and taming switch bounce . What You'll Build & Learn The finished game runs in the Thonny console and on the breadboard. Each round: a random wait, then the "go" LED lights, you press as fast as you can, and the Pi prints your time and tells you if it is a new best. Here are the fundamentals you will pick up. The Python fundamentals Variables — named boxes that store values (your start time, your reaction time, your best score) and can change as the game runs. The random module — making the computer pick unpredictable values, here random.uniform() for a random delay so you cannot cheat by anticipating. The time module — time.time() gives the current moment as a number; subtracting two readings tells you how long something took. Conditionals — if / elif / else to make decisions, such as "is this a new best score?" The while loop — repeating the game round after round. f-strings — a clean way to drop values straight into printed text, like f"{ms} ms" . The electronics fundamentals Button input — reading a push button with gpiozero's Button object (default pull_up=True , wired GPIO → button → GND). Switch bounce and debounce — why a single press can register as several, and how bounce_time fixes it. An LED as a signal — using one LED as the "go!" light, with its own 330 Ω resistor. Note: this chapter follows on from the LED and button basics earlier in the course. We will still explain each part, but it helps if you have lit a single LED before. Parts List A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. 1 × LED — any colour; green suits a "go" light. 1 × 330 Ω resistor — orange-orange-brown-gold, for the LED. 1 × push button — a small tactile switch with four legs. A breadboard. 3 × female-to-male jumper wires — one for the LED's GPIO, one for the button's GPIO, one shared ground. Careful: power off and unplug your Pi before wiring. Shut down from the menu, wait for the green light to go out, then remove the power lead. The Pi 5 GPIO is 3.3 V logic only — never put 5 V on a GPIO pin. The LED needs its own 330 Ω resistor; the button does not need an external resistor because gpiozero provides one internally. How a Button Talks to the Pi A push button is just a switch: press it and two contacts touch, completing a circuit; let go and they spring apart. gpiozero's Button object reads this for you. By default, Button uses an internal pull-up resistor. That means the GPIO pin is gently held HIGH (3.3 V) when nothing is happening. You wire the button so that pressing it connects the pin to GND , pulling it LOW. gpiozero understands this and reports the press correctly — is_pressed becomes True . The beauty is you only need two wires and no extra resistor. In plain words: a pull-up resistor keeps a GPIO input pin at a known HIGH value when nothing is pressing the button, so the pin never "floats" and reads random noise. The Pi 5 has these built in; gpiozero switches one on automatically for every Button . Note: the default is pull_up=True , so the button's other leg goes to GND . If you ever set pull_up=False instead, you would wire that leg to 3.3 V — but for this project, stick with the default and wire to GND. Wiring the button leg straight to 3.3 V while leaving the default pull-up on would be a wiring mistake, so always match the wiring to the setting. There are two everyday ways to read a button. The first is to ask it directly whether it is pressed, using is_pressed : from gpiozero import Button from time import sleep button = Button(27) while True: if button.is_pressed: print("Down") else: print("Up") sleep(0.2) Line 4 — button = Button(27) : a button on GPIO 27 with the default internal pull-up. Line 7 — if button.is_pressed: : is_pressed is a property that is True while the button is held and False otherwise. This "keep checking" style is called polling . Line 11 — sleep(0.2) : a tiny pause so we are not printing thousands of lines per second. The second way — the one our game uses — is to wait for a press with button.wait_for_press() , which stops the program at that line until the press happens. That is exactly what we want for timing: the moment wait_for_press() returns is the moment the player reacted. Switch bounce: the hidden gremlin When metal contacts inside a button slap together, they do not connect cleanly. For a few thousandths of a second they bounce apart and back, several times, like a dropped ball. The Pi is fast enough to see every one of those bounces, so a single physical press can look like five presses in a row. This is called switch bounce . Switch bounce vs a clean signal Raw button (bounces) one press → many fake edges With bounce_time one press → one clean edge → bounce_time=0.05 ignores extra edges for 50 ms Without debouncing, one press produces several rapid on/off edges. Setting bounce_time tells gpiozero to ignore further changes for a short window, turning the mess into one clean press. The cure is debouncing : after the first change, ignore any further changes for a short window (say 50 milliseconds) — long enough for the bouncing to settle. gpiozero does this for you with the bounce_time argument: from gpiozero import Button button = Button(17, bounce_time=0.05) # ignore bounces within 50 ms Line 3 — Button(17, bounce_time=0.05) : creates a button on GPIO 17 with debouncing. bounce_time=0.05 means "after a change, ignore any more changes for 0.05 seconds (50 ms)." That smooths out the bounce so each press counts once. With no bounce_time (the default None ), debouncing is off. Tip: 50 ms is a good starting value. If a fast double-tap is being merged into one, lower it; if one press still registers twice, raise it a little. The Circuit We use two GPIO pins: one drives the LED, one reads the button. Both share the same ground. Component GPIO (BCM) Physical pin LED ("go" light) GPIO 17 Pin 11 Button GPIO 27 Pin 13 Wiring diagram Reaction-Timer Wiring (LED + button) GPIO Header Pin 11 (GPIO 17) Pin 13 (GPIO 27) Pin 6 (GND) − ground rail 330Ω GO Button LED: GPIO 17 → resistor → LED → GND. Button: GPIO 27 → button → GND. The green "go" LED runs from GPIO 17 through its 330 Ω resistor to the ground rail. The button connects GPIO 27 to the same ground rail; gpiozero's internal pull-up means no button resistor is needed. Connection table From To Via GPIO 17 (pin 11) LED long leg (anode) 330 Ω resistor LED short leg (cathode) Ground rail direct GPIO 27 (pin 13) Button leg 1 jumper wire Button leg 2 (opposite side) Ground rail jumper wire Ground rail GND (pin 6) jumper wire Step-by-step wiring Power off. Shut down and unplug the Pi before touching the breadboard. Fit the LED. Push the LED in with its long leg (anode) and short leg (cathode) in different rows across the centre gap. Add its resistor. One leg of the 330 Ω resistor shares the LED's long-leg row; the other leg goes to a free row for the GPIO wire. Wire the LED. GPIO 17 (pin 11) to the resistor; the LED's short leg to the − ground rail. Fit the button straddling the centre gap so its two sides are separate until pressed. Wire the button. GPIO 27 (pin 13) to one side; the other side to the − ground rail. Common ground. Run one jumper from the − rail to a GND pin (pin 6). Re-check and power up only once every wire is confirmed. Fundamental 1: Variables and f-strings Let us meet the Python ideas one at a time before the full game. A variable is a labelled box that holds a value. You can put a value in, read it back, and change it later. best_score = None attempts = 0 attempts = attempts + 1 print(f"You have had {attempts} go(s). Best so far: {best_score}") Line 1 — best_score = None : creates a variable best_score and stores None in it. None is Python's word for "nothing yet" — we have not recorded a best score, so the box starts empty. Line 2 — attempts = 0 : a counter variable starting at zero. Line 4 — attempts = attempts + 1 : reads the current value, adds one, and stores the result back. Variables can change — that is what makes them useful for scores and counters. Line 5 — print(f"...{attempts}...{best_score}") : an f-string (note the f before the quote). Anything inside { } is replaced by the value of that variable. Here it prints the count and best score in a sentence without fiddly string-joining. In plain words: an f-string is a string with the letter f in front. Inside it, {name} gets swapped for whatever name holds. It is the tidiest way to mix words and values in one line. Fundamental 2: Random Delays If the LED always lit after exactly two seconds, you could cheat by counting. The random module makes the wait unpredictable. import random from time import sleep wait = random.uniform(2, 5) # a random number of seconds between 2 and 5 print(f"Waiting {wait:.2f} seconds...") sleep(wait) print("GO!") Line 1 — import random : brings in Python's built-in randomness module. Line 4 — random.uniform(2, 5) : returns a random decimal number anywhere between 2 and 5 (for example 3.71). uniform means every value in that range is equally likely. We store it in wait . Line 5 — f"Waiting {wait:.2f} seconds..." : the :.2f inside the braces is a format instruction meaning "show this number to 2 decimal places," so 3.71456 prints as 3.71. Line 6 — sleep(wait) : pauses for that random number of seconds, so the player never knows exactly when "GO!" will appear. Fundamental 3: Timing with the time Module To measure a reaction, we note the moment the LED lights and the moment the button is pressed, then subtract. The time module gives us those moments. from time import time start = time() # ... player reacts ... end = time() reaction_seconds = end - start reaction_ms = reaction_seconds * 1000 print(f"Reaction time: {reaction_ms:.0f} ms") Line 3 — start = time() : time() returns the current moment as a number of seconds (a big decimal). We save it as start the instant the LED lights. Line 5 — end = time() : another reading taken the instant the button is pressed. Line 7 — reaction_seconds = end - start : subtract the two readings to get how long it took, in seconds. This is a delta — a difference between two times. Line 8 — reaction_ms = reaction_seconds * 1000 : multiply by 1000 to convert seconds to milliseconds, which feels more natural for reaction times. Line 9 — {reaction_ms:.0f} : :.0f rounds to a whole number, so we print e.g. 312 ms rather than 312.4187 ms . Fundamental 4: Conditionals and while Loops To decide whether a score is a new best, and to run round after round, we need conditionals and a while loop . best = None rounds = 0 while rounds < 3: score = 250 # pretend reaction time in ms if best is None: best = score print("First score recorded.") elif score < best: best = score print("New best!") else: print("Not your best this time.") rounds = rounds + 1 Line 4 — while rounds < 3: : a while loop repeats its block as long as the condition rounds < 3 is true. The < means "less than." When rounds reaches 3, the loop stops. Line 6 — if best is None: : the first branch of a conditional . If we have no best yet, this score becomes the best. Line 9 — elif score < best: : elif means "else, if". It is only checked when the if above was false. If this new score is lower (faster) than the best, we have a new record. Line 12 — else: : runs when none of the above were true — the score was not a new best. Line 14 — rounds = rounds + 1 : count this round so the while loop eventually ends. Forgetting this line would make the loop run forever! In plain words: if / elif / else is the program making a decision — "if this, do that; otherwise, if something else, do this other thing; otherwise, do the last thing." Only one branch runs. The Full Game Now we assemble everything into the reaction-timer game. Open a new file in Thonny, type it in, and save it as reaction.py . from gpiozero import LED, Button from time import time, sleep import random led = LED(17) button = Button(27, bounce_time=0.05) # debounced button to GND best = None # best (lowest) reaction time in ms, None until first round round_number = 0 print("Reaction Timer! Press the button the instant the LED lights.") print("Press Ctrl+C in the console to quit.\n") while True: round_number = round_number + 1 print(f"--- Round {round_number} ---") print("Get ready...") led.off() wait = random.uniform(2, 5) # unpredictable delay sleep(wait) # Catch a cheat who presses before the light if button.is_pressed: print("Too soon! Wait for the light. No score.\n") sleep(1) continue led.on() start = time() # the moment the light came on button.wait_for_press() # block until the player presses end = time() # the moment they pressed led.off() reaction_ms = (end - start) * 1000 if best is None or reaction_ms < best: best = reaction_ms print(f"Your time: {reaction_ms:.0f} ms - NEW BEST!") else: print(f"Your time: {reaction_ms:.0f} ms (best: {best:.0f} ms)") print() sleep(2) Lines 1–3: import the LED and Button from gpiozero, time and sleep from the time module, and the random module. Line 5 — led = LED(17) : the green "go" LED on GPIO 17. Line 6 — button = Button(27, bounce_time=0.05) : the button on GPIO 27, debounced so one press counts once. Its other leg is wired to GND; the default internal pull-up handles the rest. Lines 8–9: two variables : best starts as None (no score yet), round_number starts at 0. Line 14 — while True: : the while loop that plays round after round forever, until you stop the program. Lines 15–17: count the round and announce it with f-strings . Lines 19–21 — random delay: turn the LED off, pick a random wait with random.uniform(2, 5) , and sleep for it so the "go" moment is unpredictable. Lines 24–27 — the cheat check: an if conditional . If the player is already holding the button before the light, we print a warning and continue — which jumps straight to the next loop iteration, skipping the timing. Lines 29–32 — the measurement: light the LED, record start = time() , then button.wait_for_press() pauses until the player presses, at which point we record end = time() and switch the LED off. Line 34 — reaction_ms = (end - start) * 1000 : the time delta in seconds, converted to milliseconds. Lines 36–40 — score check: an if / else conditional . If there is no best yet, or this time is faster than the best, record a new best and say so; otherwise just show the time alongside the current best. The :.0f rounds to whole milliseconds. Lines 43–44: a blank line and a short pause before the next round begins. Running the game Save as reaction.py in your home folder. Run with the green ▶ button or F5. Read the instructions printed in the console. Wait for the LED. After a random pause it lights — press the button as fast as you can. Read your time in milliseconds. Anything around 200–300 ms is typical for a human; under 200 ms is very sharp. Keep playing — the game tracks your best score across rounds. Press the red ◼ Stop button (or Ctrl+C in the console) to quit. Tip: challenge a friend and keep score on paper, or extend the program to track each player's best (see "Make it your own").
