Tiredness, caffeine and practice all visibly change your numbers — it makes a fun little science experiment. Understanding Your Numbers It is worth pausing on what those millisecond figures mean, because they show why we measured the way we did. A millisecond (ms) is one thousandth of a second. Human reaction to a sudden light is genuinely slow in computer terms: signals have to travel from your eye to your brain, get processed, then travel back down to your finger muscles. That round trip takes most people somewhere between 200 and 300 ms . A trained gamer or athlete might reach 150 ms; almost nobody beats 100 ms honestly — a "score" much lower than that is a sign of switch bounce or a guessed press, not superhuman reflexes. Typical human reaction times very fast typical take your time 100 ms 200 ms 350 ms 500 ms+ A score under ~100 ms usually means bounce or a guessed press, not real reflexes. Where typical reaction times fall. Most honest scores land in the 200–300 ms band; impossibly small numbers point to switch bounce. This is also why time.time() is good enough here. It measures wall-clock time to a tiny fraction of a millisecond — far finer than human reactions — so any wobble in the measurement is dwarfed by your own variation from press to press. Tracking Scores Across Rounds Our game keeps a single best value. But score tracking can be richer, and it is a great excuse to practise variables and lists together. Suppose we want to remember every time, then report the best, the worst and the average at the end. Here is a self-contained example you can try on its own: times = [] # an empty list to collect every reaction time times.append(312) # pretend three rounds happened times.append(287) times.append(341) best = min(times) # smallest = fastest worst = max(times) # largest = slowest average = sum(times) / len(times) print(f"Rounds played: {len(times)}") print(f"Best: {best} ms") print(f"Worst: {worst} ms") print(f"Average: {average:.0f} ms") Line 1 — times = [] : creates an empty list — a container that will hold every score in the order they happen. Lines 3–5 — times.append(312) : append adds a value to the end of the list. After three appends, times is [312, 287, 341] . Line 7 — min(times) : a built-in function that returns the smallest number in the list — the fastest reaction. Line 8 — max(times) : returns the largest — the slowest reaction. Line 9 — sum(times) / len(times) : sum adds them all up, len counts how many there are, and dividing gives the average. These three built-ins turn raw scores into a useful summary. Lines 11–14 — the report: f-strings print a tidy round-up, with {average:.0f} rounding the average to a whole number. Tip: to fold this into the full game, create times = [] before the loop and add times.append(reaction_ms) just after you calculate each round's score. When the player quits, print the summary. This is the basis of the "Best-of-five" idea in the next section. Note: notice how min , max , sum and len are all functions that return a value — you give them a list and they hand back a single answer. Combining a list with built-in functions like these is one of the most common patterns in all of Python. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause & fix The LED never lights LED is in backwards (long leg must face the resistor/GPIO side), or a wire is loose. Turn the LED round and re-seat the wires. One press scores twice / weird double rounds Switch bounce. Raise bounce_time , e.g. Button(27, bounce_time=0.1) . It always says "Too soon!" The button may be wired so the pin reads as pressed at rest. Confirm one leg goes to GPIO 27 and the opposite-side leg to GND, and that you are using the default pull-up. The game never reacts to a press The button's GND wire or the shared ground to the Pi is missing. Check the − rail connects back to a GND pin. Times look impossibly small (a few ms) Electrical noise or a bounce is triggering wait_for_press instantly. Make sure bounce_time is set and the button is wired firmly. No module named 'lgpio' Run sudo apt install python3-lgpio in a terminal, then restart Thonny. From the E-Waste Pile Both parts of this game are easy to salvage from broken electronics. Push buttons / micro-switches hide inside dead computer mice (the click switches), old remote controls, broken game controllers and keyboards. Desolder one carefully; it behaves exactly like a shop-bought tactile button. LEDs come from old routers, toys and appliance front panels — the longer leg is still the anode. Test salvaged buttons with a multimeter in continuity mode: it should beep only while you hold the button down. Careful: only salvage from low-voltage, unplugged gadgets — battery toys, USB devices, dead routers. Never open mains adapters, microwave ovens, CRT screens, or anything with big capacitors or lithium batteries; they can store a dangerous or lethal charge even when unplugged. Make It Your Own Best-of-five. Replace while True with while round_number < 5 and, when it ends, print the best time and an average. Keep a running total in a variable and divide. Two-player duel. Add a second button and LED; whoever presses first after the light wins the round. Compare the two reaction times with an if . Difficulty levels. Use random.uniform(1, 8) for a wider, twitchier delay range, or shrink the LED's on-time to make a "blink and you miss it" mode. Grade the result. Use if/elif/else to print "Lightning!", "Quick!", or "Keep practising" depending on the millisecond bands. Key terms Variable — a named box that stores a value and can be changed (e.g. best , round_number ). random.uniform(a, b) — returns a random decimal between a and b , every value equally likely. time.time() — the current moment as a number of seconds; subtract two readings to measure elapsed time (a delta). Conditional — if / elif / else ; the program chooses one branch to run based on tests. while loop — repeats a block while a condition stays true; while True repeats forever. f-string — a string prefixed with f where {value} is replaced by that value; {x:.0f} formats to whole numbers. Button — gpiozero's push-button object; default pull_up=True , so wire the other leg to GND. Pull-up resistor — holds an input pin HIGH at rest so it does not float; built into the Pi and enabled by gpiozero. Switch bounce — the rapid make/break of a switch's contacts that can register as several presses. bounce_time — the gpiozero argument (in seconds) that ignores further changes for a short window to debounce a switch. wait_for_press() — a Button method that pauses the program until the button is pressed. Chapter summary Variables store changing values like the start time, the reaction time and the best score. The random module's random.uniform(2, 5) gives an unpredictable delay so the player cannot anticipate the light. The time module's time.time() is read before and after the press; the difference (a delta), ×1000, is the reaction time in milliseconds. Conditionals ( if / elif / else ) decide whether a score is a new best and catch a too-soon press. A while loop runs the game round after round; continue skips to the next round. f-strings like f"{reaction_ms:.0f} ms" mix values neatly into printed text. gpiozero's Button uses a default internal pull-up, so wire one leg to a GPIO pin and the other to GND — no external resistor. Switch bounce can turn one press into many; bounce_time=0.05 debounces it in software. The "go" LED still needs its own 330 Ω resistor , and the GPIO stays 3.3 V only. Always power off and unplug before wiring, and check every connection before powering up.

title: The Salvaged Sound Machine
headings: PWM: Making a Pitch from a Pin
Why a Speaker Needs a Transistor
text: A dead toy, a binned greeting card, a stripped-out PC — each one is hiding a tiny voice you can bring back to life. In this project you will rescue a buzzer or a small speaker from the e-waste pile and teach your Raspberry Pi 5 to sing: first a clean musical scale, then a recognisable tune. Along the way you will learn three of Python's most useful ideas — dictionaries , functions , and loops — and the electronics behind sound: PWM tone generation , the difference between an active and a passive buzzer, and the all-important rule that a real speaker must never be wired straight to a GPIO pin. What You'll Build & Learn By the end of this chapter your Pi will play music through a salvaged sounder. You will build the project in three stages: a single test beep, a full eight-note scale, and finally a short melody stored as data and played back by a loop. The Python fundamentals Dictionaries — a way to store pairs of values, like a real dictionary maps a word to its meaning. Here we map each note name ( "C4" , "D4" …) to its frequency in hertz. Functions — named, reusable blocks of code. We will write a play_note() function once and call it many times. Loops — repeating actions without copying and pasting. A for loop will step through a scale and through a melody. A list of tuples — storing a melody as an ordered list where each item is a small bundle of two values: a note name and how long to hold it. The electronics fundamentals PWM and tone generation — how the Pi makes a pitch by switching a pin on and off thousands of times a second. Active vs passive buzzers — why one type only ever makes a single fixed beep, while the other can play any note. gpiozero TonalBuzzer and Tone — the friendly objects that turn a note name into a sound. Driving a speaker safely — why a small loudspeaker needs an NPN transistor driver and must never be connected directly to a GPIO pin. Note: Everything here runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. The gpiozero library and the Thonny editor are already installed, and on the Pi 5 gpiozero quietly uses the lgpio backend. There is nothing to download to get started. How Sound Actually Works Sound is nothing more than air being pushed and pulled very quickly. If you can make something vibrate back and forth — a speaker cone, a thin metal disc — it shoves the surrounding air into waves, and your ears hear those waves as a tone. The faster the vibration, the higher the pitch. In plain words: Frequency is how many times something vibrates per second, measured in hertz (Hz) . A vibration of 440 times a second (440 Hz) is the musical note A above middle C — the note an orchestra tunes to. Double the frequency and you go up one octave: 880 Hz is the A one octave higher. So to play a tune, all the Pi has to do is make a sounder vibrate at the right frequency for each note. Here are the frequencies for one octave of natural notes, which we will use throughout the chapter: Note Frequency (Hz) Where it sits C4 262 Middle C D4 294 One step up E4 330 F4 349 G4 392 A4 440 Orchestra tuning note B4 494 C5 523 One octave above middle C Tip: The "4" in C4 is the octave number. Middle C is C4. The same letter one octave higher is C5, with exactly double the frequency. You do not need to memorise the numbers — that is precisely the job we will give a Python dictionary. Active vs Passive Buzzers Before wiring anything, you need to know which kind of buzzer you have, because they behave very differently — and the code is different for each. An active buzzer An active buzzer has its own little oscillator circuit built in. Give it power and it makes a sound at one fixed pitch — that is all it can do. You cannot play a tune on it; you can only switch its single beep on and off. It is perfect for an alarm or a "ping", useless for music. A passive buzzer A passive buzzer (also called a piezo transducer) has no oscillator inside. It is silent until you feed it a rapidly switching signal — and the speed at which you switch it decides the pitch. Because you control the frequency, a passive buzzer can play any note, which is exactly what we want for a melody. In plain words: "Active" means the buzzer is active on its own — it generates its own tone. "Passive" means it just sits there passively until your Pi drives it with a changing signal. Counter-intuitively, the passive one is the clever musical one. Active buzzer vs passive buzzer ACTIVE buzzer Oscillator built IN Power on → one fixed beep gpiozero: Buzzer() PASSIVE buzzer No oscillator inside YOU set the pitch → any note gpiozero: TonalBuzzer() An active buzzer plays one fixed beep all by itself; a passive buzzer stays silent until your Pi drives it at the frequency you choose — so only the passive one can play a tune. How to tell them apart By printing on the case: some are marked. Two-leg sounders are often unmarked, though. By the legs: an active buzzer usually has one longer leg (the + ) and may have a sticker over the sound hole. A passive piezo disc often has two solder pads or two thin wires (red and black) with no polarity fuss. The battery test (the reliable one): briefly touch the buzzer's two legs to a 3 V coin cell (longer leg / red wire to +). If you hear a clear, steady tone, it is active . If you hear only a faint click, or nothing, it is passive — it needs a switching signal, which the battery cannot provide. Note: This chapter focuses on the passive buzzer (and, later, a salvaged speaker) because those are the ones that can make music. If all you have is an active buzzer, you can still follow along with the Buzzer object to make rhythmic beeps — see "Make it your own" at the end. From the E-Waste Pile You almost certainly own a dead sounder already. Here is where to find one and how to harvest it safely. Source What you'll find Type Musical greeting card A thin piezo disc with two wires Passive — ideal Dead toy that bleeps A small speaker or a piezo Either — test it Old desktop PC (motherboard) The "PC speaker" — a small piezo or buzzer Usually passive Broken radio / headphones A small loudspeaker (8 Ω coil) Speaker — needs a transistor (see later) Smoke alarm (battery type) A loud piezo sounder Often active Careful: Only ever harvest from low-voltage, battery-powered e-waste. Never open a microwave oven, a CRT (tube) TV or monitor, or any mains adapter — these can hold a lethal charge in their capacitors even when unplugged . Never cut or crush a lithium battery; it can catch fire. If a device plugs into the wall, leave its insides alone and salvage only the obviously low-voltage parts (like a clip-on speaker) after the mains section has been removed by an adult who knows what they are doing. Harvesting it Free the sounder. Snip the two wires close to the old circuit board, leaving as much wire on the buzzer as you can. If it is soldered to pads, a gentle pull with pliers usually frees it. Tidy the wire ends. Strip about 5 mm of insulation off each wire. If the buzzer has bare metal legs, leave them as they are. Test it with the coin-cell test above to decide active or passive. Tin or fit a header. To plug into a breadboard, solder a stiff jumper pin onto each wire, or twist each wire around a male jumper and tape it. Stiff legs push into breadboard holes more reliably than floppy wire. PWM: Making a Pitch from a Pin A GPIO pin can only ever be in one of two states: HIGH (3.3 V) or LOW (0 V). How can two states make a smooth musical note? The trick is speed . In plain words: PWM stands for Pulse-Width Modulation . The pin is switched on and off very fast, over and over. The number of complete on-off cycles per second is the frequency . If the pin cycles 440 times a second, the buzzer's disc is pushed and pulled 440 times a second — and you hear the note A4. So "playing a note" really means "switch this pin on and off at the note's frequency". To play A4 we cycle at 440 Hz; to play C5 we cycle at 523 Hz. Happily, gpiozero hides all the timing for us: we just tell it the note and it sets the right PWM frequency. PWM: a fast on/off square wave makes the pitch Slow switching = low note Fast switching = high note HIGH = 3.3 V LOW = 0 V More cycles per second → higher frequency → higher pitch A passive buzzer plays whatever pitch the Pi switches it at. Cycling the pin slowly gives a low note; cycling it fast gives a high note. PWM is just fast, regular on/off switching. Meet the TonalBuzzer Object gpiozero gives us two ready-made objects for sounders: Buzzer(pin) — for an active buzzer. It can only do on() , off() and beep() . TonalBuzzer(pin) — for a passive buzzer. It can play() a Tone (a musical note) and stop() . A Tone is gpiozero's way of describing a pitch. Beautifully, you can create the same tone three ways — they are all equal: from gpiozero.tones import Tone Tone("A4") # by note name Tone(440.0) # by frequency in hertz Tone(69) # by MIDI number Line 1 — from gpiozero.tones import Tone : The Tone class lives in a sub-module of gpiozero called tones . This line fetches it so we can describe musical notes. Line 3 — Tone("A4") : Creates the tone for the note A4 by its musical name. This is the friendliest form and the one we will use. Line 4 — Tone(440.0) : The identical tone, described instead by its frequency, 440 Hz. Note the decimal point — a float — which tells gpiozero you mean hertz, not a MIDI number. Line 5 — Tone(69) : The same tone again, given as a plain whole number, which gpiozero reads as a MIDI note number (69 is A4). All three lines describe exactly the same pitch. Note: TonalBuzzer plays a limited range of octaves around a middle tone (by default one octave either side of A4). The eight notes C4–C5 we are using sit comfortably inside that range. A Tiny First Test Before the full build, let us prove the buzzer works with the smallest possible program. Wire the passive buzzer for a quick test (full wiring comes next): one leg to GPIO 13 (physical pin 33), the other leg to a GND pin. A passive buzzer is gentle enough to drive straight from a GPIO pin — unlike a speaker, which we deal with later. from gpiozero import TonalBuzzer from gpiozero.tones import Tone from time import sleep buzzer = TonalBuzzer(13) buzzer.play(Tone("A4")) sleep(1) buzzer.stop() Line 1 — from gpiozero import TonalBuzzer : Imports the object for a passive buzzer. Line 2 — from gpiozero.tones import Tone : Imports the Tone class so we can name a note. Line 3 — from time import sleep : sleep(seconds) pauses the program. We use it to hold the note for a moment. Line 5 — buzzer = TonalBuzzer(13) : Creates a buzzer object on GPIO 13 (physical pin 33). The number 13 is the BCM/GPIO number, as always in gpiozero. Line 6 — buzzer.play(Tone("A4")) : Starts playing the note A4. The buzzer keeps sounding until we tell it to stop. Line 7 — sleep(1) : Waits one second while the note sounds. Line 8 — buzzer.stop() : Silences the buzzer. Always stop a tone when you are done, or it sounds forever. Save it as beep_test.py in Thonny and press the green Run button. You should hear a clear one-second tone. If you do, your salvaged sounder lives — congratulations. If not, jump ahead to Troubleshooting . Parts List A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. A passive buzzer — salvaged from a greeting card, toy, or PC motherboard (see "From the e-waste pile"), or a new one from a starter kit. 2 × female-to-male jumper wires (to reach the GPIO header from the breadboard). 1 × mini breadboard. Optional, for the speaker upgrade: a small salvaged 8 Ω speaker, an NPN transistor (2N2222 or BC548), a 1 kΩ resistor (brown-black-red-gold) for the transistor base, and a jumper to 5 V. A 1N4001 diode is a nice extra for inductive protection. Tip: If your kit included a small breadboard-friendly buzzer, it is most likely passive (the musical kind). Test it with the coin-cell trick to be sure. Wiring the Passive Buzzer Careful: Power off and unplug your Pi before wiring. Shut down from the desktop menu, wait for the green light to go out, then remove the power lead. The Pi's GPIO is 3.3 V logic — never feed more than 3.3 V into a pin. A small passive buzzer draws little current and is safe to drive directly; but a real loudspeaker or any motor must never be wired straight to a GPIO pin — that comes later, through a transistor. Only re-power once your wiring is checked. Passive buzzer wiring GPIO Header Pin 33 (GPIO 13) Pin 39 (GND) Breadboard PASSIVE signal GND Current path: GPIO 13 → buzzer → GND Purple = GPIO 13 signal · Grey = GND The passive buzzer needs just two wires: one leg to GPIO 13 (the switching signal) and the other to a GND pin. A passive buzzer draws little current, so this direct connection is safe. Connection table From To Wire colour Why GPIO 13 (physical pin 33) Buzzer leg 1 (signal) Purple Carries the PWM switching signal that sets the pitch Buzzer leg 2 GND (physical pin 39) Grey Completes the circuit back to ground Note: A passive buzzer has no polarity that matters for sound — you can swap the two legs and it still plays. (An active buzzer does care which leg is +.) GPIO 13 is one of the Pi's hardware-PWM-capable pins, which makes for a clean tone, but gpiozero works on any GPIO pin. Wiring steps Shut down and unplug the Pi. Wait for the green activity light to go out before touching any wiring. Seat the buzzer. Push the buzzer's two legs into two different rows of the breadboard so the legs are not shorted together. Run the signal wire. Female end of a jumper onto physical pin 33 (GPIO 13); male end into the breadboard row holding buzzer leg 1. Run the GND wire. Female end of a second jumper onto physical pin 39 (a GND pin); male end into the row holding buzzer leg 2. Double-check that the two buzzer legs are in separate rows and no metal is touching. Then reconnect power and boot up. Python Fundamentals: Dictionaries, Functions, Loops Let us learn the three Python ideas with tiny examples before the big program. Dictionaries — pairing keys with values A list stores items in order, fetched by position. A dictionary stores items as key → value pairs, fetched by name. That is perfect for "note name → frequency". notes = {"C4": 262, "D4": 294, "E4": 330} print(notes["D4"]) # 294 Line 1 — notes = {…} : The curly braces { } create a dictionary. Each entry is a key (the note name, in quotes) then a colon then its value (the frequency). Commas separate the entries. Line 2 — notes["D4"] : Look up a value by its key inside square brackets. Asking for "D4" hands back 294 . No need to remember any position — you ask by name. In plain words: A dictionary is like a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key ) to get its definition (the value ). Keys must be unique. Here the keys are note names and the values are frequencies in hertz. Functions — name a job once, reuse it A function wraps up a few lines under a name so you can run them again and again without repeating yourself. def greet(name): print("Hello, " + name) greet("Ada") greet("Linus") Line 1 — def greet(name): : def defines a function called greet . The word in brackets, name , is a parameter — a placeholder for a value you pass in when you call it. Line 2 — print("Hello, " + name) : The indented body. Whatever name holds gets joined onto the greeting and printed. Lines 4–5 — greet("Ada") / greet("Linus") : Two calls . Each runs the same function body with a different value for name . One definition, many uses. Loops — repeat without copy-paste A for loop walks through a collection one item at a time. for note in ["C4", "E4", "G4"]: print("Playing", note) Line 1 — for note in […]: : Take each item of the list in turn and put it in the variable note . The loop body runs once per item. Line 2 — print("Playing", note) : The indented body runs three times — once with note equal to "C4" , then "E4" , then "G4" . A list of tuples — storing a melody A tuple is a small fixed bundle of values written in round brackets, like ("C4", 0.5) . We store a melody as a list of these tuples: each one is a note plus how long to hold it. melody = [("C4", 0.5), ("E4", 0.5), ("G4", 1.0)] for note, length in melody: print(note, "for", length, "seconds") Line 1 — melody = [ (…), (…) ] : A list (square brackets) whose items are tuples (round brackets). Each tuple pairs a note name with a duration in seconds. Line 2 — for note, length in melody: : As the loop takes each tuple, it unpacks the two values into note and length in one step. This is why tuples are so handy for paired data. Line 3 — print(...) : Runs once per tuple, with the note and its length already separated out for us. The Full Program Now we combine everything: a dictionary of notes, a play_note() function, a loop to play a scale, and a melody stored as a list of tuples. Open a new file in Thonny and type it in. from gpiozero import TonalBuzzer from gpiozero.tones import Tone from time import sleep # Map each note name to its frequency in hertz NOTES = { "C4": 262, "D4": 294, "E4": 330, "F4": 349, "G4": 392, "A4": 440, "B4": 494, "C5": 523, "REST": None, } buzzer = TonalBuzzer(13) def play_note(name, length): """Play one note for a number of seconds, then fall silent.""" if name == "REST": buzzer.stop() else: frequency = NOTES[name] buzzer.play(Tone(frequency)) sleep(length) buzzer.stop() def play_scale(): """Play the eight notes of a C major scale, low to high.""" for name in ["C4", "D4", "E4", "F4", "G4", "A4", "B4", "C5"]: print("Scale:", name) play_note(name, 0.4) def play_melody(melody): """Play a melody given as a list of (note, length) tuples.""" for name, length in melody: print("Melody:", name) play_note(name, length) # "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" as a list of (note, length) tuples TWINKLE = [ ("C4", 0.5), ("C4", 0.5), ("G4", 0.5), ("G4", 0.5), ("A4", 0.5), ("A4", 0.5), ("G4", 1.0), ("F4", 0.5), ("F4", 0.5), ("E4", 0.5), ("E4", 0.5), ("D4", 0.5), ("D4", 0.5), ("C4", 1.0), ] print("Playing a scale...") play_scale() sleep(0.5) print("Now a tune...") play_melody(TWINKLE) buzzer.stop() print("Done!") Lines 1–3 — the imports: TonalBuzzer drives the passive buzzer, Tone describes a pitch, and sleep times each note. Lines 6–10 — NOTES = {…} : Our dictionary mapping note names to frequencies. The special key "REST" maps to None (Python's "nothing"), which we will treat as a silent gap. Line 12 — buzzer = TonalBuzzer(13) : Creates the buzzer object on GPIO 13. We make it once, near the top, so every function can use it. Line 15 — def play_note(name, length): : Defines our key function. It takes two parameters: the note name and how long ( length ) to hold it. Line 16 — the docstring: The triple-quoted text just under def describes what the function does. It is documentation, not code. Lines 17–18 — if name == "REST": buzzer.stop() : If the note is a rest, keep the buzzer silent. Lines 19–21 — the else branch: Otherwise, look up the frequency for that name in the NOTES dictionary and start playing it with buzzer.play(Tone(frequency)) . Line 22 — sleep(length) : Hold the note (or the silence) for the requested number of seconds. Line 23 — buzzer.stop() : Silence the buzzer before the next note, giving each note a clean, separate sound. Lines 26–30 — def play_scale(): : A function with no parameters. It loops over a list of eight note names and calls play_note() for each at 0.4 seconds. This is loops + functions + dictionary working together. Lines 33–37 — def play_melody(melody): : Takes a melody (a list of tuples). The for name, length in melody: line unpacks each tuple into its two parts, then plays it. The same function can play any melody you pass it. Lines 41–46 — TWINKLE = [...] : The tune stored as data — a list of (note, length) tuples. Storing music as data means the playing code never changes; only the data does. Lines 48–55 — the main part: Print a message, play the scale, pause half a second, then play the tune by handing TWINKLE to play_melody() . Lines 57–58 — buzzer.stop() / print("Done!") : A final tidy-up to make sure the buzzer is silent, and a friendly message. Running It In Thonny, choose File → Save and save the file as sound_machine.py in your home folder. Click the green Run button (the triangle ▶) or press F5 . Listen: you should hear a rising eight-note scale, a short pause, then the opening of "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star". The Thonny console prints each note as it plays. To stop early, click the red Stop button (the square ■). Tip: If the tune sounds too fast or too slow, change the length values in the TWINKLE list. Bigger numbers mean longer notes. You can also slow the scale by raising the 0.4 in play_scale() . Why a Speaker Needs a Transistor A passive buzzer is happy on a GPIO pin because it sips only a milliamp or two. A proper loudspeaker — the kind in a radio or headphones — is a different beast. To be loud it needs much more current than a GPIO pin can safely give. Careful: A GPIO pin can supply only about 16 mA , and the whole header together only around 50 mA. A small 8 Ω speaker can try to pull hundreds of milliamps. Wiring a speaker (or any motor) straight to a GPIO pin will overload the pin and can permanently damage your Pi . Speakers and motors are also inductive : when the current switches off they kick back a brief high-voltage spike that can punch through a GPIO pin. Always drive them through a transistor. In plain words: A transistor is an electronic switch with no moving parts. A tiny current from the GPIO pin (into the transistor's base ) controls a much bigger current flowing from the 5 V supply through the speaker. The Pi sends a small, safe signal; the transistor does the heavy lifting and the Pi is protected. We use a common, cheap NPN transistor — a 2N2222 or BC548. It has three legs: base , collector , and emitter . The GPIO pin feeds the base through a 1 kΩ resistor (which limits the small base current and protects the pin). The speaker connects between the 5 V supply and the transistor's collector ; the emitter goes to GND. When the GPIO pin pulses, the transistor switches the speaker current on and off in time — and the speaker plays the note. Driving a salvaged speaker with an NPN transistor GPIO Header Pin 33 (GPIO 13) Pin 4 (5 V) Pin 6 (GND) 1 kΩ NPN (2N2222) base collector emitter → GND Speaker 8 Ω flyback diode Pin only drives the base; 5 V does the heavy lifting through the speaker. The GPIO pin pulses the transistor's base through a 1 kΩ resistor; the transistor switches the bigger 5 V speaker current on and off. A flyback diode across the speaker absorbs the inductive kick. The Pi never carries the speaker's current. Speaker connection table From To Wire / part Why GPIO 13 (pin 33) 1 kΩ resistor → transistor base Purple via resistor Small, safe control signal; resistor limits base current and protects the pin 5 V (pin 4) Speaker terminal 1 Red Supplies the heavy current the speaker needs Speaker terminal 2 Transistor collector Black Transistor switches this current on and off Transistor emitter GND (pin 6) Grey Return path to ground Diode across speaker (band to 5 V) — 1N4001 (optional) Soaks up the inductive voltage spike when the current switches off Note: The 2N2222 and BC548 have their three legs in different orders, so always check the part's datasheet pinout (looking at the flat face, legs are typically Emitter–Base–Collector or Collector–Base–Emitter). Wiring the legs in the wrong order is the most common reason a transistor circuit stays silent. The lovely part: the code does not change at all. Your Pi still runs the exact same sound_machine.py with TonalBuzzer(13) . From the pin's point of view it is still just switching a single GPIO line on and off — the transistor and 5 V supply quietly turn that into a loud speaker note. That is the whole point of a transistor driver: it lets a tiny, safe signal control a big load. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause & fix No sound at all from the buzzer It may be an active buzzer (only beeps, cannot play tones) — try the Buzzer object instead. Or a wire is loose; reseat both jumpers. Check both buzzer legs are in separate rows. A faint click, no tone Likely a passive buzzer on too low a volume, or it is an active buzzer being driven by TonalBuzzer . Confirm the type with the coin-cell test. No module named 'lgpio' Install the backend: sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then restart Thonny. Tone plays but never stops You forgot a buzzer.stop() . Every play() needs a matching stop() eventually. "OutputDeviceBadValue" or out-of-range error The note is outside the buzzer's range. Keep notes within C4–C5, or raise octaves= when creating the TonalBuzzer . Speaker is silent (transistor build) Almost always the transistor legs are in the wrong order — recheck base/collector/emitter against the datasheet. Confirm 5 V and GND are connected. Speaker buzzes weakly even when the program stops Check the emitter really goes to GND and the base resistor is 1 kΩ, not a much smaller value. Make It Your Own You have a working instrument. Here are four ways to take it further. Add more notes. Extend the NOTES dictionary with sharps and flats (e.g. "F#4": 370 ) and a lower octave, then write a tune that uses them. Store songs in a file. Keep each melody as its own list of tuples and add a menu: print the song names, ask the user to type a number, then play the chosen one. Two-part rhythm with an active buzzer. If you also salvaged an active buzzer, wire it to another pin as a Buzzer and beep() it on the beat for a simple drum. Build a one-key keyboard. Add a push button (from Chapter 12) so each press plays the next note of a scale — a tiny playable instrument from pure e-waste. Tip: Because the melody is stored as data (a list of tuples) and the playing is done by a function , you can add a whole new song without touching the playback code at all. That separation of data from behaviour is one of the most powerful ideas in all of programming — you have just used it for real. You started with something destined for the bin and ended with a programmable instrument that plays whatever you teach it. The official gpiozero documentation at gpiozero.readthedocs.io lists every sound object if you want to dig deeper. Badge earned: Now It Sings . Key terms Frequency - How many times per second something vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz); it determines the pitch of a note. PWM (Pulse-Width Modulation) - Switching a GPIO pin on and off very fast; the number of cycles per second sets the tone's frequency. Active buzzer - A buzzer with a built-in oscillator that plays one fixed beep; controlled with gpiozero's Buzzer object. Passive buzzer - A buzzer with no oscillator that plays whatever pitch you drive it at; controlled with gpiozero's TonalBuzzer object. TonalBuzzer - The gpiozero object that plays musical notes on a passive buzzer using play() and stop() . Tone - gpiozero's way of describing a pitch, by note name ( "A4" ), frequency ( 440.0 ), or MIDI number ( 69 ). Dictionary - A Python collection of key→value pairs, looked up by key; here it maps note names to frequencies. Function - A named, reusable block of code that can take parameters and be called many times. Tuple - A small fixed bundle of values in round brackets, e.g. ("C4", 0.5) ; ideal for paired data like note-and-length. NPN transistor - An electronic switch (e.g. 2N2222, BC548) that lets a small GPIO signal control a much larger current for a speaker or motor. Flyback diode - A diode placed across an inductive load (speaker/motor) to absorb the voltage spike produced when its current switches off. Chapter summary Sound is air vibrating; the frequency of vibration (in hertz) sets the pitch — 440 Hz is the note A4. A GPIO pin makes a pitch using PWM: switching on and off at the note's frequency. An active buzzer makes one fixed beep (use Buzzer ); a passive buzzer can play any note (use TonalBuzzer with Tone ). A passive buzzer is gentle enough to wire straight to a GPIO pin (one leg to the pin, one to GND). A Python dictionary neatly maps note names to frequencies; functions let us name and reuse the "play a note" job; loops step through a scale or a melody. A melody is stored as a list of tuples — each tuple a (note, length) pair — keeping the music data separate from the playback code. A real loudspeaker draws far too much current for a GPIO pin and must be driven through an NPN transistor (2N2222/BC548) with a ~1 kΩ base resistor; a flyback diode protects against inductive spikes. Never wire a speaker or motor directly to a GPIO pin — it can permanently damage the Pi. Sounders are easy, safe e-waste to salvage from greeting cards, toys, and old PCs — but never open mains, microwave, or CRT equipment.

title: Mood Lamp from a Recycled Jar
headings: How an RGB LED Makes Colour
Python Fundamentals: Parameters, Return, while True, random
text: An empty jam jar, a frosted bottle, a single colourful LED rescued from a broken toy — together they become a soft, glowing mood lamp that drifts gently through colours and even has a flickering "lava" mode. In this project you will learn how to mix any colour from red, green, and blue light using PWM duty cycle for brightness, and you will meet three powerful Python ideas: functions that take parameters and return values , the while True loop, and the random module that gives your lamp a life of its own. What You'll Build & Learn You will build a colour-fading mood lamp inside a recycled glass jar. It will cycle through a small set of calm preset colours, and at the flick of a setting switch into a randomised, slowly shifting "lava lamp" mode. The Python fundamentals Functions with parameters and return values — a function that takes in values and hands back a result, so you can build colours and reuse calculations. The while True loop — a loop that runs forever, perfect for a lamp that glows until you switch it off. The random module — generating unpredictable numbers so the lamp never repeats itself. Gentle 0–1 maths — working with brightness as a fraction between 0 (off) and 1 (full), which is exactly how gpiozero expects colours. A list of preset colours — storing named moods as data. The electronics fundamentals PWM duty cycle as brightness — how switching a pin on for part of the time dims an LED smoothly. The RGB LED — three coloured LEDs in one package, controlled with gpiozero's RGBLED object and .value = (r, g, b) . Common-cathode vs common-anode — the two types of RGB LED and the active_high setting that tells gpiozero which you have. Colour mixing — making any colour by blending red, green, and blue light. One resistor per channel — why each of the three colours needs its own current-limiting resistor. Note: This runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. The gpiozero library and the Thonny editor are pre-installed; on the Pi 5 gpiozero uses the lgpio backend automatically. Nothing to download. How an RGB LED Makes Colour An RGB LED is really three tiny LEDs — one red, one green, one blue — built into a single clear package with four legs. By lighting them at different brightnesses and letting their light blend, you can make almost any colour your eye can see. This is exactly how a TV or phone screen works, just with millions of tiny dots instead of one. In plain words: Additive colour mixing means adding coloured light together. Red + green light makes yellow; red + blue makes magenta; all three together make white. This is different from mixing paint (where more colours make brown) because light adds up instead of soaking up. Red Green Blue Colour you see full off off Red off full off Green off off full Blue full full off Yellow full off full Magenta off full full Cyan full full full White full half off Orange Additive colour mixing: red + green + blue light Red Green Blue white R+G = yellow R+B = magenta G+B = cyan R+G+B = white Where the three coloured lights overlap, they add to make new colours. Mixing all three at full brightness gives white. Vary each one's brightness and you can reach any colour. PWM Duty Cycle as Brightness A GPIO pin can only be fully on (3.3 V) or fully off (0 V) — there is no "half voltage" setting. So how do we make an LED glow at half brightness? The answer, again, is PWM : switching the pin on and off very fast. In plain words: The duty cycle is the fraction of each cycle that the pin spends switched ON. A duty cycle of 1.0 means on all the time (full brightness); 0.5 means on half the time (looks half as bright); 0.0 means always off. The switching is so fast (default 100 times a second) that your eye blends it into a steady, dimmer glow rather than a flicker. Duty cycle sets brightness duty = 1.0 full duty = 0.5 half duty = 0.2 dim More ON time per cycle = brighter. The eye blends the fast flicker into a steady glow. Duty cycle is the proportion of each fast cycle the pin stays on. A higher duty cycle keeps the LED on for more of the time, so it looks brighter. gpiozero hides all the switching. For an RGB LED it lets you set each colour channel to a number between 0 and 1 — that number is the duty cycle, and therefore the brightness. We will set colours like (1, 0.5, 0) , meaning "red full, green half, blue off" — which is orange. Common-Cathode vs Common-Anode RGB LEDs come in two flavours, and you must know which you have, or your colours come out inverted. Common-cathode: the three colours share a single negative (cathode) leg, which goes to GND . Each colour lights when its pin goes HIGH. This is the gpiozero default ( active_high=True ). Common-anode: the three colours share a single positive (anode) leg, which goes to 3.3 V . Each colour lights when its pin goes LOW. You tell gpiozero this with active_high=False . In plain words: "Common" means shared. A common- cathode LED shares its negative leg (cathode = negative), so the shared leg goes to ground. A common- anode LED shares its positive leg (anode = positive), so the shared leg goes to 3.3 V. The longest leg is usually the shared (common) one. Common-cathode vs common-anode Common-CATHODE shared → GND active_high=True (default) Common-ANODE shared → 3.3 V active_high=False A common-cathode RGB LED shares a negative leg to GND (gpiozero default). A common-anode shares a positive leg to 3.3 V and needs active_high=False , or your colours will come out inverted. Tip: Not sure which you have? Wire it up assuming common-cathode (the default), then run a quick "red only" test. If asking for red gives you cyan (the opposite), you have a common-anode — just add active_high=False when you create the RGBLED . No rewiring needed beyond moving the shared leg between GND and 3.3 V. One Resistor Per Channel Just like a single LED, each colour inside the RGB package is a real LED with almost no resistance of its own — so each one needs its own current-limiting resistor to stop it (and the GPIO pin) burning out. Careful: You need three resistors — one in series with each of the red, green, and blue legs. A single shared resistor on the common leg will not protect each colour properly and will make the brightness change as you mix colours. Use a 330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown-gold) per channel. As always, the Pi's GPIO is 3.3 V logic — never feed more than 3.3 V into a pin. Note: Blue and green LEDs have a higher forward voltage than red, so with equal resistors the blue and green can look a little brighter than red for the same setting. That is normal and easy to correct in software — see "Make it your own". From the E-Waste Pile Two of this project's parts come straight from the recycling: the diffuser and the light itself. The jar (diffuser) Any clear or frosted glass container scatters the LED's light into a soft glow. A jam jar , a frosted bottle , or a small drinking glass all work. Frosted glass diffuses best; for a clear jar, a sheet of baking paper or tissue wrapped inside softens the light beautifully. The LED Source What you'll find Colour-changing toy / night light An RGB LED, sometimes a slow-cycling "magic" one Old computer / case fan Single coloured LEDs (use three of them) Broken fairy lights / bike light Single LEDs you can reuse one per channel Dead remote-control car Headlight LEDs and small bulbs No RGB LED to hand? Use three separate single LEDs — one red, one green, one blue — wired to the same three GPIO pins, each with its own resistor and a shared GND. gpiozero's RGBLED object treats them exactly the same. Careful: Salvage only from low-voltage, battery-powered items. Never open a mains adapter, a microwave, or a CRT (tube) TV/monitor — their capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged . Never cut or crush a lithium battery. A jar should be clean, dry, and free of cracks. Testing a salvaged LED Find the legs. A single LED's longer leg is the anode (+), the shorter leg (with the flat side) is the cathode (−). An RGB LED has one long shared leg and three shorter colour legs. Test with a coin cell. Through a 330 Ω resistor, touch a 3 V coin cell across each LED (+ to anode). A working LED glows; swap the legs if it stays dark. Identify the channels. On an RGB LED, touch each short leg in turn (sharing the long leg) to find which is red, green, and blue, and note the order. Parts List A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. One RGB LED (common-cathode preferred) or three single LEDs (red, green, blue) — salvaged or from a kit. Three 330 Ω resistors (orange-orange-brown-gold) — one per colour channel. 4 × female-to-male jumper wires (three signals + one GND), or 6 if using three single LEDs. 1 × mini breadboard. A clean glass jar or frosted bottle as the diffuser (from recycling). Wiring the RGB LED Careful: Power off and unplug your Pi before wiring. Shut down from the desktop menu, wait for the green light to go out, then remove the power lead. Use one resistor per colour channel . The Pi's GPIO is 3.3 V logic only. Re-power only once your wiring is checked. We will use GPIO 17 for red (physical pin 11), GPIO 27 for green (pin 13), and GPIO 22 for blue (pin 15). The shared common leg goes to a GND pin (for a common-cathode LED). RGB LED wiring (common-cathode) GPIO Header Pin 11 (GPIO 17) R Pin 13 (GPIO 27) G Pin 15 (GPIO 22) B Pin 9 (GND) 330Ω 330Ω 330Ω RGB LED R G B common cathode → GND Each colour: GPIO → its own 330Ω resistor → colour leg. Shared leg → GND. Red=GPIO17 · Green=GPIO27 · Blue=GPIO22 Each colour channel has its own 330 Ω resistor between the GPIO pin and the LED leg. The single shared (common-cathode) leg connects to GND. With three single LEDs, wire each one the same way and join all their cathodes to GND. Connection table From To Via Why GPIO 17 (pin 11) Red leg of LED 330 Ω resistor Controls red brightness; resistor limits current GPIO 27 (pin 13) Green leg of LED 330 Ω resistor Controls green brightness GPIO 22 (pin 15) Blue leg of LED 330 Ω resistor Controls blue brightness Common (longest) leg GND (pin 9) Direct wire Shared return for a common-cathode LED Wiring steps Shut down and unplug the Pi. Wait for the green light to go out. Seat the LED. Push the RGB LED into the breadboard so each of its four legs is in its own row. Note which leg is the long (common) one. Fit the three resistors. Place one 330 Ω resistor reaching from each colour leg's row to a free row where a jumper can meet it. Wire red. Jumper from pin 11 (GPIO 17) to the free end of the red channel's resistor. Wire green and blue. Jumper from pin 13 (GPIO 27) to the green resistor, and pin 15 (GPIO 22) to the blue resistor. Wire the common leg. Jumper from the LED's long shared leg row to a GND pin (pin 9). For a common-anode LED, take this leg to 3.3 V instead and remember active_high=False in code. Check, then re-power and boot up. Python Fundamentals: Parameters, Return, while True, random Let us learn the new Python ideas with tiny examples before building the lamp. Functions that take parameters and return a value In Chapter 26 our functions did things. Now we want functions that calculate and hand back a result, using the return keyword. def dim(colour, amount): r, g, b = colour return (r * amount, g * amount, b * amount) half_red = dim((1, 0, 0), 0.5) print(half_red) # (0.5, 0.0, 0.0) Line 1 — def dim(colour, amount): : Defines a function with two parameters : a colour (an (r, g, b) tuple) and an amount to scale it by. Line 2 — r, g, b = colour : Unpacks the tuple into three separate variables. Line 3 — return (...) : The return keyword hands a value back to whoever called the function. Here we hand back a new tuple with each channel multiplied by amount . Line 5 — half_red = dim((1, 0, 0), 0.5) : Calls the function and stores the returned value in half_red . This is the key difference from before: the function gives us something back to use. In plain words: A parameter is a value you pass into a function. A return value is the answer the function passes back out . Think of a function as a little machine: parameters go in the top, a result comes out the bottom. Gentle 0–1 maths gpiozero expects each colour channel as a number from 0 to 1 . Keeping everything in that range makes the maths easy: multiply by a fraction to dim, and you never leave the safe range. If a calculation might stray outside 0–1, we clamp it: def clamp(value): return max(0, min(1, value)) print(clamp(1.3)) # 1 print(clamp(-0.2)) # 0 Line 1–2 — def clamp(value): return max(0, min(1, value)) : min(1, value) caps anything above 1 down to 1; max(0, ...) lifts anything below 0 up to 0. The result is always safely between 0 and 1. Lines 4–5: Show it clamping 1.3 down to 1 and −0.2 up to 0 — keeping our brightness values legal for gpiozero. The while True loop A mood lamp should glow until you switch it off. The while True: loop runs its body over and over, forever. from time import sleep while True: print("still glowing...") sleep(2) Line 3 — while True: : True is always true, so this loop never ends on its own. The indented body repeats until you stop the program (the red Stop button) or press Ctrl+C. Lines 4–5: The repeating body — print a message, wait two seconds, and round again. In the lamp, this is where we will fade colours. The random module To give the lamp a life of its own we use Python's random module, which makes unpredictable numbers. import random print(random.random()) # a float from 0.0 up to 1.0 print(random.uniform(0.2, 0.8)) # a float between 0.2 and 0.8 print(random.choice(["a", "b"]))# one item picked at random Line 1 — import random : Brings in Python's built-in random-number toolkit. Line 3 — random.random() : Returns a random decimal from 0.0 up to (but not including) 1.0 — already perfect for a brightness value. Line 4 — random.uniform(0.2, 0.8) : A random decimal between the two numbers you give. Handy for keeping the lamp from going fully dark or fully bright. Line 5 — random.choice([...]) : Picks one item from a list at random — we will use it to pick a random mood. Meet the RGBLED Object gpiozero's RGBLED wraps all three channels into one object. You give it the three pins, and then set .value to an (r, g, b) tuple where each number is 0–1. from gpiozero import RGBLED from time import sleep led = RGBLED(red=17, green=27, blue=22) led.value = (1, 0, 0) # red sleep(1) led.value = (0, 0, 1) # blue sleep(1) led.value = (1, 0.5, 0) # orange (red full, green half) sleep(1) led.off() Line 1 — from gpiozero import RGBLED : Imports the ready-made RGB LED object. Line 4 — led = RGBLED(red=17, green=27, blue=22) : Creates the object, telling gpiozero which GPIO pin drives each colour. By default active_high=True (common-cathode) and PWM is on, so brightness control just works. Line 6 — led.value = (1, 0, 0) : Sets red to full (1), green and blue off (0) — pure red. Each number is the channel's duty cycle. Line 8 / 10 — blue, then orange: Changing the tuple changes the mix. (1, 0.5, 0) is red full, green at half brightness, blue off — orange. Line 12 — led.off() : Turns all three channels off. Note: If your colours come out wrong (asking for red gives cyan), you have a common-anode LED — create it with RGBLED(red=17, green=27, blue=22, active_high=False) and connect the shared leg to 3.3 V. The Full Program Now we build the mood lamp: preset moods stored as data, functions that build and fade colours, a while True loop to keep it running, and a random "lava" mode. Open a new file in Thonny. from gpiozero import RGBLED from time import sleep import random # If your colours look inverted, set active_high=False (common-anode) led = RGBLED(red=17, green=27, blue=22) # A small list of preset moods: name to (r, g, b) each 0..1 MOODS = { "sunset": (1.0, 0.3, 0.0), "ocean": (0.0, 0.4, 1.0), "forest": (0.0, 0.8, 0.2), "candle": (1.0, 0.5, 0.1), "violet": (0.5, 0.0, 0.8), } def clamp(value): """Keep a number safely between 0 and 1.""" return max(0.0, min(1.0, value)) def fade(from_colour, to_colour, steps=50, pause=0.02): """Smoothly fade from one (r, g, b) colour to another.""" fr, fg, fb = from_colour tr, tg, tb = to_colour for i in range(steps + 1): amount = i / steps # 0.0 grows to 1.0 r = fr + (tr - fr) * amount g = fg + (tg - fg) * amount b = fb + (tb - fb) * amount led.value = (clamp(r), clamp(g), clamp(b)) sleep(pause) def random_colour(): """Return a random (r, g, b) that is not too dark.""" r = random.uniform(0.2, 1.0) g = random.uniform(0.2, 1.0) b = random.uniform(0.2, 1.0) return (r, g, b) def mood_cycle(): """Slowly fade through every preset mood, then repeat.""" current = (0, 0, 0) while True: for name, colour in MOODS.items(): print("Fading to", name) fade(current, colour) current = colour sleep(1) def lava_mode(): """Drift through random colours forever, like a lava lamp.""" current = random_colour() while True: target = random_colour() fade(current, target, steps=80, pause=0.03) current = target # Choose your mode here: print("Mood lamp starting. Press Stop to switch off.") mood_cycle() # lava_mode() # comment out mood_cycle() above and use this instead Lines 1–3 — the imports: RGBLED for the light, sleep for timing, and random for unpredictability. Line 6 — led = RGBLED(red=17, green=27, blue=22) : Creates the RGB LED on our three pins. Made once, near the top, so every function can use it. Lines 9–15 — MOODS = {…} : A dictionary of preset moods, each a name mapped to an (r, g, b) tuple with values 0–1. Storing colours as data lets us add moods without touching the fading code. Lines 18–20 — clamp() : A function that returns a value safely between 0 and 1, so a fade can never ask the LED for an illegal brightness. Lines 23–33 — fade(from_colour, to_colour, …) : The heart of the lamp. It takes two colours as parameters plus how many steps and how long to pause . The loop runs steps + 1 times; amount = i / steps grows gently from 0.0 to 1.0. The lines r = fr + (tr - fr) * amount mix that fraction of the way from the start colour to the end colour for each channel — gentle 0–1 maths in action. Setting led.value each step and pausing briefly makes a smooth fade. Lines 36–41 — random_colour() : A function that returns a random colour using random.uniform(0.2, 1.0) for each channel, so the colour is lively but never fully dark. Lines 44–52 — mood_cycle() : Uses while True to loop forever. Each round, the for name, colour in MOODS.items(): line walks through every preset, fading from the current colour to the next, then remembering it as the new current . Lines 55–61 — lava_mode() : Another while True loop, but instead of presets it fades to a fresh random colour each time — slow, gentle, and never repeating. This is where parameters, return values, the forever loop, and randomness all come together. Lines 65–67 — choosing a mode: Calls mood_cycle() to start. To run the lava mode instead, comment out that line and uncomment lava_mode() . Running It In Thonny, choose File → Save and save the file as mood_lamp.py in your home folder. Click the green Run button (the triangle ▶) or press F5 . Watch the LED gently fade between the preset moods. The Thonny console prints the name of each mood as it arrives. Place the LED and breadboard inside (or beside) your jar to see the soft, diffused glow. For a clear jar, tuck a little baking paper or tissue inside. To try the lava mode, stop the program, swap which mode line is active (comment mood_cycle() , uncomment lava_mode() ), and run again. To switch the lamp off, click the red Stop button (the square ■). Careful: Use only the cool, low-power LED inside the jar — never a candle or anything hot in a sealed glass container. The LED runs barely warm, which is exactly why it is safe in a recycled jar. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause & fix Colours are inverted (red looks cyan) You have a common-anode LED. Add active_high=False to RGBLED(...) and connect the shared leg to 3.3 V. Only some colours light A resistor or jumper for that channel is loose, or that colour leg is in the wrong row. Recheck each channel separately. One colour is far brighter Normal — blue/green have a higher forward voltage than red. Scale that channel down in the colour tuples to balance. LED flickers visibly A loose common-leg wire, or PWM disabled. Ensure RGBLED is created normally (PWM is on by default). Nothing lights at all Check the common leg goes to GND (common-cathode) and that all three resistors and the LED are seated. Confirm the LED legs are in separate rows. No module named 'lgpio' Install the backend: sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then restart Thonny. Fade looks jerky / steppy Increase steps or reduce pause in the fade() call for a smoother transition. Make It Your Own Add a button to change moods. Wire a push button (Chapter 12) and use button.when_pressed to jump to the next preset on demand. Balance the colours. Add a balance() function that scales the green and blue channels down a little so white looks truly white on your particular LED. A breathing night light. Use led.pulse() (built into RGBLED ) for a slow fade in and out, like calm breathing. More moods. Add new entries to the MOODS dictionary — because moods are stored as data, the fading code never has to change. Try "midnight": (0.0, 0.0, 0.4) or "rose": (1.0, 0.2, 0.4) . Tip: Notice the same big idea from Chapter 26: colours and moods live as data (a dictionary of tuples), while the behaviour (fading) lives in functions. Add a new colour and everything just works. Separating data from behaviour is one of the most useful habits a programmer can build. You have turned a jar bound for the recycling and a salvaged LED into a calming, programmable light — and learned how screens everywhere make their colours along the way. The gpiozero documentation at gpiozero.readthedocs.io lists every trick the RGBLED object can do. Badge earned: Set the Mood . Key terms RGB LED - A single package containing red, green, and blue LEDs whose blended light can make almost any colour. Additive colour mixing - Adding coloured light together; red + green + blue at full makes white. Duty cycle - The fraction of each PWM cycle a pin spends switched on; it sets the LED's brightness (0 = off, 1 = full). PWM (Pulse-Width Modulation) - Switching a pin on and off fast; the duty cycle controls perceived brightness. Common-cathode - An RGB LED whose three colours share a negative leg connected to GND; gpiozero default ( active_high=True ). Common-anode - An RGB LED whose three colours share a positive leg connected to 3.3 V; needs active_high=False . RGBLED - The gpiozero object that controls all three channels; set .value = (r, g, b) with each number 0–1. Parameter - A value passed into a function for it to use. Return value - The result a function hands back to its caller with the return keyword. while True loop - A loop that runs forever until the program is stopped; ideal for a lamp that glows continuously. random module - Python's built-in toolkit for unpredictable numbers ( random.random() , random.uniform() , random.choice() ). Chapter summary An RGB LED is three LEDs (red, green, blue) in one package; blending their light by additive mixing makes any colour. PWM duty cycle sets brightness: a pin switched on for more of each fast cycle looks brighter. gpiozero uses a 0–1 value per channel. gpiozero's RGBLED(red=, green=, blue=) controls all three channels; set .value = (r, g, b) with each number from 0 to 1. A common-cathode LED shares a negative leg to GND (gpiozero default); a common-anode shares a positive leg to 3.3 V and needs active_high=False , or colours invert. Each colour channel needs its own resistor (330 Ω) — never share one resistor across all three. Python functions with parameters and return values let us build and reuse colour calculations like fade() and clamp() . A while True loop keeps the lamp glowing forever; the random module drives the ever-changing "lava" mode. Keeping brightness as gentle 0–1 maths makes fading easy and keeps every value safely in range. A recycled glass jar makes a perfect, safe diffuser — and the LED runs cool, so it is safe inside glass (never a candle).

title: Distance Sensor & Parking Assistant
text: Bats and dolphins find their way in the dark by sending out a squeak and timing the echo that bounces back. In this chapter you will give your Pi the very same superpower using a cheap ultrasonic sensor, then turn it into a car parking assistant — a row of green, amber and red lights plus a buzzer that beeps faster the closer you get. Along the way you will learn one of Python's biggest ideas: classes and objects , write your own little helper class, build functions that return values , and meet the single most important safety circuit in this whole course — the voltage divider that stops a 5 volt sensor from frying your 3.3 volt Pi. What You'll Build & Learn By the end of this chapter you will have a working parking assistant : point the sensor at a wall (or have a friend hold a book in front of it), and as the object moves closer the lights change from green to amber to red while a buzzer beeps faster and faster — exactly like the reversing aid in a modern car. To get there you will learn these named fundamentals : Python fundamentals Classes & objects — the idea that a "thing" in your program can bundle together its own data and its own actions. The sensor itself is an object ; you will also write your own small class , called ParkingZone , to keep your code tidy. Functions that return values — functions that hand a result back to the line that called them, using the return keyword, so you can use that result elsewhere. A little maths — converting metres to centimetres, round() ing numbers neatly, and using number ranges (is the distance between 20 and 40 cm?) to decide what should happen. Mapping a measurement to a behaviour — turning a continuous reading (distance) into a small set of clear states (safe / caution / stop). Electronics fundamentals The HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor — how it fires a pulse of sound and times the echo, and how gpiozero's DistanceSensor object turns that into a distance in metres. The voltage divider — the critical two-resistor circuit that drops the sensor's 5 V ECHO signal down to a Pi-safe 3.3 V. Skipping this can permanently damage your Pi, so we give it a whole section of its own. Driving several outputs at once — three LEDs and a buzzer working together, each LED with its own resistor. In plain words: Ultrasonic means sound that is too high-pitched for humans to hear (above about 20,000 Hz). The HC-SR04 chirps at around 40,000 Hz — silent to you, but a perfect ruler for measuring distance. Meet Classes & Objects You have actually been using objects since Chapter 12 without us making a fuss about it. Every time you wrote led = LED(17) , you created an object . Let's now name the idea properly, because it is one of the most powerful in all of programming. In plain words: A class is a blueprint. An object is one real thing built from that blueprint. LED is the class (the blueprint for "any LED"); led = LED(17) builds one specific object — the LED on pin 17. From a single class you can make as many objects as you like. Think of a class as a cookie cutter and objects as the cookies. The cutter (class) defines the shape ; each cookie (object) is a separate, real cookie you can decorate differently. An object bundles together two things: Data it remembers about itself — called attributes . For an LED, whether it is currently lit ( led.is_lit ). Actions it can perform — called methods . For an LED, led.on() , led.off() , led.blink() . You reach an object's attributes and methods with a full stop (a "dot"): led.on() means "the on action belonging to led ". The sensor we build today is an object too — we will ask it sensor.distance (an attribute) to find out how far away something is. Writing your own class — a tiny first example Before we touch any wiring, let's write a class from scratch so the idea sinks in. Open Thonny and type this small program. It models a simple Counter — something that remembers a number and can count up. class Counter: def __init__(self, start=0): self.count = start def increase(self): self.count = self.count + 1 return self.count # Make two separate counter objects from the one blueprint goals = Counter() score = Counter(start=10) print(goals.increase()) # 1 print(goals.increase()) # 2 print(score.increase()) # 11 print(goals.count) # 2 (the goals object remembers its own number) Line 1 — class Counter: : Starts the blueprint. By convention class names begin with a capital letter ( Counter , LED , DistanceSensor ). Everything indented underneath belongs to the class. Line 2 — def __init__(self, start=0): : A special method called the initialiser . Python runs it automatically the moment you build an object, to set it up. The odd-looking name is two underscores, the word init , two more underscores. self is the object being built; start=0 is an optional value the maker can pass in. Line 3 — self.count = start : Stores a piece of data on this particular object . self.count is an attribute — each object gets its very own count , kept separate from every other object. Line 5 — def increase(self): : Defines a method (an action the object can do). Every method's first parameter is self , which is how the method knows which object's data to work on. Line 6 — self.count = self.count + 1 : Adds one to this object's own count. Line 7 — return self.count : Hands the new value back to whoever called the method — our first taste of a function that returns a value , covered properly in the next section. Lines 10–11 — goals = Counter() and score = Counter(start=10) : Build two completely separate objects from the same class. goals starts at 0; score starts at 10. They do not interfere with each other. Lines 13–16: Calling goals.increase() only changes goals ; score keeps its own tally. That independence is the whole point of objects. Tip: The word self trips up every beginner. Just remember: inside a class, self always means "this particular object". You never type self when you call a method ( goals.increase() ), only when you define one. Python fills it in for you. That is the whole idea. A class gathers related data and actions under one roof so your programs stay tidy as they grow. We will write a real, useful class — ParkingZone — for the project later on. Functions That Return Values Some functions just do something (like print() , which puts text on the screen). Others work something out and hand the answer back so you can use it. The keyword for handing an answer back is return . In plain words: return is how a function gives you an answer. print() shows a value on screen and then it is gone; return passes a value back into your program so you can store it, test it, or pass it on. Here is a tiny example that turns metres into centimetres and rounds the result. Type it in and run it. def metres_to_cm(metres): cm = metres * 100 return round(cm, 1) reading = metres_to_cm(0.4267) print(reading) # 42.7 print(reading + 5) # 47.7 (we can do maths with the returned value) Line 1 — def metres_to_cm(metres): : Defines a function that takes one input, metres . Line 2 — cm = metres * 100 : There are 100 centimetres in a metre, so we multiply. Line 3 — return round(cm, 1) : round(cm, 1) rounds the number to one decimal place (42.67 → 42.7), and return sends that tidy value back. The moment Python hits return , the function ends. Line 5 — reading = metres_to_cm(0.4267) : Calls the function and captures the returned value into a variable called reading . Now reading holds 42.7. Line 7 — print(reading + 5) : Because the value was returned (not just printed inside the function), we can keep using it — here we add 5. A function that only print() ed could not do this. Note: A function with no return hands back a special value called None , meaning "nothing". If you ever see None where you expected a number, you probably forgot a return . How the Ultrasonic Sensor Works The HC-SR04 is a small blue board with two silver cylinders that look like little eyes (one is a speaker, one is a microphone) and four pins: VCC , TRIG , ECHO and GND . It measures distance just like a bat: Your Pi sends a brief electrical pulse to the TRIG (trigger) pin. The sensor chirps out a burst of ultrasound (silent to us) and starts a stopwatch. The sound travels out, bounces off whatever is in front, and comes back. When the echo returns, the sensor raises its ECHO pin HIGH for exactly as long as the round trip took. The Pi times how long ECHO stays HIGH and, knowing the speed of sound (about 343 metres per second in air), works out the distance. Because the sound travels there and back , the Pi divides the time in half before converting it to a distance. Happily, gpiozero's DistanceSensor object does every bit of this timing maths for you — you just read sensor.distance . How the HC-SR04 measures distance (echo timing) HC-SR04 speaker mic object chirp out (TRIG fires) → ← echo back (ECHO goes HIGH) distance = (speed of sound × echo time) ÷ 2 The sensor chirps when TRIG fires, then holds ECHO HIGH for as long as the round trip takes. Because the sound travels there and back, the Pi halves the time to find the one-way distance. gpiozero does this maths and gives you the answer in metres. Here is the simplest possible distance program — but do not wire it up or run it yet . First you must build the safety circuit in the next section, or you risk damaging your Pi. from gpiozero import DistanceSensor from time import sleep sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23) # ECHO via a voltage divider! while True: distance_m = sensor.distance # an attribute of the sensor object, in metres print(round(distance_m * 100, 1), "cm") sleep(0.5) Line 1 — from gpiozero import DistanceSensor : Imports the ready-made object that handles all the trigger/echo timing. Line 4 — sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23) : Builds the sensor object. We connect ECHO to GPIO 24 (physical pin 18) and TRIG to GPIO 23 (physical pin 16). Notice we name the arguments ( echo= , trigger= ) so we cannot mix them up. Line 7 — distance_m = sensor.distance : Reads the distance attribute of the sensor object. It returns a number in metres , from 0 up to 1 metre by default. Line 8 — print(round(distance_m * 100, 1), "cm") : Multiplies by 100 to get centimetres and rounds to one decimal place before printing. Line 9 — sleep(0.5) : Waits half a second so we get a steady couple of readings per second rather than a blur. The Critical Voltage Divider (Read This!) Careful — this is the most important safety point in the chapter. The HC-SR04 runs on 5 volts , and its ECHO pin sends out a 5 V signal . But the Pi 5's GPIO pins are 3.3 V only and are NOT 5 V-tolerant . Connecting ECHO straight to a GPIO pin pushes 5 V into a pin that can take 3.3 V, and there is no fuse to save it — you can permanently destroy your Pi . You MUST drop the ECHO voltage with a two-resistor voltage divider first. (The TRIG pin is the other way round — the Pi sends 3.3 V out to it, which the sensor reads happily, so TRIG needs no divider.) In plain words: A voltage divider is just two resistors in a line between the signal and ground. The voltage you want appears at the join between them. By choosing the two resistor values, you choose what fraction of the input voltage comes out — here we turn 5 V into a Pi-safe 2.94 V. The maths — turning 5 V into 3.3 V (or less) The voltage at the middle tap of a divider follows one simple formula: V out = V in × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) Here R1 is the resistor between the ECHO pin and the middle tap, and R2 is the resistor between the middle tap and ground (GND). The GPIO pin connects to the middle tap. The classic gpiozero recipe uses R1 = 330 Ω and R2 = 470 Ω . Let's plug those in with V in = 5 V: V out = 5 × 470 ÷ (330 + 470) = 5 × 470 ÷ 800 = 2.94 V 2.94 V is comfortably below the 3.3 V limit, yet still high enough for the Pi to read clearly as a HIGH signal. Perfect. The ECHO voltage divider: 5 V → 2.94 V ECHO = 5 V R1 = 330 Ω (orange-orange-brown-gold) → GPIO 24 = 2.94 V (safe) R2 = 470 Ω (yellow-violet-brown-gold) GND (0 V) Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1+R2) = 5 × 470 / (330+470) = 5 × 470 / 800 = 2.94 V ✓ safe for GPIO The ECHO voltage divider. R1 (330 Ω) sits between ECHO and the middle tap; R2 (470 Ω) sits between the tap and GND. The GPIO pin reads the tap, where the voltage has dropped from 5 V to a safe 2.94 V. TRIG needs no divider. Tip: If you do not have 330 Ω and 470 Ω to hand, any pair with roughly a 2:3 ratio works. For example 1 kΩ (R1) + 2 kΩ (R2) gives 5 × 2000 ÷ 3000 = 3.33 V — right at the limit but commonly used. The 330 Ω/470 Ω pair is gentler, so we prefer it here. Note: Some makers use a ready-made "logic level shifter" board instead of two resistors. That works too, but the resistor divider is cheaper, uses parts from your starter kit, and teaches you exactly what is happening — so that is what we build. Parts & Wiring What you need A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 1 × HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (4 pins: VCC, TRIG, ECHO, GND) 1 × 330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown-gold) — this is R1 of the divider 1 × 470 Ω resistor (yellow-violet-brown-gold) — this is R2 of the divider 1 × green LED, 1 × amber/yellow LED, 1 × red LED 3 × 330 Ω resistors — one in series with each LED 1 × active buzzer (a small buzzer that beeps when switched on) 1 × breadboard and a handful of jumper wires (male-to-male and female-to-male) Careful — power off first. Shut your Pi down fully (Raspberry Pi menu → Shutdown), wait for the green light to go out, and unplug the power lead before touching any wires . Remember: GPIO is 3.3 V logic — never feed 5 V into a GPIO input , which is exactly why the ECHO line must go through the divider. Give every LED its own 330 Ω resistor, and only re-connect power once you have checked everything. Wiring diagram Parking Assistant — Full Wiring Diagram GPIO Header Pin 2 (5 V) Pin 16 (GPIO 23 TRIG) Pin 18 (GPIO 24 ECHO) Pin 11 (GPIO 17 grn) Pin 13 (GPIO 27 amb) Pin 15 (GPIO 22 red) Pin 31 (GPIO 6 buzz) Pin 6 (GND) HC-SR04 VCC TRIG ECHO GND 5 V → VCC GPIO 23 → TRIG (3.3 V out, no divider) ECHO 5 V R1 330Ω middle tap 2.94 V → GPIO 24 (ECHO in) R2 470Ω G 330Ω A R BZ common GND rail — all − legs and the sensor GND return here to Pin 6 Red = 5 V · Purple = GPIO signal · Grey = GND. ECHO passes through the divider before reaching GPIO 24. The complete parking assistant. The sensor's VCC takes 5 V; TRIG connects directly to GPIO 23; ECHO goes through the 330 Ω/470 Ω divider so GPIO 24 only ever sees 2.94 V. Each LED has its own 330 Ω resistor, and the buzzer and every cathode share the common GND rail back to pin 6. Connection table From (component) To (Pi pin / node) Via Notes HC-SR04 VCC Pin 2 (5 V) direct The sensor needs a full 5 V to work reliably HC-SR04 TRIG Pin 16 (GPIO 23) direct Pi sends 3.3 V out — no divider needed HC-SR04 ECHO Pin 18 (GPIO 24) 330 Ω (R1) then tap to GPIO; 470 Ω (R2) tap to GND Divider is mandatory — drops 5 V → 2.94 V HC-SR04 GND Pin 6 (GND) common GND rail Same ground as the divider's R2 and the LEDs Green LED anode (long leg) Pin 11 (GPIO 17) 330 Ω resistor "Safe" light Amber LED anode (long leg) Pin 13 (GPIO 27) 330 Ω resistor "Caution" light Red LED anode (long leg) Pin 15 (GPIO 22) 330 Ω resistor "Stop" light Buzzer + (positive) Pin 31 (GPIO 6) direct A small active buzzer is fine on a GPIO pin All LED cathodes (short legs) & buzzer − Pin 6 (GND) common GND rail Shared return path Tip: Build the divider first and double-check it before anything else. The easiest way to wire it on a breadboard: push ECHO into one row, put R1 between that row and an empty middle row, run a jumper from the middle row to GPIO 24, then put R2 between the middle row and the GND rail. If in any doubt, trace it against the diagram above before powering on. Building the Parking Assistant Now we bring everything together. The plan: read the distance many times a second, decide which "zone" the object is in, light the matching LED, and beep the buzzer at a speed that depends on how close the object is. To keep the code tidy we will write our own class, ParkingZone , that bundles a zone's name, its distance range, and which light belongs to it. Step 1 — a class to describe each zone First, here is the helper class on its own so you can see it clearly. It uses everything from the earlier lessons: a class, an __init__ , attributes, and a method that returns a value . class ParkingZone: def __init__(self, name, max_cm, led, beep_gap): self.name = name self.max_cm = max_cm self.led = led self.beep_gap = beep_gap def contains(self, distance_cm): return distance_cm <= self.max_cm Line 1 — class ParkingZone: : Our own blueprint describing one band of distance, such as "caution". Line 2 — def __init__(self, name, max_cm, led, beep_gap): : The initialiser takes four pieces of information for each zone: a name , the furthest distance that counts as this zone ( max_cm ), the led object that lights for it, and beep_gap — how long (in seconds) to pause between beeps in this zone. Lines 3–6 — self.name = name … : Store each value on the object so it remembers them. Now every ParkingZone object carries its own name, range, LED and beep speed. Line 8 — def contains(self, distance_cm): : A method that answers a yes/no question: is a given distance inside this zone? Line 9 — return distance_cm <= self.max_cm : Returns True if the distance is less than or equal to this zone's upper limit, otherwise False . A function returning a True/False value like this is exactly how we map a measurement to a behaviour. Step 2 — the full program Open a new file in Thonny, type the whole program below, and save it as parking.py . from gpiozero import DistanceSensor, LED, Buzzer from time import sleep, time # --- the sensor object (ECHO wired through the 330/470 divider!) --- sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23, max_distance=1.0) # --- output objects --- green = LED(17) amber = LED(27) red = LED(22) buzzer = Buzzer(6) class ParkingZone: def __init__(self, name, max_cm, led, beep_gap): self.name = name self.max_cm = max_cm self.led = led self.beep_gap = beep_gap def contains(self, distance_cm): return distance_cm <= self.max_cm # Zones are checked closest-first. beep_gap of None means "no beeping". zones = [ ParkingZone("STOP", 10, red, 0.1), ParkingZone("Close", 20, red, 0.25), ParkingZone("Caution", 40, amber, 0.6), ParkingZone("Safe", 100, green, None), ] def read_distance_cm(): """Return the current distance in centimetres, rounded to 1 dp.""" metres = sensor.distance return round(metres * 100, 1) def pick_zone(distance_cm): """Return the first ParkingZone whose range contains this distance.""" for zone in zones: if zone.contains(distance_cm): return zone return zones[-1] # fall back to the 'Safe' zone def all_lights_off(): green.off() amber.off() red.off() print("Parking assistant running.
