Press Ctrl+C to stop.") last_beep = 0 try: while True: distance = read_distance_cm() zone = pick_zone(distance) all_lights_off() zone.led.on() print(f"{distance:5.1f} cm -> {zone.name}") if zone.beep_gap is not None: if time() - last_beep >= zone.beep_gap: buzzer.on() sleep(0.05) buzzer.off() last_beep = time() else: buzzer.off() sleep(0.05) except KeyboardInterrupt: all_lights_off() buzzer.off() print("\nStopped. Lights off.") Lines 1–2 — imports: We bring in DistanceSensor , LED and Buzzer from gpiozero, and sleep plus time from Python's time module. time() returns the current time in seconds, which we use to pace the beeps. Line 5 — sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23, max_distance=1.0) : Builds the sensor object. max_distance=1.0 tells gpiozero we care about distances up to 1 metre, which keeps readings responsive. Lines 8–11 — output objects: One LED object per light, plus a Buzzer object on GPIO 6. Each is an object created from a class — the same idea as the sensor. Lines 14–22 — the ParkingZone class: Exactly the helper class from Step 1, pasted in. Defining it here means we can stamp out several zone objects below. Lines 25–30 — zones = [ ... ] : A list of four ParkingZone objects, ordered closest-first. STOP (≤10 cm) beeps almost continuously; Close (≤20 cm) beeps fast; Caution (≤40 cm) beeps slowly in amber; Safe (everything else) shows green with no beep ( None ). Lines 33–36 — read_distance_cm() : A function that returns a value : it reads the sensor's distance attribute (metres), converts to centimetres, rounds it, and hands it back. The triple-quoted line is a docstring describing what the function does. Lines 39–44 — pick_zone(distance_cm) : Walks through the zones from closest to furthest and return s the first one whose contains() method says yes. Because the list is ordered closest-first, the tightest matching zone always wins. If somehow none match, line 44 returns the last (Safe) zone. Lines 47–50 — all_lights_off() : A small helper that switches all three LEDs off, so we start each loop with a clean slate before lighting just one. Line 55 — last_beep = 0 : Remembers the time of the most recent beep so we can space beeps out by each zone's beep_gap . Line 57 — try: : Wraps the main loop so that pressing Ctrl+C runs the tidy-up code at the bottom instead of crashing. Lines 59–60 — read & classify: Each loop we get the distance, then ask pick_zone() which zone we are in. This is the heart of mapping a measurement to a behaviour . Lines 62–63 — all_lights_off() then zone.led.on() : Clear all lights, then light only the one belonging to the chosen zone. Notice zone.led is the LED object we stored on that zone earlier. Line 65 — print(f"{distance:5.1f} cm -> {zone.name}") : An f-string showing the live reading. :5.1f formats the number in a tidy 5-character-wide field with one decimal place, so the column does not jump about. Lines 67–74 — the beeping: If the zone has a beep_gap (not None ), and enough time has passed since the last beep, switch the buzzer on for a brief 0.05 s click, then off, and record the time. Closer zones have a smaller beep_gap , so the beeps come faster — exactly the parking-sensor effect. Lines 75–76 — else: buzzer.off() : In the Safe zone there is no beeping, so we make sure the buzzer is silent. Line 78 — sleep(0.05) : A short pause so the loop runs about 20 times a second — smooth and responsive without hammering the sensor. Lines 80–83 — except KeyboardInterrupt: : When you press Ctrl+C, this runs: all lights off, buzzer off, and a friendly message. Always leaving hardware in a safe, quiet state is good manners. Running It Double-check the divider. Before powering on, trace the ECHO line one more time: ECHO → R1 (330 Ω) → middle tap → GPIO 24, and middle tap → R2 (470 Ω) → GND. This is the step that protects your Pi. Reconnect power and let the Pi boot to the desktop. Open parking.py in Thonny and click the green Run button (or press F5). Watch the console. You should see distance readings scrolling, each labelled with its zone. Move your hand (or a book) towards the sensor. The lights should step from green to amber to red, and the buzzer should beep faster as you get closer. Pull away and it relaxes back to green. Press Ctrl+C in the console (or the red Stop button) to end the program cleanly — all lights and the buzzer switch off. Tip: Ultrasonic sensors like a flat, solid target. A hand works, but a flat book or a wall gives steadier readings. Very soft or angled surfaces can scatter the sound and produce jumpy numbers — that is normal physics, not a bug. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause Fix Readings are always 1.0 m (the maximum) or jump wildly ECHO not reaching GPIO 24, or the divider tap is in the wrong place Check the middle tap goes to GPIO 24, R1 is between ECHO and the tap, R2 between tap and GND. A loose jumper is the usual culprit. No readings at all / sensor seems dead VCC not on 5 V, or GND not shared VCC must be on a 5 V pin (pin 2 or 4), and the sensor GND, divider R2 and Pi GND must all share the same ground rail. Wrong LED lights for the distance LED wired to the wrong GPIO, or zones out of order Confirm green=17, amber=27, red=22, and that the zones list is ordered closest-first. Buzzer is silent It's a passive buzzer, or wired backwards This project needs an active buzzer (beeps when simply switched on). Check the + leg goes to GPIO 6. Buzzer beeps non-stop and won't pace The last_beep timing got skipped Make sure you copied the if time() - last_beep >= zone.beep_gap: line exactly. No module named 'lgpio' The lgpio backend is missing In a terminal run sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then restart Thonny. Careful: If your Pi behaves oddly only when the sensor is connected — random reboots, USB devices dropping out — power off immediately and re-check that ECHO is going through the divider and not straight to the GPIO pin. A 5 V signal sneaking onto a 3.3 V pin is the number-one cause of mystery faults here. Make It Your Own You now have a complete sensing-and-reacting machine. Here are four ways to take it further: Add a fourth "danger close" tone. Give the STOP zone a different sound by switching to a TonalBuzzer (from Chapter 26) and playing a low note when very close and a high one further away. Smooth the readings with a method. Add a read_average() function that takes five readings and returns their average, so a single odd bounce does not flicker the lights. (Hint: collect readings in a list and return sum(readings) / len(readings) .) Make the zones configurable. Because each zone is an object in a list, you can change the ranges, colours or beep speeds just by editing the zones = [ ... ] block — no other code needs to change. Try tuning it for a model car on a desk. Build a "doorway counter". Point the sensor across a doorway and use the distance dropping below a threshold to count people walking past — a neat lead-in to the data logging you will do in the next chapter. Note: The official gpiozero documentation at gpiozero.readthedocs.io has more on DistanceSensor , including when_in_range and when_out_of_range callbacks — a tidy way to react to crossings without a busy loop, building on the event style you'll meet later. Key terms Class - a blueprint that bundles related data and actions together (e.g. LED , DistanceSensor , your own ParkingZone ). Object - one real thing built from a class, with its own data; led = LED(17) creates an object. Attribute - a piece of data stored on an object, reached with a dot (e.g. sensor.distance ). Method - an action an object can perform, also reached with a dot (e.g. led.on() ). __init__ - the initialiser method that runs automatically to set up a new object. self - inside a class, refers to "this particular object". return - the keyword that hands a value back from a function so it can be used elsewhere. HC-SR04 - an ultrasonic distance sensor that times the echo of a 40 kHz chirp. DistanceSensor - the gpiozero object for the HC-SR04; .distance gives metres (0–max_distance). TRIG / ECHO - the sensor's trigger (Pi → sensor, 3.3 V, no divider) and echo (sensor → Pi, 5 V, needs a divider) pins. Voltage divider - two resistors that drop a voltage; V out = V in × R2 ÷ (R1+R2). 330 Ω + 470 Ω turns 5 V into 2.94 V. Active buzzer - a buzzer that beeps when simply switched on; safe to drive from a GPIO pin via gpiozero's Buzzer . Chapter summary A class is a blueprint; an object is a real thing made from it, bundling its own attributes (data) and methods (actions), reached with a dot. You wrote your own class, ParkingZone , with an __init__ initialiser and a method that returns a True/False answer. Functions that return values use return to hand a result back so you can store, test or reuse it — unlike print() , which only displays. The HC-SR04 measures distance by timing the echo of an ultrasonic chirp; gpiozero's DistanceSensor reports it as .distance in metres . Critical safety: the ECHO pin outputs 5 V, which would damage the Pi's 3.3 V GPIO — you MUST use a 330 Ω + 470 Ω voltage divider (V out = 5 × 470 ÷ 800 = 2.94 V). TRIG, driven at 3.3 V by the Pi, needs no divider. The parking assistant maps the continuous distance to a small set of zones, lighting the matching LED and beeping the buzzer faster as objects get closer. Each LED still needs its own 330 Ω resistor, and all grounds (sensor, divider, LEDs, buzzer) share one common GND rail back to the Pi.

title: Plant Monitor & Data Logger
headings: Digital vs Analog & the Missing ADC
A Look at True Analog: the MCP3008
text:
A houseplant cannot tell you it is thirsty — but your Pi can listen on its behalf. In this chapter you will build a plant monitor that checks the soil and the air, then quietly writes a timestamped row to a file every few minutes, building up a history you can read back to find the driest moment of the day. You will learn how to open, write and read files , save tidy data with the CSV module, organise readings as a list of dictionaries , stamp each one with the date and time , and finish with a function that prints a daily summary. On the electronics side you will finally understand the deep difference between digital and analog — and why the Pi, alone among hobby boards, has no way to read an analog voltage directly. What You'll Build & Learn Your finished project is a data logger : every N minutes it reads a soil-moisture sensor and a temperature/humidity sensor, appends a timestamped row to a CSV file, and — at the end of a run — reads the whole file back to print a tidy summary (driest reading, warmest reading, and so on). It is the foundation of every weather station, fitness tracker and laboratory instrument ever made: sense, record, review . Python fundamentals Files — opening a file with open() , writing to it, reading it back, and why the with keyword keeps files safe. CSV — using Python's built-in csv module to save rows of data that open perfectly in any spreadsheet. Lists of dictionaries — the natural shape for "many readings, each with several named fields" (time, moisture, temperature…). datetime timestamps — labelling every reading with the exact date and time it was taken. Loops and a logging function — a function that takes one reading and appends it, called over and over on a timer. Reading data back to find min/max — loading the CSV again and scanning it to find the extremes. Electronics fundamentals Digital vs analog — the difference between a signal that is only ever ON or OFF and one that varies smoothly. Why the Pi has no ADC — every Pi GPIO pin is digital, so it cannot directly read a smoothly-varying voltage, and what to do about it. A digital capacitive soil-moisture sensor — read with gpiozero's DigitalInputDevice . A DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor — with an honest look at the messy library situation on the Pi 5, and the more reliable I²C alternative. The MCP3008 ADC over SPI — a brief look at how you would read a true analog sensor. Digital vs Analog & the Missing ADC This is the single most important electronics idea in the chapter, and it shapes every sensor choice you make on a Pi. In plain words: A digital signal has only two states — ON or OFF, HIGH or LOW, 1 or 0. An analog signal varies smoothly through every value in between, like a dimmer dial rather than a light switch. A push button is digital: pressed or not pressed. A spinning volume knob is analog: it can sit at any point from fully off to fully on. Many real-world quantities — temperature, light level, the wetness of soil — are naturally analog: they slide smoothly up and down. Digital vs Analog signals Digital — only HIGH or LOW 3.3 V 0 V jumps between two levels Analog — any value in between 3.3 V 0 V slides smoothly up and down A digital signal flips between two fixed levels; an analog signal varies continuously. Every Pi GPIO pin can only tell HIGH from LOW — it cannot measure where an analog signal sits in between. Careful — the key Pi fact: The Raspberry Pi has no analog input. It has no ADC (Analogue-to-Digital Converter) at all. Every one of its GPIO pins is purely digital — it can only ever tell whether a voltage is below or above the threshold between LOW and HIGH. This surprises people coming from boards like the Arduino, which do have analog inputs. So if a sensor produces a smoothly-varying analog voltage (like a cheap resistive soil probe), the Pi cannot read it directly . You must either choose a sensor that gives a digital output, or add an external ADC chip. In plain words: An ADC (Analogue-to-Digital Converter) is a chip that measures an analog voltage and reports it as a number a computer can understand. The Pi has none built in; the Arduino does. This is the single biggest difference beginners trip over. Your three options on a Pi Approach How it works Best for Digital-output sensor The sensor has its own little chip that decides "wet/dry" or "bright/dark" and gives a clean HIGH/LOW the Pi reads directly with DigitalInputDevice or Button . Simple yes/no questions — is the soil dry? Easiest by far. Digital data sensor (e.g. DHT22, or I²C) The sensor measures internally and sends the Pi a stream of digital bits encoding the actual number (temperature, humidity). Reading true values over one or two wires using a driver library. External ADC (e.g. MCP3008 over SPI) An add-on chip measures the analog voltage and tells the Pi the number digitally. When you must read a genuinely analog sensor (a real moisture level, a light dependent resistor). For our plant monitor we use the two friendliest options: a digital capacitive soil-moisture sensor for "wet or dry", and a DHT22 for temperature and humidity. We will look at the MCP3008 briefly at the end for when you outgrow them. Choosing the Sensors The soil-moisture sensor — choose capacitive, not resistive Cheap soil sensors come in two flavours, and the difference matters: Resistive probes pass a current through the soil between two metal prongs. They are analog (so the Pi cannot read them without an ADC) and, worse, the prongs corrode quickly because of the current. Capacitive probes sense moisture without passing current into the soil, so they last far longer. Crucially, the common capacitive modules include a small comparator chip and a sensitivity screw, giving a clean digital DO (digital out) pin: HIGH when dry, LOW when wet (or the reverse, depending on the board). That digital pin plugs straight into a Pi GPIO — no ADC needed. Tip: Capacitive sensors are the right choice for a Pi because their digital output works without an ADC and they don't rot in the pot. Turn the little screw on the board to set the wet/dry threshold: water the plant, then adjust until the onboard LED just switches as the soil dries. We read its digital DO pin with gpiozero's DigitalInputDevice : from gpiozero import DigitalInputDevice # DO pin of the capacitive sensor on GPIO 17. active_state=False means # the sensor pulls the line LOW when it detects moisture. soil = DigitalInputDevice(17, pull_up=None, active_state=False) if soil.value == 1: print("Soil is WET") else: print("Soil is DRY") Line 1 — from gpiozero import DigitalInputDevice : DigitalInputDevice is the general-purpose object for reading any HIGH/LOW input — perfect for a sensor whose DO pin is already digital. Line 5 — soil = DigitalInputDevice(17, pull_up=None, active_state=False) : Reads GPIO 17. The sensor drives the line itself, so we set pull_up=None (no internal resistor) and tell gpiozero that the "active" (detected) state is a LOW line with active_state=False . If your board reads the opposite way, swap to active_state=True . Lines 7–10 — if soil.value == 1: : soil.value is 1 when the sensor is active (moisture detected) and 0 otherwise — a clean digital read, no ADC in sight. The DHT22 — and an honest word about the Pi 5 The DHT22 (and its cheaper cousin the DHT11) measures temperature and humidity and sends the Pi a digital data stream on a single signal wire. It is popular and inexpensive — but on the Raspberry Pi 5 the software story is genuinely awkward, so let's be honest about it. Careful — outdated tutorials will fail on the Pi 5. Two libraries you will find all over the internet do not work on the Pi 5 : the old Adafruit_DHT library is archived and fails on Bookworm with Python 3.11; and the pigpio daemon (which some DHT guides rely on) is not supported on the Pi 5 either. If a tutorial tells you to pip install Adafruit_DHT or to start pigpiod , stop — it will not work. The combination that does work today is the current CircuitPython stack: adafruit-circuitpython-dht together with a recent adafruit-blinka (which routes GPIO through lgpio on the Pi 5). Because of PEP 668 on Bookworm, install them inside a virtual environment: python3 -m venv plantenv source plantenv/bin/activate pip install adafruit-circuitpython-dht adafruit-blinka Line 1 — python3 -m venv plantenv : Creates a virtual environment (an isolated, private set of Python packages) in a folder called plantenv . This sidesteps Bookworm's "externally-managed-environment" block on system-wide pip . Line 2 — source plantenv/bin/activate : Switches your terminal into that environment. Your prompt gains a (plantenv) prefix. Run your script from this same activated terminal. Line 3 — pip install ... : Installs the two libraries that actually work on the Pi 5. adafruit-blinka is the glue that lets CircuitPython libraries talk to the Pi's hardware via lgpio. Reading it then looks like this — note that the DHT22 is fussy and sometimes returns a checksum error, so we catch it and try again: import board import adafruit_dht dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4) # data pin on GPIO 4 def read_temp_humidity(): """Return (temperature_c, humidity_pct), retrying on checksum errors.""" for attempt in range(5): try: return dht.temperature, dht.humidity except RuntimeError: sleep(2) # a normal hiccup — wait and retry return None, None Lines 1–2 — imports: board names the Pi's pins the CircuitPython way ( board.D4 = GPIO 4); adafruit_dht is the working DHT driver. Line 4 — dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4) : Creates the sensor object on GPIO 4. Line 6 — def read_temp_humidity(): : A function that returns a pair of values: the temperature in °C and the humidity as a percentage. Lines 8–13 — the retry loop: The DHT22 occasionally fails its internal checksum and raises a RuntimeError . Rather than crash, we try up to five times, pausing two seconds between attempts. If every attempt fails, we return None, None so the caller can skip that reading. Tip: If you want a rock-solid reading with no checksum drama, an I²C sensor such as the SHT4x or BME280 is the most reliable teaching choice on the Pi 5. It connects to just the two I²C pins (SDA/SCL), needs no divider, and its CircuitPython library is stable. The logging code in this chapter works the same whichever sensor you read from — only the read_temp_humidity() function changes. Note: If you do not have a DHT22 yet, you can still build and learn the whole logger: replace read_temp_humidity() with a version that returns made-up numbers (e.g. return 21.4, 55.0 ). Every file, CSV and summary idea works identically with stand-in data. Files, CSV & Lists of Dictionaries Before wiring anything, let's master the data side with small examples. These are the Python fundamentals at the heart of the project. Opening and writing a file with open("hello.txt", "w") as f: f.write("Hello, plant!
") f.write("This is line two.
") Line 1 — with open("hello.txt", "w") as f: : open() opens (and here creates) a file. The "w" means "write mode" — it starts the file fresh, erasing any old contents. The with keyword is the safe way to open files: it automatically closes the file when the indented block ends, even if something goes wrong. f is our handle to the open file. Lines 2–3 — f.write(...) : Writes text into the file. 
 is a newline character, so each write ends up on its own line. In plain words: The three common file modes are "w" (write — erases first), "a" (append — adds to the end, keeping what's there), and "r" (read — look but don't change). A logger uses "a" so each new reading is added without wiping the history. Reading a file back with open("hello.txt", "r") as f: for line in f: print(line.strip()) Line 1 — open(..., "r") : Opens the file in read mode. Line 2 — for line in f: : Looping over an open file hands you one line at a time — a tidy, memory-friendly way to read even huge files. Line 3 — print(line.strip()) : .strip() removes the trailing newline so we don't print blank gaps between lines. A list of dictionaries A dictionary stores named values — perfect for one reading with several fields. A list of dictionaries is the natural shape for many such readings. readings = [ {"time": "09:00", "moisture": "wet", "temp": 20.1}, {"time": "09:05", "moisture": "wet", "temp": 20.4}, {"time": "09:10", "moisture": "dry", "temp": 21.0}, ] for r in readings: print(r["time"], "->", r["temp"], "C") # Find the warmest reading by scanning the list warmest = readings[0] for r in readings: if r["temp"] > warmest["temp"]: warmest = r print("Warmest:", warmest["temp"], "C at", warmest["time"]) Lines 1–5 — readings = [ ... ] : A list (square brackets) whose items are dictionaries (curly braces). Each dictionary holds named fields: "time" , "moisture" , "temp" . This is exactly how we'll hold our logged data in memory. Lines 7–8 — looping over the list: Each r is one dictionary; r["temp"] looks up that reading's temperature by name. Lines 11–15 — finding the maximum: Start by assuming the first reading is warmest, then loop through and keep any reading that beats it. By the end, warmest holds the dictionary with the highest temp — the classic "find the max" pattern you'll reuse on the logged file. The CSV module A CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file is the universal format for tables of data — every spreadsheet program opens it. Python's built-in csv module writes and reads it cleanly, handling commas and quoting for you. csv.DictWriter and csv.DictReader pair beautifully with our list of dictionaries. import csv rows = [ {"time": "09:00", "moisture": "wet", "temp": 20.1}, {"time": "09:05", "moisture": "dry", "temp": 21.0}, ] with open("demo.csv", "w", newline="") as f: writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["time", "moisture", "temp"]) writer.writeheader() writer.writerows(rows) Line 1 — import csv : Brings in Python's built-in CSV tools — nothing to install. Line 8 — open("demo.csv", "w", newline="") : Opens the CSV for writing. The newline="" is the recommended setting for the csv module so it controls line endings itself (this avoids blank lines on some systems). Line 9 — csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=[...]) : Creates a writer that maps dictionary keys to columns. fieldnames sets the column order. Line 10 — writer.writeheader() : Writes the first row of column names ( time,moisture,temp ). Line 11 — writer.writerows(rows) : Writes every dictionary in our list as its own row. To read it back, csv.DictReader turns each row back into a dictionary. Timestamps with datetime from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() print(now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")) # e.g. 2026-06-23 14:05:09 Line 1 — from datetime import datetime : Imports the datetime object, which represents a moment in time. Line 3 — now = datetime.now() : Captures the current date and time right now. Line 4 — now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") : Formats the moment as readable text: four-digit year, month, day, then hours, minutes, seconds. Putting a timestamp on every reading is what turns a pile of numbers into a history you can chart. Parts & Wiring What you need A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 1 × capacitive soil-moisture sensor with a digital DO output 1 × DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor (or an I²C SHT4x/BME280, or just use stand-in numbers) 1 × 10 kΩ resistor (a pull-up for the DHT22 data line, if your DHT22 module doesn't already include one) 1 × breadboard and a handful of jumper wires Careful — power off first. Shut your Pi down fully (Raspberry Pi menu → Shutdown), wait for the green light to go out, and unplug the power before wiring. Both sensors here run from 3.3 V and their data/DO lines are 3.3 V logic, so — unlike the ultrasonic sensor in the last chapter — no voltage divider is needed . Still observe the golden rule: GPIO is 3.3 V logic, and you must never feed a higher voltage into a GPIO input. Re-connect power only after checking your wiring. Wiring diagram Plant Monitor — Wiring Diagram GPIO Header Pin 1 (3.3 V) Pin 11 (GPIO 17 soil DO) Pin 7 (GPIO 4 DHT data) Pin 17 (3.3 V) Pin 9 (GND) Soil sensor VCC GND DO DHT22 + DATA − 3.3 V → soil VCC GPIO 17 ← soil DO (digital, no divider) GPIO 4 ← DHT DATA 10kΩ pull-up common GND rail → Pin 9 (both sensor grounds) Orange = 3.3 V · Purple/Teal = GPIO signal · Grey = GND. Both data lines are 3.3 V — no divider needed. The plant monitor. Both sensors run from 3.3 V; the soil sensor's digital DO goes to GPIO 17 and the DHT22's data line to GPIO 4. An optional 10 kΩ pull-up steadies the DHT data line. Because every signal is already 3.3 V logic, no voltage divider is required here. Connection table From (component) To (Pi pin) Via Notes Soil sensor VCC Pin 1 (3.3 V) direct Capacitive modules run happily at 3.3 V Soil sensor DO (digital out) Pin 11 (GPIO 17) direct Already digital 3.3 V — no divider Soil sensor GND Pin 9 (GND) common GND rail Shared with the DHT22 DHT22 + (VCC) Pin 17 (3.3 V) direct 3.3 V supply DHT22 DATA Pin 7 (GPIO 4) 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V Many DHT22 modules already include the pull-up DHT22 − (GND) Pin 9 (GND) common GND rail Shared ground Note: A bare 3-pin DHT22 needs the 10 kΩ pull-up resistor between its DATA line and 3.3 V. The common blue or white DHT22 modules on a small breakout board usually have this resistor built in, so you can skip it — check your board. Building the Data Logger Now we assemble the full program. It reads both sensors, appends a timestamped row to a CSV, repeats every N minutes, and prints a daily summary read back from the file. To keep it tidy we put the appending in its own logging function . Open a new file in Thonny, type the program, and save it as plant_logger.py . (Run it from your activated plantenv terminal if you are using a real DHT22.) import csv import os from time import sleep from datetime import datetime from gpiozero import DigitalInputDevice # --- sensor objects --- soil = DigitalInputDevice(17, pull_up=None, active_state=False) # If you have a real DHT22, uncomment these two lines and the body of # read_temp_humidity() below (and run inside your venv): # import board, adafruit_dht # dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4) CSV_FILE = "plant_log.csv" FIELDS = ["timestamp", "moisture", "temp_c", "humidity_pct"] SAMPLE_MINUTES = 5 # how often to take a reading def read_moisture(): """Return 'wet' or 'dry' from the digital soil sensor.""" return "wet" if soil.value == 1 else "dry" def read_temp_humidity(): """Return (temperature_c, humidity_pct). Replace body with real DHT22 code.""" # --- real DHT22 version (needs the venv libraries) --- # for _ in range(5): # try: # return round(dht.temperature, 1), round(dht.humidity, 1) # except RuntimeError: # sleep(2) # return None, None # --- stand-in version so the logger runs without a DHT22 --- return 21.4, 55.0 def log_reading(): """Take one reading and append it as a timestamped row to the CSV.""" temp_c, humidity = read_temp_humidity() row = { "timestamp": datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "moisture": read_moisture(), "temp_c": temp_c, "humidity_pct": humidity, } file_is_new = not os.path.exists(CSV_FILE) with open(CSV_FILE, "a", newline="") as f: writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS) if file_is_new: writer.writeheader() writer.writerow(row) print("Logged:", row) return row def print_summary(): """Read the whole CSV back and print the day's extremes.""" with open(CSV_FILE, "r", newline="") as f: rows = list(csv.DictReader(f)) if not rows: print("No data yet.") return temps = [float(r["temp_c"]) for r in rows if r["temp_c"]] dry_count = sum(1 for r in rows if r["moisture"] == "dry") print("
----- Daily summary -----") print(f"Readings logged : {len(rows)}") if temps: print(f"Warmest : {max(temps)} C") print(f"Coolest : {min(temps)} C") print(f"Times soil dry : {dry_count}") print("-------------------------
") print("Plant logger started. Press Ctrl+C to stop and see the summary.") try: while True: log_reading() sleep(SAMPLE_MINUTES * 60) except KeyboardInterrupt: print("
Stopping...") print_summary() Lines 1–5 — imports: csv for the file format, os to check whether the file already exists, sleep for the timer, datetime for timestamps, and DigitalInputDevice to read the soil sensor. Line 8 — soil = DigitalInputDevice(17, ...) : The soil-moisture object on GPIO 17, exactly as in the earlier example. Lines 15–17 — settings: CSV_FILE names our log file; FIELDS lists the column names in order; SAMPLE_MINUTES sets how often we take a reading. Change this one number to sample faster or slower. Lines 20–22 — read_moisture() : A function returning the word "wet" or "dry" based on the digital soil reading — mapping a HIGH/LOW into a human label. Lines 25–35 — read_temp_humidity() : Returns a temperature and humidity pair. The commented block is the real DHT22 code (with its checksum retry loop); the active line returns stand-in numbers so you can run the logger even without the sensor wired. Lines 38–56 — log_reading() — the logging function: This is the heart of the project. It builds a dictionary ( row ) holding a fresh timestamp plus the three readings, then appends it to the CSV. os.path.exists(CSV_FILE) tells us if the file is brand new; if so, we write the header row first. Opening in "a" (append) mode means every call adds a row without wiping the history. It returns the row in case the caller wants it. Lines 59–78 — print_summary() — reading data back: Opens the CSV in read mode and uses csv.DictReader to load every row back into a list of dictionaries . The line temps = [float(r["temp_c"]) for r in rows if r["temp_c"]] is a list comprehension that pulls out all the temperatures as numbers. Then max(temps) and min(temps) find the warmest and coolest — the "find min/max by reading data back" goal. dry_count counts how many readings found dry soil. Lines 81–88 — the main loop: Prints a start message, then loops forever: take one reading ( log_reading() ), then sleep for SAMPLE_MINUTES × 60 seconds before the next. Pressing Ctrl+C raises KeyboardInterrupt , which we catch to print the summary on the way out — a tidy finish. Tip: While testing, set SAMPLE_MINUTES to a fraction such as 0.1 (six seconds) so you don't have to wait five minutes between rows. Set it back to 5 (or higher) for real plant monitoring, where things change slowly. Running It Check your wiring against the connection table — both sensors on 3.3 V, grounds shared, soil DO on GPIO 17, DHT data on GPIO 4. Reconnect power and boot the Pi. If using a real DHT22, activate your venv first: in a terminal run source plantenv/bin/activate , then start Thonny from that same terminal so it can see the installed libraries. With stand-in numbers you can just run from Thonny directly. Open plant_logger.py and run it. You should see a Logged: {...} line appear each cycle. Watch the file grow. Open a terminal and run cat plant_log.csv to see your timestamped rows building up. Touch the soil probe (or dunk it in a glass of water vs leave it dry) and confirm the moisture field flips between wet and dry . Press Ctrl+C to stop. The program prints a daily summary — the warmest and coolest temperatures and how many times the soil was dry — read straight back from the CSV. Note: The CSV file lands in whatever folder you ran the script from (usually your home folder from Thonny). Double-click it in the Files app and it opens in LibreOffice Calc as a proper spreadsheet, ready to chart. A Look at True Analog: the MCP3008 Our capacitive sensor gives a simple wet/dry answer, which is plenty for watering a plant. But what if you wanted the exact moisture percentage, or to read a light-dependent resistor, or any genuinely analog sensor? Then you need to give the Pi the ADC it lacks. The classic, cheap choice is the MCP3008 : an 8-channel ADC chip that talks to the Pi over the SPI bus. In plain words: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is a way for the Pi to chat with add-on chips over a few dedicated pins. The MCP3008 listens on SPI, measures the analog voltage on one of its 8 input channels, and reports back a number — giving the Pi the analog reading it cannot take itself. Once SPI is enabled (in raspi-config ) and the chip is wired to the SPI pins, gpiozero makes it almost magically simple: from gpiozero import MCP3008 # An analog moisture probe on channel 0 of the MCP3008 moisture = MCP3008(channel=0) while True: level = moisture.value # a float from 0.0 to 1.0 print(round(level * 100), "% wet") sleep(2) Line 1 — from gpiozero import MCP3008 : gpiozero has built-in support for this ADC chip — no separate driver needed. Line 4 — moisture = MCP3008(channel=0) : Reads channel 0 of the chip (it has 8, numbered 0–7). Line 7 — level = moisture.value : Returns the analog reading as a number from 0.0 (0 V) to 1.0 (3.3 V) — true analog, brought into the digital Pi by the ADC. (There is also .voltage , which gives the reading in volts.) Line 8 — print(round(level * 100), "% wet") : Scales the 0–1 value into a friendly 0–100% reading. To log analog moisture instead of wet/dry, you would simply swap read_moisture() to return round(moisture.value * 100) — the rest of the logger, CSV and summary code stays exactly the same. That is the payoff of putting each job in its own small function. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause Fix Soil reading never changes Threshold screw mis-set, or wrong active_state Adjust the screw on the sensor board while watching its LED switch; if wet/dry are swapped, flip active_state between True and False. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'board' Blinka not installed, or not in the venv Activate the venv ( source plantenv/bin/activate ) and pip install adafruit-blinka adafruit-circuitpython-dht . DHT22 raises RuntimeError a lot Normal checksum hiccups, or a missing pull-up The retry loop handles occasional errors. If it's constant, add the 10 kΩ pull-up on the data line, or switch to an I²C SHT4x/BME280. You followed a tutorial using Adafruit_DHT or pigpio and nothing works Both are unsupported on the Pi 5 Use the current adafruit_dht + adafruit-blinka stack instead, as shown above. CSV has blank lines between rows newline="" was omitted from open() Always open CSV files with open(file, mode, newline="") . Summary shows no data Program stopped before any reading was logged Let at least one cycle complete (lower SAMPLE_MINUTES while testing) before pressing Ctrl+C. Make It Your Own Email or beep when the soil is dry. Inside log_reading() , if the moisture is "dry" , switch on a buzzer (from Chapter 28) or flash an LED to nag you to water the plant. Add more columns. Because each reading is a dictionary, adding a light sensor is as simple as putting a new key in row and a new name in FIELDS . The CSV grows a column automatically. Run it automatically at boot. Once you're happy, set the logger to start whenever the Pi powers on using a systemd service or a cron job, so your plant is monitored around the clock with no screen needed. Chart your data. Open plant_log.csv in LibreOffice Calc and make a line graph of temperature over time — or, looking ahead to the capstone, serve the latest reading to a web page you can check from your phone. Note: Logging to a file is the same technique professionals use for weather stations and lab equipment. See the gpiozero docs at gpiozero.readthedocs.io for MCP3008 , DigitalInputDevice and more, and the Python docs for the full power of the csv and datetime modules. Key terms Digital signal - a value that is only ever HIGH or LOW (1 or 0); every Pi GPIO pin is digital. Analog signal - a value that varies smoothly through every level in between. ADC - Analogue-to-Digital Converter; a chip that turns an analog voltage into a number. The Pi has none built in. Capacitive soil sensor - a moisture sensor that gives a clean digital wet/dry output and does not corrode; ideal for the ADC-less Pi. DigitalInputDevice - the gpiozero object for reading any HIGH/LOW input pin. DHT22 - a digital temperature/humidity sensor; on the Pi 5 use adafruit_dht + adafruit-blinka (legacy Adafruit_DHT and pigpio do not work). MCP3008 - an 8-channel ADC chip read over SPI; gpiozero's MCP3008(channel=0) gives .value 0–1. File mode - "w" write (erases), "a" append (adds), "r" read. with open(...) - the safe way to open a file; it closes automatically when the block ends. CSV - Comma-Separated Values; a universal table format handled by Python's csv module. List of dictionaries - the natural shape for many readings, each with named fields. datetime / strftime - tools for capturing the current moment and formatting it as a timestamp string. Chapter summary A digital signal is only ever HIGH or LOW; an analog signal varies smoothly. The Raspberry Pi has no ADC , so every GPIO pin can only read digital signals. To sense analog quantities you must pick a sensor with a digital output (like a capacitive soil sensor) or add an external ADC such as the MCP3008 over SPI. The capacitive soil sensor's digital DO pin reads cleanly with DigitalInputDevice ; no voltage divider is needed because it is already 3.3 V logic. On the Pi 5, the legacy Adafruit_DHT and pigpio DHT methods fail ; use the current adafruit_dht + adafruit-blinka stack (in a venv) and catch occasional checksum errors — or prefer a stable I²C sensor. Files open with open() ; use with for safety, "a" mode to append log rows, and "r" to read them back. The csv module's DictWriter and DictReader pair perfectly with a list of dictionaries , the natural shape for timestamped readings. Every reading is stamped with a datetime timestamp; reading the CSV back lets you scan for the min and max — the warmest and coolest moments of the day. Putting each job in its own small function (read, log, summarise) means swapping in a different sensor — even an analog one via the MCP3008 — changes almost nothing else.

title: Motion-Activated Alarm from E-Waste
headings: From the E-Waste Pile: Salvaging a PIR
Building the Alarm Step by Step
text: A sliver of plastic and a glittering dome of glass, pulled from a dead security light in the e-waste box, can still do one thing brilliantly: notice when a warm body moves nearby. In this project you will give that salvaged PIR motion sensor a second life as a motion-activated alarm — one that flashes an LED, sounds a buzzer, stamps the time in a logbook, and can be armed or disarmed from the keyboard. Along the way you will learn the Python idea that powers almost every interactive program in the world: event-driven programming — writing little functions called callbacks that the computer runs automatically the moment something happens. What You'll Build & Learn By the end of this chapter you will have a working intruder alarm built almost entirely from salvaged parts, and you will understand a new and powerful way of structuring programs. Here are the fundamentals this project teaches, named plainly so you know exactly what you are practising: Python fundamentals Event-driven programming. Instead of a program that marches top-to-bottom and then stops, you write code that waits and reacts . The sensor decides when things happen; your job is to say what happens. Callbacks — the functions when_motion and when_no_motion . A callback is a function you hand to another object so it can "call you back" later, at the right moment. Blocking waits with wait_for_motion() — pausing your program at one line until motion arrives. Organising code into functions and modules. You will split your program into small, well-named functions and then move the reusable pieces into a separate module (a second .py file) that you import . Counting events with a simple counter variable and the global keyword. Electronics fundamentals The PIR motion sensor (the common HC-SR501 ) and the gpiozero MotionSensor class. 3.3 V-safe digital outputs. The PIR's OUT pin already speaks 3.3 V, so — unlike the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor from Chapter 28 — it connects directly to a GPIO pin with no voltage divider . Knowing which sensors need protection and which do not is a core safety skill. Combining outputs: driving an LED and a buzzer together as the alarm's "siren". What Is Event-Driven Programming? Every program you have written so far has probably run like a recipe: do step 1, then step 2, then step 3, and finish. That style is called sequential programming, and it is perfect for tasks with a clear beginning and end. But an alarm is different. An alarm spends almost all of its life doing nothing — quietly waiting. Then, at an unpredictable moment, something happens, and it must react instantly. You cannot write that as a fixed list of steps, because you do not know in advance when the steps should run. In plain words: An event is "something that happened" — a button press, a key tap, a sensor noticing motion. Event-driven programming means you write small functions that say what to do when each event happens, then you let the program sit and wait. The events drive the program, instead of the program marching through a fixed list. The function you hand over to be run later is called a callback . The name is wonderfully literal: you give your function to gpiozero and effectively say, "don't run this now — call me back when motion happens." You met this idea briefly in Chapter 12 with a button's when_pressed . Here we lean into it properly. Two ways to wait for motion Polling (busy loop) ask, ask, ask… never resting while True: moved yet? no… moved yet? CPU stays busy the whole time Event-driven (callback) rest until something happens program waits in pause() motion! callback runs the event drives the program when_motion = someone_moved Two ways to wait. A polling loop keeps the Pi busy asking "moved yet?" thousands of times a second. Event-driven code rests in pause() and lets the motion event call your function back — simpler and far kinder to the processor. A tiny isolated example first Before wiring anything, let's see the shape of an event-driven program with the smallest possible example. You can read this even without the hardware connected yet — it shows the pattern , which is the important part. from gpiozero import MotionSensor from signal import pause pir = MotionSensor(4) def someone_moved(): print("Motion detected!") def all_clear(): print("All quiet now.") pir.when_motion = someone_moved pir.when_no_motion = all_clear pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import MotionSensor : Pulls in the ready-made gpiozero object for PIR motion sensors. You do not need to install anything — gpiozero is preinstalled on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. Line 2 — from signal import pause : Brings in pause() , which keeps an event-driven program alive and waiting. Without it the program would reach the bottom and exit instantly, before any motion could ever be noticed. Line 4 — pir = MotionSensor(4) : Creates a sensor object listening on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7). The number 4 is the GPIO (BCM) number, not the physical position on the header. Lines 6–7 — def someone_moved(): : Defines a function — a named block of instructions. Crucially, defining it does not run it. We are simply describing what should happen later. Lines 9–10 — def all_clear(): : A second function, for when the motion stops. Line 12 — pir.when_motion = someone_moved : This is the heart of event-driven programming. We hand the function someone_moved to the sensor. Notice there are no parentheses after the name — someone_moved , not someone_moved() . With parentheses you would call the function right now; without them you are pointing at it, so gpiozero can call it back later. Line 13 — pir.when_no_motion = all_clear : Same idea, registering the "all clear" callback. Line 15 — pause() : Sits here forever, letting the sensor watch in the background and fire your callbacks whenever motion starts or stops. Press the red Stop button in Thonny (or Ctrl+C in a terminal) to end it. Careful: A common beginner slip is writing pir.when_motion = someone_moved() with parentheses. That runs the function immediately , once, and then hands its return value (usually None ) to the sensor — so nothing ever happens on real motion. Always register a callback by name, with no parentheses. The other style: a blocking wait Callbacks are not the only way. Sometimes you want your program to stop at one exact line and wait for motion before going on. gpiozero gives you wait_for_motion() for precisely that: from gpiozero import MotionSensor pir = MotionSensor(4) print("Waiting for motion...") pir.wait_for_motion() print("Got it! Something moved.") Line 6 — pir.wait_for_motion() : This line blocks — the program freezes here, doing nothing else, until the sensor detects motion. Only then does it move on to line 7. This is called a blocking call because it blocks the rest of the program from running until its condition is met. In plain words: Blocking means "wait right here until I'm done". wait_for_motion() is simple and reads top-to-bottom, but your program can only wait for one thing at a time. Callbacks ( when_motion ) are more flexible: the sensor watches in the background while your program gets on with other jobs. Our alarm will use callbacks. From the E-Waste Pile: Salvaging a PIR PIR sensors are one of the most rewarding things to rescue from the e-waste box, because they are everywhere . The little white plastic boxes that switch on a porch light when you walk up the path, cheap battery alarms, motion-activated toys and ornaments — almost all of them hide a PIR module that is identical, or nearly identical, to the HC-SR501 you can buy new. In plain words: PIR stands for Passive Infrared . Everything warm — including you — glows faintly in infrared light that your eyes cannot see. The sensor is "passive" because it does not send anything out; it simply watches for a change in that infrared glow as a warm body moves across its view. That is why a PIR detects movement but not a person standing perfectly still. Where to find one Dead motion-sensor security lights — the classic source. The white dome you see on the front is the PIR's lens. The light may have failed, but the sensor module behind it usually still works. Old burglar-alarm PIR units — the wall-corner boxes. Often still perfectly good; the panel they reported to is the dead part. Motion-activated novelty toys, soap dispensers, and night-lights. How to recognise the module Once you open the plastic case (only ever low-voltage, battery or USB-powered items — see the warning below), look for a small circuit board carrying a white, faceted, half-dome lens about the size of a thumbnail. This lens is called a Fresnel lens ; it divides the sensor's view into segments so movement registers more strongly. Underneath you will usually find a board labelled HC-SR501 (or a near clone) with three pins. Those three pins are the whole story: Pin marking What it is Where it goes VCC (sometimes + or 5V ) Power in A 5 V pin on the Pi OUT (sometimes S or SIG ) The signal — goes HIGH when motion is seen Directly to a GPIO pin GND (sometimes − or G ) Ground / return A GND pin on the Pi Careful: Only ever open battery-powered or low-voltage USB gadgets. Never open anything that plugs into the mains — a security floodlight wired to your house mains, for example, must be left to a qualified electrician. Mains-powered devices can hold a dangerous charge in their capacitors even when unplugged. If you are unsure, leave it shut and pick a battery-powered item instead. When in doubt, throw it out. Tip: Even a brand-new HC-SR501 costs very little, so if your salvaged module misbehaves it is no disaster. But test the salvaged one first — most work perfectly. You will also reuse an LED and a buzzer from the earlier chapters' salvage hauls (a mouse LED and a toy buzzer are ideal). Meet the HC-SR501 The HC-SR501 has a couple of features worth knowing before you build, because they catch out almost everyone the first time. The warm-up period When you first power up a PIR, it needs roughly 30 to 60 seconds to settle . During this warm-up it calibrates itself to the room's background infrared and may fire falsely. This is completely normal. The polite thing to do is keep your alarm "disarmed" for the first minute — and our program will do exactly that. The two orange potentiometers On the board, next to the pins, you will usually find two small orange dials you can turn with a tiny screwdriver. These are potentiometers ("pots" for short) — adjustable resistors. Sensitivity — how far away motion is detected (roughly 3 to 7 metres). Turn it down if the alarm triggers from across the whole room when you only want the doorway. Time delay — how long OUT stays HIGH after motion before it resets (from a couple of seconds up to several minutes). For testing, turn this fully anticlockwise to its shortest setting so the sensor resets quickly and you are not waiting around. Note: Many HC-SR501 boards also have a tiny jumper that selects "repeat trigger" vs "single trigger" mode. For an alarm, leave it on repeat trigger (often marked H ) so continued movement keeps OUT held HIGH. gpiozero copes with either, but repeat mode behaves more naturally for an alarm. Parts & Wiring What you need A Raspberry Pi 5 running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm 1 × PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501 — salvaged or new) 1 × LED (any colour — red suits an alarm), salvaged or new 1 × 330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown-gold) for the LED 1 × active buzzer (the kind that just needs on/off — salvaged from a toy is ideal) 1 × breadboard Female-to-male jumper wires (about 7) and a couple of male-to-male wires In plain words: An active buzzer has its own tone-generating circuit inside, so you only have to switch it on and off — perfect for gpiozero's Buzzer object. (A passive buzzer needs you to feed it a tone; that is a different object, TonalBuzzer .) A small buzzer draws little enough current to drive straight from a GPIO pin. A real loudspeaker would not — that needs a transistor — but a buzzer is fine. Careful: Power off and unplug your Pi before wiring anything. Shut down from the desktop (Raspberry Pi menu → Shutdown), wait for the green light to go out, then remove the power lead. Only reconnect power once you have checked every connection. Wiring a live header is the most common way to damage a GPIO pin. The key safety fact: no divider needed Here is the single most important electronics point in this chapter. The HC-SR501's OUT pin already outputs 3.3 V logic when it detects motion, even though the sensor is powered from 5 V. That means OUT is safe to connect directly to a GPIO pin. Contrast this with the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor from Chapter 28, whose ECHO pin outputs a full 5 V that would damage a 3.3 V GPIO — so that one needs a resistor voltage divider. The PIR does not. Two sensors, both powered from 5 V, but only one needs protection on its signal pin. Knowing the difference is exactly the kind of judgement that keeps your Pi alive. Careful: Power the PIR from 5 V (its VCC needs 5 V to work), but never let that 5 V touch a GPIO pin directly. Only the OUT pin — which is already 3.3 V — goes to a GPIO. Double-check you have VCC on 5 V and OUT on the GPIO, and not the other way round. Wiring diagram Motion Alarm — Wiring Diagram 5 V GPIO signal GND LED / buzzer drive GPIO Header Pin 2 (5 V) Pin 7 (GPIO 4) Pin 6 (GND) Pin 11 (GPIO 17) Pin 13 (GPIO 27) HC-SR501 PIR VCC OUT GND 5V (red) --> GPIO4 (purple) — NO DIVIDER --> direct — no divider! 330 Ω LED (GPIO 17) Buzzer (GPIO 27) LED − and buzzer − share a GND rail back to a GND pin PIR VCC → 5 V · PIR OUT → GPIO 4 directly · everything shares GND The motion alarm wiring. The PIR's VCC takes 5 V (red), its GND joins the common ground (grey), and its OUT goes straight to GPIO 4 (purple) with no voltage divider — because OUT is already 3.3 V. The LED (through a 330 Ω resistor) sits on GPIO 17 and the buzzer on GPIO 27. Connection table From (component) To (Pi header) Notes PIR VCC Pin 2 (5 V) HC-SR501 needs 5 V to run PIR OUT Pin 7 (GPIO 4) Directly — no divider (OUT is already 3.3 V) PIR GND Pin 6 (GND) Shared ground LED long leg (+) via 330 Ω Pin 11 (GPIO 17) Resistor limits current LED short leg (−) GND rail → Pin 6 (GND) Returns to ground Buzzer + terminal Pin 13 (GPIO 27) Active buzzer, on/off Buzzer − terminal GND rail → Pin 6 (GND) Returns to ground Step-by-step wiring Careful: The Pi must be fully shut down and unplugged for every step below. Do not reconnect power until the final step. Plant the breadboard ground rail. Run a male-to-male jumper from a Pi GND pin (physical pin 6) to the breadboard's blue (−) power rail. Everything's ground will return here. Wire the LED. Push the LED into the board with its long leg (anode, +) and short leg (cathode, −) in separate rows. Connect a 330 Ω resistor from the long-leg row, then a jumper from there to GPIO 17 (pin 11) . Connect the short leg to the blue (−) rail. Wire the buzzer. An active buzzer usually has a + marked terminal (often the longer leg). Connect + to GPIO 27 (pin 13) and the other terminal to the blue (−) rail. Wire the PIR power. Connect PIR VCC to a 5 V pin (physical pin 2) and PIR GND to the blue (−) rail. Wire the PIR signal — the careful one. Connect PIR OUT straight to GPIO 4 (pin 7) . No resistor, no divider. Just confirm it really is the OUT pin and not VCC. Set the pots for testing. Turn the time-delay pot fully anticlockwise (shortest), and the sensitivity pot to roughly the middle. Set the jumper to repeat-trigger ( H ) if present. Inspect everything twice. Trace each wire from end to end. Confirm VCC is on 5 V and OUT is on the GPIO — swapping them is the classic mistake. Only now reconnect power and let the Pi boot to the desktop. Remember the PIR will need its 30–60 s warm-up. Building the Alarm Step by Step We will build the program in layers, so each new idea lands on its own. First a bare callback alarm, then we add a logbook and a counter, then we organise it into functions, and finally we split it into a reusable module and add arm/disarm control. Version 1: the siren callbacks Open Thonny (Raspberry Pi menu → Programming → Thonny) and type this first version: from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED, Buzzer from signal import pause pir = MotionSensor(4) led = LED(17) buzzer = Buzzer(27) def sound_alarm(): print("INTRUDER!") led.on() buzzer.on() def stop_alarm(): print("All clear.") led.off() buzzer.off() pir.when_motion = sound_alarm pir.when_no_motion = stop_alarm print("Arming... (give the PIR up to a minute to settle)") pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED, Buzzer : Imports all three components we need in one line: the PIR, the LED, and the active buzzer. Lines 4–6 — creating the objects: One object per piece of hardware, each tied to its GPIO number. Buzzer(27) drives an active buzzer with simple on() / off() control. Lines 8–11 — def sound_alarm(): : A function that is the alarm going off: it prints a warning, lights the LED, and switches on the buzzer. Grouping these three actions into one named function is the first step of organising code — the name says what it does. Lines 13–16 — def stop_alarm(): : The opposite: turns the siren off when motion stops. Lines 18–19 — registering the callbacks: We hand sound_alarm to when_motion and stop_alarm to when_no_motion . No parentheses — we are pointing at the functions, not calling them. Line 22 — pause() : Keeps the program alive so the sensor can fire the callbacks. Save the file as alarm.py and run it; after the warm-up, wave a hand and the LED and buzzer should burst into life. Version 2: logging the time and counting events An alarm that forgets everything the instant it happens is not much of an alarm. Let's stamp every trigger with the time and keep a running count of how many times the alarm has fired. To get the current time we use Python's built-in datetime module; to count, we use a variable. from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED, Buzzer from datetime import datetime from signal import pause pir = MotionSensor(4) led = LED(17) buzzer = Buzzer(27) alarm_count = 0 def log(message): stamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") line = f"[{stamp}] {message}" print(line) with open("alarm_log.txt", "a") as logfile: logfile.write(line + "\n") def sound_alarm(): global alarm_count alarm_count = alarm_count + 1 led.on() buzzer.on() log(f"INTRUDER! (event #{alarm_count})") def stop_alarm(): led.off() buzzer.off() log("All clear.") pir.when_motion = sound_alarm pir.when_no_motion = stop_alarm log("Alarm armed.") pause() Line 2 — from datetime import datetime : Imports Python's datetime object, which can tell us the current date and time. It is built in — nothing to install. Line 9 — alarm_count = 0 : Creates a counter, starting at zero. Because it sits outside any function, it is a module-level (global) variable that all the functions can see. Lines 11–16 — def log(message): : A reusable helper. datetime.now() grabs the moment; .strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") formats it as a tidy timestamp like 2026-06-23 14:09:02 . We build the line with an f-string, print it, and append it to a file. Line 15 — with open("alarm_log.txt", "a") as logfile: : Opens a file in append mode ( "a" ), so new lines are added to the end without erasing what is already there. The with block closes the file automatically when it finishes. Line 19 — global alarm_count : Tells Python that inside this function we mean the module-level alarm_count , not a brand-new local one. Without this line, alarm_count = alarm_count + 1 would error, because Python would treat alarm_count as a fresh local variable that has not yet been given a value. Line 20 — alarm_count = alarm_count + 1 : Adds one to the counter each time the alarm fires — this is counting events . Line 23 — log(f"INTRUDER! (event #{alarm_count})") : Calls our helper to print and save a timestamped, numbered alert. In plain words: A global variable is one defined at the top level of your file, outside every function. Functions can read it freely, but to change it they must first declare global name . This is Python's way of making sure you don't accidentally reassign an outer variable by mistake. Organising Code into a Module Our file is growing. The log() helper is genuinely useful — we would happily reuse it in other projects. This is the moment to learn a real software habit: moving reusable code into its own module . In plain words: A module is just a Python file (a .py ) whose functions and variables you can use from another file with import . You have been importing modules all along — gpiozero and datetime are modules. Now you will write your own. Create a new file called alarm_tools.py in the same folder, containing just the reusable helpers: # alarm_tools.py — reusable helpers for our alarm projects from datetime import datetime LOG_FILE = "alarm_log.txt" def now_stamp(): """Return the current time as a tidy string.""" return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") def log(message): """Print a timestamped message and append it to the log file.""" line = f"[{now_stamp()}] {message}" print(line) with open(LOG_FILE, "a") as logfile: logfile.write(line + "\n") Line 1 — the comment: A note for human readers. Python ignores anything after # . Line 4 — LOG_FILE = "alarm_log.txt" : A constant holding the filename in one place, so we never have to retype it. Naming it in CAPITALS is a common convention for "this is a fixed setting". Lines 6–8 — def now_stamp(): : Returns the formatted time. The triple-quoted line just below the def is a docstring — a short description of what the function does, which editors can show as a hint. Lines 10–15 — def log(message): : The same logging helper as before, now living in its own module so any program can import it. Now your main alarm file becomes shorter and clearer, because it borrows log from the module: # alarm.py — the main program from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED, Buzzer from signal import pause from alarm_tools import log pir = MotionSensor(4) led = LED(17) buzzer = Buzzer(27) alarm_count = 0 def sound_alarm(): global alarm_count alarm_count += 1 led.on() buzzer.on() log(f"INTRUDER! (event #{alarm_count})") def stop_alarm(): led.off() buzzer.off() log("All clear.") pir.when_motion = sound_alarm pir.when_no_motion = stop_alarm log("Alarm armed.") pause() Line 4 — from alarm_tools import log : Imports the log function from your own module, exactly the way you import from gpiozero. The only requirement is that alarm_tools.py sits in the same folder. Line 14 — alarm_count += 1 : A tidy shorthand for alarm_count = alarm_count + 1 . The += operator means "add to and store back". The rest: reads almost like plain English now, because the messy timestamp-and-file detail is tucked away in the module. That is the whole point of organising code — each file does one clear job. Tip: When you import your own module, Python may create a folder called __pycache__ next to it. That is just a cache of the compiled module to make future imports faster — it is harmless and you can ignore it. Arming and Disarming A real alarm can be switched off — otherwise you can never walk past your own sensor. We will add an armed flag: a simple True / False variable that the callbacks check before sounding. We will also use the keyboard to toggle it, and the PIR's warm-up minute will start disarmed automatically. Because we want to type commands and let the sensor fire callbacks in the background, this version uses an input() loop in the main program instead of pause() . The callbacks still run in the background whenever motion happens. # alarm.py — arm/disarm version from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED, Buzzer from alarm_tools import log pir = MotionSensor(4) led = LED(17) buzzer = Buzzer(27) armed = False alarm_count = 0 def sound_alarm(): global alarm_count if not armed: return alarm_count += 1 led.on() buzzer.on() log(f"INTRUDER! (event #{alarm_count})") def stop_alarm(): led.off() buzzer.off() if armed: log("Movement stopped.") pir.when_motion = sound_alarm pir.when_no_motion = stop_alarm print("Commands: 'arm', 'disarm', 'count', 'quit'") log("System started (disarmed). PIR warming up...") while True: command = input("alarm> ").strip().lower() if command == "arm": armed = True log("ARMED.") elif command == "disarm": armed = False led.off() buzzer.off() log("Disarmed.") elif command == "count": print(f"Alarm has triggered {alarm_count} time(s).") elif command == "quit": log("Shutting down.") break else: print("Unknown command. Try arm / disarm / count / quit.") Line 9 — armed = False : A boolean flag holding the alarm's state. Starting at False means the system is harmlessly disarmed while the PIR warms up. Lines 14–15 — if not armed: return : The first thing sound_alarm does is check the flag. If the alarm is disarmed, return leaves the function immediately, so no siren and no count. This is how one variable acts as a master switch over an event callback. Line 24 — if armed: inside stop_alarm : We only bother logging "movement stopped" when the system was actually armed, to keep the log meaningful. Line 34 — command = input("alarm> ")... : input() waits for you to type a line and press Enter. .strip() trims stray spaces and .lower() makes the command case-insensitive, so ARM and arm both work. Lines 35–48 — the if/elif/else ladder: Each branch handles one command. arm and disarm flip the flag; count reports the total; quit uses break to leave the while loop and end the program neatly. Note on the background: while you sit at the input() prompt, gpiozero is still watching the sensor on a separate thread, so motion still fires sound_alarm — it simply does nothing unless armed is True . Note: Notice we did not need global armed inside the while loop, because that loop lives at the top level of the file — the same place armed is defined. We do need global alarm_count inside sound_alarm , because that assignment happens inside a function. Running It Save both files in the same folder: alarm_tools.py and alarm.py . In Thonny, File → Save for each. Run alarm.py with the green Run button (or press F5). The shell at the bottom shows the prompt and the start-up log line. Wait out the warm-up. Leave it disarmed for about a minute while the PIR settles. Resist the urge to wave at it yet. Arm it. Type arm and press Enter. Now walk into the sensor's view — the LED should light and the buzzer sound, and a timestamped INTRUDER! line appears. Disarm it. Type disarm to silence the system so you can move freely. Check the tally. Type count to see how many times it triggered, then quit to stop. Read the logbook. Open a terminal and view your records with the command below. cat alarm_log.txt cat alarm_log.txt : Prints the whole log file to the terminal, so you can see every timestamped event your alarm recorded. cat simply means "show me the contents of this file". Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause & fix Alarm fires constantly, even with no one there The PIR is still in its 30–60 s warm-up, or sensitivity is too high. Wait a minute; turn the sensitivity pot down. Repeat-trigger mode also holds OUT high during continued movement — that is normal. Never triggers at all Check OUT is on GPIO 4, not VCC. Confirm VCC is on a 5 V pin (not 3.3 V — the HC-SR501 needs 5 V). Make sure the time-delay pot is not stuck at its longest setting. Triggers, but no light or sound LED may be backwards (swap the legs — it cannot be damaged). Check the buzzer's + is on GPIO 27 and the resistor is in the LED line. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'alarm_tools' alarm_tools.py is not in the same folder as alarm.py , or has a different name. Put them side by side and re-run. NameError: name 'alarm_count' is not defined on assignment You changed alarm_count inside a function without the global alarm_count line. Add it back. No module named 'lgpio' Install the backend: sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then restart Thonny. Buzzer makes only a faint click, not a tone You may have a passive buzzer, which needs a tone fed to it. Swap it for an active buzzer, or use gpiozero's TonalBuzzer instead (see Chapter 26). Make It Your Own You now have a complete, modular, event-driven alarm. Here are four ways to take it further: Flash instead of glare. Replace led.on() with led.blink() in sound_alarm so the warning light pulses like a real alarm beacon. Remember to led.off() in stop_alarm . Add a quiet "armed" indicator. Use a second, green LED that is lit whenever armed is True , so you can tell the system's state at a glance. Count only real intrusions. Add a few seconds of "cool-down" so repeated motion within, say, five seconds counts as one event — using datetime to compare the time since the last trigger. Send yourself an alert. Once you are comfortable, have sound_alarm also write to a file your phone can read, or — in the next chapter — surface the last alarm time on a live web dashboard you can check from anywhere in the house. Tip: The arm/disarm flag pattern you wrote here — one boolean that every callback checks first — is exactly how real software gates behaviour: feature switches, "do not disturb" modes, pause buttons. You have learned a genuinely professional idea dressed up as a fun alarm. Key terms Event-driven programming - A style where the program waits and reacts to events (like motion) instead of running a fixed top-to-bottom list of steps. Event - Something that happens at an unpredictable time, such as motion being detected or a key being pressed. Callback - A function you hand to another object so it can call it back when an event occurs; registered by name with no parentheses (e.g. pir.when_motion = sound_alarm ). Blocking call - A line such as wait_for_motion() that pauses the whole program until its condition is met. Module - A Python file whose functions and variables another file can use via import ; you wrote your own ( alarm_tools.py ). Global variable - A variable defined at the top level of a file; to reassign it inside a function you must first declare global name . PIR sensor - Passive Infrared sensor; detects movement by sensing changes in the infrared (heat) glow of warm bodies. HC-SR501 - The common, inexpensive PIR module with VCC/OUT/GND pins, a Fresnel lens, two adjustment pots, and a 30–60 s warm-up. Fresnel lens - The faceted white dome that splits the PIR's view into segments so movement registers more strongly. Potentiometer (pot) - An adjustable resistor; the HC-SR501 has two, for sensitivity and time delay. Active buzzer - A buzzer with its own tone circuit; you only switch it on/off, so gpiozero's Buzzer object drives it. Docstring - A short triple-quoted description placed just under a def to explain what a function does. Chapter summary Event-driven programming means writing callbacks — functions that run automatically when an event happens — instead of a fixed sequence of steps. Register a callback by name with no parentheses: pir.when_motion = sound_alarm . Adding parentheses runs it immediately by mistake. when_motion and when_no_motion fire on the rising and falling edges of motion; wait_for_motion() instead blocks until motion arrives. The HC-SR501 PIR is powered from 5 V , but its OUT pin is already 3.3 V , so OUT connects directly to a GPIO with no voltage divider — unlike the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, whose 5 V ECHO does need one. The PIR needs a 30–60 s warm-up and has two pots (sensitivity and time delay) for tuning. PIR modules are commonly salvaged from dead motion-sensor lights and alarms — but only ever open battery or low-voltage devices, never mains-powered ones. Organising code into small named functions, then into an importable module ( alarm_tools.py ), keeps the main program short and reusable. A global declaration is needed to reassign a module-level variable (like the event counter) from inside a function. An armed boolean flag, checked at the top of the callback, lets the same alarm be switched on and off — the same gating pattern used throughout professional software.

title: Capstone: Your Sensor Dashboard on the Web
headings: Client and Server: The Big Idea
Reading the Sensors as a Module
The JavaScript That Makes It Live
Running It and Viewing on Your Phone
text:
Everything you have built so far has lived inside the Pi — flashing its own LEDs, printing to its own screen. In this final project you will set it free. You will build a small web server on the Pi that reads your sensors and serves a live dashboard you can open on your phone from the sofa, showing temperature, distance, motion, and the time of the last alarm — updating itself every second. To do it you will pull together everything you know in Python and meet, for the first time, three new languages that run the web: HTML , CSS , and JavaScript . What You'll Build & Learn This is the capstone. Rather than one new gadget, you are wiring together the whole course into a single, genuinely useful, full-stack project — and getting a real taste of the languages of the web. Python fundamentals (putting it all together) Modules — organising sensor-reading code into its own file and importing it, exactly as you did in Chapter 30. A dictionary as a shared state object — one dict that holds every current reading, passed around and updated in one place. A small Flask web server — the @app.route decorator, returning JSON with jsonify , and serving an HTML page with render_template . The correct Bookworm install of Flask using a virtual environment (because of PEP 668). Other languages (a real taste) HTML — the structure of a web page (tags, elements, ids). CSS — a few rules to style the page and make it readable on a phone. JavaScript — fetch() to ask the server for fresh data, setInterval() to poll repeatedly, and updating the page (the DOM) live. The client/server split — what runs on the Pi, what runs in the phone's browser, and how they talk. There is far less wiring here than in other chapters — you are reusing sensors you have already built. The new ground is software, and the leap from "a program on the Pi" to "a service other devices can use". Client and Server: The Big Idea Every website works the same way, whether it is a giant social network or the tiny dashboard you are about to build. There are always two halves: a server and a client . In plain words: The server is a program that waits for requests and sends back answers — here, it is your Pi. The client is whatever asks the questions — here, the web browser on your phone. The client sends a request ("please give me the latest sensor data"); the server sends a response ("here it is, as JSON"). That back-and-forth, over your Wi-Fi, is the whole of the web in miniature. How the Client Talks to the Server CLIENT Phone browser HTML + CSS + JS runs in the browser SERVER Raspberry Pi Flask (Python) reads the sensors on the GPIO pins REQUEST: GET /api/data RESPONSE: JSON data { "temp_c": 21.4, "distance_cm": 35, ... } ...repeated every second by JavaScript over your home Wi-Fi The client (your phone's browser) sends a request to the server (Flask on the Pi). The server reads the sensors and replies with JSON. JavaScript on the client repeats this every second to keep the dashboard live. In plain words: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a simple, universal text format for data. It looks almost exactly like a Python dictionary — {"temp_c": 21.4, "motion": true} — which is why it is the perfect bridge between your Python server and the JavaScript client. Both ends understand it instantly. Installing Flask the Bookworm Way Flask is the small Python library we will use to be a web server. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm there is a right way and a wrong way to install it, and the wrong way fails on purpose. In plain words: Flask is a lightweight Python web framework — a toolkit for writing web servers. With a handful of lines it can serve pages and answer data requests. It is the most popular way to put a Raspberry Pi project on the web. Why plain pip is blocked If you simply type pip install flask on Bookworm, you will hit a wall: error: externally-managed-environment This is not a bug — it is a deliberate safety rule called PEP 668 . Bookworm protects its system Python (which the OS itself relies on) by refusing to let pip install packages into it. If it let you, a bad package could break parts of the operating system. In plain words: A virtual environment (venv) is a private, self-contained copy of Python that lives in a folder of your project. Anything you pip install goes only in there, never touching the system Python. It is the correct, recommended fix for PEP 668 — clean, reversible, and exactly what professionals use. Create the project and its venv Open a terminal and run these commands one at a time: mkdir dashboard cd dashboard python3 -m venv venv mkdir dashboard : Makes a new folder to hold the whole project. cd dashboard : Moves into that folder, so the next commands act inside it. python3 -m venv venv : Creates a virtual environment in a sub-folder called venv . The first venv is the tool; the second is just the folder name we chose for it. Now activate the environment and install Flask into it: source venv/bin/activate pip install flask source venv/bin/activate : Switches your terminal into the virtual environment. You will see (venv) appear at the start of your prompt — that is how you know it is active. From now on, python and pip mean the private copies inside venv . pip install flask : Now this works perfectly, because it installs Flask inside the venv , not into the protected system Python. No PEP 668 error. Note: You only create and install once. But every new terminal starts outside the venv, so each time you come back to work on the project you must re-run source venv/bin/activate first. To leave the venv, simply type deactivate . If you ever prefer not to use a venv at all, sudo apt install python3-flask installs a system-tested Flask instead — but the venv approach is the cleaner habit. Reading the Sensors as a Module Following the modular habit from Chapter 30, we will keep all the sensor-reading code in its own file, sensors.py , and the web code in app.py . That way the web server does not need to know how a reading is taken — it just asks for one. Here is sensors.py . It uses the components from earlier chapters: an ultrasonic distance sensor and a PIR. (If you do not have the hardware to hand, the note below shows how to run the whole dashboard with fake readings so you can still build the web side.) # sensors.py — read the hardware, return tidy values from gpiozero import DistanceSensor, MotionSensor # ECHO via a 330 Ω/470 Ω divider (5 V -> ~2.9 V); TRIG direct distance = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23) pir = MotionSensor(4) def read_distance_cm(): """Distance to the nearest object, in centimetres.""" return round(distance.distance * 100, 1) def read_motion(): """True if motion is being detected right now.""" return pir.motion_detected def read_temperature_c(): """Placeholder CPU-ish temperature. Swap for a real sensor.""" with open("/sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp") as f: return round(int(f.read()) / 1000, 1) Line 2 — imports: Brings in the two gpiozero sensor classes you have already used. Line 5 — DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23) : Recreates the HC-SR04 from Chapter 28. Remember its ECHO pin outputs 5 V, so it must go through a 330 Ω/470 Ω voltage divider before reaching GPIO 24 — unlike the PIR. Line 6 — MotionSensor(4) : The PIR from Chapter 30 on GPIO 4, OUT wired directly (no divider). Lines 8–10 — read_distance_cm() : distance.distance gives metres, so we multiply by 100 for centimetres and round to one decimal place. Wrapping it in a named function means the web server just calls read_distance_cm() and gets a clean number. Lines 12–14 — read_motion() : Returns True or False from the PIR's motion_detected property. Lines 16–19 — read_temperature_c() : A real, always-available reading: the Pi's own CPU temperature, read from a system file. Swap this for a real room sensor (e.g. an I2C BME280) when you have one — the rest of the dashboard will not need to change, because it only calls this function. Note: No hardware to hand? Replace the bodies of these functions with fixed or random values, for example return round(random.uniform(20, 24), 1) (with import random at the top).
