The web side works identically — the whole point of the module is that the server does not care where the numbers come from. The Shared State Dictionary The dashboard needs to report several things at once: temperature, distance, motion, and the time of the last alarm. Rather than juggle four separate variables, we keep them together in a single dictionary — one object that is the current state of the system. In plain words: A dictionary stores data as key: value pairs, like a labelled box of drawers. state["temp_c"] looks in the drawer labelled "temp_c" . Using one dictionary as the single source of truth — a shared state object — keeps everything in one place and, conveniently, converts straight to JSON for the browser. state = { "temp_c": None, "distance_cm": None, "motion": False, "last_alarm": "never", } def update_state(): """Refresh every reading in the shared state dictionary.""" state["temp_c"] = read_temperature_c() state["distance_cm"] = read_distance_cm() moving = read_motion() state["motion"] = moving if moving: state["last_alarm"] = now_stamp() return state Lines 1–6 — the dictionary: Four labelled values, all starting empty or default. None means "no reading yet"; "never" is a friendly starting value for the last-alarm time. Line 8 — def update_state(): : One function that refreshes the whole dictionary by calling each sensor reader and storing the result under the right key. Lines 13–15 — updating last_alarm: If motion is happening right now, we record the current timestamp (using a now_stamp() helper like the one from Chapter 30) under "last_alarm" . So the dashboard always shows when motion was last seen. Line 16 — return state : Hands back the whole dictionary, ready to be turned into JSON. The Flask Server (app.py) Now the centrepiece. This is the Python file that ties everything together and serves the web. Read the labelled block carefully — every web project you ever build will have this same shape. # app.py — PYTHON (the server) from flask import Flask, jsonify, render_template from datetime import datetime from gpiozero import DistanceSensor, MotionSensor app = Flask(__name__) distance = DistanceSensor(echo=24, trigger=23) # ECHO via 330Ω/470Ω divider pir = MotionSensor(4) # OUT direct, no divider state = {"temp_c": None, "distance_cm": None, "motion": False, "last_alarm": "never"} def now_stamp(): return datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S") def update_state(): with open("/sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp") as f: state["temp_c"] = round(int(f.read()) / 1000, 1) state["distance_cm"] = round(distance.distance * 100, 1) state["motion"] = pir.motion_detected if pir.motion_detected: state["last_alarm"] = now_stamp() return state @app.route("/") def index(): return render_template("index.html") @app.route("/api/data") def data(): return jsonify(update_state()) if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000) Line 2 — from flask import Flask, jsonify, render_template : Imports the three Flask tools we need: Flask (the app itself), jsonify (turn a dict into a JSON response), and render_template (serve an HTML page). Line 6 — app = Flask(__name__) : Creates the web application. __name__ is a built-in Python variable that tells Flask where the app lives, so it can find your templates folder. Lines 8–9 — the sensors: The same objects as in our module. (For clarity we have inlined them here; you could equally from sensors import update_state to keep app.py tiny.) Lines 16–23 — update_state() : Refreshes the shared dictionary from the live sensors each time it is called, so every request returns fresh numbers. Line 25 — @app.route("/") : A decorator . It tells Flask: "when a browser asks for the home page (the URL / ), run the function just below." The index() function returns the HTML page. Line 27 — return render_template("index.html") : Sends the file templates/index.html to the browser. Flask automatically looks in a folder named templates . Line 30 — @app.route("/api/data") : A second route, for data rather than a page. When the browser asks for /api/data , Flask runs data() . Line 32 — return jsonify(update_state()) : Reads the sensors and returns the state dictionary as JSON — the response the JavaScript will fetch. Line 35 — app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000) : Starts the server on port 5000. The crucial part is host="0.0.0.0" : it means "accept connections from any device on the network", which is what lets your phone reach it. (The default of 127.0.0.1 would only allow the Pi itself.) In plain words: A decorator (the @app.route(...) line) is a label you stick above a function to give it an extra job. Here it connects a URL to a function, so visiting that URL runs that function. You do not need to understand how decorators work internally to use them — just match a URL to the code that should answer it. Careful: host="0.0.0.0" exposes the server to everyone on your local network. That is exactly what we want for a home dashboard, but it means anyone on your Wi-Fi can open it. Flask's built-in server is for development and home projects, not for putting on the open internet. Keep it on your home network. The HTML Page (templates/index.html) Now we leave Python and meet the first web language. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure of a page: what text and boxes appear, and in what order. It is made of tags in angle brackets, usually in pairs that wrap content. In plain words: An HTML tag like

opens an element and

closes it; together they wrap a paragraph. An id (e.g. id="temp" ) is a unique name for one element, so our JavaScript can find it and change its text. Think of HTML as the skeleton, CSS as the skin and clothes, and JavaScript as the muscles that make it move. Save this as templates/index.html (create the templates folder inside your project). title: Reanimate a LEGO Mindstorms NXT Robot with AI
headings: Meet the NXT 2.0 Parts You Can Reuse
Driving the Motors Safely — the H-bridge
Code: a Robot Class You Can Drive
Reading a Sensor — the Touch Bumper
Make It Your Own / Where to Go Next
text: Somewhere in a cupboard sits a dusty LEGO MINDSTORMS NXT 2.0 set — the orange-and-grey brick that could only ever be as clever as its own little firmware allowed. In this chapter you will tear that ceiling off. You will salvage the NXT's motors and sensors, wire them to a Raspberry Pi 5 through a proper motor driver, and give the whole thing a brain that runs real Python and a pair of AI eyes from a Pi Camera. By the end you will have built an autonomous rover that sees an object, thinks about where it is, and acts by steering itself towards it. Along the way you will learn to write a class of your own, decode an unusual connector, drive a DC motor safely through an H-bridge , read a quadrature encoder , and bend a 5 V signal down to a Pi-safe 3.3 V. What You'll Build & Learn This is the Maker Lab finale, and the most ambitious build in the course. We are going to reanimate a LEGO NXT robot: keep its Technic frame, motors and sensors, but replace its old brain with your Pi 5 — which can run an on-device AI model that recognises objects in a camera image. The finished rover rolls forward, and when its camera spots a target (a ball, a person) it turns to keep that target centred and drives towards it. That one sentence hides three whole disciplines, and you will learn the named fundamentals behind each. Python fundamentals Classes & objects — you met these in Chapter 28; here you will write a Robot class of your own that wraps the two drive motors and gives them friendly methods: forward() , backward() , turn_left() , turn_right() and stop() . Bundling the messy motor wiring inside one tidy object is exactly what classes are for. gpiozero Motor and RotaryEncoder — two ready-made objects: one drives a motor through an H-bridge with speed control, the other counts the clicks of the wheel's built-in encoder. Functions and a control loop — a while loop that reads the world, decides, and acts, over and over: the heartbeat of every robot. Integrating a callback — feeding the camera's "I see something" result into the Robot so vision and motion become one program. This reuses the AI ideas from Chapter 19 ("Run AI on your Pi"). Electronics fundamentals The RJ12 6P6C connector and the NXT pinouts — the odd little plug LEGO used, why ordinary phone leads do not fit, and exactly which of the six coloured wires does what. The DC motor plus quadrature encoder — an NXT motor is a plain 9 V DC motor with a clever optical sensor built in that counts how far the shaft has turned. The H-bridge motor driver — the circuit that lets a tiny 3.3 V GPIO pin command a hungry 9 V motor in either direction, without the motor ever touching the Pi directly. A separate motor battery and a common ground — why the motors get their own battery pack, and why that pack's negative terminal must still join the Pi's ground. Level-shifting / a voltage divider — the NXT's sensor and encoder lines can sit near 5 V, so we drop them to 3.3 V before they reach a GPIO pin (the same trick as Chapter 28). A touch of I²C — the NXT ultrasonic sensor talks over the two-wire I²C bus, which we meet briefly. AI fundamentals On-device object detection driving real motors — a camera image goes into a small neural-network model that returns boxes around objects it recognises; your code turns the box's position into a steering decision. This is the see → think → act loop at the heart of all robotics. Note: You do not need a complete NXT set to follow along. If you only have one motor, build the single-motor parts; if you have none, the wiring and code still teach you everything, and any cheap 6 V–9 V DC gear-motor works in their place. We will always say "your motor" rather than assume a particular kit. Meet the NXT 2.0 Parts You Can Reuse Before we cut a single wire, let's be honest about what is easy to reuse on a Pi and what is genuinely hard. The NXT was a sealed system, so some parts give up their secrets readily and others fight back. NXT 2.0 part What it really is How reusable on a Pi? Servo motors (the big interactive ones) A 9 V DC motor + gearbox + built-in optical encoder Easy. Drive through an H-bridge; read the encoder through a divider. This is our main build. Touch sensor A simple push switch (two wires close when pressed) Easy. Wire as a gpiozero Button to a GPIO pin and GND. Ultrasonic sensor A distance sensor that talks over I²C Medium. Works over the Pi's I²C bus, but has timing quirks and needs level-shifting. Advanced / optional. Colour / light sensor (NXT 2.0) A digitally-clocked sensor with a tri-colour LED, driven by a fiddly custom protocol Hard. Be honest: not worth the pain. Swap for a Pi-friendly colour sensor (e.g. a TCS34725 over I²C) instead. Sound sensor (from the first NXT set) A microphone producing an analog voltage Medium. The Pi has no analog input, so you need an ADC chip (e.g. MCP3008) to read it. Technic frame, gears, wheels, axles Plastic — no electronics at all Trivial. Reuse freely. This is the easiest and most valuable part to keep. Tip: The single best thing you keep from an NXT set is the mechanics : the Technic beams, the wheels, and especially the geared motors. Building a sturdy rolling chassis from scratch is hard; LEGO already solved it for you. Mount the Pi on the frame and you are halfway there. We will build the two drive motors and the touch bumper fully, cover the ultrasonic honestly as an optional extra, and be upfront that the colour sensor is best replaced. Now, the connector. The NXT Connector, Decoded Every NXT motor and sensor ends in the same plug: a six-position, six-conductor modular connector, written 6P6C . It looks almost exactly like the RJ12 connector on an old telephone handset cable — and that "almost" is the whole problem. In plain words: 6P6C means "6 positions, 6 conductors" — a little clear plastic plug with six gold contacts in a row, held in by a springy plastic latch. RJ12 is the common name for the wiring standard that uses this exact plug. LEGO played a sneaky trick: on an NXT plug the locking latch is offset to one side (the right) rather than centred. A standard phone or RJ12 lead has a centred latch, so it pushes into an NXT socket but will not seat or click home — the contacts do not line up reliably. This was deliberate, to stop people plugging the wrong things in. That leaves you two routes to the wires: Buy NXT-compatible RJ12 sockets. A handful of breakout sockets with the correct right-offset latch are sold cheaply (search "NXT/EV3 RJ12 jack breakout"). You plug an unmodified LEGO cable in and screw-terminals or header pins come out. Tidy, reversible, and you keep your cables intact. This is the gentlest option. Cut a LEGO cable open — the salvage route. Take a spare NXT lead, snip it in the middle, and strip back the grey outer sheath to expose the six coloured inner wires . Now you have six tinned ends you can poke straight into a breadboard. You sacrifice one cable but need no special parts. This is the route we will assume, in the spirit of the e-waste pile. Careful: Only ever cut a cable that is not plugged into anything, and never the cable to a sensor you cannot replace. Strip the outer sheath gently with wire strippers (or careful fingernails) so you do not nick the thin inner wires. Once exposed, the six wires follow a fixed colour code, which we map next. The NXT 6P6C plug and its six coloured wires latch (offset right!) 1 2 3 4 5 6 pins 1–6, latch facing away from you grey sheath 1 White 2 Black 3 Red 4 Green 5 Yellow 6 Blue A centred phone-lead latch will NOT seat in an NXT socket — the latch is offset to the right. Cut a spare lead and strip the sheath to expose the six colours, or use an NXT-compatible RJ12 breakout socket. An NXT 6P6C plug: six gold contacts and a right-offset latch. Cutting a spare cable exposes the six inner wires in a fixed colour order (white, black, red, green, yellow, blue from pin 1 to pin 6). Note: The colour of each inner wire is consistent across LEGO cables, but the wire colour does not follow the resistor/power conventions you have used elsewhere — here "red" is a ground wire and "green" is a power wire, which feels back-to-front. Always go by the table below, not by what a colour "usually" means. Inside the NXT Motor An NXT servo motor sounds fancy, but electrically it is two simple things in one housing: a plain 9 V DC motor with a built-in gearbox (strong but not fast), and a built-in optical quadrature encoder that reports how far the shaft has turned. In plain words: A DC motor spins when you put a voltage across its two terminals; swap the two wires over and it spins the other way. There is no "position" built in — it just turns while powered. It is not a hobby servo (those expect a special pulse signal); it is much simpler than that. In plain words: A quadrature encoder is a sensor that counts how far a shaft has rotated by watching a striped disc spin past two light sensors. "Quadrature" means the two sensors are offset by a quarter-step so that, by comparing which one changes first, you can tell both how far and which direction the shaft turned. The NXT encoder gives roughly one count per degree — about 360 counts per full revolution of the output shaft. That is plenty to drive a precise distance or keep two wheels matched so the robot rolls straight. The motor's six-wire pinout Here is the exact mapping for a MOTOR cable. Pin 1 is on the left when you look into the plug with the latch facing away from you. Pin Wire colour Function Goes to… 1 White Motor power A One output of the H-bridge 2 Black Motor power B The other output of the H-bridge 3 Red Encoder ground (0 V) Common GND 4 Green Encoder supply (+4.3 V) Pi 3.3 V (powers the encoder) 5 Yellow Tacho / encoder channel A GPIO input via a divider 6 Blue Tacho / encoder channel B GPIO input via a divider The two power wires (white/black) carry the heavy current that spins the motor — these never go near the Pi, only the driver. The other four belong to the encoder : a power pair (green/red) and the two signal channels (yellow/blue) we read. Electrical specs you must respect Motor voltage: about 9 V (a fresh 6×AA pack). It will also run more gently at 6 V. No-load current: low — only a few tens of milliamps when spinning freely. Stall current: high — up to roughly 1 A when the motor is jammed and cannot turn. This is the figure that matters when choosing a driver. Encoder supply: the green wire wants about 4.3–5 V; the Pi's 3.3 V rail powers it well enough in practice for our purposes, and keeps the signal swing lower (a bonus for the divider). Careful: Never connect the motor's white/black power wires to a GPIO pin or to the 3.3 V/5 V pins. A motor drawing up to ~1 A would instantly overload the Pi, and when a spinning motor is switched off it generates a sharp reverse voltage spike (we explain this next) that can destroy a GPIO pin. Power wires go to the H-bridge, full stop. NXT motor — six wires, two jobs DC motor + encoder Pin 1 White + Pin 2 Black = motor power → H-bridge only (up to ~1 A, ~9 V) NEVER to a GPIO pin encoder (counts ~1° per step) Pin 3 Red = GND · Pin 4 Green = +supply Pin 5 Yellow = channel A Pin 6 Blue = channel B A & B → GPIO via a voltage divider The NXT motor's six wires split into two groups: a high-current power pair (white/black) that goes only to the H-bridge, and a four-wire encoder (red, green, yellow, blue) whose two signal channels feed the Pi through a divider. Driving the Motors Safely — the H-bridge You already know the golden rule from Chapters 26 and 28: never drive a motor straight from a GPIO pin. It is doubly true for an NXT motor. Current. A GPIO pin can safely source only about 16 mA. An NXT motor wants tens of milliamps to spin freely and up to ~1 A if it stalls — fifty times too much. The pin (and possibly the whole Pi) would burn out. Inductive kickback. A motor is a coil of wire. Cut the current to a coil suddenly and it fights back with a sharp voltage spike of the opposite polarity. Fed into a 3.3 V GPIO pin, that spike is lethal. The answer is an H-bridge : a small chip between the Pi and the motor. The Pi sends gentle low-current 3.3 V logic signals; the chip switches the motor's heavy current on its behalf and can reverse its direction. In plain words: An H-bridge is four electronic switches arranged in an "H" shape around the motor. Close one diagonal pair and current flows one way (motor forwards); close the other pair and it flows the other way (motor backwards). The chip also contains protection diodes that safely swallow the inductive kickback so it never reaches the Pi. Which driver to use For a pair of NXT motors, a small dual H-bridge (two motors on one board) is ideal. Three good choices: Driver Motor voltage Current per motor Verdict for NXT motors DRV8833 (recommended) 2.7–10.8 V ~1.5 A continuous, 2 A peak Perfect. Handles a 9 V pack and the NXT's ~1 A stall with margin to spare. Small, cheap, efficient. TB6612FNG 2.5–13.5 V ~1.2 A continuous, 3 A peak Also excellent and very efficient. A great alternative if you have one to hand. L298N (the cheap classic) up to ~35 V ~2 A Works, but it is bulky, wastes ~2 V as heat, and needs a heatsink. Use only if it is what you already own. We will use the DRV8833 . Each of its two channels has two inputs ( IN1 , IN2 ) and two outputs ( OUT1 , OUT2 ). The Pi drives the inputs; the outputs go to one motor's white/black power pair. gpiozero's Motor(forward=IN1, backward=IN2) drives those inputs for you, pulsing them rapidly (PWM) to control speed. In plain words: PWM (pulse-width modulation) means switching a pin on and off very fast. If it is on 30% of the time the motor behaves as though it is getting 30% of full power, so the wheel turns slowly. gpiozero does this automatically when you call motor.forward(0.3) . The separate-battery and common-ground rule This is the most important wiring idea in the chapter, so read it twice. Give the motors their own battery. The Pi's 5 V supply is for the Pi's brain; it cannot spare amps for motors, and motor noise can crash the Pi. Use a separate ~9 V pack (six AA cells is ideal) wired to the driver's motor-power input (often labelled VM or VMOT ). But join the grounds. The motor battery's negative terminal, the driver's GND and the Pi's GND must all connect to one shared ground . That shared "0 V" reference is what lets the Pi's 3.3 V logic signals mean anything to the driver. Without a common ground nothing works, and floating grounds behave unpredictably. Careful — the safety rules for this build: Power off and unplug the Pi before wiring anything. Only re-power after a full check. Use a separate battery for the motors — never try to spin them from the Pi's 5 V pin. Share a common ground between the motor battery, the driver, and the Pi. Never feed motor voltage back into the Pi. The motor's 9 V power pair touches only the driver's outputs. Level-shift the sensor and encoder lines down to 3.3 V (with a divider) before they reach any GPIO input — these lines can sit near 5 V. DRV8833 H-bridge wiring (one motor channel) Raspberry Pi 5 GPIO 20 → AIN1 GPIO 21 → AIN2 GND DRV8833 AIN1 AIN2 AOUT1 AOUT2 VM GND motor White (A) Black (B) 6×AA ≈ 9 V separate motor battery +9 V → VM COMMON GROUND: Pi GND + driver GND + battery − all joined One motor channel of the DRV8833. The Pi's 3.3 V logic drives AIN1/AIN2; a separate ~9 V battery feeds VM; the motor's white/black pair connects to AOUT1/AOUT2. Crucially, the Pi's ground, the driver's ground and the battery's negative all meet at one common ground. Connection table — both motors From To Notes Pi GPIO 20 DRV8833 AIN1 Left motor forward input (3.3 V logic) Pi GPIO 21 DRV8833 AIN2 Left motor backward input Pi GPIO 19 DRV8833 BIN1 Right motor forward input Pi GPIO 26 DRV8833 BIN2 Right motor backward input Left motor White / Black AOUT1 / AOUT2 High-current pair — never to the Pi Right motor White / Black BOUT1 / BOUT2 High-current pair 6×AA pack + DRV8833 VM Separate ~9 V motor supply 6×AA pack − Common ground rail Joins Pi GND and driver GND DRV8833 GND Common ground rail Same 0 V as the Pi Pi GND (e.g. pin 6) Common ground rail The shared reference Tip: If your DRV8833 board has a pin marked EEP , SLP or STBY ("sleep"/"standby"), tie it to 3.3 V to keep the chip awake. Many breakout boards already pull it high for you — check your board's markings. Code: a Robot Class You Can Drive Time for Python. We will start with one motor to prove the wiring, then wrap both motors in a Robot class so the rest of the program can say robot.forward() without caring about pins. First, one motor Open Thonny and type this short test. It assumes the left motor's inputs are on GPIO 20 and 21. from gpiozero import Motor from time import sleep left = Motor(forward=20, backward=21) left.forward(0.5) # half speed forwards sleep(2) left.backward(0.5) # half speed backwards sleep(2) left.stop() Line 1 — from gpiozero import Motor : Imports the ready-made Motor object, which knows how to drive a two-input H-bridge channel. Line 4 — left = Motor(forward=20, backward=21) : Creates a motor object. forward=20 is the GPIO that drives AIN1; backward=21 drives AIN2. Naming the arguments stops us mixing the two up. Line 6 — left.forward(0.5) : Spins the motor forwards at half speed. The 0.5 is a fraction from 0 (stopped) to 1 (full speed); gpiozero turns it into PWM on the input pin for you. Line 7 — sleep(2) : Keeps it running for two seconds so you can watch. Line 8 — left.backward(0.5) : Reverses direction at half speed by driving the other input. Line 10 — left.stop() : Switches both inputs off, letting the motor coast to a halt. Note: If "forward" actually spins the wheel backwards, you have two easy fixes: swap the motor's white and black wires at the driver output, or swap forward= and backward= in the code. Either is fine — pick one. Now the Robot class A wheeled robot's two motors must do coordinated things: both forward, both backward, or one each way to spin on the spot. Rather than repeat motor commands everywhere, we bundle the pair into a Robot class with friendly methods. Save this as robot.py . from gpiozero import Motor class Robot: """Two NXT motors wired to a DRV8833, wrapped as one robot.""" def __init__(self, left_pins, right_pins, speed=0.6): self.left = Motor(forward=left_pins[0], backward=left_pins[1]) self.right = Motor(forward=right_pins[0], backward=right_pins[1]) self.speed = speed def forward(self, speed=None): s = speed if speed is not None else self.speed self.left.forward(s) self.right.forward(s) def backward(self, speed=None): s = speed if speed is not None else self.speed self.left.backward(s) self.right.backward(s) def turn_left(self, speed=None): s = speed if speed is not None else self.speed self.left.backward(s) self.right.forward(s) def turn_right(self, speed=None): s = speed if speed is not None else self.speed self.left.forward(s) self.right.backward(s) def stop(self): self.left.stop() self.right.stop() # A quick demo when you run this file directly if __name__ == "__main__": from time import sleep robot = Robot(left_pins=(20, 21), right_pins=(19, 26)) robot.forward(); sleep(1.5) robot.turn_right(); sleep(0.7) robot.forward(); sleep(1.5) robot.stop() Line 1 — from gpiozero import Motor : We will build two Motor objects inside our class. Line 4 — class Robot: : Starts our own blueprint. Anything indented underneath belongs to it. The triple-quoted line just below is a docstring describing the class. Line 7 — def __init__(self, left_pins, right_pins, speed=0.6): : The initialiser, run automatically when you build a Robot . It expects the two pins for each side (as a pair like (20, 21) ) and a default driving speed. Lines 8–9 — self.left = Motor(...) / self.right = Motor(...) : Build one Motor object per side and store them on this robot . left_pins[0] is the forward pin, left_pins[1] the backward pin. Line 10 — self.speed = speed : Remembers the default speed so methods can fall back to it. Line 12 — def forward(self, speed=None): : A method. speed=None means "if you don't pass a speed, use my default". Line 13 — s = speed if speed is not None else self.speed : Picks the speed to use: the one passed in, or the stored default. A compact one-line if . Lines 14–15 — drive both motors forward: Calls forward() on each side at the chosen speed, so the robot rolls straight ahead. Lines 17–20 — backward : The mirror image — both motors reverse. Lines 22–25 — turn_left : Spins on the spot to the left by running the left wheel backward and the right wheel forward . Lines 27–30 — turn_right : The opposite — left forward, right backward. Lines 32–34 — stop : Stops both motors. We will call this whenever the program ends so the robot never runs off. Line 38 — if __name__ == "__main__": : Code under this line runs only when you launch robot.py directly, not when another file imports the class. It is a tidy way to ship a class with a built-in self-test. Lines 40–45 — the demo: Build a robot with our pin choices, drive forward, turn, drive forward again, then stop. A short, safe shake-down run. Run steps Lift the wheels off the ground. Rest the chassis on a mug or box so the wheels spin freely in the air. Never test-drive a new robot on the floor. Fit fresh batteries in the motor pack and switch it on. Power up the Pi separately. Open robot.py in Thonny and press the green Run button (F5). Watch the wheels: both should spin forward, then the right side should reverse briefly for the turn, then both forward again, then stop. If a wheel goes the wrong way, swap that motor's white/black wires. Press the red Stop button in Thonny if anything misbehaves — it cuts the program and the motors. Reading the Wheels — the Encoder Driving blind is fine for a demo, but a real robot wants to know how far it has gone. That is the job of the motor's built-in quadrature encoder , read via its two channels (the yellow and blue wires) with gpiozero's RotaryEncoder object. Wiring the encoder — through a divider The encoder's two signal wires can swing up towards 4–5 V, which is too high for a 3.3 V GPIO input. So each one goes through the same kind of voltage divider you built in Chapter 28 before reaching the Pi. Green (encoder +supply) → Pi 3.3 V pin. Powering the encoder from 3.3 V keeps its output swing lower, which is kinder to the divider. Red (encoder GND) → common ground. Yellow (channel A) → through a 330 Ω / 470 Ω divider → GPIO input. Blue (channel B) → through a second 330 Ω / 470 Ω divider → GPIO input. Careful: Even powered at 3.3 V the encoder output can briefly exceed the Pi's safe limit, so keep the dividers in place. Reusing the proven 330 Ω (R1, signal-to-tap) and 470 Ω (R2, tap-to-GND) pair drops 5 V to about 2.94 V — safely readable as a HIGH. The GPIO pin connects to the tap between the two resistors. Here is a short program that counts one wheel and prints how far it has turned. Save it as encoder_test.py . from gpiozero import RotaryEncoder from time import sleep # Channel A on GPIO 16, channel B on GPIO 12 (both via dividers) enc = RotaryEncoder(a=16, b=12, max_steps=0) print("Turn the wheel by hand. Ctrl+C to stop.") try: while True: steps = enc.steps degrees = steps # ~1 count per degree on an NXT motor print(f"steps={steps:6d} ~{degrees}°") sleep(0.3) except KeyboardInterrupt: print("\nDone.") Line 1 — from gpiozero import RotaryEncoder : Imports the object that watches two pins and keeps a running count of how far, and which way, the shaft has turned. Line 5 — enc = RotaryEncoder(a=16, b=12, max_steps=0) : Builds the encoder object. a and b are the two GPIO pins reading channels A and B (each via its divider). max_steps=0 tells gpiozero not to wrap or clamp the count, so it can grow as large as we like. Line 10 — steps = enc.steps : Reads the steps attribute — the live count. It rises as the wheel turns one way and falls as it turns the other. That sign is the "quadrature" magic: the object compares which channel changed first to know the direction. Line 11 — degrees = steps : Because an NXT encoder gives roughly one count per degree, the step count is already an approximate angle. For precise distance you would calibrate this against your wheel size. Line 12 — print(...) : Shows the count and approximate angle. ° is just the degree symbol (°). Lines 14–15 — except KeyboardInterrupt : Lets Ctrl+C end the loop cleanly. Driving a set distance with when_rotated Instead of polling in a loop, the encoder can call a function of yours each time it moves, using its when_rotated event. Here is the idea — drive forward until the left wheel has turned a target number of steps, then stop. from gpiozero import RotaryEncoder from robot import Robot from signal import pause robot = Robot(left_pins=(20, 21), right_pins=(19, 26)) left_enc = RotaryEncoder(a=16, b=12, max_steps=0) TARGET = 720 # ~two full wheel turns (720 ° at ~1 °/count) def check_progress(): if abs(left_enc.steps) >= TARGET: robot.stop() print("Reached target distance.") left_enc.when_rotated = check_progress robot.forward(0.5) print("Driving... will stop after the target.") pause() Line 2 — from robot import Robot : Reuses the Robot class you wrote earlier by importing it from robot.py . This is why classes pay off — one tidy object, used everywhere. Line 6 — left_enc = RotaryEncoder(a=16, b=12, max_steps=0) : The encoder for the left wheel, on the same two divider-protected pins as before. Line 8 — TARGET = 720 : Our goal in encoder counts. At roughly one count per degree, 720 is about two full turns of the wheel — adjust to suit your wheel diameter. Lines 10–13 — check_progress() : A function that asks "have we gone far enough?". abs(...) ignores direction so it works whichever way the count runs. When the target is reached it stops the robot. Line 15 — left_enc.when_rotated = check_progress : Hands our function to the encoder as a callback . From now on, every time the wheel moves, gpiozero calls check_progress for us — no busy loop needed. Line 17 — robot.forward(0.5) : Starts both wheels rolling at half speed. Line 19 — pause() : Keeps the program alive so the callback can keep firing until the target is hit. Tip: To drive straight , read both wheels' encoders and nudge the faster wheel's speed down a little until the two counts match. Real robots wobble because no two motors are identical; the encoder is how you correct for it. Reading a Sensor — the Touch Bumper The touch sensor is the easiest part to reuse: under the plastic it is just a push switch — press it and two wires connect, release and they part. That is exactly what gpiozero's Button expects. Find the two wires that close — the robust method Rather than trust a fixed pinout (touch-sensor wiring varies, and a salvaged cable can be wired either way round), find the switch contacts yourself with a multimeter. This always works. Set your multimeter to continuity (the mode with the little speaker/diode symbol that beeps when two probes are connected). Expose the six wires of the touch sensor's cable (cut-and-strip, as before). Touch the probes to pairs of wires and press the sensor button. The pair that beeps only while pressed is your switch. On most NXT touch sensors these are the two signal/ground wires, but verify — do not assume. Mark those two wires. One becomes "signal", the other "ground". Wire the "signal" wire to a GPIO pin and the "ground" wire to a Pi GND pin. gpiozero's Button switches on an internal pull-up or pull-down so you need no extra resistor. Save this as bumper.py . from gpiozero import Button from robot import Robot from signal import pause robot = Robot(left_pins=(20, 21), right_pins=(19, 26)) bumper = Button(17) # the touch sensor's switch wires: GPIO 17 + GND def on_bump(): robot.stop() print("Bump! Stopped.") bumper.when_pressed = on_bump robot.forward(0.4) print("Rolling forward until the bumper is hit. Ctrl+C to quit.") pause() Line 1 — from gpiozero import Button : Brings in the Button object, perfect for any simple on/off switch — including a salvaged NXT touch sensor. Line 6 — bumper = Button(17) : Creates the button on GPIO 17. The sensor's other switch wire goes to a GND pin. No external resistor is needed — gpiozero handles the pull internally. Lines 8–10 — on_bump() : What to do when the bumper is hit: stop the robot and say so. Line 12 — bumper.when_pressed = on_bump : Registers our function as the press callback, so a bump instantly halts the wheels. Line 14 — robot.forward(0.4) : Rolls gently forward; the robot will keep going until something presses the bumper. Line 16 — pause() : Keeps the program running so the callback stays armed. The ultrasonic sensor (advanced / optional): The NXT ultrasonic sensor is not a simple switch — it is an I²C device . I²C is a two-wire bus (a clock line and a data line, the yellow and blue wires here) that lets a chip and the Pi exchange numbers. You enable I²C in raspi-config , level-shift the two lines to 3.3 V, and read the sensor's distance register over the bus. Be honest with yourself: the NXT ultrasonic has fussy timing and was designed for LEGO's own brick, so it is a fiddly afternoon project, not a five-minute one. If you just want reliable distance, the HC-SR04 from Chapter 28 is far easier — reuse that instead. Giving the Robot AI Eyes Now the exciting part. In Chapter 19 you ran an AI model on your Pi; here we point it at a camera and let it steer the robot. The plan is the classic robotics loop, see → think → act : See — grab a frame from the Pi Camera with Picamera2 (the modern camera library on Bookworm). Think — run the frame through an on-device object-detection model that returns boxes around things it recognises. Act — find the target box's horizontal position and turn the Robot so the target moves towards the centre, then drive forward. In plain words: Object detection is an AI task where a model looks at an image and draws a box around each thing it finds, with a label ("person", "ball", "cup") and a confidence score. We only care about where our chosen target's box is, left-to-right. Two ways to run the model TensorFlow Lite on the Pi 5 — a small model (MobileNet-SSD) runs on the Pi's own CPU. It needs no special hardware beyond a Camera Module 3, but on a Pi 5 you should honestly expect only a handful of frames per second for detection. That is plenty for a slow follower robot. The Raspberry Pi AI Camera (Sony IMX500) — this clever camera runs the neural network inside the camera module itself and hands the Pi the results directly, so the Pi's CPU stays free and the frame rate is much higher. If you have one, it is the smoother choice. Either way the Python pattern is the same. See → Think → Act: the vision control loop SEE Picamera2 frame THINK object-detection model → boxes TFLite / IMX500 decide left? right? centre? ACT Robot motors repeat, several times a second The see → think → act loop. A camera frame goes to an object-detection model; the model's boxes feed a steering decision; the decision drives the motors; then it all repeats. On a Pi 5 with TFLite expect a few frames per second — enough for a gentle follower. The follower program This program follows the first person it sees (change the label to follow anything in the model's vocabulary). It keeps the AI part simple so the steering logic is clear. Save it as follower.py . from picamera2 import Picamera2 from robot import Robot import numpy as np # 'detector' wraps your chosen model. See ch19 for loading a TFLite model. from detector import detect_objects # returns a list of {label, score, cx} robot = Robot(left_pins=(20, 21), right_pins=(19, 26)) picam = Picamera2() picam.configure(picam.create_preview_configuration( main={"size": (320, 240)})) picam.start() TARGET_LABEL = "person" DEAD_ZONE = 40 # pixels either side of centre we call "centred" CENTRE_X = 320 // 2 # the middle column of a 320-wide frame print("Following. Ctrl+C to stop.") try: while True: frame = picam.capture_array() objects = detect_objects(frame) targets = [o for o in objects if o["label"] == TARGET_LABEL and o["score"] > 0.5] if not targets: robot.stop() # nothing to follow — wait continue target = max(targets, key=lambda o: o["score"]) offset = target["cx"] - CENTRE_X if offset < -DEAD_ZONE: robot.turn_left(0.4) # target is to the left elif offset > DEAD_ZONE: robot.turn_right(0.4) # target is to the right else: robot.forward(0.4) # centred — approach it except KeyboardInterrupt: robot.stop() print("\nStopped.") Line 1 — from picamera2 import Picamera2 : The modern camera library on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm. It gives us frames as plain image arrays. Line 5 — from detector import detect_objects : We hide the AI details behind one helper, detect_objects(frame) , which returns a list of detections — each a small dictionary with a label , a confidence score , and cx , the horizontal centre of the box in pixels. Building that helper from a TFLite model is exactly the Chapter 19 material, so we reuse it here rather than repeat it. Lines 9–12 — set up the camera: Create a Picamera2 , configure a small 320×240 preview (small frames are faster to detect), and start it. Line 14 — TARGET_LABEL = "person" : The thing we want to follow. Swap for any label the model knows. Line 15 — DEAD_ZONE = 40 : A tolerance band around the centre. If the target is within 40 pixels of the middle we treat it as "centred" and drive straight, rather than twitching left/right forever. Line 16 — CENTRE_X = 320 // 2 : The middle column of the frame — the position we want the target to sit at. Line 21 — frame = picam.capture_array() : "SEE": grab the latest camera image as a numbers array. Line 22 — objects = detect_objects(frame) : "THINK": run the model and get back every object it found. Lines 24–25 — filter: Keep only detections matching our target label and confident enough ( score > 0.5 ), discarding the rest. Lines 27–29 — nothing found: If no target is visible, stop and loop again. A follower that charges off when it loses sight of its target is a runaway robot. Line 31 — target = max(targets, key=lambda o: o["score"]) : If several match, pick the most confident one. Line 32 — offset = target["cx"] - CENTRE_X : How far left (negative) or right (positive) of centre the target is. This single number is the whole "decision". Lines 34–39 — "ACT": If the target is well to the left, turn left; well to the right, turn right; otherwise it is roughly centred, so drive forward to approach. Steering to reduce offset towards zero is what keeps the target in front of us. Lines 41–43 — clean stop: Ctrl+C stops the motors so the robot never keeps rolling after the program ends. Note: Be realistic about speed. A TFLite detection on a Pi 5 might take a couple of hundred milliseconds, so the robot reacts a few times a second, not instantly. Keep the drive speed low (0.3–0.4) so it does not overshoot between decisions. The IMX500 AI Camera, doing the maths on-sensor, reacts much faster. Putting It All Together You now hold every piece of an autonomous object-following rover: A chassis built from the NXT's Technic frame and two drive motors. A DRV8833 H-bridge with its own ~9 V battery and a common ground to the Pi. A Robot class giving clean forward/turn/stop control. An encoder on each wheel for distance and going straight. A touch bumper as a safety stop. A camera + AI model closing the see → think → act loop. To combine them, run the follower loop as the main program, but keep the bumper's when_pressed callback armed so that a physical bump always wins and stops the robot, no matter what the camera thinks. A good robot has a reflex that overrides its brain. A safe start (arm / disarm) Never let a vision robot leap into motion the instant the program starts — the camera might already see its target and bolt. Add a simple "armed" guard: the robot only drives once you have pressed the bumper once to say "I'm ready", and the same bumper stops it again. armed = False def toggle_arm(): global armed armed = not armed if not armed: robot.stop() print("ARMED" if armed else "DISARMED") bumper.when_pressed = toggle_arm # inside the main loop, only move when armed: # if armed and targets: # ... steer ... # else: # robot.stop() Line 1 — armed = False : A flag that starts off , so the robot is still until you say otherwise. Lines 3–8 — toggle_arm() : Flips the flag each press. global armed lets the function change the outer variable. When disarming, it stops the motors immediately. Line 10 — bumper.when_pressed = toggle_arm : One press arms, the next disarms — a simple, physical on/off you can reach without the keyboard. Lines 12–16 — the guard (shown as a comment): In your main loop, only steer when armed is true; otherwise hold still. This is the difference between a controllable robot and one that surprises you. The Easy Route: BrickPi3 Sidebar — don't fancy soldering or cutting cables? The BrickPi3 (originally Dexter Industries, now Modular Robotics) is a HAT that sits on top of your Pi and provides four proper NXT/EV3 sockets — for both motors and sensors — with the correct right-offset latch. You plug your unmodified LEGO cables straight in and control everything from a Python library, with the H-bridges and level-shifting already done on the board. Pi 5 support: the BrickPi3 does work with a Pi 5, but with caveats — the Pi 5 draws more power than the BrickPi3 can comfortably supply, so power the Pi separately, and the acrylic case/fan clearance is tight. Check the current BrickPi3 notes before you buy. When to choose it: if you want to reuse NXT/EV3 parts with the least fuss, or you are teaching a class and cannot have students cutting cables, the BrickPi3 is the gentle path. You lose the deep understanding of H-bridges and dividers that the DIY route teaches — which is precisely why this chapter builds the DIY version first. Careful: The official Raspberry Pi Build HAT is not a substitute here. It uses LEGO's newer LPF2/SPIKE connector, not the NXT's RJ12, so NXT motors and sensors will not plug into it. For NXT parts, it is DIY-with-an-H-bridge or a BrickPi3. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause Fix Motors do nothing at all No common ground, or driver in standby Join the motor battery −, driver GND and Pi GND. Tie any SLP/STBY pin to 3.3 V. Check the battery is switched on. One wheel spins backwards That motor's power pair is reversed Swap its white and black wires at the driver output, or swap forward= / backward= in code. Pi reboots when motors start Motors drawing from the Pi, or grounds bouncing Confirm motor power comes from the separate battery's VM, not the Pi's 5 V. Use fresh cells. Keep motor wires short. Encoder count never changes Wrong wires, no encoder power, or divider error Green→3.3 V, Red→GND, Yellow/Blue→GPIO via dividers. Confirm the GPIO taps to the join between R1 and R2. Encoder count jumps erratically Floating input or no divider Make sure both channels go through their dividers and that the encoder shares the common ground. Bumper never triggers Wrong two wires chosen Re-do the multimeter continuity test; use the pair that beeps only while pressed. Camera follower never moves Model not loaded, or label not in its vocabulary Test detect_objects on its own first (print the labels it returns). Pick a label the model actually knows. Robot overshoots / weaves Drive speed too high for the frame rate Lower the speed to 0.3, widen the DEAD_ZONE , or use the faster IMX500 AI Camera. No module named 'lgpio' The lgpio backend is missing Run sudo apt install python3-lgpio , then restart Thonny. Safety Checklist Before every powered test, run down this list. It takes ten seconds and saves Pis. Separate motor battery. Motors are powered by their own ~9 V pack at the driver's VM — never from the Pi. Common ground. Battery −, driver GND and Pi GND all meet at one shared 0 V rail. Level-shifted signals. Every NXT sensor/encoder line that can exceed 3.3 V passes through a divider before reaching a GPIO pin. Motor isolation. The motors' white/black power wires touch only the driver outputs — never a GPIO or power pin. Current within limits. The driver is rated above the motor's ~1 A stall current (the DRV8833 is, comfortably). Wheels off the ground first. Test new code with the chassis propped up so a bug cannot send it off a table. Power off to rewire. Shut down and unplug the Pi before changing any wiring; re-power only after a full check. Make It Your Own / Where to Go Next You have built a genuinely intelligent robot from a box of "obsolete" LEGO. Here is where to take it: Line following. Point a downward camera (or a swapped-in Pi-friendly light sensor) at the floor and steer to keep a dark line centred — the same offset-to-steering idea, no AI model needed. Obstacle avoidance. Add the NXT ultrasonic over I²C (or an HC-SR04 from Chapter 28) and have the robot back up and turn when something gets too close. Voice control. Combine with the speech work from Chapter 19 so you can say "follow me" or "stop" and have the robot obey. A web joystick. Wrap the Robot class in a small Flask app (Chapter 31) so you can drive it from your phone's browser — manual override for when the AI gets confused. Go EV3. The newer EV3 motors and sensors use the same RJ12 plug and similar ideas; a BrickPi3 or careful DIY wiring reuses those too. Tip: Keep your Robot class as the foundation for all of these. Because the messy hardware lives inside one tidy object, every new project — line follower, web-driven car, voice rover — just imports Robot and gives it new orders. That is the real lesson of classes: write the hard part once, reuse it forever. Key terms 6P6C / RJ12 - the six-contact modular plug LEGO used; the NXT version has a right-offset latch so ordinary phone leads don't seat. Quadrature encoder - a two-channel sensor that reports how far and which way a shaft turned; the NXT motor's gives ~1 count per degree. H-bridge - a driver chip that switches a motor's heavy current and reverses its direction from gentle 3.3 V logic, absorbing inductive kickback. DRV8833 - a recommended dual H-bridge (2.7–10.8 V, ~1.5 A/channel) ideal for two NXT motors. PWM - rapid on/off switching that controls motor speed; gpiozero applies it when you pass a speed like 0.4. Separate battery + common ground - motors get their own ~9 V supply, but its negative must join the Pi's ground as a shared 0 V reference. Voltage divider / level-shift - two resistors dropping a >3.3 V signal (sensor or encoder line) to a Pi-safe level before a GPIO input. Motor / RotaryEncoder - the gpiozero objects that drive an H-bridge channel and count an encoder ( .steps , when_rotated ). Robot class - your own class wrapping both motors with forward/backward/turn_left/turn_right/stop . Object detection - an AI task returning labelled boxes around things in an image; we use the box's horizontal centre to steer. See → think → act - the robotics loop: capture a frame, run the model, decide, drive the motors, repeat. BrickPi3 - a HAT with proper NXT/EV3 sockets that does the H-bridge and level-shifting for you (works on a Pi 5 with power caveats). Chapter summary An NXT motor is a plain 9 V DC motor with a built-in quadrature encoder (~1 count/degree); its six RJ12 wires split into a power pair (white/black) and a four-wire encoder (red, green, yellow, blue). The NXT's 6P6C plug has a right-offset latch , so you either use an NXT-compatible breakout socket or cut a spare cable to reach the six colours. Motors must be driven through an H-bridge (we used the DRV8833), never a GPIO pin, because of their current draw and inductive kickback. Separate ~9 V battery for the motors, but a common ground with the Pi — the single most important wiring rule here. The encoder's and sensors' lines can exceed 3.3 V, so they reach the Pi through a voltage divider (level-shifting). You wrote a Robot class wrapping two gpiozero Motor objects, read wheels with RotaryEncoder , and read a touch bumper as a Button . The AI layer follows the see → think → act loop: Picamera2 frame → object-detection model → steer the Robot towards the target. Expect a few frames per second on a Pi 5 with TFLite, faster with the IMX500 AI Camera. The BrickPi3 is the easy off-the-shelf alternative; the Pi Build HAT is not, as it uses the newer LPF2 connector.

title: Recycle an Old Smartphone into Pi Parts
headings: The Honest Truth About Phone Parts
Reuse 1 — the Battery as Backup Power
Reuse 4 — the Whole Phone as a Wireless Camera
What You Genuinely Can't Do — and Why
Make It Your Own / Where Next
text: There is a dead smartphone in a drawer in almost every home — a cracked-screen Galaxy, a swollen-battery iPhone, a hand-me-down that simply stopped charging. The internet is full of breathless promises that you can rip out its camera, its screen, even its "graphics card", and plug them straight into a Raspberry Pi. The honest truth is that most of a modern phone cannot be reused that way at all — and this chapter will explain plainly why. But a handful of parts genuinely can be given a second life, and there is one brilliant trick that turns the whole phone into a wireless camera for your Pi. Along the way you will name and practise some real Python (functions, loops, and using external libraries like gpiozero and OpenCV) and real electronics (lithium-ion safety, a transistor motor driver, a class-D audio amp, and a boost converter) — with safety, always, coming first. The Honest Truth About Phone Parts Before we salvage a single screw, let us set expectations honestly. A modern smartphone is one of the most tightly integrated pieces of electronics ever made for the home. Tiny, proprietary, glued, and soldered — it is built to be a sealed unit, not a parts bin. That is exactly the opposite of the friendly, modular world of breadboards and jumper wires you met earlier in this Part. In plain words: integrated means many separate jobs have been squeezed onto one chip or one tiny board. The more integrated a device is, the harder it is to pull one job back out and reuse it on its own — there are no neat, documented connectors, and no spare drivers to make it work elsewhere. So the realistic picture is: a few parts are reusable, most are not, and being clear about which is which will save you hours of frustration (and protect your wallet and your Pi). Here is the honest map. A phone’s parts: reusable vs not ✗ NOT practically reusable proprietary, fused, no drivers • Camera module — proprietary MIPI CSI-2 link, no published driver • AMOLED screen — proprietary MIPI DSI, custom power rails • The “GPU” — there is none to remove; it is fused inside the SoC • SoC, RAM — soldered silicon • UFS storage — soldered BGA chip • Modem / radios — proprietary • Tiny MEMS microphone — skip it No connector, no driver, no realistic path to a Pi. ✓ Genuinely reusable simple, standard, or whole-device • microSD card (if it has a slot) • Li-ion battery (carefully!) • Loudspeaker (with an amp) • Vibration motor (with a driver) • Buttons (as GPIO inputs) • USB-C port & cables • Glass back / frame as enclosure • THE WHOLE PHONE as a wireless camera / sensor These have standard interfaces — or skip the wiring entirely. The honest map. The red column lists parts that are proprietary, fused or undocumented and so cannot realistically reach a Pi. The green column lists what genuinely works — ending with the best trick of all: reuse the whole phone over Wi-Fi. Part Reusable on a Pi? Why Camera module No Connects over proprietary MIPI CSI-2 with no published driver, ISP tuning or matching connector AMOLED screen No Proprietary MIPI DSI, custom power/backlight rails, per-panel driver — not a beginner job "Graphics card" / GPU No (does not exist) There is no removable GPU; it is fused permanently inside the SoC silicon SoC, RAM, UFS storage, modem No Soldered, proprietary silicon — nothing to plug in elsewhere microSD card Yes A standard removable card — slots straight into the Pi Li-ion battery Yes, with great care A standard lithium cell — but dangerous; needs a protected charger and a boost converter Loudspeaker Yes, with an amp A small 8 Ω driver; the Pi 5 has no analog jack, so it needs an I²S amplifier Vibration motor Yes, with a driver A tiny DC motor; never driven from a pin directly — needs a transistor Buttons, USB-C, cables, frame Yes Simple switches, standard connectors, and a ready-made enclosure The whole phone Yes — best of all Run an app and stream over Wi-Fi; the Pi reads it with OpenCV Note: this is not pessimism — it is the path of least frustration. By skipping the impossible reuses, you spend your energy on the four that genuinely pay off: three small hardware builds, and one pure-software trick that is the most powerful of the lot. Name the Fundamentals As always in the Maker Lab, we name out loud exactly what you are learning so that the skills stick and carry into your next project. This chapter is a little different from a single build — it is four mini-builds — so it touches several fundamentals, each taught with a small example before it is used. Area Fundamentals (named) Python functions and loops ; using external libraries ( gpiozero for hardware, OpenCV for vision); a frame-capture loop that reads images one after another; a quick recap of PWM for motor intensity Electronics lithium-ion battery safety & charging (a protected TP4056 charger + a 5 V boost converter); the transistor motor driver + flyback diode (the same rule you met for the speaker); a class-D I²S audio amplifier (MAX98357A); and the idea of a boost converter that lifts a low voltage up to 5 V In plain words: a library is a bundle of ready-written code someone else has tested, so you do not have to solve the hard parts yourself. gpiozero hides the fiddly details of GPIO pins; OpenCV (the "Open Computer Vision" library) hides the fiddly details of reading and showing video. You import them and call simple commands. Two of these — functions and loops — you will use everywhere. Let us warm up with a tiny isolated example before any hardware, so the camera code later feels familiar. def buzz_pattern(times): for i in range(times): print(f"buzz {i + 1} of {times}") buzz_pattern(3) Line 1 — def buzz_pattern(times): : defines a function named buzz_pattern that takes one input (a parameter ) called times . The indented lines below are its body and only run when the function is called. Line 2 — for i in range(times): : a loop . range(times) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2… up to (but not including) times , and the body runs once for each, with i holding the current number. Line 3 — print(f"buzz {i + 1} of {times}") : an f-string prints a tidy message; we add 1 to i so it counts from 1 for a human reader. Line 5 — buzz_pattern(3) : calls the function with the value 3, so the loop runs three times. Wrapping repeated steps in a function like this is exactly how we will drive the vibration motor in buzz patterns later. Safety First: the Lithium-Ion Talk Of everything in a phone, the lithium-ion battery is both the most tempting reuse and by far the most dangerous part. This section is firm on purpose. Read it fully before you so much as pick a cell up. The same iron rule you met in the e-waste lesson applies here, only closer up: never deform a lithium-ion cell. In plain words: a lithium-ion cell stores a lot of energy in a very small space, separated by a microscopically thin membrane. Damage that membrane — by a puncture, a bend, a crush, or a short circuit — and the two sides touch internally. That causes a runaway chemical reaction called thermal runaway : the cell heats itself, vents flammable gas, and can catch fire or explode. Swelling (the cell puffing up with gas) is often the warning sign that comes first. Careful — never use a damaged cell. If a phone battery is swollen, bulging, puffy, hot, hissing, leaking, or deformed in any way , do not use it, do not charge it, and never try to "deflate" it by pressing or piercing it. Put it somewhere non-flammable and take it to a battery recycling point. A swollen cell is a fire that has not happened yet. Careful — never puncture, bend, crush or short a cell. Do not cut into it, drop it, drill it, or let its two terminals touch a piece of metal (or each other). Any of these can trigger thermal runaway in seconds. Treat a bare cell with the same respect you would a small petrol container. Careful — never remove the protection PCB, and always charge attended. Many phone cells have a small protection circuit board (PCM) on their tab that stops dangerous over-charge, over-discharge and short circuit. Never peel it off. When charging a salvaged cell, do it attended , on a non-flammable surface (a ceramic tile or metal tin, never on a sofa or carpet), and never overnight or unattended . Tip — the responsible default: for most learners, the genuinely sensible choice is not a bare harvested cell at all, but a purpose-built Raspberry Pi UPS HAT or an 18650 power-bank UPS module . These are designed and certified for the job, include proper protection, and are matched to the Pi's power needs. Reuse the harvested cell only if it is in perfect condition and you understand every warning above. There is no shame in choosing the safe, ready-made option — it is the grown-up move. Reuse 1 — the Battery as Backup Power The dream is simple: power your Pi from a salvaged phone cell, or at least keep it running for a few minutes when the mains drops out. It can be done, but only through the correct chain of parts — and with an honest understanding of its limits. A single phone cell sits between about 3.0 V (empty) and 4.2 V (full) . The Pi wants a steady 5 V . So we need two helper boards between the cell and the Pi. The two boards you need A TP4056 charging module with protection (the variant with a DW01 + FS8205 protection chip, usually with a USB-C input). It safely charges the cell to 4.2 V using a constant-current then constant-voltage profile, and — crucially — cuts the load off if the cell is over-discharged or shorted. A plain TP4056 with no protection chip must never be used on a bare cell. A 5 V boost converter (a "step-up" converter). The cell's 3.0–4.2 V is below 5 V, so we cannot simply use it; a boost converter lifts the lower voltage up to a steady 5 V output. In plain words: a boost converter is a small board that takes a lower input voltage and raises it to a higher, steady output voltage. Think of it as a tiny pump that lifts the pressure up to where the Pi needs it. (Its sibling, a buck converter, lowers voltage instead.) The battery power path: cell → TP4056 → boost → Pi 5 V Li-ion cell 3.0–4.2 V (keep PCM on) TP4056 + protection charge & protect USB-C in 5 V boost step-up to steady 5 V Pi 5 5 V in Common ground (GND) shared by every board Power flows left → right; the boost makes a steady 5 V for the Pi. The only safe power path. The cell charges and is protected by the TP4056, the boost converter lifts its voltage to a steady 5 V, and every board shares one common ground. Never connect the bare cell straight to the Pi. From To Notes Li-ion cell + tab TP4056 B+ The cell's positive terminal (keep its protection PCM attached) Li-ion cell − tab TP4056 B- The cell's negative terminal TP4056 OUT+ Boost converter IN+ Protected output feeds the step-up board TP4056 OUT- Boost converter IN- Shared negative (ground) Boost OUT+ (set to 5.0 V) Pi 5 V (header pin 2 or a USB-C lead) Adjust the boost to 5.0 V with a multimeter before connecting the Pi Boost OUT- Pi GND (e.g. header pin 6) Common ground — essential Careful: set the boost converter's output to exactly 5.0 V using a multimeter on its output terminals before you ever connect it to the Pi . Many boost boards ship set higher; feeding more than 5 V into the Pi can damage it. Also confirm common ground across the cell, charger, boost and Pi — without a shared ground the circuit will behave erratically or not at all. And as always: charge attended, on a non-flammable surface. Careful — the honest Pi-5 caveat. The Raspberry Pi 5 wants up to 5 V at around 5 A (25 W) at its busiest, and if it does not detect a proper 5 V/5 A supply it limits its own USB ports to 600 mA. A single salvaged phone cell (only a few watt-hours) feeding a cheap boost converter simply cannot deliver that peak current — under load the voltage sags and the Pi browns out or reboots. This makes a harvested cell suitable only for light, headless use (a sensor node with nothing plugged in) or a short backup for a graceful shutdown. For anything more, use a purpose-built Pi 5 UPS HAT matched to your load. That is the responsible recommendation. Notice there is no Python code in this reuse: it is pure power wiring, with no GPIO involved. The cell does not talk to your code — it just keeps the lights on. The next two reuses, by contrast, are real GPIO builds with code. Reuse 2 — the Vibration Motor (Haptics) Inside the phone is a tiny vibration motor — the part that makes your phone buzz silently in your pocket. Salvaging it is easy and safe, and it is a lovely way to add haptics (touch feedback) to a Pi project: a buzz when a sensor trips, a pattern to signal a notification, a pulse when a button is pressed. In plain words: a phone's vibration motor is a small DC motor with an off-centre weight on its shaft (an ERM , eccentric rotating mass) or a flat coin-shaped version. When it spins, the lopsided weight throws the whole motor side to side — that wobble is the buzz you feel. It is still a motor, and that means the same firm rule you met when driving a speaker applies here: never connect a motor straight to a GPIO pin. A motor pulls far more current than a pin can safely give, and worse, when its coil switches off it kicks back a sharp voltage spike that can destroy the pin. We protect the Pi with three cheap parts. An NPN transistor (a 2N2222/PN2222A or a BC548) acting as a low-side switch — the tiny GPIO signal controls a much bigger current. A base resistor (about 470 Ω, anything from 330 Ω to 1 kΩ is fine) between the GPIO pin and the transistor's base, to limit the small control current. A flyback diode (a 1N4001) across the motor — mandatory — to soak up that switch-off voltage spike. In plain words: a transistor is an electronic switch with no moving parts: a small current into its base lets a much larger current flow through it. A flyback diode is a one-way valve placed across a motor (or any coil) that gives the switch-off voltage spike a safe loop to die away in, instead of blasting back into your circuit. Driving a salvaged vibration motor with an NPN transistor GPIO Header GPIO 17 (pin 11) 5 V (pin 2) GND (pin 6) 470 Ω NPN 2N2222 base collector emitter M motor flyback 1N4001 The GPIO pin pulses the transistor's base through a 470 Ω resistor; the transistor switches the bigger 5 V motor current on and off. The flyback diode (band toward 5 V) absorbs the switch-off spike. The Pi never carries the motor's current. From To Wire / part Why GPIO 17 (pin 11) 470 Ω resistor → transistor base Purple via resistor Small, safe control signal; the resistor limits base current and protects the pin Transistor emitter GND (pin 6) Grey The return path; this is a "low-side" switch Transistor collector Motor − terminal Grey The transistor sinks the motor's current to ground Motor + terminal 5 V (pin 2) Red The motor is powered from 5 V, not from the pin Diode across motor (band → 5 V side) — 1N4001 Soaks up the inductive spike when the motor switches off — mandatory Careful: power off and unplug the Pi before wiring, and only re-power once you have double-checked every connection. Get the diode the right way round — its silver band must point toward the 5 V side; backwards it shorts your supply. And check the transistor's leg order against its datasheet: the 2N2222 and BC548 number their emitter, base and collector legs differently, and a swapped leg is the commonest reason the motor stays still. The code: buzz patterns From the Pi's point of view, this is just one GPIO line going on and off — exactly like blinking an LED. The transistor and 5 V supply quietly turn that into a buzzing motor. We will use gpiozero 's DigitalOutputDevice for simple on/off buzzes, then upgrade to PWMOutputDevice for adjustable intensity. from gpiozero import DigitalOutputDevice from time import sleep motor = DigitalOutputDevice(17) def buzz(times, length=0.2, gap=0.15): for i in range(times): motor.on() sleep(length) motor.off() sleep(gap) buzz(3) # three short buzzes sleep(0.6) buzz(1, length=0.8) # one long buzz Line 1 — from gpiozero import DigitalOutputDevice : imports a simple on/off output object from the preinstalled gpiozero library. Unlike LED , the name DigitalOutputDevice makes clear this is a general output, here switching a transistor. Line 2 — from time import sleep : brings in sleep() , which pauses the program for a given number of seconds — how we set the length of each buzz. Line 4 — motor = DigitalOutputDevice(17) : creates the output object on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11). Setting it HIGH sends the small base current that switches the transistor — and the motor — on. Line 6 — def buzz(times, length=0.2, gap=0.15): : defines a function for a buzz pattern. times is how many buzzes; length and gap have default values , so you can call buzz(3) and still get sensible timing, or override them. Line 7 — for i in range(times): : a loop that repeats the buzz the requested number of times. Lines 8–11 — motor.on() / sleep(length) / motor.off() / sleep(gap) : turn the motor on, hold it for length seconds, turn it off, then pause for gap seconds before the next buzz. Lines 13–15 — the calls: buzz(3) gives three short buzzes; after a pause, buzz(1, length=0.8) gives one long one — by passing a different length we reuse the same function for a new pattern. That is the payoff of writing a function. To control the strength of the buzz rather than just on/off, swap to PWM. PWM (pulse-width modulation) switches the pin on and off thousands of times a second; the fraction of time it is on (the "duty cycle", 0 to 1) sets the average power, and so the motor's speed. from gpiozero import PWMOutputDevice from time import sleep motor = PWMOutputDevice(17) for level in (0.4, 0.7, 1.0): motor.value = level sleep(0.5) motor.off() Line 1 — from gpiozero import PWMOutputDevice : imports the PWM-capable output object, which can hold any level between fully off and fully on. Line 4 — motor = PWMOutputDevice(17) : creates the PWM object on the same GPIO 17 driving the transistor. Line 6 — for level in (0.4, 0.7, 1.0): : loops over three intensity levels — a gentle 40%, a firmer 70%, then full power. Line 7 — motor.value = level : sets the duty cycle. At 0.4 the pin is on 40% of the time, so the motor gets roughly 40% of full power and buzzes more softly. Line 8 — sleep(0.5) : holds each level for half a second so you can feel the difference. Line 10 — motor.off() : stops the motor cleanly at the end. Note: a very small ERM motor may not turn at all below a certain level (say 0.3) because there is not enough power to overcome friction. Experiment to find the lowest level that reliably starts your salvaged motor, and start each pattern at or above it. Reuse 3 — the Loudspeaker The phone's tiny loudspeaker is genuinely reusable — but with an important catch you must know about the Pi 5. The Raspberry Pi 5 has no analog headphone jack. Earlier Pis had a 3.5 mm socket; the Pi 5 removed it. Audio now comes only over HDMI , USB , Bluetooth , or the I²S digital audio pins on the GPIO header. So you cannot simply solder a speaker to an audio jack — there is not one. Careful — a common myth. Any tutorial that tells you to wire a speaker to the Pi 5's "audio jack" is out of date: the Pi 5 has none. Ignore that advice. We will use the modern, clean route instead: a small digital amplifier on the I²S pins. In plain words: I²S (Inter-IC Sound) is a digital audio "language" spoken over a few GPIO pins. The Pi sends the sound as numbers; a small amplifier board turns those numbers into the analog waveform a speaker needs. A class-D amplifier does this very efficiently by rapidly switching, so it stays cool and sips power. The recommended board is the MAX98357A — a tiny, cheap I²S class-D mono amplifier that connects directly to the GPIO header and drives a small 8 Ω speaker at up to about 1.8 W from 5 V. It needs only four signal connections plus power. MAX98357A I²S amplifier → salvaged 8 Ω speaker GPIO Header 5 V (pin 2) GND (pin 6) GPIO 18 (BCLK) GPIO 19 (LRC) GPIO 21 (DIN) MAX98357A VIN GND BCLK LRC DIN SD + − amp --> SD → 5 V (un-mute) 8 Ω speaker speaker --> The MAX98357A takes I²S audio from GPIO 18/19/21, powers from 5 V and GND, and drives the salvaged 8 Ω speaker from its + and − outputs. Tying SD to 5 V keeps the amp un-muted. MAX98357A pin Pi connection Why VIN 5 V (pin 2) Powers the amplifier GND GND (pin 6) Common ground with the Pi BCLK GPIO 18 (pin 12) Bit clock — the I²S timing signal LRC GPIO 19 (pin 35) Left/right word-select clock DIN GPIO 21 (pin 40) The audio data itself SD 5 V (or a GPIO to mute) Shutdown pin; high = the amp is on. Tie to 5 V to keep it playing Speaker + / − Salvaged 8 Ω speaker The amplified mono output Enable I²S, then play a sound The MAX98357A needs the Pi's I²S audio output switched on with a small device-tree overlay. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, edit the firmware config and reboot: sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt : opens the Pi's firmware configuration file in the nano text editor with administrator rights ( sudo ). On Bookworm this file lives at /boot/firmware/config.txt (older guides may say /boot/config.txt ). Find the line dtparam=audio=on and put a # in front of it to disable the old analog audio, then add the I²S overlay on a new line at the end of the file: #dtparam=audio=on dtoverlay=hifiberry-dac Line 1 — #dtparam=audio=on : the leading # comments out (disables) the built-in audio so it does not clash with our I²S amplifier. Line 2 — dtoverlay=hifiberry-dac : loads a generic I²S DAC overlay. The MAX98357A is electrically compatible with this widely-used overlay, so the Pi presents it as a normal sound card after a reboot. Save with Ctrl+O , exit with Ctrl+X , then run sudo reboot . After rebooting, the amplifier appears as a normal audio device, so you can play sounds the ordinary way. Here is a tiny Python program that plays a WAV file by calling the system's aplay tool: import subprocess def play(path): subprocess.run(["aplay", path]) play("/usr/share/sounds/alsa/Front_Center.wav") Line 1 — import subprocess : imports Python's subprocess module, which lets your program run other command-line programs and wait for them to finish. Line 3 — def play(path): : wraps the playback in a function so you can reuse it for any file by name. Line 4 — subprocess.run(["aplay", path]) : runs the aplay command (the ALSA WAV player that ships with Raspberry Pi OS), passing the file path as its argument. Giving the command as a list of separate strings is the safe way to call external programs. Line 6 — play(...) : calls the function with a test sound that comes preinstalled, so you can confirm the amp works before supplying your own audio. Note — be honest about the speaker. A salvaged phone speaker is a tiny driver: it is usually 8 Ω but rated only a fraction of a watt, with little bass and a modest maximum volume. The MAX98357A can output up to about 1.8 W, so do not drive it hard or you will hear distortion (and may damage the little driver). It is perfect for beeps, spoken alerts and gentle tunes — not for filling a room. Tip: if you would rather use an analog amplifier such as a PAM8302 , feed it from a cheap USB sound card (the Pi 5 has no analog line-out of its own). Analog amps are simple but can "pop" at start-up and pick up more noise; the I²S route above is cleaner for most projects. Reuse 4 — the Whole Phone as a Wireless Camera This is the big one — the reuse that makes the whole chapter worthwhile. You cannot harvest the phone's camera module , but you absolutely can use the phone's camera by leaving it exactly where it is, inside the working phone, and reading its video over Wi-Fi . This sidesteps every proprietary connector and missing-driver problem in one stroke. The trick: install a free IP-webcam app on the phone (popular ones are IP Webcam , DroidCam , or Iriun ). The app turns the phone into a little web server that streams its camera over your home network. Your Pi then reads that stream with OpenCV , the standard computer-vision library, in just a couple of lines. The whole phone as a wireless camera IP Webcam Phone (camera on) Wi-Fi router Pi 5 OpenCV reads the stream router --> MJPEG stream pi --> http://PHONE-IP:8080/video The phone runs an IP-webcam app and streams its camera over Wi-Fi; the Pi reads the stream with OpenCV at a URL like http://PHONE-IP:8080/video . No connectors, no drivers — just the network. Install OpenCV the Bookworm way OpenCV is not preinstalled. Because Bookworm protects the system Python (the PEP 668 rule you met earlier), install it inside a virtual environment : python3 -m venv ~/cvenv source ~/cvenv/bin/activate pip install opencv-python Line 1 — python3 -m venv ~/cvenv : creates a private, self-contained Python environment in a folder called cvenv in your home folder, so anything you install stays separate from the system Python. Line 2 — source ~/cvenv/bin/activate : switches your terminal into that environment; your prompt gains a (cvenv) prefix. Now pip installs inside the venv. Line 3 — pip install opencv-python : downloads and installs OpenCV into the venv, with no PEP 668 error because you are no longer touching the system Python. (As a quicker alternative you can run sudo apt install python3-opencv system-wide.) The frame-capture loop Now the heart of computer vision: a frame-capture loop . Video is just a fast sequence of still images called frames . We open the stream once, then loop forever, reading one frame at a time and doing something with it (here, showing it in a window). import cv2 cap = cv2.VideoCapture("http://PHONE-IP:8080/video") while True: ret, frame = cap.read() if not ret: print("No frame - is the phone app running?") break cv2.imshow("Phone camera", frame) if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord("q"): break cap.release() cv2.destroyAllWindows() Line 1 — import cv2 : imports OpenCV. The module is named cv2 for historical reasons; it is the external library that does all the heavy video work for us. Line 3 — cap = cv2.VideoCapture("http://PHONE-IP:8080/video") : opens the phone's video stream. Replace PHONE-IP with the address the app shows (for example 192.168.1.42 ); the IP Webcam app serves its MJPEG stream at the /video path on port 8080. Line 5 — while True: : the frame-capture loop — it repeats forever until we deliberately break out of it. Line 6 — ret, frame = cap.read() : grabs the next frame. read() hands back two things: ret , a True/False saying whether a frame arrived, and frame , the image itself (a grid of pixels). Lines 7–9 — if not ret: : if no frame came through (the app stopped, the phone locked, or the network dropped), print a friendly message and leave the loop instead of crashing. Line 10 — cv2.imshow("Phone camera", frame) : shows the frame in a window titled "Phone camera". Each pass of the loop replaces it, so the stills blur into smooth video. Line 11 — if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord("q"): : waits 1 millisecond for a key press; if you press q , it breaks the loop. This also gives the window time to redraw — without a waitKey the image never appears. Lines 14–15 — cap.release() / cv2.destroyAllWindows() : tidy up after the loop: free the stream and close the window. Always release the capture when you are done. Once you have frames flowing, you can do far more than display them. A small tweak saves a snapshot to disk instead of showing it: import cv2 cap = cv2.VideoCapture("http://PHONE-IP:8080/video") ret, frame = cap.read() if ret: cv2.imwrite("snapshot.jpg", frame) print("Saved snapshot.jpg") cap.release() Line 4 — ret, frame = cap.read() : grabs a single frame (no loop this time). Lines 5–7 — if ret: cv2.imwrite("snapshot.jpg", frame) : if a frame arrived, cv2.imwrite writes it to disk as a JPEG image, and we print a confirmation. This is the basis of a time-lapse or a doorbell snapshot. Line 8 — cap.release() : frees the stream straight away, since we only needed one frame. Tip: these very same frame images can be fed to the AI vision and object-detection code from the earlier chapters — the phone simply becomes the eyes. Wherever those chapters used a Pi camera, you can hand them frames from this stream instead. Careful — the real-world gotchas. Free app tiers often cap the resolution (commonly 640×480). Android may stop the camera when the screen locks or the app goes to the background , so keep the app in the foreground and the screen awake (and ideally the phone on charge). Usually only one program can read the stream at a time. And of course the phone and Pi must be on the same Wi-Fi network . Other Useful Bits Beyond the four headline reuses, a phone yields a few smaller treasures worth pocketing. The microSD card — if the phone has a card slot, that card is a completely standard removable card. Pop it into the Pi's slot (after backing up anything you want to keep). It is the one piece of phone "storage" that genuinely transfers. The buttons — the volume and power buttons are simple momentary switches. Desoldered (carefully), each can become a Button GPIO input with gpiozero's internal pull-up, exactly like the push button you wired earlier. The USB-C port and cables — ready-made 5 V power leads and data cables.
